26 ఆగస్టు 2026న నేపాల్లో సంభవించిన ఆకస్మిక వరదల్లో మరణించిన వారి మృతదేహాలను చూపుతున్న దృశ్యాలంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో బాగా ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: ఆగస్టు 2026 నేపాల్ ఆకస్మిక వరదల్లో మరణించిన వారి మృతదేహాలను చూపుతున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియోకి నేపాల్ వరదలకు ఎలాంటి సంబంధం లేదు. ఇది ఒక ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ క్రియేటర్ వినోదం కోసం చిత్రీకరించిన స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియో. నేపాల్ వరదలు ఆగస్టు 26న సంభవించగా, ఈ వీడియో ఆగస్టు 3నే అప్లోడ్ చేయబడింది. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియోని (ఆర్కైవ్) Simran SK అనే కంటెంట్ క్రియేటర్ తన ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ ఖాతాలో 03 ఆగస్టు 2026న అప్లోడ్ చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. దీన్ని బట్టి, ఈ వీడియోకు 26 ఆగస్టు 2026 నాటి నేపాల్ వరదలతో సంబంధం లేదని, నేపాల్ విపత్తుకు కొన్ని రోజుల ముందే ఈ వీడియో చిత్రీకరించబడిందని స్పష్టమవుతోంది.
ఇక Simran SK ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ ఖాతాను పరిశీలించగా, అందులో కామెడీ వీడియోలు, స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియోలు అప్లోడ్ చేస్తున్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. అలాగే, కొందరు వ్యక్తులు శవాల్లా నటిస్తున్న మరికొన్ని స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియోలు (ఆర్కైవ్) కూడా లభించాయి. అంతేకాకుండా, జూలై 2026లో సంభవించిన అస్సాం వరదల సమయంలో కూడా, ఇదే ఇన్స్టాగ్రామ్ ఖాతాకు చెందిన ఒక స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియోని నిజమైన ఘటనగా సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారమైనప్పుడు మేము రాసిన ఫ్యాక్ట్-చెక్ ఆర్టికల్ను ఇక్కడ చూడవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, 2026 నేపాల్ వరద బాధితుల మృతదేహాల దృశ్యాలంటూ ఒక స్క్రిప్టెడ్ వీడియోను తప్పుగా షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

The Meaning of the Lindsay Clancy Mistrial
Everyone has a theory. But what if this case means nothing at all?
During the five weeks of her murder trial, Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three young children in 2023, spoke barely a word. She has been on display for the entirety of her livestreamed trial, sitting in her wheelchair beside her lawyer at the defense table. At one point, when the prosecution walked the jury through the children’s autopsy reports, she hunched over, racked with sobs, crying out, “I can’t do this!” But mostly, Clancy has remained silent and wide-eyed, her gaze wandering around the courtroom as though searching for something.
The judge in the case has just declared a mistrial because the jury has been unable to reach a unanimous verdict. But the viewing public, in the absence of Clancy’s own explanation of her experiences leading up to and after the killings, has projected its own ideas onto the case and rendered its own verdict. Some people have interpreted Clancy’s trial as a referendum on women’s postpartum mental health. Others have developed elaborate conspiracy theories maintaining that Clancy’s ex-husband, Patrick, is actually the guilty party. Still others have construed Clancy’s story as evidence for their own niche political beliefs.
These are all comforting narratives, in some sense, because they imply an underlying logic that imbues the events with meaning and provides a road map for catharsis. Yet the jury’s inability to arrive at a verdict makes plain that a careful evaluation of the facts does not yield an easily intelligible conclusion. The reality may be darker and more despairing: that something so dramatic and destructive could, in the end, mean nothing at all.
As Clancy’s trial has progressed, dozens of women wearing pink have appeared at organized rallies outside the courthouse in Plymouth, Massachusetts, holding signs signaling a kind of support for her. “Any one of us who have dealt with mental health, anxiety, depression, postpartum—I think we just know that any one of us could be sitting in her chair,” the organizer of a recent event billed as an opportunity to “stand in peace for Lindsay” told a local news outlet.
There is something inherently unsettling about any public expression of support for a confessed killer, but these gatherings and their associated social-media movements have not seemed aimed at improving Clancy’s odds of success in court. Instead, these demonstrations suggest that Clancy has for some women become a symbolic figure: the devoted but suffering mother martyred by the relentless, punishing demands of her children’s early years and left to suffer by a flawed and fractured health-care system. Many women have felt overwhelmed to the point of drowning in the months after giving birth, and many have sought help but failed to receive it. Clancy’s case, in her supporters’ imagination, appears to be the sum of all those biological and social hazards. What happened to Clancy, in this view, was predictable, and thus preventable.
That’s a tidy narrative about what took place in Duxbury that night in 2023, when Clancy strangled her three young children to death, then attempted to end her own life by swallowing prescription drugs, slashing her neck and wrists, and then jumping out of a window. A possible upshot of this view is that it may raise awareness about the inadequacy of treatment options for postpartum mental illnesses—to the degree that raising awareness about any given issue ever meaningfully changes anything. And some elements of it seem inarguably true, such as the idea that Clancy’s psychiatric care was woefully uncoordinated. But this theory also has the odd effect of making Clancy the star of her own murder trial, for whom the viewer at home may be encouraged to root, which risks eliding the gravity of what she did.
Simultaneously believing that someone is relatable and vulnerable and that they are nevertheless guilty of and accountable for heinous crimes is, however, cognitively tricky. I suspect that that tension is the origin of a similarly enormous groundswell of conspiracy theorizing about Clancy’s case that has pervaded social media. Although those theories vary, they generally maintain that Clancy is factually innocent of the killings and that her ex-husband is instead guilty of murdering the children, attempting to murder Clancy, and framing his ex-wife for the deaths. Proponents typically cite as proof any number of purported facts presented at trial, such as that Clancy’s fingerprints weren’t found on the exercise bands used to strangle the children, or that her core body temperature upon her arrival to the hospital called the prosecution’s timeline of events into question. Clancy is, in these tellings, a victim of spousal abuse akin to torture, whose partner cruelly exploited her postpartum suffering in order to dispose of his family.
That, too, is a tidy story with symbolic significance: For those who deny her guilt, Clancy’s life and fate become a nightmare of female subjugation. This view morphs a reasonable claim that Patrick ought to have been more attentive to Clancy’s deteriorating mental state into a much stronger insistence that he is in fact fully culpable for what happened, having carefully plotted the entire sequence of events. Clancy’s story, then, becomes a parable about male violence against women.
Yet this embrace of Clancy as the true victim of her crimes has triggered an online backlash on the political right that maintains that liberal-female support for Clancy is a naked expression of latent female tendencies toward violence against children and an indication that liberal women are unstable and dangerous. (This despite the fact that women actually have varying views on the case, and that men kill the majority of children murdered in the United States.) That thinking also mistakenly takes Clancy to be a representative Everywoman, this time standing in for the threatening volatility of liberal women writ large.
All of these views of Clancy’s case strive to make sense of her alleged crimes: This trial must mean that mothers in America are crucially underserved, or that men in America are chauvinistically exploitative, or that women in America are secretly a danger to themselves and others. Some of those readings are more compelling than others, but they all seem to overemphasize what is generalizable about the case while understating what is unique, particular, and hyper-specific about what happened. The broader the statements about this case are, the less they have to do with the events as they really occurred.
Clancy’s experience was inarguably extreme. If, as the defense claims, she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, it was an ultra-rare expression of an already uncommon condition. Her psychiatric care was, per a subsequent malpractice lawsuit, allegedly mismanaged, and the severity of her purported adverse reactions to widely used medications was highly unusual. She was undoubtedly suffering in the months leading up to the murders, and it’s possible that the right degree of support could have prevented what happened, but it’s likewise true that nobody could have reasonably predicted what happened. More than any general theme or idea, Clancy’s crimes seem to have hinged on a moment of catastrophic dysfunction. Life, in the end, defies a great deal of neat storytelling.
For the past several weeks, Clancy’s case has been heard in the court of public opinion. At this point, people seem desperate for answers about why these deaths happened and what they mean, or at least a guarantee that something we’ve learned from this case will prevent similar tragedies from happening in the future. Many such onlookers have hoped that the trial verdict will supply such insights. This hope now appears to have been in vain.
Prosecutors in Clancy’s case must now decide whether to retry her, negotiate a plea deal, or drop the charges altogether. No matter what they choose, this case will continue to frustrate those trying to make sense of it.
Clancy herself, with her haunted, bewildered gaze, seems to already understand what her well-meaning supporters and their opponents can’t yet come to terms with: There is no making sense of what happened, and no greater wisdom to learn from it. At the core of all of this is a void, and nothing emanates from it but the assurance of everlasting pain.

Tamil Nadu recorded nearly 45,000 fewer births in 2025 than the previous year, with the number of births falling by 5.3% from 8.47 lakh in 2024 to 8.02 lakh, pointing to a continuing decline in births in the State.
The decline comes against the backdrop of a long-term fall in fertility in the State. In 2026, five lakh-odd births were recorded so far, according to Civil Registration System data.”
While the decline in births reflects a broader demographic transition, with implications for the workforce and ageing population, experts say greater attention must be paid to education, childcare, social security, elderly care and standard of living.
T. Sundararaman, former executive director, National Health Systems Resource Centre, said the total fertility rate among women of reproductive age fell below the replacement level of 2.1 in Tamil Nadu nearly 20 years ago. “We continued to have a positive population growth rate because of population momentum. We have now moved beyond this phenomenon and a decline in the population is likely to occur,” he said.
S. Irudaya Rajan, chairperson, International Institute for Migration and Development, Thiruvananthapuram, pointed out that Tamil Nadu is better placed compared with Kerala, which has recorded around three lakh births.
“There will be no short-term impact. The State government can focus on creating a productive, healthy population of eight lakh-plus by investing in quality education over the next 20 to 25 years. The focus should be on quality rather than quantity,” he said.
“First of all, there is no need to worry about the low fertility rate or the decline in births,” Padmavathi Srinivasan, independent research consultant in demography, said, adding: “This opens up opportunities to increase and improve the standard of living and enable people to better access the State’s resources. The State government should seize this opportunity and capitalise on low fertility.”
Observing that politicians would worry about what would happen to the State’s labour force, she said, “but this is the time to focus on education and employment opportunities. Tamil Nadu is a prosperous State, but this prosperity needs to translate to better living standards.”
“It would be an injustice if the State focussed on increasing fertility and channelled government funds towards it. Rather, it should focus on the existing population, especially the youth. The State should pay attention to the foundations, such as quality education and the nutritional status of children. There are still pockets of people living in poverty, those who have no access to opportunities and have not benefitted from the State’s economic growth.”
Financial incentives to reverse low fertility rates have never worked, as evidenced in many developed countries, she said, asking: “So, why go down that route, when there are much more pressing issues we need to tackle.”
Professor Rajan said the State government’s “Thaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam”, under which one-gram gold rings will be gifted to babies born in government hospitals, is unlikely to help increase births. Increasing maternity leave to women government employees for a third child cannot be considered a meaningful incentive, he believed.
Policies alone will not help much. At best, they may add another 5,000-odd births, he said. “Children are assets, but when you ask couples today, many consider them liabilities. This mindset should change. Increasing the fertility rate is not simple, given factors such as delayed marriages. To motivate young couples to have children, we need out-of-the-box, innovative ideas.”
Priority areas
Professor Sundararaman said increasing longevity means that there will be more people aged 65 or 70 and above. “At the same time, we will have less working age population and a larger elderly population that needs to be cared for. This has already happened in most developed countries that have stronger social security systems and better elderly care,” he said.
“I am less worried about productivity and more concerned about social security and elderly care. We need policies that anticipate these changes,” he added.
Efforts simply to increase childbearing are unlikely to work. What can make a difference is providing child care support for the first two children, he said. “We need to have innovative thinking and creative community-based efforts for elderly care. Our priorities should include elderly care, social security, child care support, good quality primary education and measures that make it easier for working women for childcare. Funds should be better utilised to establish facilities, such as creches for working women,” he added.

NEW DELHI: Lashkar terrorist Yasir, a Pakistani national linked to Hafiz Saeed's outift, was killed by security forces in the higher reaches of Yusmarg in central Kashmir, on Saturday.He was suspected of being involved in several major terror attacks in Jammu and Kashmir in 2024, including the ambush of an Indian Air Force convoy in Poonch and the killing of soldiers and civilian workers near Gulmarg.Yasir was gunned down on Friday during Operation Ashdar, launched after security forces received intelligence about the movement of a group of terrorists through the Pir Panjal mountains. Jammu and Kashmir Police identified the slain terrorist as Yasir and said he was affiliated with the banned Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT).The police also posted a message on X after the operation, saying, "You Can Run But You Can't Hide!"
Yasir's role in the 2024 attacks
Security agencies had first detected Yasir's presence in the region in 2024. Officials said intelligence inputs pointed to his involvement in at least three major terror attacks that year.The first was the ambush of an IAF convoy in Poonch on May 4, 2024. Terrorists opened fire on the convoy near Shahsitar in the Surankote area as the personnel were returning to their base at Sanai Top. One IAF member was killed and four others were injured.Yasir was also suspected of involvement in the October 20 attack at Gangangir near Sonamarg, where terrorists killed seven people, including a local doctor.
Four days later, on October 24, terrorists attacked an Army vehicle in Bota Pathri near Gulmarg. The attack killed five people, including three soldiers and two civilian porters. Officials said Yasir was part of the group behind the attack.
Link to Lashkar
Yasir was reportedly operating with a Lashkar-e-Taiba group led by commander Junai Ahmed Bhat. Bhat was killed by security forces in the Dachigam forest on the outskirts of Srinagar on December 3, 2024.After the Bota Pathri attack, Yasir and another Lashkar terrorist, identified as Musa, are believed to have remained hidden in the Yusmarg and Pulwama areas. Officials said they later crossed to the Jammu side of the Pir Panjal range before returning to the Valley earlier this month.
The latest operation began after security forces tracked the movement of the terrorist group from Ashdar Gali in Poonch towards Pakherpora in Pulwama through Yusmarg.The Army, J&K Police and CRPF established a cordon in the area on September 1. They made contact with the terrorists on September 3 at Ashdar Gali, a remote mountain ridge. Yasir was eventually killed in the exchange of fire. An AK rifle was recovered from the site.The operation is still continuing as security forces search for Musa, who is believed to be hiding among large boulders and natural caves. The encounter site lies between 12,000 and 15,500 feet in the Pir Panjal range, where heavy rain and visibility of as little as five metres have made the operation particularly difficult.

Tesla’s Cybercab, a distinctive two-seater without a steering wheel or brake pedals, is set to start picking up members of the public in Austin, Texas, this evening. But the vehicle is already under investigation by the US federal government, which is probing whether it meets federal safety standards.
The investigation comes just hours after the electric automaker welcomed hundreds of fans to downtown Austin to ride in the driverless Cybercabs. Tesla plans to deploy the vehicles on its Robotaxi ride-hail network, which is currently operating in a handful of cities in Texas and Florida.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is updating vehicle standards to make it easier and faster for driverless cars to deploy on public roads. It’s currently tweaking eight rules, including those requiring car parts that driverless cars don’t really need: brake pedals, windshield wipers, and rearview mirrors. But for now, years-old standards remain in place.
Meanwhile, unusually shaped robotaxi companies have been told to apply for an exemption from federal rules before they start picking up passengers. Amazon subsidiary Zoox, whose vehicles do not have steering wheels or manual controls, won the first of these exemptions this summer, which limits its operations to 2,500 vehicles this year.
Tesla, however, has said it doesn’t need an exemption because its vehicles comply with all existing safety standards.
The investigation, called an Audit Query, will examine the data and process that Tesla used to make that determination, according to a government filing.
In a statement, NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said his agency “fully supports the safe development and deployment of automated vehicles. But as the federal regulator, we need to ensure that all of our laws are followed.”
Tesla did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Ann Carlson, a former acting NHTSA administrator who is now a professor of environmental law at UCLA, says the investigation is likely “an indication that NHTSA is super frustrated with Tesla.” The agency made clear through the Zoox case that it expects driverless vehicle developers to go through the exemption process. “For Tesla to slap them in the face and ignore that—that is gobsmacking,” she says.
This kind of federal investigation can prove consequential. NHTSA can require an automaker to change its vehicle or process. The agency can also pursue enforcement actions, including civil penalties. Volvo Group North America paid $130 million in penalties in 2023 after an investigation into its recall process. The company also agreed to three years of oversight by a third-party auditor.
The Cybercabs are, in many ways, symbols of Tesla’s intended future. CEO Elon Musk has said that Tesla should no longer be regarded as an automaker, but as a robotics and autonomous vehicle company. While 45 of these vehicles are in Texas’ Tesla fleet right now, a state database shows, the company intends to deploy millions annually.

Kal Dosanjh charged with theft, fraud and breach of trust offences dating back to 2017
Vancouver police say a high-profile officer who was arrested on Thursday allegedly defrauded at least 19 victims of a total of about $3 million.
Kal Dosanjh, a 26-year veteran of the Vancouver Police Department (VPD) and the CEO of the KidsPlay Youth Foundation, is facing four counts of fraud over $5,000, four counts of theft over $5,000 and one count of breach of trust dating back to 2017.
At a Friday news conference, Vancouver police Chief Steve Rai said Dosanjh had been suspended, and that he had recommended to the Vancouver Police Board that the suspension be served without pay.
He added that investigators believe there may be additional victims who have yet to speak to police.
"These allegations are deeply troubling not only because of their seriousness, but because they have the potential to undermine the trust that our members work very hard, very hard to build and maintain with the public," Rai said.
"This officer had a profile in the community and internally, and officers are angry and disappointed."
Dosanjh was arrested in Surrey in what police described as a "controlled" traffic stop. He has been released on conditions and relieved of his service weapon, police said.
Rai said police began a large-scale, covert investigation in December 2023 after multiple alleged victims came forward.
He said that after consulting with the RCMP, it was "determined with collective judgment" that the VPD would head the investigation because it was best equipped with the expertise and resources to handle the file.
Property developments targeted
According to court documents, multiple charges relate to alleged fraud and theft from investors in the Azura, Queen's Park and Sahara development projects.
Sarabjit Singh Gill, who police described as Dosanjh's business partner, is listed as a co-defendant in those charges.
"It began over a series of years until such a point that victims then started to question the veracity of those things," said Supt. Mike Ritchie, who led the 2½ -year investigation. "We were not made aware internally until 2023."
Dosanjh also faces two charges alleging fraud and theft from the KidsPlay Youth Foundation. Dosanjh founded the charity in 2015 with the stated aim of "keeping B.C. kids away from a life of crime."
Ritchie confirmed police had searched KidsPlay's offices.
Ritchie said the province's Civil Forfeiture Office has been engaged in a separate but parallel process for "quite some time," and added that police weren't ruling out additional criminal charges.
Municipal election ripples
Dosanjh's arrest has already had ripple effects in Surrey's upcoming municipal election, where his wife was running for council.
On Friday, the Conservative Party of Surrey announced that Sandy Dosanjh was no longer one of its council candidates.
Sandy Dosanjh is not named or accused in any of the charges or allegations her husband is facing.
He has, however, participated in her campaign as a speaker and supported her campaign on social media.
Richmond City Coun. Kash Heed, a former West Vancouver police chief and B.C. solicitor general, said the move was not a surprise given the election was just weeks away.
"When you have something of this nature, your significant other under such a cloud, it's going to be difficult to maintain the credibility and confidence of the public that are going to elect you to serve in office," he said.
"Certainly it will override anything that she is positively able to add as the individual running for municipal government."
In a statement on Thursday, Dosanjh's law firm Alliance Lawyers said it was "inappropriate to draw conclusions" based on the reported arrest of their client.
"Mr. Dosanjh has committed no crime and is innocent of any wrongdoing," the statement reads.
"An arrest, or a report that an arrest has occurred, is not evidence of guilt, misconduct, or criminal responsibility."
None of the charges have been tested in court.
Anyone who believes they may be a victim can contact police at 604-717-2601.

సోషల్ మీడియాలో ఒక వీడియో విస్తృతంగా వైరల్ అవుతోంది. ఈ వీడియోలో ఒక మహిళపై కొంతమంది వ్యక్తులు దాడి చేస్తుండగా, పోలీసులు ఆమెను రక్షిస్తున్నట్లు కనిపిస్తోంది. ఈ వీడియోను “బంగ్లాదేశ్లో హిందూ మహిళా టీచర్పై ఇస్లామిస్టులు దాడి చేశారు” అనే వాదనతో షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ). ఈ వాదనలో నిజమెంత ఉందో ఇప్పుడు పరిశీలిద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: బంగ్లాదేశ్లో ముస్లింలు ఓ హిందూ టీచర్పై దాడి చేస్తున్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్ : వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపిస్తున్న మహిళ పేరు జాకియా సుల్తానా. ఆమె రాజ్బారీలోని కదేరియా మార్కెట్లో ‘ఆస్థా పోషాక్ శిల్ప’ అనే బట్టల వ్యాపారాన్ని నిర్వహిస్తున్నారు. ఈ ఘటన జాకియా సుల్తానా, ఆమె మాజీ ఉద్యోగి షహానా పర్వీన్ బ్రిష్టి మధ్య జరిగిన వ్యాపార వివాదం కారణంగా జరిగినట్లు సమాచారం. రాజ్బారీ సదర్ పోలీస్ స్టేషన్ అధికారి ఉత్తమ్ కుమార్ ఘోష్ ఈ ఘటనలో ఎలాంటి మతపరమైన కోణం లేదని తెలిపారు. కాబట్టి, ఈ పోస్టులో చేస్తున్న వాదన తప్పు.
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని కీ ఫ్రేమ్లతో రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇవే దృశ్యాలు కలిగి ఉన్న పలు బంగ్లాదేశ్ మీడియా కథనాలు లభించాయి(ఇక్కడ , ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ). ఈ కథనాల ద్వారా వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపిస్తున్న మహిళ పేరు జాకియా సుల్తానా అని తెలిసింది. ఆమె రాజ్బారీలోని కదేరియా మార్కెట్లో ‘ఆస్థా పోషాక్ శిల్ప’ అనే బట్టల వ్యాపారాన్ని నిర్వహిస్తున్నారు. జాకియా సుల్తానా, ఆమె మాజీ ఉద్యోగి షహానా పర్వీన్ బ్రిష్టి మధ్య జరిగిన వ్యాపార వివాదం కారణంగానే ఈ ఘటన జరిగినట్లు ఈ కథనాలు పేర్కొన్నాయి.
జాకియా తెలిపిన ప్రకారం, బ్రిష్టి తన దుకాణంలోని లెక్కలు పూర్తిగా తేల్చకుండానే అక్కడి నుంచి వెళ్లిపోయి, ఆ తర్వాత సొంతంగా వ్యాపారం ప్రారంభించింది. కొంతమందితో కలిసి బ్రిష్టి తన దుకాణానికి వచ్చి తనను బెదిరించిందని జాకియా ఆరోపించింది. ఈ వివాదానికి పరిష్కారం కోసం మార్కెట్కు వెళ్లిన సమయంలో తనపై దాడి చేశారని కూడా ఆమె పేర్కొంది. అయితే, వ్యాపారులు ఇతర స్థానిక వర్గాల ప్రకారం, బ్రిష్టి జాకియా దుకాణం నుంచి వెళ్లిపోయి అదే మార్కెట్లో సొంతంగా వ్యాపారం ప్రారంభించడంతో ఈ వివాదం తలెత్తింది.
రాజ్బారీ సదర్ పోలీస్ స్టేషన్ అధికారి ఉత్తమ్ కుమార్ ఘోష్ తెలిపిన ప్రకారం, ఈ ఘటన వ్యాపార వివాదానికి సంబంధించినది. సమాచారం అందిన వెంటనే పోలీసులు ఘటనాస్థలానికి చేరుకుని, అక్కడి పరిస్థితుల నుంచి జాకియాను రక్షించి, ఆమె భద్రత కోసం పోలీస్ స్టేషన్కు తీసుకెళ్లారు. వైరల్ వీడియోలో పోలీసులు అక్కడే ఉండగా, కొంతమంది వ్యక్తులు జాకియాపై దాడి చేస్తున్న దృశ్యాలు కనిపిస్తున్నాయి.
ఫ్యాక్ట్లీ రాజ్బారీ సదర్ పోలీస్ స్టేషన్ అధికారి ఉత్తమ్ కుమార్ ఘోష్ను వాట్సాప్ కాల్ ద్వారా సంప్రదించింది. ఈ ఘటనకు ఎలాంటి మతపరమైన కోణం లేదని ఆయన స్పష్టం చేశారు. ఘోష్ తెలిపిన వివరాల ప్రకారం, బాధితురాలు జాకియా సుల్తానా ముస్లిం మహిళ. ఈ ఘటనకు సంబంధించి నిందితులుగా ఉన్న ముగ్గురూ ముస్లింలే అని, వారిని పోలీసులు అరెస్టు చేసినట్లు ఆయన తెలిపారు.
చివరిగా, బంగ్లాదేశ్లో హిందూ టీచర్పై ముస్లింల దాడి అంటూ వైరల్ అవుతున్న ఈ వీడియో ఫేక్.

UN says Israeli settler violence in West Bank displaced 2,500 Palestinians in 2026
Israeli settler violence has resulted in the displacement of more than 2,500 Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
OCHA said in a statement that since 2023, more than 6,400 Palestinians in 130 communities across the West Bank have been displaced due to the settler violence and related access restrictions.
Half of the 2,500 forced out this year alone are children, OCHA said.
That has left 48 Palestinian communities fully displaced since 2023, including a dozen just this year.
The statement said that humanitarian partners have warned that the cumulative impact of repeated displacement, recurrent settler attacks, damage to homes and infrastructure, and restrictions on access to land and essential services is deepening humanitarian needs.

Donald Trump has long embraced vengeance. “I am your retribution,” he declared to an admiring audience at the 2023 Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) as he commenced his march back to the White House.
It is unlikely Argentina, and far-flung holdovers of the former British empire, were on the US president’s mind at the time.
But the tide of international events in the past three and a half years have turned Trump’s vindictive mindset to the advantage of Javier Milei, the boisterous rightwing Argentinian president.
Trump’s notorious fixation with payback was almost entirely the trigger for Milei’s televised address to his fellow Argentinians on Thursday, as he stated his intention to reopen his country’s claim to a set of windswept islands in the south Atlantic – known to Britain as the Falklands, and to Argentina as the Malvinas.
The centuries-old dispute over the islands’ sovereignty has lain dormant since 1982, when the two countries fought a brief, but bloody, conflict that began after Argentina’s ruling military dictatorship invaded the territory.
Britain reclaimed them after troops in a naval taskforce dispatched by the then prime minister, Margaret Thatcher – ironically lionized by Milei as a political exemplar and inspiration – stormed the territory and eventually forced Argentina’s surrender.
An uneasy peace has reined in the generation since, although Argentina, which returned to democracy the year after the conflict, has never renounced its claim to the isles – despite the adamant insistence of their less than 2,000 inhabitants that they remain British.
This week, however, Trump suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falkland Islands. Why would the president go out on a limb to threaten this fragile peace? And why now?
Milei jumped on Trump’s comment that he was “reviewing” the US’s longstanding neutral stance on the territory’s sovereignty, which amounts to a de facto recognition of Britain’s control.
Fueling Trump’s animus is grievance that Britain, under former prime minister Keir Starmer, declined to support the US president’s decision to go to war on Iran, another irony given that country’s deep-rooted suspicions of Britain and its imperial past.
The president’s obsession that allies declined to help him in a war he never consulted them on runs deep and wide – from Westminster to Seoul – and has the potential to upend US relationships around the globe, if unchecked.
And Milei’s attempt to capitalize on Trump’s vengeance underlines the potential for ripple effects of this war to reach waters far beyond the Gulf.
In what has become a repetitive refrain, Trump laid bare his sense of wounded affront in an interview with a rightwing British cable channel on Thursday.
“Your country was not there to help me,” he told GB News. “We didn’t need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader, ‘Why don’t you send a couple of ships?’ He said, ‘We don’t have any.’ It was pretty sad, the whole thing.”
Milei’s opportunism could also be used by Trump as a bargaining chip – to lever more money from the cash-strapped UK treasury for defense spending and Nato contributions, after the new British chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, recently suggested that it might not reach increased spending targets.
It is a sorry pass for the “special relationship”, fostered through alliances in two worlds wars and deepened during the cold war and subsequent conflicts. Yet Britain is hardly alone in feeling the heat of a wrathful Trump.
Vengeance has been targeted in recent months at numerous other allies, now regarded with more hostility by the White House than traditional adversaries such as Russia and China.
Annual joint military exercises with South Korea – a vital ally of Washington since the Korean war broke out in 1950 – were suddenly scaled down and cut short by six days last month, on Trump’s orders, because of his irritation that the Seoul government declined to join the fight against Iran.
He has repeatedly threatened to bomb or “blow up” the tiny Gulf kingdom of Oman, which has had friendly ties with the US for 200 years, if it impedes his efforts to reopen the strait of Hormuz, which Iran has closed to most commercial shipping.
The White House also announced the withdrawal of 5,000 US troops from Germany after the country’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, rebuffed pressure to get involved in the Iran conflict and said Trump had been “humiliated” in the conflict.
Threats of retribution have also been aimed at Spain, which has resisted pressure to boost defense spending, and Italy, whose prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, was a former Trump ally.
Turbulence under Trump
But Milei, a self-styled “anarcho-capitalist” who has paraded with a chainsaw to signify his attitude to public spending and attended Trump’s 2025 inauguration, remains on the US president’s good side.
Last year, the administration extended his troubled government a $20bn loan guarantee to stabilize the infamously shaky Argentinian economy – but premised the money on Milei’s party defeating the leftist opposition in forthcoming congressional elections, which it duly did.
This time there are no guarantees, other than that of never-ending turbulence at the hands of Trump. Such rough currents may be the “winds of change” Milei referenced in Thursday’s speech, delivered – Trump-style – with his cabinet members flanking him.
But he may have been aware the phrase had other, historical connotations – evoking the words of a famous speech in 1960 by then British prime minister Harold Macmillan in Cape Town, heralding independence for Britain’s former colonial possession in Africa.
“The wind of change is blowing through this continent,” Macmillan said then. “Whether we like it or not, this growth of national consciousness is a political fact.”
In his address, Milei suggested the sun was setting on Britain, just as it once did on its empire, citing multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. “It is clear that they are on a path of decline,” he pronounced.
He did not mention his own falling political popularity – a factor which may also have played a key role in the former military junta’s decision to seize the islands in 1982, as opposition grew against the backdrop of mass disappearances of political dissidents and multiple human rights abuses.
Then, too, Britain was grappling with tensions over immigration and race riots, soaring unemployment and long-term economic decline that Thatcher had been elected pledging to reverse. In the late winter of 1982, there was little sign that she was capable of doing so – until the Falklands conflict sparked a sudden upturn in her political fortunes.
But she had the solid backing of the special relationship, and her ideological soulmate, Ronald Reagan, in the White House. Andy Burnham, Britain’s newly installed Labour prime minister, must contend with the chill wind emanating from the menacing and destabilizing presence of Trump.

Kissing apes, anti-splash urinals: This year's Ig Nobels showcase surprising science
This year's Ig Nobel Prizes — which are awarded for humorous, yet thought-provoking research — have been announced, but not on their home turf.
For the first time in the ceremony's 35-year history, officials are holding the Ig Nobel ceremony outside of the United States — in Zurich, Switzerland.
The reasons, they say, have to do with the increasingly hostile climate in the U.S. toward science and foreigners.
"Before last year, almost every winner would find a way to travel to the ceremony from around the world," says Marc Abrahams, who founded the Ig Nobels in 1991. "Last year, of the 10 winners, we ended up with only six of them at the ceremony."
Four did not want to travel to the U.S., citing safety concerns related to unpredictable immigration and visa protocols.
"They'd been seeing news reports of people being possibly sent right home when they arrived here, people being badgered about their personal lives in great detail, of people potentially being grabbed and put in prison or stuck on an airplane and sent to some other country, or who knows what else," explains Abrahams.
Abrahams says that, in part, he sees this change as an opportunity.
"When you've been doing something for 35 years, what's the chance you're ever going to get to start it all over again afresh?" says Abrahams.
Still, he and others involved say it's bittersweet to host the awards abroad.
"It's a sad decision to move from where it all started, but it's also opening new horizons for us and new audiences," says Kees Moeliker, retired director of the Natural History Museum Rotterdam and a former Ig Nobel winner. "It's a very positive thing for all our fans we have in Europe."
"Unfortunately, the decision that they're making to hold their ceremony outside the U.S. is quite rational," says Holden Thorp. He's the editor-in-chief of the Science family of journals and doesn't play a role in the Ig Nobels.
Thorp says the move reflects a broader trend where international scientists are now less enthusiastic to come to the U.S. for study, work and awards.
"A principle by which the United States built its scientific excellence," says Thorp, "which is that we welcome the best scientific talent from all over the world — that is no longer the case."
Urination optimization
After opting to host the Ig Nobel ceremony overseas, Abrahams has remained focused on the unwavering goal of the initiative — "to get people interested in things that otherwise they might never ever let themselves become interested in," he says.
That includes fluid mechanics. This year's physics prize was awarded to a research group that built the theory around — and then prototyped — a splash-free urinal.
"I don't know if you've ever been in a urinal and wore sandals, you sometimes feel those droplets," says Tadd Truscott, a fluid dynamicist at the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology in Saudi Arabia and a member of the winning team. "They could be yours, they might be your neighbor's. Well, the idea was to stop that completely."
Truscott helped determine the optimal stream angle to minimize splashback, which is less than 30 degrees. His colleagues then took it a step further.
"They were able to redesign a urinal so that any direction that you urinate into it," he says, "it maintains this minimum angle so that you always have no splash."
When Truscott got the news of the Ig Nobel, he was beyond thrilled. "I almost passed out, I was so excited," he says, laughing. "They didn't ask me if I was sitting down. And I think that would have been good!"
All winners received a statuette (this year, a slab of blue cheese topped by a foot erupting with toadstools in honor of this year's broader theme of "fungi") and 10 trillion Zimbabwean dollars. But that currency cratered years ago, so it isn't actually worth anything.
A rather long kiss
This year's economics prize went to a group that found that those in higher social classes were more likely to take from a children's candy stash.
A late researcher who examined the aerodynamics of nose blowing received the medicine award.
And the biomechanics prize was given to a team for developing a more rigorous definition of kissing — "a non-agonistic interaction involving directed, intraspecific, oral-oral contact with some movement of the lips/mouthparts and no food transfer."
This definition allowed the researchers to study the long history of kissing behavior in humans and beyond.
"To understand how a trait has evolved, you can't just look at it in one species," says Matilda Brindle, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Oxford and part of the winning team. "You've got to look across different species."
She and her colleagues found that kissing occurs in most living large apes and likely, they believe, in Neanderthals. In fact, they argue that early humans and Neanderthals may have even kissed one another. "That's really exciting," Brindle says, "cause it just puts such a romantic spin on human-Neanderthal relationships."
"Next time you kiss someone," she says, "you can think, 'This is a 21.5 million-year-old tradition that I'm honoring here. It's not just a modern human behavior. It's really ancestral.' And to us, that suggests that it probably has quite a useful evolutionary function."
That function may be to facilitate mate choice or exchange beneficial oral microbes.
Despite the change in location, the Ig Nobel laureates were honored as they are every year: They were showered with the traditional volley of paper airplanes — a celebration still filled with splash and affection, if on a new continent.

It’s Bullitt meets Christine meets Waymo.
Robotaxis enter their villain era
Road Rage is a new short film in production that casts a murderous autonomous car as the bad guy — and taps into everything people already fear about AI on the road.
Robotaxis enter their villain era
Road Rage is a new short film in production that casts a murderous autonomous car as the bad guy — and taps into everything people already fear about AI on the road.
A new short film imagines a San Francisco car chase where the other driver isn’t human — and the car may be trying to kill you. That a robotaxi can now be cast as the villain with almost no explanation says something about the present moment. Autonomous cars have gone from sci-fi curiosities to fixtures in some American cities, where they’ve become stand-ins for anxieties about AI job displacement, Big Tech surveillance, and machines making decisions once left to humans.
Road Rage, the planned short film awaiting $40,000 on Kickstarter to fund production, leans into all of it. The film pits Joa, a ridehail driver in a manual-transmission car, against Roboride, an autonomous vehicle that takes a minor road-rage incident very personally, according to a synopsis by its director, Romain Thomassin. Roboride lightly clips Joa’s mirror. Joa gives it the finger. The car decides to kill him.
“It’s analog versus artificial,” Thomassin told The Verge.
The AI bad guy will be played by an old Prius transformed with cold LED lights across the front — à la Tesla — fake cameras, a spinning lidar-like device on the roof, a black exterior, and a menacing, ever-blinking red dot. Thomassin calls the intended result a “nasty Waymo.”
“I really wanted to play the nasty, gritty look of the ’70s car chase, but with today’s robotaxi in today’s San Francisco,” he said.
The chase itself will be a throwback: real cars, real actors, and real stunts.
“I really wanted to play the nasty, gritty look of the ’70s car chase, but with today’s robotaxi in today’s San Francisco.”
— Road Rage director Romain Thomassin
“What makes Joa the good guy is not only his instinct but also his authenticity,” Thomassin said, noting a scene in which the character has an unexpected conversation with his passengers. “This type of human interaction doesn’t happen in a robotaxi.”
Thomassin doesn’t actually think robotaxis are inherently evil. But as a movie villain, they come preloaded with tension. For one thing, they’re replacing the kind of worker his protagonist represents. Joa is a Mexican immigrant trying to make a living driving in an increasingly expensive San Francisco. Robotaxis are already competing with ridehail drivers, just as generative AI is competing with workers in Thomassin’s own industry.
“Driving here is a metaphor for what’s happening in cinema, in filmmaking,” Thomassin said.
Then there’s surveillance. Autonomous cars are covered in cameras and sensors, constantly observing the streets — and people — around them. That, more than the prospect of being driven around without a human behind the wheel, is what actually unnerves Thomassin.
In Road Rage, that anxiety is pushed toward dystopia. There’s a brief encounter involving immigration enforcement, and Thomassin imagines a feature-length version in which autonomous cars identify people, trap passengers inside, or deliver them directly to authorities. The progression, as he describes it, is observation, surveillance, then control.
“The next step is that [autonomous vehicles] could become the police,” he said. And because robotaxis operate as connected fleets, the threat can scale beyond one vehicle. “Imagine an army rising up,” Thomassin said.
Robotaxis also make unusually good revenge-movie villains because people already treat them like adversaries. Thomassin points to the indignities Waymos have endured on San Francisco streets: people immobilizing them with traffic cones, tagging and vandalizing them, and even setting them on fire.
“They are being bullied,” he said. In Road Rage, that mistreatment becomes the motivation: “They want to take revenge.”
Thomassin describes Roboride as absorbing the behavior it observes around it — including the behavior of human drivers. The car is simply learning road rage from humans.
“Humans are known to be the worst versions of themselves on the road,” he said.
That makes Roboride a very 2026 update to the killer car idea in Stephen King’s Christine. There, the menace is supernatural. Here, it comes from something more contemporary: a machine that watches humans, learns from them, and inherits some of their worst traits along with the useful ones.
On the other side of the chase is Joa and his stick shift — a deliberately analog counterpoint. To Thomassin, driving stick is a deeply human act: The driver remains in control of the vehicle, physically responding to the road. What separates Joa from Roboride, in Thomassin’s telling, is instinct — and even irrationality.
During one confrontation, Joa takes his hands off the steering wheel while facing down the autonomous car. The move is so reckless that Roboride backs off. The human wins by becoming less predictable than the machine.
“Respect your madness. Be a little mad and creative in your way of doing things, and you will be able to rise against the machines.”
— Romain Thomassin
“Respect your madness,” Thomassin said. “Be a little mad and creative in your way of doing things, and you will be able to rise against the machines.”
Despite its skepticism toward AI, Road Rage may use some of the technology itself. Thomassin says the filmmakers are considering AI-generated imagery to depict what Roboride sees, while shooting the human driver’s world with traditional cinematography. To him, that distinction matters. He sees AI as a creative tool when it serves the story, rather than simply a way to replace workers.
For all the menace he sees in robotaxis, Thomassin isn’t afraid to ride in them. He signed up for Waymo as soon as he could and uses it when visiting friends and family for rides.
“I don’t feel in danger,” he said.
That may be what makes Roboride such an effective 2026 villain. The scary part isn’t necessarily that the machine will crash. The scary part is that the machine works.

“It’s a girl!” Melissa Peterson exclaims.
Just outside the operating room, the hallway erupts in cheers. Joseph Dewane, an ob-gyn, has just delivered a healthy baby via C-section; Autumn Joi Goodwin-Samson, a neonatalist, tends to the newborn still slick with a waxy film.
It’s a successful delivery just like any other except for one, minor, difference: The patient is an orangutan.
Ruhana—or just “Ru” for short—is one of eight orangutan babies born in a collection of US zoos since the beginning of 2025. For these critically endangered primates, that’s a staggering figure. It’s also not random: The baby boom is the result of a meticulous breeding plan and decades of research to weave a conservation safety net, one birth at a time.
“It might seem like it was all a coincidence that everyone was born at the same time, but it was very carefully planned,” says Angie Selzer, a senior animal care specialist with the Fort Wayne Zoo in Indiana and the Orangutan Species Survival Plan (SSP) program coordinator.
The SSP has been coordinating breeding recommendations since 1985; every two years, the program creates a breeding and transfer plan for animals at zoos accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA). Geneticists from the SSP consult a “studbook,” which contains the pedigree of all the animals in their system.
“We want to maintain a healthy and sustainable population that mimics the natural history of wild orangutans while ensuring successful mother-rearing of offspring,” Seltzer tells WIRED. Their recommendation accounts for a number of breeding factors, including underrepresented genetic lines, each animal’s unique personality, and group dynamics—always aiming for the lowest relation between breeding pairs.
“We’ve had a very good, happy outcome,” she says. It all started in February 2025 when the Indianapolis Zoo welcomed Edi, a healthy baby boy. After that, Weila was delivered at the Hogle Zoo in Utah in June; Bintang arrived at the Los Angeles Zoo, and in December, the Memphis Zoo welcomed Ruhana. Peterson, the associate primates curator at the Memphis Zoo says being present for that moment was a “remarkable experience.” The run of babies has continued this year, with baby girls born at the Cameron Park Zoo in Waco, Texas, Sedgwick County Zoo in Wichita, Kansas, and Fort Wayne Zoo in Indiana. Just a few months ago, the Denver Zoo welcomed a baby boy named Rambutan.
Humans share over 90 percent of their DNA with orangutans, a figure well-evidenced in how they breed and give birth. Orangutans in the program are routinely given human birth control and human prenatal vitamins; they’re taught to pee on human pregnancy tests; they gestate for nearly nine months; and after humans, their offspring have the longest childhood of any mammal. While C-sections like Jahe’s are rare, some zoos keep ob-gyns on call for their orangutans and other primates.
“Looking at their eyes and their hands, it’s like a mirror,” says Matthew Lenyo, assistant curator of predators at Denver Zoo. “It’s humbling.”
As with humans, maternal behaviors are learned; training is a critical part of ensuring the health of orangutan babies. For first-time mom Hesty, the Sumatran orangutan at the Denver Zoo, training involved teaching her to pass the baby to and from keepers for essential health checks and nursing since Hesty’s mother had struggled with it.
For many zoos, prebirth training involves other orangutans in their care too. To be successful, this training requires a deep and hard-earned trust between keepers and these animals, and can prove invaluable if an orangutan cannot be cared for by their biological mother.
That happened at the Hogle Zoo, when Weila’s biological mom failed to bond with her. She was hand-reared by keepers while they prepared Acara—a proven foster who raised her younger brother—to take over as mom using a stuffed animal as a proxy. They slowly introduced the two to each other, rewarding Acara for properly handling Weila. “She also has a gentle behavior” and uses a very gentle touch, says Hannah Comstock, the animal care supervisor of primates at Hogle Zoo. The pair live together full-time now. Acara is a model parent, and Weila is thriving; she has even started adopting some of Acara’s mannerisms.
Still, zookeepers aim to be as hands-off as possible. “We do all this work, but then at the same time, the best outcome is when you’re not needed,” says Lenyo.
It’s estimated that there are around 100,000 Bornean orangutans and 11,000 Sumatran orangutans left in the wild. The population of Tapanuli orangutans is even more dire, with estimates indicating a few more than 700 are left in the wild. The rainforest habitat they rely on in their native Borneo and Sumatra is being razed to create palm oil plantations, and the great apes are also targeted by traffickers who kill orangutan mothers, kidnap their babies, and sell them on the black market as pets. Some estimates indicate that orangutans could go extinct in the wild within 50 years; some experts caution it could be even sooner, in the next 10 to 20 years.
While these new orangutan babies will not be released into the wild, they are a critical part of species conservation. Zookeepers call them ambassadors; when visitors can see the apes, abstract ideas like climate change and deforestation become more real.
But the captive population also has a direct impact on the well-being of wild and rehabilitated populations: Research conducted at AZA zoos on everything from disease management to quality of life is then relayed back to teams in Southeast Asia. Felicity Oram is a conservation practitioner and co-director of OrangJUGA, a Borneo-based conservation organization. Her research on orangutan’s teeth has been critical in the care of young orangutans rescued from the pet trade who live in rehabilitation and rescue centers. She quips that “captive orangutans can help their cousins in the wild and in rehabilitation centers just by opening their mouths.”
Before Oram’s research, estimating age was an imperfect science at best. “It’s very difficult with size,” Oram says. “It’s just like with human children—you go, ‘Isn’t that a cute 4-year-old!’ And then they tell you it’s 2.” She partnered with zoos, using data collected from captive orangutans to link tooth stages to behavioral and developmental stages. In turn, this research allowed rescuers to more accurately make critical decisions about nutrition, medical care, and socialization, giving these orangutans the best shot at having a successful life—and maybe one day having offspring of their own.

Back in 2009, Ars wrote about what was being reported as a leaked trailer for the then-upcoming Left 4 Dead 2, saying the footage “looks like it’s straight from a high-gloss action movie.” Today, we need to offer an important update to this crucial, 17-year-old story: The trailer “leak” was orchestrated by Valve itself.
That news comes courtesy of former Valve writer Chet Faliszek, who said in a newly posted video about cut lines in the game that “for Left 4 Dead 2 with the ESRB… we leaked our trailer ahead of time because they wouldn’t let us release the trailer.”
Faliszek is referring to the Entertainment Software Rating Board, the self-regulating industry group that, since 1994, has offered sometimes questionable age-appropriateness ratings for thousands of games submitted to its purview. While many smaller and/or online-focused game makers skip out on getting those ratings these days, at the time, any publisher that wanted space on major retailers’ shelves needed to submit to the ESRB’s standards.
Those standards included restrictions on how companies could market their games as well. And looking back at the “leaked” Left 4 Dead 2 trailer on YouTube, you could argue that it falls afoul of guidelines that prohibited trailers with “graphic and/or excessive depictions” of “violence… the use of weapons… [and] blood and/or gore” as well as those with “crude and/or offensive language.”
At the time, Valve had some recent firsthand experience with the ESRB’s sometimes onerous enforcement of its marketing standards. Earlier in 2009, the ESRB requested a change to a Left 4 Dead 2 promotional image featuring a hand with three gnawed-off fingers, leaving two intact digits indicating the number of the sequel. To pass the ESRB’s muster, Valve shot a new version with two of those fingers back in place (and simply curled down) that eventually appeared on the game’s box art.
“Faliszek pointed out that this is a game where people are torn apart using a chainsaw,” we reported at the time. “But bitten off fingers on the logo? That’s crossing some line.”
“Likely to cause serious offense to the average consumer”
The ESRB of nearly two decades ago could also be quite restrictive regarding game trailers in particular. In 2007, the ratings group requested the removal of trailers for D3’s Dark Sector and 2K’s The Darkness after they had already been shared across the web (behind age gates on most major news sites). In a statement at the time, the ESRB’s Patricia Vance said that “the mere presence of an age gate does not permit a publisher to simply put whatever content it wishes into the trailer. All trailers must still conform to [the Advertising Review Council]’s Principles and Guidelines, which prohibit the display of excessively violent content or any content likely to cause serious offense to the average consumer.”

Argentine couple to return Nazi-looted painting to rightful owner
- Published
A painting which was stolen by the Nazis and only recovered in Argentina last year must now be returned to the heir of its rightful owner, a court has ruled.
The late-baroque Portrait of a Lady was lost for 80 years until it was spotted in photographs of a house for sale near Buenos Aires.
The house belonged to Patricia Kadgien, the daughter of a Nazi fugitive who had fled there after the Second World War, and she has now agreed to return the painting in exchange for not being prosecuted for concealing it from the authorities.
Portrait of a Lady was among over 1,000 artworks looted from the collection of Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker after the Nazi invasion of the Netherlands in 1940.
His daughter-in-law and sole heir Marei von Saher intends for the painting to be exhibited on a temporary loan at the Holocaust Museum of Buenos Aires to spread awareness of the issue, Argentine newspaper Clarin reports.
Von Saher has previously said her family "aims to bring back every single artwork robbed from Jacques' collection, and to restore his legacy".
This painting was first recognised in August 2025 by the Dutch Algemeen Dagblad (AD) newspaper on an estate agent's website of a property in the coastal town of Mar del Plata.
It was hanging above a green sofa in the living room of Patricia Kadgien, whose father Friedrich Kadgien had been a top adviser to Hermann Goring, Adolf Hitler's deputy. Goring plundered thousands of works across Europe.
Last September, Patricia Kadgien and her husband were charged with concealment and placed under house arrest after a search of her property initially failed to find the painting.
But at Friday's hearing in Mar del Plata, all criminal proceedings were suspended against the couple.
The agreement reached between the families and prosecutors means Kadgien and her husband will give up all rights to the artwork and must donate 4.8 million pesos (£2,356; $3,185) to local hospitals.
Portrait of a Lady, also known as Contessa Colleoni, is attributed to the work of the late-baroque artist Giuseppe Ghislandi.
However, experts have questioned the artwork's provenance, with some scholars attributing it to Giacomo Ceruti - another Italian artist from the same period.

AI data centres are booming in Australia - but at what cost?
- Published
The sheer size and noise of data centres are what people tend to notice first. Some say they sound like a jet plane about to take off, others complain of a high-pitched whine.
When Lucy* puts her child to bed, she hears a constant humming. "I'll hear it and think, 'What is that? What is going on?'," she says.
And then she'll remember that the noise is a data centre just 350m (0.2 miles) from her front door in the desirable suburb of Lane Cove, in Sydney's lower north-shore. Another four are in the pipeline at the local industrial park.
Australia has quickly become a global destination for data centres, with investors attracted to the country's abundance of clean energy, natural gas reserves, and land to power and house their technologies.
Earlier this year, OpenAI's CEO Sam Altman said Australia could become a data centre capital of the world, if it wanted to.
Australia is already headed in the direction of big tech's wishes. There are 162 data centres across the country, with plans for 90 more, and an estimated more than A$155bn (£80bn) of investment money lined up.
If approved, one of the world's biggest data centres will be built in western Sydney. At one gigawatt, it is expected to be Australia's largest single energy user.
And in Marsden Park, also in western Sydney, the biggest data centre in the Southern Hemisphere is already under construction only 100m away from a local community.
But as more Australians find themselves living next door to data centres - triggering concerns about water supplies, energy use and the environment - many are asking whether joining the artificial intelligence (AI) race is worth it.
'What happens if we don't?'
Data centres have been essential to the digital economy since the arrival of the internet.
They were originally built to process and store data for things like emails, online banking and cloud services. But everything changed after 2022 when ChatGPT launched and AI exploded in popularity. This prompted a sudden race to build more data centres to power the technology.
The location of these large, windowless buildings filled with beeping servers and cables also became important to latency – the time it takes for data to travel from its source to its destination.
Delays for things like air traffic control, robotic surgery or even Netflix would not be tolerated today, Belinda Dennett, CEO of Data Centres Australia, says.
Australia has roughly 13.6 million users of AI every month, making them the sixth most active users of the tech globally.
And experts say having data centres in Australia will lower the barrier to building more of its own AI companies.
"If we think about it in reverse, what happens if we don't build infrastructure here", Dennett says. "We get none of the value chain, we are just importing tools from someone else and we become just a user."
Australia is also an attractive market for foreign investment, as "we've got availability of land, we've got political stability, and we've got the Five Eyes security alliance," Dennett says.
"We've also got a skilled workforce, a pretty stable energy grid, and an abundance of renewable energy potential."
Leading business experts and economists say that without Australia's data centre boom over the last couple of years, the country would likely have headed into a recession.
Jon Whittle, a former director of the digital research centre at the country's national science agency CSIRO, who is now a leading voice in AI and business, agrees with this. He says the government doesn't really have a choice but to continue down the investment path.
"There's some very serious considerations around this, but my main message would be we need to lean into it," he says.
Fears over power and water supplies
But leading energy and environmental experts argue Australia has little capacity to meet the massive energy and water demands of new data centres.
The Australian Energy Market Operator says data centre energy demands could triple by 2030 nationwide.
Without significant new renewable generation and storage, data centres could push power prices 26% higher in New South Wales (NSW) by 2035, according to the Climate Council, an independent non-profit that provides expert advice.
Because data centres need uninterrupted power at a scale and speed that wind and solar cannot match, there are fears the current boom will trigger a new generation of coal and gas power plants.
No data centre operator analysed in a recent report by Greenpeace Australia Pacific adequately proved their claim of driving the country's renewable energy growth.
In the US, many data centres are not waiting to build more renewable energy and have found it cheaper to build new gas-fired power stations instead.
Just a 90-minute drive from Sydney's central business district, the Australian-owned data group Cloud Carrier plans to build three gas-fired power stations to generate energy for an existing data centre and two more in the future.
Moreover, if energy demands place too much pressure on the grid or there is a power outage, data centres, like in Lane Cove, will rely on backup diesel generators.
But NSW Treasurer Daniel Mookhey says Australia's investment boom in data centres is being accompanied by a boom in renewable energy.
"We don't see the two [as] unrelated," he tells the BBC. "We see data centres allowing us to replace a lot of our old coal-fired power with clean, green renewable energy with the private sector picking up a large amount of the tab because otherwise households would."
The new private investment will help with renewable energy and create "new industries that are likely to employ future generations", Mookhey says.
But data centres also consume large amounts of water - some up to 40 million litres a day, which is equivalent to 80,000 households - to prevent their servers from overheating. In a drought-prone country that is a potentially huge problem.
Sydney already needs to increase its drinking water supply over the next five to 10 years in order to provide for its growing population, according to Water Services Association of Australia (WSAA).
But if that water is used for data centres, households are likely to pay the price for sourcing water from elsewhere, such as through desalination, which costs more than traditional water sources.
Sydney Water, Australia's largest water utility, says data centres could use up to 25% of Sydney's drinking water by 2035.
In July, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced a new legal obligation for "large-scale" data centres to underwrite power supplies, limit water use, and pay for any extra water infrastructure needed.
But the prime minister also told media that the legislation, which will be introduced in 2027, would only apply to new proposals, not projects that were already built or under construction.
In response, environmental and community groups want a pause on all data centre development.
"We've got the government rolling out the red carpet saying we want to be the data centre capital of the world," Sydney's Lane Cove deputy mayor, Rochelle Flood, says.
"But can we actually do that sustainably or is it going to set us back in terms of net zero and our water storage targets?"
'What is it for?'
On a rainy Monday night during a town hall event led by Greenpeace Australia Pacific at the Lane Cove library, locals say they were never consulted on their area becoming a data centre hub.
One of the proposed centres from the cluster is 16m from the nearest home and 160m from a local primary school.
In addition, Flood says if the four data centres get approved in the industrial park, 50% of the current businesses will have to move - taking their jobs with them.
Felipe Tanaka, 40, is a manager of a business in the industrial park who has been told he must relocate for a data centre.
"We never knew that something like this would happen," Tanaka tells the BBC. "Thousands of jobs are going to be gone from this area in the next few years."
While a large data centre can employ more than a thousand workers during construction, research says that number drops to more like 100 jobs once the centre is operational.
"Most of our 300 to 400 workers here are locals," Tanaka says. "Having to move will probably see half of my employees gone."
NSW Treasurer Mookhey says the jobs that data centres will bring come not from those who work in them but from those who use them.
"When Microsoft and Amazon do business here in NSW, it's pleasing to see they are committed to providing some of their more skilled operations and locating them here," he says.
But what other skilled jobs might be created is not clear, and effectively what the data centres will be used for. As some critics have pointed out, many AI users are making cat GIFs, which uses the equivalent amount of energy as running a microwave for an hour.
"They're telling us this is essential... that we need to have these centres in our neighbourhood but they're not saying what it's for," Flood says.
"When our drinking water, energy and land is being used for generative AI slop, that is not giving any value back."

The Schism Within the Trump Administration on Mexico
Officials are veering between praise for cooperation and threats to attack.
To hear Ronald D. Johnson tell it, the United States and Mexico have entered an era of blissful cooperation. Johnson, a former Army and intelligence officer who took up his post as U.S. ambassador to Mexico in the spring of 2025, has chronicled on his social-media feeds joint efforts to incapacitate drug cartels, tackle the screwworm pandemic, halt illegal immigration, imprison wildlife traffickers, dismantle criminal finance networks, and expand soybean exports. That’s just over the past two weeks.
For Johnson, the U.S.–Mexico relationship is defined by “close coordination,” “decisive action,” “information shared,” and “the security of both our nations.” His hashtag of choice is #TogetherWeAchieveMore. Johnson’s Mexico is one in which the country’s security chief, nicknamed Batman, has made remarkable strides against criminal networks.
Other members of the Trump administration see things differently. Stephen Miller’s Mexico has a cartel-dominated government that has obstinately refused to cooperate in the fight against drugs and illegal immigration. It’s a place where terrorist organizations “kill, extort, kidnap, or murder anybody who gets in their way,” as he said in a July speech. Miller’s Mexico is one in which the U.S. military might need to do what an ineffectual Mexican government cannot.
Perhaps no other bilateral relationship has exposed so publicly the stark disconnects within the Trump administration. Mexican officials say they have become accustomed to bipolarity—a “doble discurso,” they call it—in their interactions with the U.S. government. Some meetings suggest that things are going swimmingly. Others seem to telegraph the possibility of an American air strike. “Sometimes they say one thing, and other times they say another” was how Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum explained the vacillation during a press conference in August.
Last week, after Johnson’s run of public praise, U.S. officials revived a periodic critique against Mexico in meetings in Washington between Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Mexican foreign minister, Roberto Velasco: Mexico isn’t doing enough to stop its own citizens from migrating to the United States. More than half of the people apprehended by U.S. Border Patrol in July were Mexican. U.S. officials asked why Mexico couldn’t halt the flow of its own citizens.
To Mexican officials, it felt like an unfair demand, given how much they had already offered the U.S. on immigration enforcement. Although overall apprehensions at the U.S.-Mexico border are up slightly from last year, they are down roughly 90 percent from 2023, thanks in part to Mexican cooperation. And although Mexican authorities have made it much more difficult for migrants from other countries to approach the border, deterring Mexicans presents a different sort of challenge. Detaining Mexicans moving through their own country “would be a violation of Mexican law,” the country’s former immigration chief Tonatiuh Guillén López told us. “It would pin the state against its own citizens.”
Johnson had posted on X that the Rubio meeting “reflects our commitment to work together to stop illegal migration.” But the secretary’s office struck a different tone, suggesting that Rubio wasn’t satisfied with what he had heard. Rubio, a post-meeting readout from the department explained, had “called for decisive action to end illegal immigration, stop the trafficking of fentanyl and other illicit drugs into the United States, and dismantle foreign terrorist organizations and cartels and deprive them of arms.”
Asked about the inconsistency in messaging about Mexico, the White House echoed Miller’s sentiments. “As President Trump has said, and as the U.S. government has repeatedly and clearly communicated, it is unacceptable that foreign terrorist organizations control vast territories across Mexico, including the entire region that directly borders the United States,” the White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told us in a statement.
The United States’ most important trade agreement could get caught in the tug-of-war over whether Mexico is doing enough to further U.S. interests. As the United States, Mexico, and Canada work through the annual review of the trilateral USMCA trade deal, Miller has privately floated the possibility that the U.S. could use the occasion to pressure Mexico into doing more on immigration enforcement, one U.S. official said. Although the focus of the USMCA review has been more on granular disputes over supply chains and the origins of raw materials, the U.S. could decide to withdraw from the deal entirely. If that happened, the economic blow to all three countries would be substantial.
U.S. law-enforcement officials based in Mexico gush about the kind of close security coordination that they’re seeing now, but that hadn’t existed for more than a decade. Since Sheinbaum’s election in 2024, Mexico has acted on U.S. intelligence to take down top cartel leaders; it has extradited more than 100 alleged criminals to the United States; it has detained thousands of migrants en route to the U.S. border and permitted thousands of non-Mexican deportees from the U.S. to be sent to southern Mexico. Sheinbaum’s predecessor openly considered stripping Drug Enforcement Administration agents of diplomatic immunity; now those agents have supported a series of major security operations.
“On security cooperation, what we’ve seen is a massive improvement under Sheinbaum. We’re getting things that were blocked for years—from extraditions to action against cartels,” one recently retired U.S. official who had been based in Mexico told us.
But for another group of U.S. officials, those actions are grossly insufficient. Miller in particular has lobbied for unilateral U.S. action against Mexican cartels. When he meets with Mexican officials, he typically complains about the country’s inaction. During Fox News interviews, he has used Mexico City, along with Baghdad, as examples of the world’s most dangerous cities. Sheinbaum has responded by saying she asked her foreign minister to send “this White House official the data concerning Mexico City, which perhaps he is not aware of.” (Mexico City has roughly the same homicide rate as Portland, Oregon.)
In recent weeks, U.S. diplomatic and trade officials have grown worried that the USMCA, negotiated during Trump’s first term, could be blown up if some of the president’s advisers get their way. U.S.-Canada relations are already strained over bilateral disputes; now negotiators fear that the broader pact could become a casualty of Trump’s immigration and cartel crackdowns.
Peter Navarro, a senior adviser to Trump on trade and manufacturing, has cast doubt on the deal, arguing that it needs major changes or should be scrapped altogether. Mexico is the United States’ largest trading partner—another point that Johnson makes frequently, but something that Navarro and other members of the Trump administration seem to view as a liability.
The deal enables a regional supply chain in which parts of a final product are sourced and assembled across the three countries. If the USMCA were to be abandoned or weakened, manufacturing costs throughout North America would rise dramatically. But the stakes of any USMCA renegotiation go well beyond the future of a trade pact. If the administration uses the deal to gain leverage over immigration and security policy, it would blur the line between trade policy and national security, and put the basic rules governing North American commerce at the mercy of disputes far outside trade. For Mexico, that could make the USMCA review less a negotiation over tariff rates than a test of how far the government is willing to bend to Washington’s demands. Mexico is already watching the U.S.-Canada rupture closely as it prepares for its own talks with Washington.
Trump allies have long touted his unpredictability as an asset, and Mexican journalists and security analysts are now debating whether the incoherence within the administration is perhaps part of a broader strategy. “Ambiguity is the tool. As long as Mexico doesn’t know for sure what will trigger the Pentagon and what will satisfy the DEA, it continues to hand over information,” Ghaleb Krame, an analyst and a former Mexican official, wrote in an August Substack post.
Other Mexican intellectuals argue that it’s Sheinbaum—the leader of a populist, leftist political party—who has revealed her own doble discurso in her dealings with the Americans. She “employs an anti-imperialist discourse for domestic consumption, while being discreetly and selectively subservient to the United States,” Ricardo Pascoe Pierce, a former Mexican congressman and ambassador, wrote in the newspaper El Heraldo de México. Sheinbaum has been particularly critical of the treatment of Mexican immigrants by U.S. immigration authorities, asking U.S. state attorneys general to investigate the deaths of 17 Mexican nationals in ICE detention or enforcement operations. But that anger has apparently not affected Mexico’s cooperation with the U.S. on security or immigration enforcement.
Johnson was the first U.S. ambassador in Trump’s second term to have an official Truth Social account. There and on X, he is careful to tag the president in his posts, signaling Mexico’s progress and growing cooperation. Johnson, who declined an interview request, has good reason to make sure the White House is aware of his messaging: Trump himself has embodied the kind of duality in his remarks about Mexico that ripples across his administration. He has called Sheinbaum “terrific” and “elegant,” with “a beautiful voice.” He has also said, repeatedly, that “the cartels rule Mexico.”
Johnson’s efforts to convey to Trump the payoff from Mexican cooperation may be working. Even though Miller has promoted a unilateral strike on Mexico—presumably targeting a cartel hideout or fentanyl lab—no such attack has occurred. U.S. officials in Mexico know that unilateral action would have an immediate chilling effect on bilateral cooperation, and they hope that it can be deterred. They have privately told their Mexican counterparts that anticartel efforts will be coordinated jointly.
Even some of the U.S. officials most critical of Mexico seem to recognize the value of the country’s assistance. DEA Administrator Terry Cole in July called the Mexican government and cartels “one and the same.” But a month later, at a presentation in Argentina, he told a story about Mexico’s security chief, Omar García Harfuch, calling to inform the Americans that Mexican security forces had killed Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as El Mencho, arguably the most dangerous drug trafficker in the region. Cole sat next to Harfuch as he recounted the story and described the joint celebration after El Mencho’s death. “Omar and I share information daily,” he said.
It was another disorienting twist for those following U.S.-Mexico relations, trying to parse what exactly the Trump administration makes of its southern neighbor. Former U.S. officials told us that part of the apparent inconsistency in White House messaging is related to Mexico’s own internal contradictions: a country with a $2 trillion licit economy where organized crime controls large swaths of territory; a government that attacks cartels even as some of its own members are accused of aiding organized crime. The U.S. government has always had difficulty capturing that nuance in its messaging. Now it doesn’t even seem to be trying.
