‘Very distressing’: SC judge says ‘dismayed’ to see police personnel assault Jantar Mantar protesters
SC judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan's comments came days after he said students must not face punitive action for expressing a different opinion or asking questions.
Supreme Court judge Justice Ujjal Bhuyan said on Friday that seeing police personnel assault students and other protesters at Jantar Mantar in July was "distressing" and "a matter of grave concern".
His comments came days after he said students must not face punitive action for expressing a different opinion or asking questions.
ALSO READ | 'Metallic foreign bodies’ removed in surgery from protester's body in Delhi, report shows
‘Very distressing to observe’: SC judge on police action against students
Justice Bhuyan reportedly made the remarks at the launch of "Policing the Republic", a book by former secretary (security) Yashovardhan Azad. The event took place at Viceroy Hall in the national capital.
"All of us are dismayed when we see young officers of the Indian Police Service personally going and assaulting protesters and demonstrators. This is something very, very distressing to observe," he was quoted as saying by news agency PTI.
"The detachment expected of police officers somehow seems to be disappearing, and this is indeed a matter of grave concern," he added.
Justice Bhuyan said the police can maintain effective law and order without using excessive force or violating people's rights.
"For most common people, a policeman on the street wearing a whistle and a lathi represents the power and authority of the state. When they feel wronged, they seek the help of the police. It is, therefore, of utmost importance that the police force maintains its credibility," he said.
"It can do so only by strictly adhering to the Constitution, by functioning as a truly professional force, acting impartially, displaying courage and acting with conviction, maintaining integrity and adhering to secular principles, thereby upholding the rule of law," he added.
He also raised concerns over the growing number of cases involving custodial torture and deaths in the country, calling it one of the worst crimes in a civilised society.
He said there is a need to reform the police system and warned against political interference in its functioning.
Congress MP P Chidambaram, former Maharashtra DGP D Sivanandhan and several others attended the event, according to the report.

Punishing students for asking questions is unconstitutional: SC judge
A few days ago, Justice Ujjal Bhuyan had said on Sunday that students should not face the threat of punitive action for holding a different view or asking questions, as doing so is unconstitutional and amounts to misuse of power.
He said universities should provide space for "established positions" to be "examined and questioned", while differences of opinion should not be treated with hostility.
The Supreme Court judge was speaking at the 13th convocation ceremony for postgraduate students of National Law University, Delhi.
"When students express a different point of view, when students ask questions, they cannot be threatened with punitive action. That is unconstitutional. That is a misuse of power and office," said Justice Bhuyan.
His remarks came after the Bar Council of India (BCI) withdrew an August directive that had asked state bar councils not to enrol graduates from NALSAR University of Law in Hyderabad. The directive followed a boycott by some students of an event where CJI Surya Kant was the chief guest.

Chelsea Women: Sonia Bompastor and Ellie Carpenter on Blues' transitional moment as they target WSL and Champions League success
Chelsea are morphing into a new team under Sonia Bompastor; they are taking learning from a disappointing 2025/26 season, with a clear change in playing personnel; they want to return to WSL and domestic glory, as well as competing in the Champions League
Saturday 5 September 2026 07:31, UK
"Chelsea are going through a transitional moment and it takes time for the club to rebuild."
Not pundit analysis, but the thoughts of Chelsea head coach Sonia Bompastor to Sky Sports ahead of the new WSL season.
And despite the hint of cliché, it works. There has been plenty upheaval over the last two years, starting with Bompastor replacing Emma Hayes.
Then, there was the shock departure of Paul Green as head of women's football in February. Alongside Hayes, the duo oversaw years of unprecedented success. It is something hard to sustain and even harder to replicate.

But that is the task that falls at Bompastor's feet. She managed to keep it going in her first season with an unbeaten domestic treble - some may say with Hayes' influence still in play - but her second campaign exposed the realties. Chelsea were not the team of old and a new era was beckoning.
Now in her third pre-season with the Blues, Bompastor believes she has the backing of the club to do just that.
"I think now I understand what the club is about a lot more," she said. "I also understand what we want to achieve and bringing my input into that.
"It's good to be in a place where I feel the confidence and the trust coming from the hierarchy in the club. As much as I know my job, we need to get good results in order for me to stay as long as possible, but it's also important to feel like we also have time to rebuild the team in order for us to compete against the best."
How last season informs the next
Chelsea only won the League Cup last season and finished third in the league behind Manchester City and Arsenal. It was the first time in six years they had not walked away with the WSL title.
Bompastor reflected: "We wanted last season to be a more successful season because Chelsea is a club who is used to winning. We only won one trophy, but if you analyse it, we have some good learnings to take and that's really important for us to reflect on.
"We spoke a lot about the environment and the culture we want to create here at Chelsea.
"It's a lot about standards, behaviours, how you show up every day, how much you are committing to work hard to achieve your goals and what are the type of behaviours you want to show up every day, off and on pitch.
"Who do we want to be as a team? How do we want people to talk about Chelsea? These things are really important for us to be able to achieve the goals we have.
"Chelsea are a club who are used to winning and we need to make sure we put everything together in order for us to achieve that.
"I'm quite happy with the squad of players I have, the quality we have, but it's also important alongside that quality to bring the right mentality."
Experience and youth informing transfer policy
This summer does have the air of a new start about it, especially in terms of playing personnel.
Players who have been the face of Chelsea for years have left. Former captain Millie Bright retired, legendary goalscorer Sam Kerr moved to the USA. Niamh Charles, Guro Reiten and Johanna Rytting Kaneryd also departed. They represent years of service, experience and trophies.
"We lost some really important players in terms of the environment and culture," Bompastor said. "Some of them had been here for many years and it's difficult to replace them.
"So it's for us, the staff and club, to think about how and what is the best way to replace them. It's about the recruitment, but also again linked back to the environment and the culture we want to create.
"We have also great leaders who have the right mentality about when you are on pitch, it's about winning games. Off the pitch, it's about the behaviours you need and showing up every day in order for us to work hard on the pitch to achieve the goals."
Chelsea's transfer strategy of mixing experience and youth is clear and epitomised by two of their four summer signings so far in Katie McCabe and Nelly Las.
McCabe needs little introduction. Indeed, Bompastor herself told Sky Sports she did not need to speak on the defender's quality, and it is clear she goes a long way in replacing some of the leadership Chelsea lost.
"She has already started to impact the squad in terms of the behaviours and the standards," Bompastor added. "I'm really pleased she's a Chelsea player now."
Las, meanwhile, is an exciting 18-year-old prospect who joined from Leicester. She made 16 WSL appearances across the last two seasons, and has featured for England's youth teams.
"It's important to have the right balance between experienced players, but also the youth into the squad," Bompastor said. "Players having versatility to play in different positions is also really important for me.
"I'm a manager who really loves to work with young players, to invest time to develop them and I'm really keen to bring these players into the squad and see how they can develop to contribute to the success we will have in the future."
Carrying on a legacy
There will always be pressure to win at Chelsea given their history, and they now have a balance to strike - maintaining that legacy while also forging a new way forward and meeting the standards Bompastor has set out.
That falls, in part, to the team's senior players - no matter how long they have played for the club.
One of those is defender Ellie Carpenter. She may have only been at Chelsea for a year, but as a multiple-trophy winner and regular starter, she will likely now step into a leadership role among the group.
"Chelsea are going through a bit of a transition phase at the moment. A lot of legends have gone and they left such a great legacy," she told Sky Sports. "Now it's our turn to do that, follow in their footsteps and to build on what Chelsea is as a club.
"As a footballer, you love those opportunities and moments in your career and it's a perfect time to be stepping into that role for this club.
"Our aim this season is to fight for those trophies back and show what Chelsea is about. We want to do it as a team, winning in that way and enjoying it and hopefully getting the results on the way as well.
"We have a great team this season and pre-season has felt good so I'm excited."
Champions League - is this the year?
One way this squad can cement themselves into Chelsea history is by winning the one trophy that continues to elude them - the Champions League.
For a long time, the Blues' recruitment strategy has been geared towards European glory while the domestic trophies took care of themselves.
Bompastor won it as a manager with Lyon and was a key reason for her appointment in 2024. Carpenter was in her victorious squad, as was new striker Melvine Malard and defender Kadeisha Buchanan. McCabe won it with Arsenal. Lucy Bronze - who signed a new Chelsea deal this summer - has been crowned Europe champion five times.
But none of those have come in Chelsea blue and every year, we ask the same question: is this the year the wait is over?
"Winning the Champions League is one of the main goals for us," Bompastor said. "We'll work as hard as possible to achieve that and I know everyone is expecting Chelsea to always be at their best.
"But the competition now in Europe is getting higher and higher. Many clubs now are in a position where they can compete to win the Champions League. I don't want to shy away from us and our ambitions, but I also know it's difficult.
"But that's the one trophy we're missing in the club and we will try as hard as possible to fight for that."
"It's always what Chelsea want," Carpenter added. "It's what their ambition is, what the fans want, what everyone here wants and what we work towards every day.
"This squad is young, but multiple people have won it in the team, so that helps a lot to bring the experience and what it takes to win.
"But we're just going to go game-by-game this season. We don't want to put too much pressure on ourselves. When we're enjoying football, we're playing our best football."
Getting comfortable with scrutiny
While it may seem a tedious back and forth on the Champions League each year, that is the kind of scrutiny that comes with being at Chelsea and despite changes elsewhere, will never alter.
It has perhaps been one of the learnings for Bompastor in her two years at the club, and something she must instil in the squad she is assembling.
"I've never been in a place before where the scrutiny is so high like at Chelsea, but I'm comfortable with it," she reflected.
"It means people care about us and really think we are a really important club. That's what comes with our standards and Chelsea being one of the best clubs in the world, so we need to get comfortable with that.
"We need to make sure when we go into the season, we don't have any regrets and we give our all any time we step into the pitch."
What is for sure is the Blues are in the process of morphing into something new. Consistent evolution was one of the secrets to Hayes' success, and Bompastor will be hoping the same is true now.

Microsoft’s Copilot rarely reproduces even full sentences from news articles and books, let alone substantive chunks that could substitute for the original, the company says in new legal filings as it fights copyright claims from publishers including The New York Times and book authors.
Microsoft says virtually nobody was grabbing NYT articles through its chatbot
Fewer than 1 percent of more than 8 million chat logs regurgitated at least 16 words.
As part of the lawsuit’s discovery, Microsoft provided 8.2 million Copilot chat logs to an expert hired by news publishers. The logs, it claims, were specifically chosen “because they hit on keywords implicating use of News Plaintiffs’ websites, and therefore the most likely to contain News Plaintiffs’ works.” It says the resulting analysis shows that 59,545 of these contained at least 16 words in common with news content used to ground the AI model. An expert for the Center for Investigative Reporting found 51 instances of “substantial overlap” with CIR work in the dataset, Microsoft says. Similarly, an expert in the authors’ suit found that the 8.2 million conversations with Copilot only had 24 responses that contained at least 30 matching words. Only 10 of the 212 books evaluated had any matches, Microsoft claims. The Times, CIR, and Authors Guild did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Microsoft argues that the numbers bolster its case that using copyrighted content for AI training datasets should be considered fair use. While systems like Copilot rely on using copyrighted material, it says, the resulting systems are used for significantly different purposes than the original. The fact that they sometimes reproduce sections of text, it concludes, “hardly undermines the transformative purpose of LLM training.”
The filings were made as part of a legal battle brought by publishers and authors against Microsoft and OpenAI, which the plaintiffs claim built products on their works and now compete with them directly, in part by regurgitating copyrighted content. The news publishers’ and books authors’ claims were consolidated under one judge to streamline the process, despite objections from the publishers and authors. Microsoft submitted its filing on Friday as it argues for the judge to issue a summary judgement, which would end the case at an early stage. (The Trump administration also filed a statement of interest in the New York Times case this week, supporting OpenAI.) If the judge sides with the publishers and authors, the legal battle will continue in court.

UN adopts new map: Africa bigger, North America and Europe smaller
The US was the only vote against the resolution for a shift to the Equal Earth cartographic projection over the traditional Mercator map
The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday to back a resolution spearheaded by several African countries to adopt a map that makes their continent bigger while shrinking North America and Europe.
Aimed at “a more accurate representation” of continental landmasses, the resolution was supported by 164 countries while the US voted against it and six other states abstained.
The new map – known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection – “is a relevant option for improving the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world”, the resolution said.
It urges member states to adopt the new map in place of the traditional Mercator projection, which was designed for maritime navigation by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569.
Foreign Minister Robert Dussey of Togo, which drove the resolution, said maps “guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions”.
“They are therefore never neutral, when they present a distorted image of our planet, they risk perpetuating inaccurate representation that are passed down through generation.”

There’s been a lot of excitement in the cancer research field recently. Preliminary results from a trial with patients who had melanoma or skin cancer, showed that a ‘cancer vaccine’ had been successful in reducing the recurrence of melanoma tumours. This vaccine, called instamaren autogene, is based on mRNA technology – the same tech that was used to manufacture Covid vaccines during the pandemic. A number of other trials across the world are also looking into how mRNA vaccines can help prevent the recurrence of certain hard-to-treat cancers.
So what are these new therapies and what cancer do they treat? Why are they called vaccines when they don’t actually prevent cancer? How does mRNA tech work and how is AI helpful in this? Will these personalised treatments be available in India any time soon and how expensive will they be?

Sydney sweats in spring hot spell, faces 'extreme' bushfire risk
Temperatures in Sydney are expected to hit 33 degrees Celsius on Saturday (Sep 5), nearly 13 degrees above average.
SYDNEY: Australia's most populous city Sydney baked in a burst of sweltering spring heat on Saturday (Sep 5), raising the risk of bushfires and prompting authorities to issue a ban on lighting fires.
The heat comes as a powerful El Nino weather pattern in the Pacific, expected to be among the strongest in decades, drives hotter and drier conditions across southern Australia during the September-November spring season.
On Saturday, the nation's weather forecaster said temperatures in the New South Wales capital, home to 5.6 million people, were set to hit 33 degrees Celsius, nearly 13 degrees above average.
At Sydney Airport, the temperature was already 28.6 degrees Celsius at 11.30am (9.30am, Singapore time), more than seven degrees above the September mean maximum temperature, according to forecaster data.
"Fresh to strong and gusty northwesterly winds developing during the morning, combined with dry, unseasonably warm conditions, will result in elevated fire dangers across the Greater Sydney Region today," the forecaster said.
State fire authorities issued a total fire ban for Sydney where they rated fire risk as "extreme", the second highest danger rating.
Climate change is causing extreme heat and fire weather to become more common in Australia, a bushfire-prone country of around 27 million. In January, thousands of firefighters battled bushfires in the southeast that razed homes, cut power to thousands of homes and burned swathes of bushland.

As Carney advances Vancouver port expansion, environmentalists raise concern for at-risk species
Aug. 29 notice part of larger push by federal government to fast-track projects amid trade war with U.S.
The federal government is advancing the process to potentially designate the Roberts Bank Terminal 2 port expansion in Vancouver as a project of national interest.
A notice published in the Canada Gazette on Aug. 29 marks the start of a 30-day consultation period on whether to list the port expansion as a project of national interest under the Building Canada Act.
The law allows projects deemed to be in the national interest to have their approval process, including environmental assessments, expedited.
In announcing the potential listing of both the terminal and the Mackenzie Valley Highway project in the Northwest Territories, the Liberal government said the projects "have the potential to strengthen Canada's transportation and trade networks ... and support Canada's long-term economic sovereignty."
However, environmental groups are concerned that potentially fast-tracking the port expansion could allow the government to bypass environmental protections.
The Roberts Bank Terminal 2 (RBT2) port expansion project, led by the Vancouver Fraser Port Authority, is a proposed three-berth container terminal that would increase the port's capacity by nearly 50 per cent and generate approximately $100 billion in annual trade capacity, according to the port authority.
The federal government approved the project in 2023, imposing 370 legally binding conditions intended to address environmental concerns. That same year, B.C. issued the project an environmental assessment certificate that included 16 additional conditions.
In their decisions, both levels of government acknowledged that the project would likely cause significant adverse environmental effects, but were "justified in the circumstances."
The RBT2 project is still in the process of securing final environmental permits, including legal approval from Fisheries and Oceans Canada related to compliance with the Species at Risk Act (SARA).
However, if the project is granted national-interest status, Carney's cabinet could obtain the discretionary power to grant it exemption from SARA.
In July, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced $10 billion in federal support for the expansion project as part of a broader agreement with British Columbia.
The expansion would be built in the Fraser River estuary, a location that environmentalists say is integral to the survival of hundreds of species, many of them endangered.
'Mega port' in an 'incredibly important breeding ground'
"This is an incredibly important breeding ground ecosystem for over a hundred at-risk species," said Julia Levin, associate director of national climate with Environmental Defence, a Canadian environmental advocacy group. "It's putting a mega port in the middle of that, destroying nearly 200 hectares of this really biodiverse estuary."
Last year, a Federal Court judge dismissed a lawsuit launched by multiple environmental groups who said the project would destroy vital chinook salmon habitat and threaten the survival of southern resident killer whales.
Southern resident killer whales — also known as orcas — are among more than 600 wildlife species listed under the Species at Risk Act. Only 75 southern residents remain.
Chinook salmon, currently under consideration for listing under SARA, are one of the southern resident's main food sources. But the area has lost approximately 85 per cent of its salmon habitat due to development and infrastructure, according to a 2021 study.
In response to environmental concerns, the port authority said in an emailed statement to CBC News that it plans to restore 102 hectares of habitat in collaboration with First Nations to "support key species like juvenile Chinook salmon and Dungeness crab."
The port authority said it is also advancing protections for southern resident killer whales, including requiring ships to participate in slowdown programs designed to reduce underwater noise.
B.C.'s Environmental Assessment office pointed to the legally binding conditions, saying in an emailed statement to CBC News that when construction begins, officers would "monitor the project for compliance with all provincial requirements over the life of the project."
Last spring, the federal government also proposed $258 million over five years to protect whales and their habitats, including $95 million over five years and $16.5 million annually thereafter specifically for the protection of southern resident killer whales.
But Levin and other environmental groups say the government's potential fast-tracking of these projects is a way to get them built at "any cost," including at the southern resident's expense.
Getting projects built at 'any cost'
"The federal government is clearly pursuing multiple avenues to bypass environmental safeguards," said Levin.
Along with potentially fast-tracking several major projects, including a new West Coast pipeline that would end in Roberts Bank, the Carney government is considering further changes to environmental regulations, including the Species at Risk Act, that it says would allow for quicker approval and construction of major projects.
"All of this is about overriding environmental protections, environmental laws and species protections to get certain projects built at any cost," Levin said.
The changes the government is considering would render the Species at Risk Act — and the protection it provides — "meaningless," wrote multiple scientists in a press release last month.
In May, two federal discussion papers proposed a number of possible changes, including exempting certain projects from the "jeopardy test" in the Species at Risk Act. Following criticism from First Nations and environmental groups, the government extended the engagement period, which ended in July.
"We're suggesting, rather strongly and bluntly to the minister, maybe this is not the way you want to do this," said David Green, a biologist and professor emeritus at McGill University who is one of the former COSEWIC chairs behind the letter.
"You don't have to just give yourself carte blanche to do whatever you want without mulling it over."

'Silence is complicity' - top footballer hits out over Cameroon femicides
- Published
The killing of at least eight women in a week has sparked outrage in Cameroon, with many calling on the government to do more to protect women and girls.
Among those who have spoken out is renowned footballer Nchout Njoya Ajara, who has called for an end to the "tragic wave" of targeting women, saying "silence is complicity".
The government has also raised concern about the rise in attacks. At least 50 women have been killed between January and April this year, compared to 77 last year, according to official figures.
In the latest case on Tuesday, a 44-year-old woman was killed in a hotel room in the capital, Yaoundé. She was allegedly stabbed to death by a 22-year-old who was later arrested.
"Being a woman in Cameroon should never be a risk," said Ajara, who is one of Cameroon's greatest female footballers.
The 33-year-old striker has played professionally in Russia, Sweden, Norway, Spain, Italy and Saudi Arabia for clubs including Atlético Madrid and Inter Milan.
"In the face of the tragic wave of femicides that has hit our country in recent days, silence is complicity," Ajara said.

In a statement, the opposition Cameroon Renaissance Movement (CRM) party said it was outraged by the "tragic recurrence of domestic femicides" and accused the government of being passive about the issue.
The femicide cases, most of which are attributed to domestic violence, have been reported in different parts of the country.
In a video published by state media, the minister for Women's Empowerment and the Family, Marie-Thérèse Abena Ondoa, condemned the "worrying" rise in the number of the killings, and said the government was working to address the problem.
She mentioned a bill to protect women against gender-based violence, which she said was being reviewed by the prime minister.
But civil society and women's rights groups have denounced what they perceive as the government's delay in turning the bill into law.
A parliamentary session, the last one for the year, is due to be held in November. However, Viviane Tathi, whose organisation documents cases of femicide in the country, told the BBC she was not sure that the bill would be passed at the session.
"We are worried because the November parliamentary session focuses on budgetary debates…So, we don't know by what magic this bill will be passed," she said.
She has called for the creation of a special court to handle family disputes, which lead to domestic violence.
According to the latest UN data, Africa had both the highest total number of femicide victims and the highest rate relative to its population in 2024 - with an estimated 22,600 cases, external.
The numbers are an estimate as some cases of femicide are believed to go unreported and many governments do not consistently record the information.

Flares reportedly set off and items thrown at players during junior AFL grand final in Canberra
Two people were briefly taken into custody at a junior AFL grand final in Canberra last night after reports of flares being set off and items thrown at players.
Officers were called to Phillip Oval around 8:30pm after receiving reports of a disturbance during the Under 18s AFL Canberra Grand Final between Marist College and the Belconnen Magpies.
"Reports received by police were that from a group of between 50 and 75 teens, items had been thrown at players, flares had been discharged, and multiple patrons were intoxicated," ACT Policing said in a statement.
"Two people were briefly taken into custody and released at the venue."
'Chaotic scenes' at conclusion of the match
In a message to parents of Marist AFL players, the college's deputy principal Liam Stakelum said the end of the game was "chaotic", with spectators taken into custody for "anti-social behaviour".
"They were part of a group that exhibited considerably poor behaviour throughout the match," Mr Stakelum said.
"After [quarter] time, we made the decision to keep our students down one end to ensure they were safe and away from the potential risk.
"I will state that it does not look like these [spectators] were affiliated with Belconnen."
ACT Policing said after the match concluded, event management staff advised all spectators to clear the venue.
"All patrons left the scene without further incident," the ACT Policing statement said.
Mr Stakelum said in his message to parents that officers believed the group posed a risk to students, and wanted to limit their engagement with the group as much as possible.
"I know the chaotic scenes at the conclusion of the match are hard to reconcile, but I do want everyone to know that the police were the ones who were in control," he said.
"The decision to remove everyone from the ground again was [made by] the police.
"This was done because they couldn't differentiate between the true Belconnen supporters, and the spectators who were causing the trouble.
"We may not agree with the decision, but coming from a safety perspective, I can understand the intent. Scenarios like this are not easy to manage."
An AFL spokesperson said the safety of players, officials and spectators was "of paramount importance" to the AFL.
"[Safety] guided all decision-making during last night's U18s boys' grand final,"
"The AFL worked closely with ACT Policing throughout the event and took appropriate steps to contain the situation and ensure the safe conduct of the match."
The Belconnen Magpies Football Club has been contacted for comment.

Netflix has ordered a live-action adaptation of D&D's Ravenloft
Alfonso Cuarón will executive produce the dark fantasy vampire story.
Dungeons & Dragons is a sprawling, ever-expanding world. That's part of what makes it so appealing for players and, more recently, has made it such a popular choice for film and TV adaptations. Netflix is the latest to roll for initiative, ordering a live-action series called Ravenloft. This gothic fantasy will center on the backstory of Darklord Strahd von Zarovich, a popular vampire villain from the Ravenloft setting. Deadline reports that legendary filmmaker Alfonso Cuarón will executive produce the project, as will John August, who is attached as the series' writer. Hasbro Entertainment
This isn't Cuarón's first collaboration with the streaming service; he wrote and directed the critically acclaimed Roma for Netflix in 2018. It would have been extra exciting to have him ply those skills for Ravenloft. But August, who has been a screenwriter on Tim Burton film projects including Big Fish and Corpse Bride, also seems like a solid match.
You could be forgiven for thinking that you'd already heard about a D&D adaption. There was a movie version in 2023 starring Chris Pine, Michelle Rodriguez and Regé-Jean Page. And HBO is working on a Baldur's Gate 3 show, which is practically a D&D expansion taking video game form.

During a tense vote on a data center being built in her drought-stricken Arizona district last summer, Tucson City Councilmember Nikki Lee made an unlikely pitch: “We’re going to get a little out-of-this-world for a second, so just bear with me.”
Elon Musk wants to put data centers in space. Should we let him?
What Big Tech’s sci-fi dream reveals about the infrastructure America actually needs.
Like many of her constituents, Lee did not want Project Blue, a sprawling 290-acre data center, gobbling up an ounce of her local drinking water. “We need to put data centers where they belong,” she said, and “we don’t think data centers belong in the desert.”
President Donald Trump’s recent bluster aside, it’s possible that the only thing as bipartisan as loving Dolly Parton is hating data centers, whose construction has become so controversial, so costly, and so backlogged here on Earth that companies like Google, Meta, and of course, SpaceX, are actively flirting with the idea of flinging them into orbit instead. Soon after the Tucson City Council rejected Project Blue’s attempt to connect to city utilities, Amazon Web Services, the secretive intended beneficiary, pulled out of the project, and another Jeff Bezos company, Blue Origin, filed a plan with regulators for tens of thousands of possible new data centers, this time, destined for orbit.
Sure, launching a hyperscale AI data center into space is still unprecedented engineering-wise, carries an unfathomably large price tag, could engender its own severe environmental risks, and may or may not draw unwelcome attention from the hunters among the stars. But for AI companies, such trade-offs might still be preferable to the terrestrial roadblocks, among them an explosive populist backlash and a 12-year wait to connect to the power grid.
SpaceX’s gargantuan initial public offering earlier this summer was predicated on the idea that it would launch a thus-far-unrealized fleet of orbital data centers to fuel much of the AI economy. The company claims that by the end of this decade, possibly as early as 2028, it will have successfully assembled an AI data center in orbit, with plans to eventually harvest a staggering 100 gigawatts of new solar energy for AI annually, equivalent to one-fifth of all US electricity consumption last year. (As always, that’s a very iffy promise.)
And Google, which has its own plan to deploy dozens of space-based data centers, released a study last December positing that as launch costs go down, they could become cost-competitive with terrestrial data centers within the next decade.
Experts tell me that it’s no longer a question of if space-based data centers could be technically feasible, but rather when they’ll be ready to launch, and perhaps more importantly, whether the math of using them to power something like AI will make much financial sense anytime soon. As of now, building a one-gigawatt data center in space would cost about $51.5 billion, according to an analysis by aerospace engineer Andrew McCalip, compared with $16 billion for one on land.
“They’re not breaking any rules of physics. Yes, there are going to be engineering challenges, but they are all solvable with enough time and money,” said Jason Aspiotis, a leading space systems engineer who now leads an orbital data center startup. “The gray area is, well, what about the economics?”
But even if this astronomically kooky plan does take off, it may not change much for those of us left on terra firma: Our energy bills will remain high, even if data centers aren’t there to drive them up. Our earthly infrastructure — affordable housing, public transit, and more — may be just as hard to build as ever. Harder even, maybe, given that crucial resources and untapped tax revenue will be literally rocketing up out of our reach.
No, if these tech giants succeed, it will not fix what’s wrong here on Earth, but merely prove once again their exemption to the gravitational forces holding the rest of us down.
Space-based data centers, explained
My father spent most of his career working in the satellite industry, and would sometimes let me waltz inside the quaint little data center housed in his office, a room I remember as roughly the size of my school’s computer lab, hosting rows upon rows of servers that I couldn’t touch, churning with a cool, mechanical hum as they crunched zeroes and ones.
AI data centers work similarly to that server room but on an exponentially larger scale, requiring far more land and energy to run, and much more extravagant cooling systems. Sending his office’s data center into orbit would have been extraordinarily difficult, and getting one of the facilities that powers modern LLMs aloft would be an even larger, more ambitious undertaking. But the benefits — namely, “cheap space (no pun intended) and power,” as my dad put it to me recently — are even more enticing.
An orbital data center need not negotiate with an elected official like Lee over precious water rights to the Colorado River, though it would need to install bigger-than-football-field-sized heat radiators to keep itself cool. You can’t simply launch something that big into orbit, meaning a space-based hyperscale data center — the size of which would likely rival that of the International Space Station — would need to be assembled piece by piece, probably by robots. And while the sun would provide an endless supply of solar power to process your ChatGPT queries, it would also inflict incessant radiation on delicate circuitry. If something breaks, you can’t send a technician up to fix it. Many experts are also concerned that if an excess of space junk, which extraterrestrial data centers would inevitably produce, begins colliding like bumper cars in Earth’s low orbit, it could knock out the orbital infrastructure we already rely on, like GPS navigation and weather satellites.
Even plastic decays in space, said Sven Bilén, a professor of aerospace engineering at Penn State, who, like Aspiotis, believes that early orbital data centers will probably be “processing data from space, like spatial imaging satellites or weather satellites, as opposed to, you know, cat videos” or AI-generated reality TV slop.
But even if AI is not the lowest-hanging fruit for deploying compute into space, it is certainly the deepest-pocketed, meaning that many investors and companies like SpaceX and Google seem quite willing to shoulder the start-up costs anyway. And considering how difficult it’s gotten to build data centers on Earth, or at least in the United States, it’s indeed possible that space could become the cheaper, or at least most convenient option, more quickly than one might think.
“In some form or another, in five years, we are going to have some orbital data centers in space for sure,” Krishna Muralidharan, who leads the Center for Semiconductor Manufacturing at the University of Arizona, told me, but it’s hard to say right now whether those consist of just a few expensive prototypes, or the beginning of a much bigger swing toward orbital compute. “Only time will tell whether you’re going to have a business case for it.”
Can we send our data center problem into space?
So, is it better to have a data center in space or in your backyard?
David Reid, a member of Virginia’s House of Delegates representing Loudoun County, home to more data centers than anywhere else on Earth, says the question has repeatedly come up at his town hall meetings. Reid is the rare politician — apart from the president, anyway — willing to defend terrestrial data centers, calling them a “money-printing machine” for local schools and infrastructure. Having spent decades working in the defense and technology sectors, he is doubtful that the math on orbital data centers will ever make sense.
“I believe this is, for lack of a better term, fictional nonsense,” he said, and is “creating a distraction from the fact that local officials here on Earth still need to make better zoning decisions.”
If most of the AI industry can eventually be powered by space, as SpaceX claims, it will require millions of sprawling new satellites, in an orbit currently dotted by fewer than 20,000 of them. Though “space is really big,” as Elon Musk has put it, one million satellites would still profoundly and, likely irrevocably, transform our night sky into one in which data centers outnumber visible stars.
“Will humanity notice if there are fewer stars in the sky? Well, not so much right now,” given light pollution in many cities, said John Barentine, an astronomer and environmental advocate for the night sky. “But what if they’re replaced by these artificial stars in the night sky? Is that the point at which people will say, ‘Wait a minute, we don’t want this. We want the benefits, but we don’t want this as a consequence.’”
This is, of course, the tension also at the heart of building data centers here on Earth. To some extent, they’re the most tangible representations of how little power we have to shape the course of a transformative new technology that few trust, and even fewer asked for. It’s one thing to object to a hulking data center, but it might be another altogether to see the sigils of our digital overlords illuminating the firmament. Would a place like Tucson, one of the most beautiful places to stargaze in the world, prefer a Project Blue to a starscape marred by blinking servers in the sky?

Major Australian alpine resorts are closing their ski operations up to a month early after a winter that broke multiple records for heat with limited snow falls being washed away by rain.
Predictions in June that a building El Niño could combine with global heating for a challenging ski season came to pass, with seven resorts either already closed or announcing ski lifts will stop operating this weekend.
This week the Victorian resorts of Mount Buller, Mount Hotham and Falls Creek, together with Charlotte Pass in New South Wales, all announced ski operations would end this weekend.
The Victorian resort of Mount Baw Baw, the NSW resort at Selwyn and Tasmania’s Ben Lomond have already closed. Resorts typically aim to stay open until the first weekend of October.
Resorts blamed “challenging” weather conditions and lack of snowfall. Two other major NSW resorts at Perisher and Thredbo remain open.
“The season was frankly a shocker. This was the fourth disappointing season since 2020,” said Dr Andrew Watkins, a climate scientist and adjunct professor at the Monash University and a science adviser to the campaign group Protect our Winters.
“The problems were El Niño and climate change. It was not that dry this year, but the problem was the warmth. The heat just did us in.”
Watkins, who is also a keen skier, said winter temperatures had been too high and precipitation that might have fallen as snow, had instead fallen as rain.
“Rain is the natural enemy of a snowpack. It melts it and then washes it away,” he said.
Data from the Bureau of Meteorology show Falls Creek and Mount Hotham had their wettest winters in more than 30 years but, together with Mount Buller, they also had their warmest winters on record for average maximum and minimum temperatures.
Watkins said data from weather observations at Cabramurra in Kosciuszko national park suggested alpine winters had warmed by about 2C since the 1960s.
He said that temperature rise would have been the difference between precipitation falling as rain instead of snow. “It would have been a bumper season if it had been 50 years ago,” he said.
The El Niño currently in place in the Pacific Ocean can promote hotter and drier temperatures in Australia’s south-east in winter and spring.
This week the bureau forecast the current El Niño would be the strongest on record and Australian scientists said climate change had made the strength of the event six times more likely.
A bureau spokesperson said this winter’s heat was consistent “with a developing strong El Niño” and the season had seen long periods of high pressure in the Tasman Sea that directed warmer air from the north over alpine regions.
“But winter 2026 also experienced relatively warm nights, with cloud cover and moist soils resulting in less overnight cooling,” the spokesperson said.
“This is in contrast with historical El Niño events. This is all occurring against the background of a globally warmer climate, with daily global surface air temperatures since June close to or above the record levels in 2024.”
New South Wales, Tasmania and Victoria all recorded their hottest winters on record this year.
In July, many ski resorts broke all-time heat records for the month with temperatures during one hot spell up to 12C above average.
Climate scientists have been warning for decades that global heating will create a challenging future for Australia’s ski resorts and alpine habitats.
Josh Elliott, chief executive at the representative body Snow Resorts Australia, said there was “no question it has been a challenging season for natural snowfall”.
“This winter was shaped by a combination of abnormally warm weather and climatic variability, but it’s important to remember that in any outdoor environment, that variability can result in some seasons being better than others.
“This is an abnormal season and shouldn’t be considered in isolation as a reflection of what future seasons will look like.”
He said skiing, snowboarding and snow play had still been available in NSW, Victoria and the ACT “since the June long weekend, with all resorts across Australia operating through the July school holidays and beyond”.
“What this season has shown is the importance and value of the investment resorts have made in snow making, with underlying demand for snow holidays remaining strong through July and August.”

The Japanese yen has soared by more than 2% against the dollar amid speculation the Bank of Japan is set to raise interest rates.
The latest jump on Thursday lifted the yen to its highest level against the dollar in a month, at 155.57, and followed a 0.9% move the previous day.
Global markets remain jittery after this week’s dramatic government bond sell-off – caused by fears of a fresh inflation increase as a result of higher oil prices.
Investors have been reassessing their expectations for the future path of interest rates, in Japan and across other major economies.
Remarks by a Bank of Japan policymaker, Hajime Takata, suggesting it needs to move more “nimbly”, appeared to have heightened the prospects of a decisive move.
The chief executive of the financial adviser deVere, Nigel Green, said the scale of the yen appreciation over such a short time period underlined the febrile state of markets. “Markets this jumpy don’t need a shock to move hard, a rumour is enough,” he said.
Citi said in a note to clients that Takata’s remarks were the “strongest messaging we’ve heard from the board and reintroduces the idea of an expedited rate hike trajectory”.
The Bank of Japan has been incrementally raising rates for the past two years, after the economy finally shrugged off decades of deflation, or falling prices – but its main policy rate was left unchanged at 1% in July.
Markets now believe there is a 77% chance of a rate rise at the BoJ’s next meeting, which starts on 17 September.
Commenting on the latest market moves, Japan’s vice-finance minister for international affairs, Atsushi Mimura, said he was “neither satisfied nor reassured”, and policymakers “remain on a state of heightened alert”.
The global bond market sell-off – pushing up the yield, or interest rate, on government borrowing – intensified earlier this week after the US Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, used a speech last Friday to indicate that he was determined to bring inflation back to target.
Warsh had previously baffled some investors by withdrawing the Fed’s approach of signalling future rate moves, known as “forward guidance” – but in Friday’s speech at the central bankers’ conference in Jackson Hole, he said that if inflation did not move towards the 2% target the Fed would have “more to do”.
The dollar weakened on Thursday after the Fed governor Christopher Waller indicated he was leaning towards keeping interest rates steady at this month’s meeting of Fed rate-setters.
“I’m going to paraphrase John Lennon here: ‘give disinflation a chance’. We can wait one meeting,” Waller told Reuters.
The dollar dropped further against the yen after his comments, and was also weaker against the pound and the euro.
The bond sell-off appeared to have eased on Thursday, with yields on 10-year UK government bonds, known as gilts, hovering at about 5.1% in morning trading – having touched the highest level since 2008, close to 5.3%, earlier this week.

Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka kept her US Open title bid on track with a controlled 6-3, 6-4 win over Kamilla Rakhimova in the third round, moving into the last 16 and extending her push for a fifth major crown.
Playing in a packed Louis Armstrong Stadium during a hot morning session, the world number one broke early in the opener and dominated on serve, finishing with four aces and losing only four first-serve points.
Sabalenka later described the experience as a dream, saying it was her first time playing a morning match in front of a full stadium and that she was grateful for the atmosphere.
ALSO READ: High on tennis: Sabalenka interrupts US Open match over cannabis smell
Rakhimova raised her level in the second set, holding serve more comfortably and saving four break points, but Sabalenka eventually manufactured the crucial break with an aggressive return before closing out the match on her own serve.
Sabalenka praised her opponent’s resistance, noting that Rakhimova pushed her hard and helped bring out her best, and expressed satisfaction at finishing in straight sets.
The victory stretched Sabalenka’s US Open winning streak to 16 matches, putting her in line to become the first woman since Serena Williams (2012–14) to win three consecutive titles in New York.
She will next face the winner of the fixture between Taylor Townsend versus Diana Shnaider, with a potential rematch of her French Open quarter-final loss to Shnaider on the horizon.

Justice Minister Hiroshi Hiraguchi said Friday he will ask an advisory panel to consider a law revision barring the use of evidence submitted in civil trials for purposes not directly related to court proceedings.
Hiraguchi told a news conference that he will ask the Legislative Council, which advises the justice minister, at its meeting on Sept. 14 to consider the change to the Code of Civil Procedure.

Wolves announce signing of defender Konan

Wolves have announced their final signing of the summer transfer window - almost 23 hours after it closed - by bringing in Portugal-based Ivory Coast defender Ghislain Konan.
The 30-year-old 57-times capped left-back, who played under new Wolves head coach Cesar Peixoto at Gil Vicente in the Portuguese Liga last season, has signed on a one-year deal.
He fills the gap in the squad left by David Moller Wolfe's departure to SV Hamburg on deadline day.
Konan started his career with Ivorian club ASEC Mimosas before moving to Portugal with Vitoria Guimaraes.
He then moved in 2018 to Stade de Reims, where he spent five years, before a stint in the Saudi Pro League, first at Al-Nassr, then Al-Fayha, half a season with Spanish second tier side Burgos and then last season's time with Gil Vicente.

On Thursday, Elon Musk’s X won a court order blocking Operation Bluebird from launching a new app taking over the Twitter name.
In his opinion, Chief Judge Colm Connolly explained that Operation Bluebird was unlikely to prove that X had entirely abandoned the Twitter name. Therefore, X was likely to succeed on trademark infringement and dilution claims tied to the platform’s former name.
Most compellingly, X argued that it still uses the Twitter name in the current listing for the X app in Apple’s App Store. In the first sentence of that listing, written in the same size font as the rest of the text, a single clause clinched the early court win for X by stating, “Welcome to X (formerly known as Twitter).”
X’s legal director, Naser Baseer, testified that X “deliberately” added that clause “to ensure that people who were searching for the Twitter app within the App Store, as well as people who were searching for the Twitter app outside of the App Store, would find the Apple app link and have an understanding that this is one and the same app, same platform,” Connolly said.
Additionally, survey evidence showed that people still think Twitter’s a “famous” brand, and X showed that despite wiping the name from its platform, the company still “takes advantage” of the “goodwill” that the “commercially strong” initial brand maintains by associating X with Twitter in the App Store, Connolly wrote.
“By virtue of the parenthetical, the listing is telling customers that what they knew as Twitter is now X and can be accessed by downloading the X app from the Apple App Store,” Connolly said.
It may also strengthen X’s case that twitter.com redirects to x.com, but Connolly did not yet have to weigh that question. Because X could be irreparably harmed if Operation Bluebird benefits from using the Twitter name at X’s expense, Operation Bluebird will be blocked from using the name until litigation is resolved, Connolly ruled.

Australia’s property market is facing a rare price correction, as rising interest rates and less favourable tax settings for investors accelerate a downturn.

US President Donald Trump is pushing American companies to take a bigger role in his planned Golden Dome missile defence shield, as his administration moves to turn an ambitious proposal into a functioning system despite ongoing concerns over its technology, cost and funding.
The project envisages a nationwide, multi-layered defence network designed to detect and intercept missiles before they can reach the United States.
Trump has presented it as a central part of his national security agenda and has said he wants the system to be fully operational before the end of his second term.
The scale of the plan goes well beyond Israel's Iron Dome, which provides ground-based protection against shorter range rockets and missiles. Golden Dome is intended to combine a ground-based system with a large network of satellites capable of detecting missile launches and tracking threats. Its proposed space-based architecture could also include interceptors designed to destroy missiles soon after launch.
That ambition is what makes the project both strategically significant and technically difficult.
Trump's administration has been looking to defence contractors and technology companies to provide the different pieces of the system. Lockheed Martin, L3Harris Technologies and RTX have also been identified as potential major contractors, while SpaceX, Palantir and Anduril have also emerged as companies with potentially important roles
Reuters has reported that the programme will draw on existing missile-defence technologies while pursuing newer space-based capabilities.
Lockheed Martin has already positioned itself publicly around the programme, describing Golden Dome as a layered defence shield that would use sensors to identify incoming projectiles, calculate their trajectories and deploy interceptors.
The funding, however, remains less certain than the presidential rhetoric might suggest.
Republican lawmakers have proposed an initial $25 billion allocation for Golden Dome within a wider $150 billion defence package. The funding has faced political obstacles, raising concerns over whether the money required to meet the administration's timetable will arrive quickly enough. Reuters previously reported that uncertainty over the financing could put the project's schedule at risk.
There is also a much larger question about the eventual bill. The Congressional budget Office has previously estimated that a version of Golden Dome could cost around $1.2 trillion over 20 years, although Pentagon officials have disputed the assumptions behind that estimate and argued that it does not accurately reflect the architecture the department intends to build.
The system's proposed use of space has meanwhile attracted international concern. China and Russia have described Golden Dome as deeply destabilising, arguing that deploying interceptors in orbit could turn outer space into an arena for military confrontation. In a joint statement, Beijing and Moscow said the programme would encourage the development of weapons designed to operate in space.
Those concerns come as the US, China and Russia are already developing increasingly sophisticated military space capabilities. Analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies have warned that Golden Dome could contribute to an arms race in space, while also noting that Beijing and Moscow are developing their own countermeasures.
Trump has also said Canada could participate in the project. Ottawa has confirmed discussions with Washington about strengthening NORAD and related initiatives, including Golden Dome.
For now, the administration is trying to move the programme from concept to construction. The challenge is not simply finding companies willing to build it. It is developing a system capable of doing what Trump has promised, securing the money to pay for it and ensuring that its increasingly ambitious space-based elements do not create a new set of security risks while attempting to reduce existing ones.

Following Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s startling announcement in July that the US military would begin mandatory testosterone screening for personnel, the Pentagon released a clinical guidance document on September 2 outlining the new medically questionable policy.
The next day, though, the clinical guidance document disappeared, as did an accompanying statement by spokesperson Sean Parnell. The withdrawal was first reported by Reuters.
In a statement sent to Ars Technica, the Pentagon said that the document, titled “Clinical Guidance for Health and Human Performance Optimization,” had been temporarily rescinded on September 3 to allow for updates.
“The Department remains committed to addressing hormone deficiencies, protecting the long-term health of its Service members, and enabling peak operational performance,” the Pentagon said. An interim guidance remains in effect, and “the final clinical guidance will be issued shortly,” it added.
The Pentagon declined to provide more information regarding what was being updated about the guidance and why it needed to be updated so quickly after its release.
Reuters reported that the rescinded guidelines called for men aged 30 and older to be screened through a questionnaire that could then trigger a blood test for testosterone levels and, if needed, testosterone hormone therapy. Women were also to be screened through a questionnaire, which could lead to treatment for hormonal imbalances.

South Korea jails care home head for sexually assaulting disabled residents
- Published
A South Korean court has jailed the former head of a disabled care home for sexually assaulting multiple residents, in a case that shocked the nation.
The man, surnamed Kim, was handed a 15-year prison term for abusing three residents at the Saekdongwon facility in Incheon City, west of Seoul. The ruling is subject to appeal.
Police started investigating Kim after one of his victims, a woman with a severe intellectual disability, came forward in February last year.
The case has prompted the government to inspect 1,507 care facilities for disabled people across the country, where 33 cases of suspected abuse were found.
South Korean Prime Minister Kim Min-seok had described the abuse at Saekdongwon as "a grave matter that calls into question the very reason for the state's existence".
An in-depth assessment of residents commissioned by Ganghwa County found that 20 current and former female residents may have experienced sexual abuse.
Many in South Korea have asked how such a case could still occur, especially after laws were strengthened in 2011 to protect people with disabilities from sexual assault.
Some have also raised questions on how the director's actions could have gone undetected for so long.
Ganghwa County has ordered Saekdongwon to close, while Incheon City officials revoked the licence of the foundation that operated it.
However, the closure has been deferred until the remaining residents have been relocated and arrangements for independent living have been completed.
The foundation has filed an administrative lawsuit challenging the revocation of its licence.

In Summary
- The Poco M8x is the latest phone from Xiaomi’s sub-brand, Poco, and is targeted at the budget segment.
- The phone is the first in the Indian market to come with the new Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 processor and also boasts a massive 7900 mAh battery.
- At Rs 20,999, the Poco M8x packs a punch in everyday use. It cuts some corners in the display department, but remains a very good option for those wanting reliable performance on a budget.
Even as smartphone prices head north, a new budget contender has entered the Indian smartphone market. Xiaomi’s sub-brand Poco has launched the Poco M8x 5G. With a starting price of Rs 20,999, the smartphone is the first in India to be powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 processor and also packs in a huge 7900 mAh battery. It also packs in some good specs and some decent ones, but is that enough to help it deliver a performance that can make it stand out in a segment which is not as spec-forward as it once used to be? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
Poco M8x Appearance and Design: Premium looks even at a budget price
The Poco M8x may be a budget smartphone but does not look like it. We received the Leather Green variant, and it is, without a doubt, the best-looking version of the device. There are plain-ish black and blue colors on offer too, but the combination of muted gold and that vegan leather back makes the Leather Green look very good indeed.
The back has a rectangular camera unit with rounded sides. This is slightly raised and comes with a matte gold finish and a shiny metallic gold outline around it. There are two large, dark camera lenses arranged vertically on the left side of the camera unit, while the flash is encased in a long, vertical pill-shaped island on the right. The Poco badge appears on the lower portion of the back, which is covered with textured green eco-leather goodness. This not only helps the phone stand out from the usual budget segment crowd but also keeps scratches and smudges at one arm’s distance. We are guilty of packing multiple gadgets in the same bag compartment, which often roughs them up, but the Poco M8x still looks brand new in spite of many such crowded trips.
The front of the phone is more regular-looking. It is all about a tall display, surrounded by bezels which can be termed “thick” now, for those who notice them. There is a punch-hole notch in the middle of the top of the display, which is home to the front camera. The sides of the phone also come in the same gold shade as the camera unit and house ports and buttons. The left side of the frame is completely plain, while the right side carries the volume rocker and the power/lock button, which doubles up as a physical fingerprint scanner as well. While it has been written off in almost every other smartphone segment, you do get to see the mighty 3.5 mm audio jack in the budget segment. The Poco M8x comes with one right on top of the phone, although the trademark IR blaster has been skipped. The base holds the hybrid SIM card tray, along with a USB Type-C port and a speaker grille.
The Poco M8x is a big phone, and this is immediately noticeable – it is 170 mm tall and 78.4 mm wide. It is relatively slim at 8.8 mm, but at 232 grams, it makes its presence felt both in hand and in pocket. While the phone feels very good in hand, one needs both hands to use. It is a pretty sturdy customer too – it comes with an IP64 rating which provides some dust and water resistance, while the screen has Corning Gorilla Glass 7i protection.
Poco M8x Spec sheet: Fit for its segment
Its design may look more premium than its price, but the Poco M8x’s spec sheet slots very well in the budget segment, or rather the new budget segment that has been defined by increasing component prices. It is the first smartphone in India to be powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 processor. This is paired with 4 GB and 6 GB RAM and 128 GB storage, which can be expanded up to 2 TB using a microSD card.
The display on the phone is big – a 6.9-inch HD+ LCD display (yep, those have made a comeback) with a 120 Hz refresh rate. There are two cameras on the back of the phone, one being the main 50-megapixel sensor and the other an “auxiliary” one, while the one on the front for selfies and video calls is an 8-megapixel sensor.
One of the major spec USPs of the Poco M8x is its battery. The phone comes with a large 7900 mAh battery, with support for 45 W fast wired charging and 22.5 W reverse wired charging as well. The Poco M8x comes with Android 16 out of the box with Xiaomi’s HyperOS 3 on top of it, with a promise of 4 years of OS and 6 years of security updates. In the sound department, it features stereo speakers and a 3.5 mm audio jack as well. Since it has an LCD display, the fingerprint scanner is on the side. All in all, these are good specs for the price the Poco M8x charges.
Poco M8x Performance: A consistent daily driver
The Poco M8x delivers the performance its spec sheet promises. The processor and RAM combination is budget-level, and the phone manages to get through everyday smartphone tasks with ease. Jumping from one app to another, social media scrolls, messaging, emails, photography, and calls are all handled without strain. Casual games like Tetris and Subway Surfers run with ease too. The phone is not designed to handle high-end games – we tried Genshin Impact, and not surprisingly, the experience was laggy even with tweaked settings.
The display is big, and the 120 Hz refresh rate does make the process of scrolling on social media a pretty smooth one. However, it is an LCD display with HD+ resolution, which makes the content feel a little less sharp, even though the colors do seem quite vibrant. This, combined with stereo speakers and a 3.5 mm audio jack, makes the Poco M8x a good device for those who like to watch content on their smartphones.
We had said waaay back in 2020 that the real home of a fingerprint scanner is on the side of the phone, so the fingerprint scanner placed on the side of the Poco M8x is something we actually liked. It worked smoothly and was easy to access. There is the option of using face unlock as well, which turned out to be impressively accurate and speedy, although it is supposed to be less secure than the fingerprint scanner. Call quality was good, and we did not face any abrupt call drop issues. In short, the Poco M8x is a terrific daily driver, handling everyday life and delivering entertainment with ease.
Poco M8x Cameras: Good main and selfie camera for the price
The Poco M8x comes with a 50-megapixel main sensor on the back paired with an auxiliary lens. The daylight performance of the main camera is pretty good. It captures basic shots well, with a decent amount of detail. The colors look a little muted as compared to the natural settings, but still turn out good enough for a quick social media post. You get a 2x digital zoom, which basically crops an image. The details do get compromised here, but it comes in handy when you need a closer look. The camera, however, struggles a bit if you push it out of its comfort zone.
It struggles to capture macro photos – you have to keep your hand very (very) steady to get a decent photo, and the portrait mode on the phone did not really add a lot of visible difference – the bokeh added was very light and almost negligible, which was disappointing. The low light performance of the phone is nothing too special either. As the light dims, details take a hit, and the colors remain muted here as well. There is a night mode which makes results a bit better, but low-light pictures in general take a second to process, and it is very important you keep your hands very steady for that second (there’s no OIS, remember). The phone comes with a number of modes like Document, Dual video, and Pro, that give users more shooting options and utility.
The front camera also performs surprisingly well for a modest-sounding 8-megapixel shooter, in terms of both color and detail. With beauty mode off, it can capture skin texture well, and colors seem good too. The portrait mode on the selfie camera actually delivers deeper bokeh than what we got from the primary camera. It does not catch edges very well (blurred out my ear once), but the photos are good enough for social media posts. There are a number of beauty filters, all of which do their job well. However, it follows the path of the primary camera and struggles with details and color in low light. The primary camera is capable of capturing full HD videos at 30 fps. Videos also turn out well in daylight but get noisy in low light. All said and done, we were actually surprised by the cameras on the Poco M8x, which performed well beyond our expectations (we still don’t know what difference the auxiliary camera makes, though).
Poco M8x Battery: Where the phone is BOSS
This is one department where the Poco M8x shines most brightly, and how. The phone comes with a massive 7900 mAh battery, and it is safe to say it just keeps going on and on. The combination of a low-resolution display, an efficient everyday processor, and a big battery is a terrific one. The Poco M8x comfortably lasted for two days of hectic usage, with hours of Instagram scrolls, YouTube, and some Modern Family episodes here and there, emails, messaging, WhatsApp, calls, sessions of Tetris, and some photography. The phone handled it all like a champ.
With a bit of careful usage, we even got it to last the third day. It is safe to say this is perhaps the best battery performance we have experienced in this segment. The phone comes with 45 W fast charging support and a 45 W adapter in the box, which took about one hour 15 minutes to go from 20 percent to full. But so big is the battery that even a 30-minute charge session can easily give you a full day’s battery. And as it comes with a 22.5 W reverse charging feature as well, it can double as a power bank for your other devices, including smartphones and wearables. This is pretty much the battery boss of the segment.
Poco M8x UI and software: A mixed bag of functionality and third-party apps
The Poco M8x comes with Android 16 with Hyper OS 3, and on budget devices, Hyper OS is a bit of a mixed bag. The first thing that hits you when you fire up the phone is the large number of third-party apps. It is a little overwhelming – there are even multiple casual games of the same type. Although there are also popular apps like Instagram, YouTube, YouTube Music, and LinkedIn, the interface can seem very crowded. Thankfully, these can be uninstalled, and we recommend doing so.
Now on to the good bits. HyperOS is otherwise quite functional and customizable. There are a number of personalization options – from icons to fonts, to themes and wallpapers; you can personalize them all to your liking. There are also features like interconnectivity that allow you to connect your device to other Xiaomi products and carry out functions over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi, and you can also link your device to a Chromebook.
There are some basic AI features on the phone as well – Google Gemini for writing and other assistance, and features like Circle to Search. Of course, given its specs, we do not recommend pushing the phone too hard in the AI zone. Finally, the phone has an array of accessibility features (divided into general, vision, physical, and hearing), which aim to make the experience smooth for all users. Get rid of the bloatware, and the Poco M8x’s UI experience can be a pleasant one.
Poco M8x Price: In line with the new budget zone
The Poco M8x comes with a starting price of Rs. 20,999 for its 4 GB/ 128 GB version, while the 6 GB/ 128 GB version is priced at Rs. 22,999. Keeping in mind the rising prices of smartphones, the Poco M8x is quite fairly priced for the specs it offers. It does face competition, though.
One of its most notable competitors is the Samsung Galaxy M17, which starts at Rs 17,999 and comes with triple cameras on its back (50 MP+ 5 MP+ 2 MP), a 13-megapixel front camera, and most notably, a Super AMOLED Full HD+ display with a 90 Hz refresh rate. That said, its display and battery (with no charger in the box) and its Exynos 1330 processor are a step behind the Snapdragon 4 Gen 5 on the Poco M8x. There is also the Moto G37 Power 5G, which starts at Rs 19,999 and is powered by MediaTek Dimensity 6400, and has RAM that goes up to 8 GB, but comes with a smaller display and battery and also starts with a 4 GB/ 64 GB version.
Poco M8x Review Verdict: The big battery boss of the budget segment
For its starting price of Rs. 20,999, the Poco M8x is a pretty budget smartphone. It mainly shines in two areas: design (Green Leather variant) and battery. It also does well in other departments, and we can see many people liking its large display, good speakers, and main and selfie cameras (in good light conditions). It also delivers very consistent everyday performance and comes with a very functional OS as well. All of which make it a great option for those who are looking for a good-looking but reliable device with days of battery life.
- Leather Green design stands out
- Good main and selfie cameras
- Great battery life
- Handles everyday tasks well
- Big display and screen combo make it great for consuming content
- Relatively low-resolution HD+ display
- LCD display, rather than an AMOLED one
- Portrait shots from the main camera are disappointing
- Bloatware in the UI

Fire dept wants TMC youth wing to vacate Kolkata office over fire safety
The West Bengal fire services department asked occupants to vacate the two floors, citing inadequate fire safety measures and an expired certificate.
Trinamool Congress (TMC) MP Abhishek Banerjee has been asked to vacate his youth wing office at Kolkata’s Camac Street after a fire safety audit found the sixth and seventh floors lacked adequate fire safety measures, officials said.
The West Bengal fire services department on Friday sent a letter to Rama Devi Goenka, owner of the sixth and seventh floors of the eight-storey building. The two floors were leased out to the Trinamool Youth Congress in March 2020 for a period of 10 years.
“Considering the fact that due to non-maintenance and inadequacy of the required fire safety measures, the occupancy is unsafe from fire and life safety point of view. It poses imminent threat to the safety of life and property of the building and its surroundings. You are directed to vacate the occupants immediately. You are further directed not to use the occupancy until and unless the fire safety measures are complied with and the renewal of fire safety certificate is obtained,” the fire department’s letter to Goenka said.
This comes days after the fire brigade department sent a team to conduct an audit of the two floors from which Banerjee runs the office of the TMC’s youth wing.
TMC leaders, including Abhishek Banerjee, didn’t comment on the developments till the time of filing this report.
On August 27, a scuffle broke out between TMC leaders and workers and the police when a team of officials from the Kolkata Municipal Corporation removed an allegedly unauthorised TMC billboard from the building where Abhishek Banerjee’s office is located. A case was registered against Banerjee and police questioned him on Tuesday. On Thursday, a group of armed masked men ransacked and looted Banerjee’s office on Camac Street in the early hours.
Sagnika Banerjee, advocate representing Rama Devi Goenka, said, “A lease agreement was signed with TMC Youth Congress on March 1, 2020 for 10 years. He (Banerjee) was supposed to occupy the floors and operate legally after we received the completion certificate (CC) from the civic authorities. Obtaining CC is a statutory requirement. But he forcefully took possession of the floors even before the CC could be procured.”
According to the letter sent by the state fire brigade department, the fire safety certificate was renewed on August 10, 2023 for a period of three years. It has expired and wasn’t renewed this year.
Advocate Sagnika said that the signatory of the lease was TMC leader Debraj Chakraborty, a close aide of Abhishek Banerjee. He was arrested by the STF in July on various charges, including extortion, money laundering, criminal intimidation and possession of assets disproportionate to income. He is now in custody.
