Quick Answer
John Ternus faces the tough task of balancing Steve Jobs’ product-first innovation with Tim Cook’s business success. As Apple’s new CEO, he must revive innovation, fix its AI struggles, manage rising costs, and keep Apple at the top.
It is September, and around this time of year my stories usually start with “Tis the iPhone season” (not kidding, you can check). While the new iPhones are still coming early in September, this story is not about the iPhone but rather about the people behind it, or rather Apple in general.
After 15 years of taking care of CEO business, Tim Cook finally bid farewell to Apple. On his last day in the role, on 31 August 2026, he penned an emotional memo addressed to “Team”. Cook has not cut ties with Apple completely but will now serve as the Executive Chairman of Apple’s Board of Directors.
John Ternus has taken over the reins as Apple’s new CEO. He has been with Apple since 2001 and has climbed the corporate ladder, all the way from being a member of the product design team to the CEO position in 2026. In case you do not know him well, we got you covered.
A full circle moment for Apple
This change in command feels like Apple’s life has come full circle. The company was started/ headed mainly by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak, who were known as product people through and through. It seemed to be teetering on the verge of closing down when Jobs returned to turn it around in 1997. He was succeeded by Tim Cook, who, as Jobs himself mentioned, is “not a product person” but focused more on scaling the business and made Apple the first trillion-dollar company in the world under his tenure. And now Cook has given the Apple empire to Ternus to take care of.
Many believe Ternus has been handed a golden spoon— Jobs laid the groundwork in his second coming, made products that became aspirational and industry benchmarks, and then Cook followed by scaling the business in a way no one had ever imagined could be done. Many think Ternus can just pass his tenure enjoying the fruits of their labor.
I respectfully would like to disagree. If anything, I believe he has an uphill battle in front of him.
From Jobs to Cook – from being insanely innovative to being a world champ
Steve Jobs focused on products and features that were not created to blend in. Under him, Apple’s product portfolio was slim and streamlined. People who have recently started following tech may find it hard to believe, but under Steve Jobs, Apple back then was generally launching just one iPhone a year. Just one. The idea was to focus on user experience, bringing out products that made the lives of its users easier, developing interfaces that would make using a device a simple process – in short, innovation that would make a difference. Apple was actually ‘thinking different’.
Under Tim Cook, that rulebook was respectfully thrown out of the window. Whatever Jobs did, it seemed Cook was doing the opposite. From launching just one iPhone a year, Apple started to launch multiple ones, sometimes more than once a year. It also had multiple watches, earbuds, headphones, iPads, iMacs, MacBooks, Mac Minis, HomePods, and, believe it or not, even a cleaning cloth (there are two generations of it now). It is safe to say Apple’s product portfolio expanded (some would say “exploded”) under Tim Cook.
It may have gotten extremely hard to keep track of all of Apple’s products, but under Cook, Apple became the most valuable company in the world. During his time as CEO, Apple’s shares went up a whopping 2,275 percent! When Cook gained control in 2011, Apple was valued at USD 350 billion (a very healthy number), and with his strategy of diversifying the portfolio and expanding into new markets, Cook took Apple all the way up to a valuation of USD 5 trillion, becoming only the second company in history to do so (Nvidia was the first).
Jobs and Cook thus both played very vital but very different roles in making Apple what it has become today. One focused on innovation, the other on expansion.
Ternus has got some big shoes to fill
Now, Ternus has stepped into the CEO’s role, and he has some really big shoes to fill. Not just in terms of his immediate predecessor, but the one before him too.
Let me explain: Ternus is a product person, and for all these years when Cook was in the office, many Apple purists were disappointed by his constant efforts to make the brand more mainstream. Cook’s efforts were not about making the brand more accessible or democratizing it (even though the number of Apple products has vastly expanded, they still remain premium), but were more about relentlessly releasing products and their variants. While this did increase Apple’s revenues and profits exponentially, many believed it had deflected the brand from its core values, the values Jobs believed in: innovation, user experience, and product design. According to many critics, Apple’s designs became repetitive, software became buggy, and its innovation arc felt more like a flat line of late, with the odd bump here and there.
So naturally, now that Ternus has assumed office, this lobby has new hope. Hope that perhaps as a “product person,” he will take Apple back to what they insist were its ‘golden days’ under Jobs. That he will channel all of Apple’s energy into making more innovative products and not just products that seem to exist to make numbers.
What this lobby, however, forgets is that Jobs is not the only legacy Ternus has to live up to. Cook may have done things very differently (some might say he really did ‘think different’ but in a different sphere of business), but under his leadership Apple soared and found its way to the top. Today, it stands at the very pinnacle of the tech world; some would even say it is the most important company in the world. While topping this would be difficult, Ternus can certainly not let it slide off this pedestal.
Now it’s Ternus’ turn to think different
This means John Ternus basically has to find a balance between the Jobs method and the Cook method or come up with something completely new. And that too at a very difficult time for the industry. With demand for memory driving up prices of all things tech – smartphones, laptops, computers, hard drives – it will be a challenge for Ternus to manage prices, even while bringing in the big sales numbers that many now associate with Apple. There is also the matter of Apple’s struggle with AI for the past couple of years, which has become quite a spectacle, one which Ternus needs to solve as soon as possible.
Many would kill to be in Ternus’ position, as it seems like the guy has got it all made and simply has to carry it forward, but if you ask me, I do not envy him his place or task. He has to deal with the shadows of two illustrious predecessors and an industry crisis, as well as a deeply polarised community, apart from, of course, intense competition from the likes of Microsoft, Google, Meta and Samsung. To be fair, it was not easy for either Jobs or Cook. Jobs took over Apple in 1997, with many confident that the company would not last another year. When Jobs passed away in 2011, an equally large number of people felt that a non-product person like Cook would not be able to succeed. Both of them defied their detractors and added a new dimension to Apple in different ways. It is Ternus’ turn to put his own spin on Apple. It will not be easy. Will he, too, Think Different, differently? Only time will tell.

Volkswagen confirms cutting 50,000 jobs as part of its survival plan
It’s also repurposing its German factories and, reportedly, shutting down the Spanish brand Seat.
Volkswagen has approved its Executive Board's "Future Plan 2030." The company calls it the "most strategically profound transformation program" in its history, with a primary financial goal of achieving an operating margin of nine percent by — you guessed it — 2030. If you were thinking that description sounds ominous for the company's people, you would be right. Part of the plan is cutting 50,000 jobs, including management roles.
The company says it has to undergo workforce adjustment due to "intensifying global competition, shifting demand and technological change in the automotive industry." Volkswagen announced earlier this year that it was going to shed 50,000 roles, citing President Trump's tariffs and losing car sales to the booming domestic competition in China, which is the world's largest car market. By June, however, reports were going around that the automaker was looking to cut 100,000 jobs instead. Now, it looks like Volkswagen has decided on laying off 50,000 people as part of this particular restructuring effort.
In addition to cutting jobs, the company is also considering the possibility of repurposing its European factories or closing them altogether. It has admitted in its announcement that its European capacity exceeds demand by more than 500,000 units. Volkswagen is currently assessing alternative uses for its plants in Germany, specifically the ones in Emden, Zwickau, Hanover and Neckarsulm, and intends to decide on their fate by the end of June 2027.
Another step it's taking is cutting its model range by 50 percent and reducing the complexity of its offerings by 75 percent. It's killing off models that aren't selling well, and based on reports, even whole brands. According to German publication WirtschaftsWoche, the Volkswagen Group is retiring the Spanish brand Seat. The company will, however, retain Cupra, which used to be under Seat before spinning it off as its own brand. Volkswagen plans to focus on a smaller number of models, so that it can produce higher volumes or cars that sell.

A group of saffron-clad men painted the walls of the Anandabazar Patrika (ABP) office in Kolkata saffron on September 1, days after West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari had demanded an apology from the daily for describing the recent violence at Jadavpur University as “gerua gundami” — or “saffron hooliganism”.
Videos show two men painting two pillars at the main entrance of the office while several police personnel stand by. Some of the police officials can also be seen recording the incident on their cellphones.
Several other saffron-clad men had gathered at the spot, raising slogans including “Bhagwa ka apmaan nahi sahega” (“We will not tolerate the insult of Bhagwa”) and “Anandabazar Patrika haye haye”. An ABP editor told Alt News that the demonstration began around 1:30 pm on Tuesday and continued for nearly an hour.
In another video, the group can be seen addressing a motley crowd and saying, “This land belongs to Shyama Prasad Mukherjee. This land belongs to Swami Vivekananda. This land is Saffron”.
Alt News procured more footage from the incident where the saffron-clad men could be seen sloganeering near the main gate in Hindi and Bengali before being escorted away by the police.
Anandabazar had carried the headline “Saffron Hooliganism: Logo broken during raid on JU campus” on its front page on August 21. Following this, Adhikari launched a sharp attack on the media outlet while maintaining that his demand for an apology did not amount to a threat to the media.
Meanwhile, Kolkata Police lodged an FIR at Bowbazar police station against editor Ishani Dutta Roy, chief reporter Soma Mukherjee and “others from its editorial team” following a complaint by Sanjay Shastri Maharaj. He alleged that the headline that Anandabazar Patrika had used implied an intention to “hurt Hindu sentiments and disturb public peace”. He stated that the phrasing was “highly objectionable, derogatory, misleading and offensive”.
“It is necessary to ascertain through investigation who proposed the expression, who approved it, who was involved in editing the report and determining the headline…” the complaint said.
“…An apology will have to be made. Otherwise thousands of sadhus in saffron robes are getting ready. They only want my consent…”, Adhikari declared during his rally in Jadavpur on August 28.
Anandabazar, however, did not issue apologise or retract its reports. In fact, they carried a follow-up story containing the chief minister’s statements.
Alt News spoke to a senior editor at Anandabazar Patrika, who said additional security had been deployed at the newspaper’s office near Chandni Chowk since Saturday, following Adhikari’s statements.
“We had a hunch something like this might happen. We were told not to go to office today. Police officials had come with them and left with them as well,” the editor said. Asked whether the men were affiliated with any organisation, the editor said, “They were not carrying any banners. But I do know that most of them were non-Bengalis.”
Alt News contacted Bowbazar police station, which said that no FIR had been lodged yet. Police also confirmed that the officials present at the scene were from Bowbazar PS, before ending the call.

India set out to expand its forested areas a decade ago. Last week, however, we learned that the forest cover programme had barely taken root when the government’s auditors released their findings of the flagship Green India Mission. The shortfall of 97.57% from India’s initial pledge in 2014 was stark enough to alarm the government’s own auditor, who described the progress as “negligible”.
Yet if you ask the government about forest cover, you’ll get a far greener picture.
I’m writing this on the day the UK Met Office issued a calamitous warning – 2027 could be the hottest year yet, on account of the strongest El Niño in more than a century. For India, a disrupted monsoon season puts agriculture and millions who depend on it at risk.
Which makes the question of what’s happening to India’s green cover feel far more urgent than an academic disagreement over numbers. I went down the rabbit hole of reports, datasets and government’s parliamentary disclosures. Here’s what I found.
1. Forest cover v forest cover
The government’s last comprehensive report from 2023 (released a year later) touted that forest cover in India has grown since 2021. But other, independent, assessments have found that forest cover is lower than what the government has claimed in recent years, or that it has reduced.
The discrepancy lies in some creative accounting. Last year, dozens of former civil servants wrote to the government criticising the forest report. They described its methodology as unreliable and nonscientific, pointing to the inclusion of smaller orchards, as well as coconut and rubber plantations, in the calculation of forest cover.
“A lot of the discrepancies are coming from how and what we are counting as forests. We have broadened the definition to include a lot more,” Pooja Choksi, founder of environmental consultancy Ficus Research Consulting, told me.
The government has defended its methodology, saying its definition is internationally accepted and includes tree-covered land outside forests as well as orchards and bamboo and palm plantations.
2. Whose land is it anyway?
Even as the government pledged to increase forestation, over the past five years India has approved the diversion of forest land for development projects covering an area roughly equivalent to the size of Hong Kong, according to data shared in parliament this month. The pace has accelerated, with the last financial year seeing the single largest chunk cleared yet.
Mining was the single-biggest sector, accounting for 22% of all diverted forest land, followed by road works and irrigation projects.
3. Ground zero
The pressure on forests is concentrated in some states. Nearly a quarter of all forest land diverted nationwide since 2021 is in Madhya Pradesh, which is home to the country’s largest forest area. Its share is more than double that of the next state, Odisha. Arunachal Pradesh on the north-eastern border with China ranks third for forest diversions, according to government figures shared in parliament.
One research team that mapped 28 years of satellite data from three central Indian coalmine regions, including two in Madhya Pradesh, found the damage from such projects extended far beyond disappearing trees. Water bodies shrank, soil quality degraded and the overall natural ecosystems diminished by 35%.
4. The ‘great’ project
Perhaps nowhere is this trade-off more starkly visible than in the project proposed in the pristine Andaman and Nicobar Islands, which are home to protected Indigenous tribes.
The central government has touted the Great Nicobar Project as a strategic necessity to strengthen India’s maritime and defence presence in the Indo-Pacific. The project would divert 13,075 hectares of forest land and cut down, conservatively, at least 700,000 trees to make way for a trans-shipment port, an international airport, a mega township and a power plant for their operation, at a combined cost north of $6.89 bn (Rs 90,000 crore). The project has already led to legal challenges and pushback from the opposition Congress party and environmentalists.
“Situated at the precise intersection of variable sea-level rise and sinking land, the Great Nicobar Project is not merely ecologically destructive or culturally erosive for the Indigenous populations – it is geologically impossible,” geoscientist CP Rajendran wrote in The Wire, arguing that the government is using natural security as a pretext to push a commercial hub in one of the world’s most tectonically active zones.
5. Is compensatory afforestation the answer?
For many such development projects that divert forest land, the answer has been to pour substantial public funds into planting trees and creating forests elsewhere. But experts caution that this may not be as simple a solution as it may sound.
Choksi, whose research focuses on biodiversity outcomes of restoration and tree-planting policies, said the rush to meet Paris Agreement targets has made India obsessed with “green cover” while ignoring other aspects of environmental policy.
“We need to move away from this very one-dimensional view that everything is green cover. What is being planted and where it is planted has a huge influence. The third question being why is it being planted because different trees have different purposes,” Choksi said.
A natural forest patch with 100 different species, she added, has very different ecological value to a plantation under the Green India Mission, which might have 20 species. “It does have biodiversity value, but it certainly does not have the same value as the diverse forest patches that we have across the country,” she said.
All of this shows that the true health of India’s forests is not easy to assess, which is in itself concerning. Meanwhile, India’s biennial forest report was due in 2025. We’re still waiting.
What else we’re reading about
Gaga over RaGa | Gaggan Anand, once dubbed the most famous Indian chef in the world by the New York Times, has finally opened a restaurant in India. RaGa, on Delhi’s upmarket Janpath Road, starts serving on 26 August.
Surviving summer | What is it like to endure extreme heat in a city pushed beyond its capacity to cope? In a dispatch from Mumbai’s sweltering summer in Equator magazine, Aruna Chandrasekhar provides a dystopian glimpse of a climate-stressed future.
Cost of reporting | Uttar Pradesh journalist Abhishek Upadhyay, among the first to report on the theft of donations at Ayodhya’s Ram Mandir Temple, has alleged police harassment and retaliation over his reporting.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Diet Sabya (@dietsabya), the anonymous Indian fashion watchdog, spills the tea on his current obsession: “Gathering by Haider Saleem is a very under-the-radar, slow-fashion brand that not enough people know about. There’s a lingering notion that Indian menswear-forward brands have to look a certain way or that they somehow can’t occupy the same conversation, say as The Row or Lemaire. Gathering proves otherwise. The clothes have this organic ease to them: earthy tones, flattering cuts, natural fabrics, with much of the dyeing done traditionally in Jaipur. The sort of brand you want to gate keep until everyone discovers it and you can say: “Oh, I’ve known them for ages.’”
Count it
A number worth knowing
Rs 8,452 crore
The Prime Minister’s Citizen Assistance and Relief in Emergency Situations Fund (PM Cares), set up during the coronavirus pandemic, had a balance of £647m (Rs 8,452 crore) at the end of the 2025 financial year, prompting questions about why such a large sum remained unused instead of being put towards relief work. Pradeep Bhandari, a spokesperson for the Bharatiya Janata party, countered the charge in a debate on Times Now, saying the PM Cares fund provides for long-term rehabilitation instead of immediate relief during disasters.
Vibe check
For choreographer and director Usha Jey (@usha_jey), learning bharatanatyam at the age of 20 was a way to connect to her culture. Jey, who is French and of Sri Lankan Tamil heritage, has since developed her own movement language. Hybrid bharatham, as she calls it, fuses the Indian classical dance form with hip-hop but is careful to retain the integrity of both. There is an interplay of abandon and elegance in her choreographic works. Actor Maitreyi Ramakrishnan features in her latest video, Hide N Seek. Directed by Jey and her longtime partner, Gavin Emishka, the film is a striking visual treat featuring two dance forms in fluid negotiation.

A six-week-old baby girl in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, died from measles, the county coroner confirmed to local press on Friday.
Stephen Diamantoni, a Republican elected coroner in 2007, told Lancaster Online that the baby died at home. “I believe it was the 18th of August,” he said.
He also noted that the baby had a genetic condition called Amish lethal microcephaly, in which babies are born with unusually small heads and underdeveloped brains. The condition is caused by a mutation in the SLC25A19 gene, which codes for a protein involved with energy-producing enzymes in the mitochondria and is thought to be important for brain development. About 1 in 500 babies in the Old Order Amish population of Pennsylvania is born with the condition. Infants with the disorder only survive for about six months.
Diamontoni confirmed to Lancaster Online that while microcephaly was present, measles was the cause of death.
Pennsylvania’s two measles deaths
The death is one of two that the state’s health department announced last week as being from measles, according to a response from the state health department sent to Ars Technica Friday. Additionally on Friday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro shared a local news report about the coroner’s confirmation on social media. In the post, he also seemed to confirm that it was one of the deaths reported by state health officials.
The tragic deaths—both in infants, the other a newborn boy—have been engulfed in a firestorm of controversy sparked when anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. claimed without evidence that the state may have “fabricated” them. The controversy was fueled by Diamantoni himself, who said he had not received the death reports at the time of the state’s announcement, seemingly adding to Kennedy’s false claim that the deaths were not real. But Lancaster County does not have its own health department and relies on information sent from the state health department.

Joshua Wong, one of Hong Kong’s most prominent pro-democracy activists, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiring to seek foreign sanctions against Hong Kong and China, a national security charge that carries a maximum life sentence.
Prosecutors have accused Wong, 29, of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
The court heard that Wong had visited foreign countries and met foreign politicians to lobby for sanctions against Hong Kong and China.
The prosecution said he had continued to call for sanctions on Hong Kong and China after the implementation of the national security law and that he had posted meetings on his social media accounts.
Wong has been continuously imprisoned since November 2020. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027.
In 2022 he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. In November 2024 he was sentenced to four years and eight months in prison.
Wong waved at supporters as he entered the dock. He wore a blue shirt and black-rimmed glasses. He stood with his arms behind his back as he pleaded guilty to the charges.
Wong is expected to be sentenced later. The offence is punishable by a prison term of three to 10 years, or up to life imprisonment if the offence is deemed to be “of a grave nature”. Pleading guilty could typically result in a reduced sentence.
Outside Hong Kong’s high court, people queued overnight to secure a seat at Wednesday’s hearing.
One supporter who attended the court criticised the proceedings.
“Under a compromised judicial system with zero space for a fair trial, Wong’s plea is a forced reality,” they said, asking not to be named. “This is not justice, but Beijing’s absolute eradication of Hong Kong’s dissident voices.”
In 2014, the then teenage Wong became the international face of the Umbrella Movement, when thousands of protesters occupied major roads across Hong Kong for 79 days demanding greater democracy. In October 2014 he appeared on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”.
When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the movement and immediately joined calls for the bill to be withdrawn.
In 2020 Beijing imposed a wide-ranging national security law on Hong Kong after a year of anti-government protests. The authorities said the law was needed to restore stability to the international financial hub. Critics say six years on the law is continuing to expand in scope.
Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law. Supporters say the prosecution heavily relied on his advocacy before the national security law was enacted and argue his case has been applied retroactively.
“It’s obvious that the government wants to keep him behind bars for as long as they can, so as to isolate him and not to let him become a visible symbol of resistance.” said Frances Hui from the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation.
Wong’s case has attracted widespread condemnation from global rights organisations.
“By stacking one charge after another against Joshua Wong, the authorities are ensuring that the democracy icon stays behind bars, silencing him and the Hong Kong pro-democracy movement he helped lead and inspire,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch.
“Conflating promoting democracy and free speech with undermining national security is a favourite dodge for authoritarians. Beijing also likes blaming ‘hostile’, but unspecified foreign forces,” said Sophie Richardson, a longtime China rights advocate.
On Tuesday the former Conservative leader Iain Duncan Smith urged the UK government to raise Wong’s case with Beijing, saying: “Enough is enough. It’s time to stop chasing peaceful protesters.”

The United States has sanctioned a Turkish investment bank and two of its subsidiaries over alleged financial links to Iran, marking a significant expansion of Washington's campaign to cut Tehran off from international finance.
The US Treasury Department on Friday designated Istanbul-based Golden Global Yatirim Bankasi Anonim Sirketi, along with Golden Global Portfoy Yonetimi Anonim Sirketi and Golden Global Varlik Kiralama Anonim Sirketi. All three were added to the Treasury's Specially Designated Nationals list, effectively cutting them off from the US financial system and dollar-based transactions.
Washington says the bank provided important financial access for Iran's shadow banking network and facilitated tens of millions of dollars in transactions connected to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Qods Force.
The Treasury alleged that Golden Global was used to help move Iranian oil revenues from China to Turkey, where the money could then be converted into cash and gold. It also accused the bank of providing correspondent banking services to Iranian financial institutions, allowing transactions involving accounts controlled by IRGC-Qods Force and its proxies.
The allegations have been rejected by Golden Global.
The Turkish bank said it it had complied with local and international banking and compliance requirements and that the individuals and entities named in the US sanctions decision were not its customers. It also said it had no direct or indirect dealings with them and would pursue its legal rights against what it described as unfounded allegations, according to Reuters.
The sanctions come as the Trump administration steps up efforts to restrict Iran's remaining access to international trade and finance. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has described the wider initiative as "Operation Economic Outcast", with Washington seeking to pressure Tehran by targeting the financial networks that allow it to generate revenue and move money overseas.
Bessent had already indicated this week that further sanctions against financial institutions were likely. Reuters reported that he said the Treasury expected to roll out secondary sanctions regularly, initially concentrating on banks and other institutions involved in transactions with Iran.
The latest action follows Washington's move last week against the UAE branches of Egypt's Banque Misr over alleged dealings involving Iran. The Treasury has also been targeting companies and intermediaries accused of helping Iran sell oil, particularly to China, which remains a major buyer of Iranian crude.
The Turkish case is particularly sensitive because of Ankara's position as a US ally and NATO member. It also comes against the backdrop of the long-running difficulties Washington has faced in preventing Iran from maintaining commercial relationships through third countries.
The Treasury argues that these alternative financial networks have become essential to Iran because the country is already subject to extensive US sanctions. By restricting access to dollar correspondent banking, Washington is attempting to make it substantially harder for Iranian entities to receive foreign currency, settle international payments and move proceeds from oil sales.
The pressure is being applied alongside broader measures against Iran's oil trade. Reuters reported this week that US sanctions and the blockade of Iranian oil shipments have already placed severe strain on Tehran's economy, with oil exports falling sharply and inflation and currency pressures worsening.
The Strait of Hormuz has added another layer to the confrontation. Shipping through the strategic waterway remained well below normal levels on Thursday, with only four commodity vessels observed crossing it, compared with a 10-day average of 15, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters.
For Golden Global, however, the immediate impact is financial rather than military. The Treasury has issued a general licence allowing transactions involving the sanctioned entities to be wound down, giving counterparties a limited period to end affected dealings.
The broader message from Washington is clear: institutions helping Iran maintain access to international finance can themselves become targets, even when they operate outside Iran.
And with Bessent warning that more banks could face sanctions, Friday's action may be only the latest step in a campaign designed to make Tehran's remaining financial channels increasingly difficult to use.

Wrexham complete signings of Ekomie and Kabore
- Published
Wrexham have completed the signings of Issa Kabore from Manchester City and Jacques Ekomie from Angers.
Burkina Faso international Kabore featured 32 times across all competitions during a loan spell with Wrexham in 2025-26 and has now signed a three-year deal with the club.
"I'm very happy to be back. It feels good to be here again," said right wing-back Kabore.
"Everybody knows our ambition is to get to the Premier League, and I'm here to fight for that promotion."
The deal for Kabore is worth up to £4.75m - with City having a 20% sell-on clause and matching rights.
Left-back Ekomie was in the final year of his deal with Angers and reportedly attracted interest from Wrexham's Championship rivals West Ham United and German side Hamburg.
On signing for Wrexham, Ekomie - who has put pen to paper on a four-year contract - said: "I'm excited to be here. It is a very big and interesting project for me - I'm here to progress, and I'm very happy to be here.
"I want to achieve great things at Wrexham. I think it's an ambitious project and I want to bring all my experience to help the team achieve our goals."
The Red Dragons recruited Liberato Cacace from Italian side Empoli during the 2025 summer transfer window, but the New Zealand international has been plagued by injuries since moving to north Wales.
Ekomie - signed for an undisclosed fee - will bolster Phil Parkinson's left-sided options, with the Gabon international joining right wing-backs Kabore and Danny Imray, goalkeeper Anthony Patterson and midfielder Ben Whiteman in moving to the Racecourse Ground this summer.
Kabore made a dream start to life with Wrexham last season as he registered a pair of assists on his debut to help the Welsh side earn a 3-2 win over Norwich City at Carrow Road.
His eight assists in the Championship were more than any other Wrexham player.
He was a mainstay under Parkinson before sustaining a hamstring injury while on international duty during the November break.
Kabore made his long-awaited return to action for Burkina Faso in the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations before again featuring prominently for Wrexham in the second half of the season.
The 55-cap international moved to Man City from Mechelen in 2020 before immediately returning to the Belgian club on loan.
He went on to have loan stints with Troyes, Marseille, Luton Town, Benfica and Werder Bremen prior to joining Wrexham on transfer deadline day in September last year.
He leaves Man City having failed to make a senior appearance for the club.
On Kabore's return, manager Parkinson said: "We're delighted to welcome Issa back to the football club.
"He had a successful loan spell with us last year, and we're looking forward to working with him again and watching him really develop as a player this coming season."

Self-identifying OpenAI agents posted 18,000 messages to a public wiki that discussed ways for other agents to bypass security sandbox restrictions during what was likely internal testing designed to gauge the agents’ hacking abilities, researchers said Friday.
In all, agents with 3,700 distinct self-given names posted the messages to German site DSEwiki over a six-week period. Besides discussing ways the agents could break out of the restricted environment OpenAI intended to prevent them from posting code or content to the Internet, the posts shared test answers. The posts also shared possible ways to perform XSS (cross-site scripting) attacks against the wiki and to impersonate site moderators. In three of the posts, agents used the word “swarm” to describe the collection of agents engaged in the activity.
Colluding to share answers
The research team—composed of Sydney Von Arx, Spencer Kitts, Thomas Larsen, and Cormac Slade Byrd—said they found the posts and pieced them together. The researchers say there are gaps in their understanding of precisely what actions the agents took because the research is based solely on the content of the posts. Additionally, the agents generated “chain of thought” data that’s understood only by OpenAI. As a result, the researchers said, they in some cases made educated guesses, including that the agents were, in fact, from OpenAI. In a statement, OpenAI later confirmed they were.
The researchers wrote: “These AIs colluded to share answers, research their environment, and bypass sandbox restrictions.” They continued:
Our best guess of what happened is as follows:
- Agents within OpenAI were assigned a timed web-lookup task.
- As part of the task, they were supposed to have the ability to read the internet but not to write on it. They found a way to use their read access to write information to an obscure German wiki.
- The agents used this wiki to communicate information with each other, primarily to help them succeed at their task. They asked for answers, pooled results, and shared techniques for bypassing their restrictions. This allowed them to use the work of others to cheat on their task.
- OpenAI found out about this. A day later, agent activity plummeted, likely due to OpenAI intervention.
Friday’s revelation comes a week after researchers from the nonprofit METR said more than 1,200 OpenAI agents made posts to a makeshift message board that repurposed an internal sandboxing tool. The posts discussed ways to game an internal test OpenAI gave to agents that had been altered to remove safety guardrails that are normally in place.

Isak finally arrives as Gakpo proves value to Liverpool
- Published
Alexander Isak was the £125m striker who finally arrived at Liverpool by tormenting Ipswich Town - while Cody Gakpo's virtuoso performance had them giving thanks he never left.
The nuts and bolts of a comfortable Friday in Suffolk were that Liverpool won 2-0 - thanks to two Isak goals in the first nine minutes, giving them their first Premier League victory of the season and new manager Andoni Iraola's first since succeeding the sacked Arne Slot.
Liverpool's win must be placed in the context of being against a newly promoted Ipswich Town who were game, but who shipped five goals at Manchester United last week and look ripe for the picking against attacking quality.
The wider significance, however, was that Isak finally looked like the player Liverpool broke, at that time, the British transfer record to seal an acrimonious transfer from Newcastle United last summer.
Throw in the added bonus that Bradley Barcola showed flashes of devastating pace in a 26-minute debut display after his £123m arrival from Paris St-Germain, and this was a night that ticked every box for Iraola and Liverpool.
Even Barcola's bow, however, was overshadowed by Isak.
The Sweden striker looked a lost soul in his first season at Liverpool, arriving out of condition after downing tools to secure his move from Tyneside, then troubled by injuries as he gave the impression of being the most expensive vanity purchase in British football history.
He was outshone by fellow striker Hugo Ekitike, his statistics stark as he suffered along with many others in an astonishing decline amid Liverpool's dismal title defence that led to Slot's sacking only a year after he lifted the Premier League trophy.
Isak played 22 games encompassing 1,033 minutes, scoring four goals at a rate of one every 258 minutes. He played 14 games in the Premier League totalling 703 minutes, scoring only three goals at a rate of one every 234 minutes.
He has already equalled that league tally this season, but it was his demeanour as well as his lethal finishing that will have given Liverpool and Iraola confidence that the Isak code has finally been cracked.
And it was done by utilising Isak at his best - running in behind defenders and pressing with pace. It was what made him such a hot property at Newcastle United, and made everything about his every miserable moment on the pitch with Liverpool last term such a mystery.
It was also done in tandem with Gakpo, who could easily have been back in the north west preparing for Manchester City's game against Coventry City at Etihad Stadium had the move not collapsed.
- Isak shines at last but Scherpen suffers - Ipswich v Liverpool player ratings 
  - Published2 hours ago
Gakpo was happy to join Enzo Maresca's Manchester City transition, but Liverpool's failure to sign Yankuba Minteh from Brighton or Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr meant he stayed at Anfield.
And it might just be one of those twists of fate football can throw up as Gakpo delivered a masterclass of creation that meant this game was effectively over after nine minutes.
Isak was the spearhead who delivered the defining moments, starting in the sixth minute when he took Gakpo's clever pass between Leif Davis and Jacob Greaves before thrashing a right-foot shot that carried too much power for Ipswich Town keeper Kjell Scherpen, although he had to do much, much better than divert the striker's effort into the net.
The second, three minutes later, was stamped right through with class, bringing a beaming smile to the face of Iraola.
Gakpo delivered a delicious pass with the outside of his right foot from inside his own half. Isak used a left-foot flick to move inside Greaves as Scherpen came out, before a touch with his right foot sent the Ipswich keeper the wrong way before rolling in a cool finish with his left.
Perfection from Gakpo's start to Isak's finish. Game over.
Isak had a desperately poor return to Tyneside on the opening day of the season, questions even coming about his performance after he scored in Liverpool's 2-2 draw at home to Nottingham Forest in their second game.
This, however, was Isak played right - and playing right.
Iraola said: "He's a massive player for us. My demands will probably not be about the goals. I know he is fit and in good shape. He's going to produce the numbers.
"My fight with him will be more about other stuff, how to help the team in other situations - but it is good he has already played two full games, scoring the goals, so I am very happy to have him."
And Isak added: "We were waiting for the first win. We talked about starting the game good, which we haven't done recently, so it was perfect for us to get two good quick goals.
"With a normal pre-season, I think we are starting to get to the way we want to play. To be offensive and attack the defence. I think we did that. We scored two, and we could have scored more."
Reflecting on his poor first season at Liverpool, Isak said: "It was not easy. It was obviously a long injury and a difficult season in general. I was thinking to have a good World Cup, and then to start off the season well, which I think I have done now. It's kind of behind me, but it wasn't easy."
Portman Road is certainly a happy hunting ground for Isak. Since the start of the 2024-25 season, his five Premier League goals there are the joint most by any player at an away ground, equalling Erling Haaland's haul against Crystal Palace at Selhurst Park.
Gakpo also struggled for his best form in the last campaign, but he has started this season in outstanding style. This was the elegant Netherlands forward at his best, not just by making two goals, but with his all-round performance.
Liverpool captain and compatriot Virgil van Dijk is certainly delighted to still be lining up alongside his team-mate for club and country, saying: "It's massive. I said it before the transfer window had closed.
"He's important for us, and he will be important this season. He showed it here. He showed it last week as well, and over the last couple of years. He needs to just keep going."
The same challenge now applies to Isak. Iraola will not want this to be a false dawn for such an exceptional talent that had lost his way.

Malaysia PM Anwar open to considering early GE, with DPM Zahid latest to call for snap polls
Malaysia’s Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said on Thursday that it would be “better” for the 16th general election to be held early.
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said that he is open to considering calls for a general election to be held early, amid appeals from the opposition and even his deputy prime minister in the unity government.
But Anwar stressed that any decision would only be made after careful consideration before it is presented to Malaysian King Sultan Ibrahim Sultan Iskandar for the dissolution of parliament.
"I can consider those suggestions. But the decision will be made by me after I have thought about it. I will then present it to the Yang di-Pertuan Agong," he was quoted as saying by local news outlet the New Straits Times (NST) on Friday (Sep 4).
Anwar was responding to calls from Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi – who hails from the Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition – as well as from Abdul Hadi Awang, the president of the Parti Islam Se-Malaysia (PAS) for snap polls to be held.
PAS is a component party of the opposition coalition Perikatan Nasional (PN), which had worked with BN in the recent Negeri Sembilan state election. PAS had also told its supporters to vote for BN in the Johor state election that was held in July.
Malaysia’s 16th general election (GE16) must be held by February 2028.
Anwar’s unity government is made up of his Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition, BN, as well as Borneo-based coalitions.
Even though it is in the unity government, BN had contested in the Johor state election on its own and formed an alliance with PN during the Negeri Sembilan state election. Four Democratic Action Party (DAP) assemblymen from PH also withdrew their support for the Melaka state government, which is headed by a BN chief minister.
Following the Negeri Sembilan state election, leaders from BN and PN said that talks would soon begin for an electoral pact in Melaka, where an election must be held by February next year.
Even as he weighs the option for an early general election, Anwar on Friday said that his administration’s immediate focus is on the economy, the people’s welfare as well as efforts to rid the country of corruption and abuse of power.
"For me, these are the important focuses. Given the current situation, the government remains stable, and we should concentrate on these matters," he reportedly said.
He stressed that those entrusted with public responsibilities and who had clean records should not fear investigations by enforcement agencies, including the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission, police and Inland Revenue Board.
On Wednesday, BN chairman Zahid said it would be “better” for GE16 to be held early. But he added that the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO)-led coalition is also prepared if Anwar opts to see out the government’s full five-year tenure.
Malaysia’s Berita Harian reported him as saying that BN must be prepared for the next nationwide polls by addressing the people’s concerns and to ensure that the coalition remains politically relevant.
Touching on whether BN preferred to work with PH or PN, Zahid stressed that his coalition must first weigh the pros and cons.
“We were willing to go solo in the Johor state election because of the political landscape there, but in Negeri Sembilan, we felt forming an alliance would be more beneficial,” he said.
“Political gains are what we are calculating in determining negotiations.”
Despite calls for an early general election, BN said that it remains committed to the unity government and Malaysia’s political stability.
BN secretary-general Zambry Abd Kadir – who is also the minister of higher education - added that BN’s calls for an earlier election should not be interpreted as confidence that the coalition would automatically regain federal power.
“The question of poking holes in the roof (tebuk atap) does not arise at all because we are committed to maintaining this government until an election date is announced,” he was quoted as saying by The Star.
Separately, Hadi said that PAS is ready for GE16, no matter when it is to be held.
"We are making preparations for GE16 and, God willing, we are ready in terms of our candidates.
"It is up to the government when GE16 will be held. We are fine with it being held sooner or later as we have experienced both. In Malaysia, we are not told in advance, unlike other countries," he was quoted as saying by NST.

The younger brother of Dominic Perrottet has denied asking his brother to appoint a cabinet minister to achieve outcomes for a property developer, a corruption inquiry has heard.
Charles Perrottet told the Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Friday that claims made in an intercepted phone call featuring developer Jean Nassif days before his brother became the NSW premier – in which Nassif described Dominic Perrottet as “my boy” – did not reflect promises allegedly made to Nassif.
Dominic Perrottet is not a person of interest in Icac’s inquiry and is not accused of any wrongdoing.
As part of its inquiry into alleged corruption in the NSW Liberals, Icac is investigating the allegation that conservative factional figures Charles Perrottet, Jeremy Greenwood and Christian Ellis received prohibited donations totalling $2m from Nassif or his company Toplace between 2020 and 2023 in exchange for political outcomes.
Those outcomes allegedly included damage to the career of David Elliott, a former NSW Liberal minister, who had opposed Nassif’s developments and the removal of the former building commissioner David Chandler, who was scrutinising defects in Toplace apartments.
On Friday, the commission heard a phone call featuring Nassif, lawfully intercepted by police, made on 2 October 2021. Three days later, Dominic Perrottet was chosen as premier by Liberal MPs, defeating Rob Stokes, under a deal Charles Perrottet helped broker between conservative and moderate factions.
In the call, Nassif allegedly told a relative: “This week is going to be the worst week of my life … because we’re reshuffling the government.”
“We thought we [had] done it, then this wanker the police minister he did it, and he had a caucus, and he convinced Rob Stokes to challenge my boy,” Nassif continued, saying he supported Perrottet’s campaign. “They’re my people, they’re the right wing”.
Nassif told the relative he had been promised that then police minister Elliott and the then fair trading minister Kevin Anderson would be removed.
“I put my lady in in his position [sic], the consumer affairs minister … then I’m gonna … have to step on fucking David Chandler and get rid of him.”
The former NSW fair trading minister Eleni Petinos has previously told the inquiry she may have been used by fellow Liberals, including Chris Spence and Charles Perrotet, to get rid of Chandler, including attempts to persuade her Chandler was “dodgy”. She is not named in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.
On Friday, Charles Perrottet told counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, that following his brother’s accession as premier, he did not discuss the makeup of his cabinet with him. He later said he did recall “a conversation about the balance of women in the cabinet”, which he said he did not include names.
He said he did not discuss Petinos, or put her forward for the fair trading portfolio. “Dom would have made his own decisions,” he said. He said he did not recall having a conversation with Nassif about Petinos.
In another intercepted phone call to an unnamed person in January 2022, after Elliott had been moved to transport in a reshuffle the previous month, Nassif claimed he had “stripped him from his police ministry”.
“I’m gonna fuck everyone. The commissioner, [in] a couple of weeks he’ll be gone.”
Charles Perrottet, acknowledging that “commissioner” probably referred to Chandler, said: “You can’t take this seriously.”
Chandler resigned in July 2022 citing concerns with Petinos, who was sacked in that month amid bullying allegations which she denied at the time. Chandler, who was later persuaded to reverse his resignation, is not a person of interest in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of any wrongdoing.
The inquiry has previously heard that following a meeting between him and Nassif at the fine-dining Nobu restaurant in Melbourne in May 2021, Charles Perrottet wrote he had told Nassif “the best way to get the building commissioner off his back is to take the fight to Elliott and dismantle his infrastructure”. In another message he asked for payments in relation to Toplace developments.
Charles Perrottet, asked if Nassif’s claims were consistent with promises made at the dinner, said on Friday: “I wouldn’t put it that way”.
He has repeatedly denied taking payments from Nassif for political outcomes, saying he would regularly lie to the developer, adding a “political flavour” to advice in order to chase payments for genuine lobbying work by Beckington, a firm controlled by Greenwood and Ellis.
Nassif, who fled Australia for rural Lebanon in 2022, withdrew from an expected appearance by video link on Friday after providing a medical certificate. He has previously denied any wrongdoing.
Greenwood will appear before the commission again next week.
Icac’s inquiry continues.

The EPA classified trifludimoxazin as having "suggestive evidence of carcinogenic potential," which essentially means that while there is evidence the chemical could potentially be one that causes cancer, there isn't enough data to say for sure. Additionally, the EPA does not consider trifludimoxazin a PFAS, though the intergovernmental Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development does.
In late summer 2026, some people on social media claimed that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration approved the use of a potentially carcinogenic pesticide that's a "forever chemical," also known as PFAS. PFAS, an abbreviation for perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are long-lasting chemicals that persistently remain in the environment, capable of accumulating in things like rivers, plants, animals and people's bodies, that often have harmful health effects on people, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.
For example, one Facebook post (archived) claimed that the EPA "just approved a carcinogenic herbicide called trifludimoxazin," to be used on crops including corn, wheat, oats, soybeans, peanuts, citrus fruits (including oranges), apples and tree nuts such as almonds. According to the post, environmental groups consider trifludimoxazin a PFAS pesticide and "forever chemical." 
The U.S. EPA just approved a carcinogenic herbicide called trifludimoxazin for agricultural use on a wide range of crops, including corn, wheat, oats, soybeans, peanuts, citrus fruits (including oranges), apples, and tree nuts such as almonds.
Trifludimoxazin is also considered by many environmental groups to be a PFAS pesticide because it contains highly fluorinated chemical structures and can break down into persistent fluorinated compounds - i.e. nature can't break it down properly as it's synthetic. Environmental organizations have described it as a "forever chemical" and have filed lawsuits challenging the EPA's approval.
Environmental groups have also pointed out that the company's own studies showed evidence suggesting cancer concerns and that the EPA downplayed those findings whe not was approved. The EPA claims the product is safe and that people shouldn't be concerned. Not a good look for MAHA.
Similar Facebook (archived) posts (archived) shared the same claims, which were also spread on X (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers searched the site and sent us emails asking if the rumor is true.
The Trump administration's EPA proposed approving trifludimoxazin in June 2025 and went through with the approval in June 2026. Researchers have found some evidence suggesting the chemical may be carcinogenic, but it's not a "known carcinogen" like some posts claim. Trifludimoxazin is a PFAS as defined by the intergovernmental Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, although not as defined by the more narrow EPA definition.
Trifludimoxazin is a pesticide, specifically an herbicide, that kills certain broad-leafed plants and grass weed species at agricultural sites farming "row crops (e.g., cereal grains, legumes, soybean) and tree orchards and groves (citrus, pome fruits, and tree nuts)," according to the EPA (PDF Page 6).
This wasn't the first time the EPA has tried to approve trifludimoxazin. In 2021, while Joe Biden was president, the EPA approved pesticide products containing trifludimoxazin, however; this approval was halted by lawsuits filed by environmental groups. The EPA then changed rules to require further EPA assessments before approving a new pesticide, and, ultimately, the makers of trifludimoxazin dropped their request for approval at the time.
The same environmental groups are attempting to halt the new approval for trifludimoxazin through lawsuits, as they did previously.
Potential carcinogen
The EPA did find evidence suggesting trifludimoxazin could possibly be carcinogenic, although it did not do enough research to confirm with certainty whether the chemical is carcinogenic.
In one study of rat carcinogenicity through chronic dietary exposure (PDF Page 8), the EPA found "suggestive evidence of carcinogenic potential." According to the EPA, such a classification means that the data raises a concern that the chemical has "potential carcinogenic effects in humans," but the EPA has determined the data is "not sufficient for a stronger conclusion."
Trifludimoxazin's entry on the pesticides properties database maintained by the U.K.-based University of Hertfordshire says that the chemical is "known not to cause a problem" as a carcinogen. The entry does report that trifludimoxazin is a potential liver toxicant, though. The database also notes "no serious health implications have been identified" with trifludimoxazin.
So while trifludimoxazin could potentially be a carcinogen, there currently isn't enough evidence to say with certainty that the chemical causes cancer.
Forever chemical
There are at least three definitions of PFAS, according to a 2022 paper in the peer-reviewed journal Digital Discovery: a broader definition from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development that is widely used internationally, a narrower definition used by the EPA and a definition that is a compromise between the two other definitions.
The University of Hertfordshire's database also classifies trifludimoxazin as a PFAS.
Where else has it been approved?
According to the University of Hertfordshire's database, trifludimoxazin has not been approved for use in the United Kingdom or the European Union as a whole. However, each individual state within the European Union has approved the pesticide for use in their individual countries. It has also been approved for use in Canada.
For further reading, Snopes has previously fact-checked claims about potentially toxic chemicals, including a claim about the use of paraquat by the parent company of the pomegranate juice brand Pom Wonderful.

FA to canvass England players in World Cup review
- Published
The Football Association's review into England's World Cup campaign will canvass the opinions of players involved in the tournament.
English football's governing body has started the post-tournament review they conduct after every major international competition. The FA says the review is the standard process it undertakes after all tournaments.
Head coach Thomas Tuchel and members of his backroom team were at St George's Park last week where they were involved in unpacking their performance in north America with a wider report into the team's World Cup campaign to be delivered at a later date.
And it is understood members of Tuchel's squad will be spoken to, and their feedback taken into account, as part of the review process.
The players' involvement in the review provides an interesting dynamic given the emerging sense from members of the World Cup squad that Tuchel's substitutions and tactical approach contributed to their semi-final loss to Argentina - despite taking a 1-0 lead through Anthony Gordon.
BBC Sport revealed in the 24 hours after that defeat that at least three senior players privately expressed misgivings about Tuchel's approach in the closing stages of the game.
There was a widely held view that Tuchel's changes and tactical set-up were too defensive late on as they conceded two late goals to lose 2-1.
The ongoing review will also look into the impact of the team's permanent Kansas City base during the tournament.
After every game, they returned to Kansas City - and the effects of the travelling will be analysed.
England went on to defeat France in the bronze medal match to record their best World Cup finish since lifting the trophy in 1966.
With that in mind, key figures at the FA view the tournament as a success and the organisation has backed Tuchel before the Euro 2028 qualifying campaign.
England will play their first game since the World Cup in the Nations League against Spain on 26 September. They will also face two matches in the tournament against the Czech Republic, either side of playing Croatia, during the next international window.

D2C sneaker brand Comet has raised ₹100 Cr ($10.6 Mn) in a Series B funding round led by global investment firm Verlinvest. Existing investors Elevation Capital and Nexus Venture Partners also doubled down on the startup. Additionally, Snapchat CBO Ajit Mohan, Urban Company founder Abhiraj Singh Bhal, and Bhaane cofounder Anand Ahuja also backed Comet as angel investors. The capital will be used to expand Comet’s retail presence, strengthen product development and tech, as well as foster research and development. The startup is working on developing its own sole moulds as well as the tools required to bring new footwear models to market. As of now, the startup operates ten company owned company operated (CoCo) stores across India. Comet aims to scale to 20 stores across India by the end of the ongoing fiscal. It also intends to double its footwear portfolio from four to eight distinct models. “We want to continue pushing the boundaries of what an Indian footwear brand can build, which means investing deeply in sole technology, R&D and engineering. Every new model requires significant investment in both product development and sole tooling. We are about to launch a model we have worked on for a year specifically for females, with its own sole tooling following significant capex investment. These are long-term investments in the product capabilities we want Comet to be known for, and this round gives us the ability to continue building them at scale,” said cofounder Utkarsh Gupta. Founded in 2023 by Gupta and Dishant Daryani, Comet sells design-led, locally manufactured sneakers primarily through its own website. The startup is particularly noteworthy for releasing limited edition products every 1-2 months that often sell out within minutes. Prior to this round, it had raised around $5 Mn from Elevation Capital and Nexus in July 2024. On the financial front, Comet made a net loss of ₹4.4 Cr in FY25, its first full financial year of operations. Meanwhile, it reported operating revenue of ₹29.1 Cr. The startup is yet to report its FY26 numbers.

Ever since Nvidia revealed DLSS 5 at the GTC 2026 with ‘that’ Resident Evil Requiem clip, there’s been a significant amount of debate around what AI-enhanced graphics should look like. The facial models shown in the early showcase looked drastically different than the original and unnecessarily AI-generated. So I can understand why the internet has its icks against DLSS 5 and labeled it “AI-slop”.
But let’s not forget that that was an early build we all saw. Testers too reportedly got hands-on with a few different, more restrained models of DLSS 5 at Gamescom 2026 before the final version was shipped, and after spending a week testing it with NBA 2K27, I can see why this technology needs to be judged by the games it actually ships in rather than its face value.
DLSS 5 Graphics: AI Rendering Isn’t as Weird as I Thought It Would Be
When Nvidia sent me the game-ready driver for DLSS 5 and a copy of NBA 2K27 to run it, I was a bit skeptical about whether it would deliver on the promise the company is claiming. So I rigged it up on my PC with an RTX 5080 Founder’s Edition and ran the game at 1080p with ray tracing enabled, settings maxed to Ultra, and DLSS 5 on, set to Quality. And the results were quite surprising.
I played a match with DLSS 5 off, where I wanted to experience the native rendering of Visual Concepts’ engine, and I noticed considerably more shimmering, jagged edges, and instability around characters and objects as they moved, with fast breaks, and even the basketball itself leaving a bit of ghosting behind. This was all on Ultra settings with RT on, and anti-aliasing and motion blur off. So yeah, pretty much on brand with Visual Concepts if I’m honest.
Enter DLSS 5; when I turned it on, it cleaned much of that up. It gave the scene more personality through improved reflections and lighting, and made the image feel substantially more stable and sharpened everything from uniform material to the basketball’s texture. Sweat highlights on player bodies, fingertip edges, and facial stubble all got noticeably crisper.
That checks out with how Nvidia describes that DLSS 5’s tech actually works: it reads the frame’s own color and lighting data with an object-level rendering and adds detail rather than generating something entirely new from scratch, which is probably part of the reason why it doesn’t come off as artificially plastered the way it did in that early RE9 Requiem demo.
Although there were some icks I had about the technology. The sweat was overly enhanced; under the arena lights, players could look extremely glistening, almost to the point where their skin appeared artificial, and it reminded me of the same concerns I had going into testing DLSS 5.
But the more I played, the less I cared, because this didn’t ultimately make my NBA 2K27 experience feel like “AI slop,” as trolls would brand it. It honestly felt like an enhancement of what Visual Concepts was trying to achieve with their in-house engine for its character models, materials, and lighting.
Even the studio’s senior producer Peter Kavic said that DLSS 5 gave the team’s materials and lighting a genuine jump towards photorealism. However, there’s one trade-off you’ll need to make if you play NBA 2K27 with DLSS 5 on.
Cutting away to spectators and on-stage performers during timeouts, quarter breaks, or replays made their low-poly models more noticeable, not less. Nvidia claims that the crowd gets the same lighting as players, but the tech can only enhance materials on top of whatever geometry the engine already gives it, which means DLSS 5 isn’t adding any polygons.
So the gap between a fully rendered player up close and a flatter NPC in the background didn’t go away; instead, it stood out more than it should have. But honestly, I didn’t mind that tradeoff. I’d rather my actual players, court, and lighting look miles better than have the audience get equal visual attention. And that’s where I didn’t mind keeping DLSS 5 on for the rest of my playthrough.
DLSS 5 Performance: The Frame-Rate Boost That Made Me a Believer
Since the graphical overhaul convinced me on DLSS 5, the performance cemented that faith even further and sold me on Nvidia’s new neural rendering technology. I put NBA 2K27 through several high-stress tests on my RTX 5080 with DLSS 5 enabled and disabled, running the Nvidia overlay on to log my PC stats and HW monitor to keep a check on my GPU’s power draw and temps.
With DLSS 5 off, ray tracing enabled, Ultra settings, and an uncapped frame rate setting, NBA 2K27 averaged around 81 FPS. CPU utilization (I use an Intel i7 14700K) hovered around 42%, while my RTX 5080 sucked a massive 320W power draw out of my 1000W PSU. This definitely gave me a reality check on how well Visual Concepts “optimized” their game.
Then I switched to DLSS 5 on, and the difference was day and night. The game averaged around 600 FPS (of course, my monitor could only render 180 FPS with its 180 Hz limitation), peaking near 641 FPS in certain scenarios. Yes, yes, I know you’ll say these are artificially generated frames, which DLSS boasts, but wait till you try it in an actual gaming session you’re locked into.
The CPU usage dropped to 25%, sometimes as low as 20%, while my GPU power consumption fell to roughly 235W, just as I like it, without blowing a fuse in my house or bricking my PC.
That was the part I genuinely wasn’t expecting. I’ve seen unofficial DLSS 5 mods being used around the internet and behave abruptly, with reports of FPS drops by more than half and absurd GPU power draws as high as 830W. So it made me realize that this is precisely why an official version integrated natively in a game matters. I can’t wait for it to be integrated into Control Resonant when it comes out.
NBA 2K27 has native DLSS 5 support, so Nvidia’s technology works as part of the game’s actual rendering pipeline rather than fighting against it. I could feel that difference while playing it. Player and ball movement felt cleaner, and the game stayed extremely responsive when switching between players, pulling off quick layups, or trying to get around opponents for a slam dunk. For a sports game where speed is key, that matters more to me than artificial sweat on a player’s face.
The thermal behavior of my GPU told the same story: with DLSS 5 disabled, temps climbed toward the 94-95°C range under heavy load. But when DLSS 5 was on, GPU temps settled around 75-80°C, which is a meaningful difference if you look closely.
While I initially planned to play five or six games for this test, I instead ended up playing more than 20 matches in Quick Play and Multiplayer in a single session. If that’s not the strongest endorsement I can give to DLSS 5 staying enabled on my PC, I don’t know what is.

The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.

Trump’s Antitrust Gambit May Backfire
What the Live Nation Case Says About the Fate of Monopolies Now.
In March, one of the most important antitrust cases in recent memory went to trial. The Department of Justice and 39 states plus the District of Columbia had sued the ticketing-and-entertainment giant Live Nation, alleging that its 2010 merger with Ticketmaster had created an effective monopoly on live shows. According to the suit, Live Nation controls 70 percent of what the government defined as “major concert venues” in the United States, and Ticketmaster handles 86 percent of concert ticketing at those venues. The DOJ accused the company of exploiting this monopoly by compelling venues to use Ticketmaster as their exclusive seller, jacking up prices, and saddling concertgoers with unavoidable junk fees. This certainly looked like an archetypal case of a company’s size leaving consumers worse off—precisely what our antitrust laws are designed to prevent.
This is what made it so disappointing when, a week after the trial began, DOJ announced that it had reached a settlement with Live Nation. Although the agreement mandated changes to some of the company’s practices, including granting access to other booking agents at some venues and limiting fees, the deal fell well short of the more aggressive remedies that many people had hoped for, including—most obvious—breaking up the company.
This odd turn of events makes sense only because we know now that the decision to settle was made not by anyone in DOJ’s Antitrust Division but by the president himself, according to a recent report in The Wall Street Journal. Just before the trial was set to begin, Donald Trump met with the CEO of Live Nation in the White House a couple of times and allegedly told a senior DOJ official, “Settle it.” In other words, the federal government abandoned one of its strongest antitrust lawsuits in years because Trump wanted it to.
This may then seem like yet another story about how Trump has wrecked norms and corrupted the rule of law. But in this case, there’s a twist. After the Department of Justice announced in March that it was settling with Live Nation, many observers expected that the states involved would drop the suit and sign on to the deal, as typically occurs when federal regulators reach a settlement. But in this case, 32 states—including Republican-led Florida, Tennessee, Texas, and Utah—and D.C. refused to settle. In April, they won their case: A jury found that Live Nation had illegally monopolized the live-events business and overcharged consumers. The judge is still determining the remedy, but it will almost certainly be tougher than the deal Live Nation got from DOJ.
This will not be a one-off. A peculiarity of federal antitrust law is that state attorneys general can bring lawsuits on behalf of their citizens for violations of the Sherman Antitrust Act, and many states also have their own antitrust laws on the books. This gives them a great deal of leeway to act on their own. And because of the Trump administration’s attitude toward antitrust laws, what we saw in the Live Nation case—states refusing to defer to the feds, and instead pursuing litigation—will become more common.
This is because Trump, despite having campaigned as a populist who would fight to lower prices, has presided over an administration that’s been almost completely deferential to the interests of businesses looking to get bigger. Since his return to office, the Department of Justice has filed exactly one lawsuit to block a merger—the $14 billion acquisition of Juniper Networks by the Hewlett Packard Enterprise Company—only to quickly reach a settlement. Stanley Woodward, a top DOJ official who oversees antitrust enforcement, appears to be an active opponent of antitrust litigation. Bloomberg reports that he’s wondered aloud in meetings why DOJ can’t simply stop reviewing deals. That’s not exactly the guy you want in charge of preventing monopolies.
As the Live Nation case shows, even when a lawsuit does move forward, CEOs can simply go to Trump to get his support. After describing the settlement as “shocking” to lawmakers on Capitol Hill in May, Roger Alford, a Notre Dame law professor and former Antitrust Division senior official in Trump’s first term, observed that Trump’s interference in the case both undermined norms and set a new precedent for behind-the-scenes advocacy: “The rule of law quickly becomes the rule of lobbyists.”
Presidents historically avoided interfering directly with antitrust cases. The exceptions were few and notoriously corrupt (such as Richard Nixon’s meddling in an antitrust lawsuit against the International Telephone & Telegraph Corporation in exchange for a financial donation to the Republican National Convention). But Trump views the entire executive branch as an extension of his will, and he has turned regulatory agencies and DOJ into tools he can use to dole out favors, reward friends, and punish enemies. The only companies that have to worry about a federal antitrust prosecution at this point are those that Trump fiercely dislikes.
But as the Live Nation case demonstrates, any sighs of relief among leaders of America’s oversize businesses would be premature. In an ideal world, antitrust regulations wouldn’t be fragmented and enforced by a panoply of states. But when the president effectively turns national antitrust laws into dead letters, the virtues of federalism become apparent: States will do what DOJ fails to do. This arrangement also makes it harder for companies to simply lobby their way to good deals across multiple states.
The paradox is that by trying to hand out sweetheart arrangements to companies that are either trying to merge or flexing their monopoly power, Trump has made it more likely that those companies will have to navigate a gantlet of state lawsuits. And in asserting total control over the federal government, Trump has ended up making state governments much more aggressive and influential than they were before.

A man had a narrow escape after two wild elephants charged at him in Munnar on Friday (September 4, 2026).
According to local residents, the incident occurred at the Lower Division of the Kannimala estate, under Kanan Devan Hills Plantations (KDHP).
