Former WA and Victorian MP Peter Katsambanis dies, aged 60
Former MP Peter Katsambanis has been remembered as one of the Liberal Party's "fiercest and finest" warriors following his death, aged 60.
Mr Katsambanis served in the parliaments of Western Australia and Victoria, and was a prominent Greek Australian.
His wife Karalee Katsambanis said his family was "devastated" by his death.
"He was a great man: loved, adored, treasured and respected by so many people," she wrote in a tribute on social media.
"As his wife, I've lost my soulmate and love of my life and I thank everyone for all their support."
She also thanked the heart transplant team at The Alfred hospital who had been caring for him.
Mr Katsambanis served in the WA parliament from 2013 to 2021, first in the Legislative Council and then in the Legislative Assembly as the member for Hillarys.
The seat had been a Liberal heartland before Mr Katsambanis was defeated by Caitlin Collins in Labor's landslide victory in the 2021 state election.
He had held the positions of opposition spokesperson for police, road safety, justice and industrial relations.
He was also a member of the Victorian parliament, from 1996 to 2002.
Liberals mourn loss
The Liberal Party of WA's state director Simon Morgan said Mr Katsambanis would be sorely missed.
"Peter Katsambanis was the fiercest and finest of warriors for the Liberal cause as a student, a trusted adviser and as a member of parliament in both Victoria and Western Australia," Mr Morgan said.
"Our party is poorer for his loss and we extend our heartfelt sympathies to Karalee and to all of Peter's children at this sad time."
WA Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas said Mr Katsambanis made an incredible contribution to the Liberal Party and to public life in two states.
"Service always came first for Peter, he was such a committed representative and he occupies a rare place in Australian politics, having served in the Victorian parliament and in both houses of the parliament of Western Australia," Mr Zempilas said.
"He will be greatly missed by his friends and former colleagues and we extend our very sincere condolences to Karalee and all the family."
Mr Zempilas also acknowledged his "significant contribution" to the Greek Australian community.
Mr Katsambanis served as president of the World Hellenic Inter-Parliamentary Association from 2017 to 2021.
He was also a vice-president of the Hellenic Community of Western Australia.
His family will provided details in the coming days for his funeral, which will be held in Melbourne.

Thank you for joining us for our continuing coverage of the aftermath of Wednesday’s catastrophic flash floods in the Himalayan mountains near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Poor weather has hampered aerial rescue operations in Nepal as the search for thousands of people missing enters its fourth day.
Nepal’s finance minister says his country will need up to $5bn to rebuild after the floods, believed to have been caused by a melting glacier high up in the mountains that set off a deadly cascade of water into the valleys below.
Finance minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters today those figures are “just an estimate” and that “loss and damage is being assessed”.
Here’s a summary of what we know so far:
Nearly 3,000 people are missing. Nepal’s disaster agency on Saturday said 2,426 people were missing on its side of the border, while China’s Xinhua news agency reports the total number of missing in Tibet is now 554.
The death toll in Nepal has now risen to 626, while China’s Xinhua news agency earlier today reported seven people confirmed dead in Tibet.
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far but at least 93,000 people are estimated to have been affected by the disaster, according to the Red Cross.
At least 777 foreigners are missing, with Nepal’s disaster agency on Friday reporting 517 foreigners unaccounted for – which could include tourists and foreign workers – and Chinese officials putting the number of foreigners missing at 260.
India said it is increasing surveillance of glaciers and glacial lakes in its Himalayan regions bordering Nepal and China.
The deadly floods on the Nepal-Tibet border were believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse that was detected as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event by geologists. You can read this explainer to find out more about how a collapsing glacier can generate a powerful flood, and whether the climate crisis is contributing to the risk.
Madan Kaushik, state disaster management minister in India’s Himalayan state of Uttarakhand, said: “Since we share a border with Nepal, as a neighbour, and also have a similar geographic situation … we have asked our department to monitor all the glaciers and known glacial lakes in the region.”
Uttarakhand is one of the most ecologically sensitive regions of India, with 1,266 glacial lakes. As glaciers melt, water can accumulate in lakes held back by natural barriers. If those barriers fail, vast volumes of water can be released suddenly, triggering devastating floods.
“We have asked our teams to be vigilant and monitor if a similar situation is emerging anywhere in the state,” Kaushik told AFP.
‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal
The Guardian’s south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen and journalist Gaurav Pokharel report from the Nepalese town of Bidur, where rescue efforts are being coordinated. They spoke to survivors mourning loved ones and confronting the loss of their homes and livelihoods after devastating floods swept through their communities.
Among those caught in the floods was Sangke Dolma Tamang, who described the moment she watched her husband being swept away and returned to find her home and village destroyed:
Sangke Dolma Tamang, 61, had been cheerily cooking snacks in her village of Mailung in the Rasuwa district when the floods came without warning. The whole family ran uphill for safety, but as she grabbed for her husband, he slipped from her grip and was washed into the dark, fast-moving waters.
“Others tried to pull him to safety, but the flood swept him away,” she said, tears rolling down her weathered cheeks. There was, she said, nothing left of her village now. She had spent a night sheltering on higher ground, until an army helicopter arrived and brought to her safety at the barracks. Her son too was missing since the disaster, and she waited anxiously for any news.
“Now I have nothing left to live for,” said Tamang. “The whole house is gone. We couldn’t salvage anything.”
Nepal’s government has appealed for financial help as it faces the daunting task of recovering from the devastating flash floods and braces for the possibility of more flooding.
Entire communities have been swept away, leaving families homeless or sheltering in temporary facilities.
“Multiple bridges have been washed away and major roads disrupted, leaving some of the worst-affected communities extremely difficult to reach,” the Red Cross says.
At least 18 schools have been destroyed and another 20 damaged, leaving about 10,000 school-age children affected, according to the UN Children’s Fund.
The disaster comes just ahead of the anniversary of last year’s 8-9 September mass anti-corruption protests that toppled the government.
Nepal is now led by prime minister Balendra Shah, a 36-year-old rapper turned politician widely known as “Balen”. The former Kathmandu mayor swept March elections on a wave of euphoria calling for political change.
The risk of a lake formed after the glacier collapse bursting near the China-Nepal border where the devastating flood occurred earlier this week has decreased, Chinese authorities said today, as its size appears to have shrunk.
Satellite images from Thursday this morning suggest water in the lake – straddling the China-Nepal border at the confluence of two rivers – has been slowly flowing through, decreasing the reservoir gradually, state broadcaster CCTV reported, citing the water resources ministry.
The ministry said satellite imagery of the surface area of the lake at Purepu Tsangpo river showed it was 99,000 sq metres in size this morning – around the size of 14 football fields combined – having shrunk by 21,000 sq metres compared with images from Thursday.
Experts and authorities have warned of the extremely high risk of secondary disasters in the valley, especially from the lake that was formed by glacier debris, potentially endangering rescue operations downstream.
State-owned engineering and rescue enterprise China Anneng, which has been monitoring the lake since Thursday, dispatched a 15-member team on Friday with reconnaissance drones, portable satellite stations and mobile surveillance cameras to gather more data about the lake.
An overflow from the lake on Friday temporarily halted rescue work before further assessment deemed the risks manageable.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Chimpanzees used for vaccine research get health checks as part of long-term care
Chimpanzees once used in hepatitis B vaccine experiments are getting health checks at their new home in Liberia
ABUJA, Nigeria -- A group of chimpanzees that were once used for hepatitis B vaccine experiments in laboratories have received health checks at their new home in Liberia, in hopes of giving them a second chance at a normal life.
The West African chimpanzees received checks ranging from teeth cleaning to X-rays and pedicure at the Humane World for Animals’ Second Chance Chimpanzee Refuge in central Liberia, Liliana Pacheco Ricote, director of the sanctuary, told The Associated Press.
More than 400 of the chimpanzees had been used by American researchers in Liberia in the hepatitis B vaccine experiments from the 1970s until early 2000s, Ricote said, many of them captured in the wild as infants.
Liberia has the second-highest number of chimpanzees in West Africa, after Guinea. The West African chimpanzees are classified as critically endangered species because of their rapidly declining numbers.
“They were used in very invasive research … (and) went through a lot of experiments and pain,” Ricote said.
Humane World for Animals said that in 2015, it assumed permanent responsibility for 60 of the chimpanzees that were remaining at the end of the research program. The chimps now mostly live at the sanctuary on a series of mangrove forest-covered islands.
The checks carried out under anesthetic gave the chimpanzees head-to-toe exams to assess their long-term health, detect any early signs of disease and tailor care plans for individuals as they age, Humane World for Animals said in a statement to the AP.
The tests included dental examination, the heart, lungs and nervous system as well as blood. They get booster vaccinations and fingernail trims, it said, adding that plans are in place to carry out the checks on the remaining ones.
“The health checks are a vital part of caring for these chimpanzees who have been through so much,” said Belen Perez Hernando, the sanctuary’s veterinarian.
The extent of the impact of the experiments on the chimps, whose average age is 30 to 35, is unclear, as findings from the assessments are yet to be concluded. However, “for those who were under experiments, you could still feel the hurt and the pain that they went through,” Ricote said.
“Seeing how much they hurt about what we’ve done, it gives me a lot of pleasure … to give them this second chance to live with dignity the life that they deserve,” she added.

A woman has lived with a pig kidney for more than nine months without needing dialysis, a record-setting achievement.
The woman underwent the operation at Massachusetts General Hospital on November 22 last year. As of Thursday, the kidney has been functioning for 285 days, according to Cambridge, Massachusetts-based eGenesis, the biotech company that used Crispr gene editing to make the organ fit for human transplantation. Previously, the record for a person living with a transplanted pig kidney was 271 days, set by Tim Andrews.
Most people in need of a kidney transplant wait three to five years on average to receive one, though it can take longer depending on blood type and other factors. While they wait, patients often need dialysis, in which a person’s blood vessels are hooked up to a machine that removes excess fluid and waste from the bloodstream. Dialysis typically requires four-hour sessions three times a week and can damage blood vessels over time, making the procedure hard on the body.
Pig kidneys could offer an alternative until a human organ is available. Pig organs are similar in size and function to human organs and are being investigated as a way to ease the shortage of human donor organs. To make them more suitable for humans, scientists are genetically editing them to prevent immediate rejection and reduce the risk of pig viruses being passed on to transplant patients.
Patients' health gets worse the longer they're on dialysis, “and their odds of getting a human transplant aren't rising fast enough to meet their declining health,” says Mike Curtis, CEO of eGenesis. The company used Crispr to remove certain pig genes that could cause an immune response and add a handful of human genes.
“What we saw with Mr. Andrews was a radical improvement in his overall health while he was on the pig kidney versus if he had stayed on chronic dialysis,” Curtis says.
The woman who has crossed the nine-month mark is the fifth person to receive an eGenesis kidney through a special regulatory pathway known as expanded access. The Food and Drug Administration allows patients with serious or life-threatening conditions to gain access to experimental treatments when there are no good alternatives.
Andrews’ case shows that pig kidneys may provide a temporary solution. He received a pig kidney in January 2025 and had it removed in October last year after a period of decreasing kidney function. He returned to dialysis but received a human kidney transplant in January this year. A second person has also successfully received a human transplant after having a pig kidney for eight months, according to eGenesis.
Curtis says the company is learning more with each transplant. In a paper published on Thursday in The Lancet medical journal, the surgical team that performed the transplants details Andrews’ experience. They determined that Andrews’ pig kidney eventually failed due to thrombotic microangiopathy, which means tiny blood clots formed in the transplanted organ.
The team is using that information to adjust the immunosuppressant medications that pig kidney recipients receive and how frequently they need to take those drugs. People who receive human organ transplants also need to take immunosuppressive drugs to prevent their body from rejecting the transplanted organ. Organ rejection can happen at any time following a transplant, ranging from minutes after the surgery to many years later.
Kidneys are the most-needed organ, with more than 95,000 people waiting to receive one in the US. But due to a shortage of donor organs, fewer than 28,000 kidney transplants were performed in the US in 2025.
The FDA has given eGenesis the green light to conduct a more formal trial in up to 33 patients with kidney failure who are between 50 and 70 years old and on the wait list for a human kidney. That trial will not happen until 2027, but eGenesis plans to perform additional transplants under the expanded access pathway in the meantime. Their next goal is to get a transplanted pig kidney to function for a year.

Nepal rescuers try to reach dozens trapped in tunnel after two found alive
- Published
Rescuers in Nepal are stepping up efforts to find scores of workers believed to be trapped in tunnels, nine days after the devastating flash floods which hit the area on the border with Tibet in China.
Hopes have risen after two people were pulled out alive on Friday. The body of a third person was also found in one of the tunnels used to supply hydropower stations.
The massive flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through a Himalayan valley last Wednesday, wiping out entire villages.
There are now 1,311 confirmed dead and 5,330 still missing in Nepal and Tibet. Hundreds of foreign citizens are believed to be among those missing, from at least 34 countries.
The full impact of the flood in Tibet is unclear. China has released information through state media outlets showing the devastation around the border, but has given few details about the victims or the impact on local villagers.
In Nepal, however, rescue operations are taking place at seven hydropower tunnels in which more than 150 people are feared trapped - as well as in 19 other areas.
In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices at the Trishuli 3A hydropower site.
According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay".
Crews clambered in to find Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan - both had injuries on their hands and legs, "possibly" from crawling through the tunnel. Both were airlifted to the Army Hospital in the capital, Kathmandu.
Maharjan, who was rescued second, is in a critical condition, the prime minister's office said. Shah was also undergoing medical tests.
The body of a third person was found in the same tunnel later. A local official said it was swollen and could not be immediately identified.
Officials believe another 39 people are in the Trishuli 3A tunnel, although it is not clear if all are alive.
Col Jhabindra Reshmi said that his teams had rescued more than 400 Nepali nationals and 270 foreign citizens following the flash flooding on 26 August.
He has said mud and rocks have made entering tunnels difficult and rescuers were having to dig access holes to get underground.
Engineers have been pumping air into the tunnels.
Last week's floodwaters washed away a lot of heavy machinery, making it harder for rescuers to unblock tunnels, says a representative for Nepalese power companies.
Uttam Bhlon Lama, vice president at Independent Power Producers of Nepal, told the BBC's Newsday programme that the rescue of the two men on Friday would "motivate the rescuers to do more".
"The flood level is still very high," Lama added.
Nepalese authorities have warned that rainfall may cause additional flooding in the region.
At least 1,287 people are known to have died in Nepal, with 5,083 still missing.
On the Tibetan side, the death toll reported by Chinese media on Friday was 31, with 531 people unaccounted for.
Emergency teams in Tibet appear to be focusing on helping the living rather than holding out hope for more survivors.
Scientists are still studying the exact cause, but it is believed to have been caused by a glacial collapse and climate change may have been a factor.
Moments after the seismic event, which was initially thought to have been an earthquake, a massive wall of water and debris crashed downstream, taking buildings, roads and vehicles with it.
Experts from the Asian Mountain Academic Alliance, the Stimson Centre and China's Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment said there was evidence of growing instability around the glacier in the days before the collapse and better early-warning systems could have saved lives.

SaaS startup Meritto’s parent NoPaperForms has filed its updated draft red herring prospectus (UDRHP) with Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) for its initial public issue (IPO). The startup’s proposed public offering will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth ₹375 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) component of up to 3.8 Cr equity shares. As reported earlier, only investor Info Edge will participate in the OFS. As per the UDRHP, the venture capital giant, via Startup Investments (Holding) Ltd, will offload 3.8 Cr shares. Around ₹148 Cr of the fresh proceeds will be utilised to bolster its tech stack and cloud infrastructure, while ₹96 Cr will be deployed for customer acquisition and retention. A chunk of the capital will also be used for general corporate purposes and fueling inorganic growth via acquisitions. This nearly a year after the enterprise tech startup first filed its DRHP with the market regulator via the confidential route in November 2025. It then received SEBI’s nod to float its IPO in March this year. Founded in 2017 by Naveen Goyal and Suraj Sapra, NoPaperForms offers two products: Meritto and Collexo. The former offers SaaS-based enrolment automation and CRM tools for educational institutions, helping them manage student recruitment, admissions and fee collection. Under Collexo, it offers fee-collection and payments-related solutions for educational institutions. Its Pixi brand, under Collexo, also sells co-branded cards to students. The startup also enables educational organisations to deploy AI agents across student-facing and institutional workflows with its Mio AI suite. The startup claimed to have catered to 1,183 customers in the fiscal year ended March 2026, including 104 overseas clients. India accounted for 91.2% of its total revenue in FY26, while international operations contributed the remaining 8.8%. NoPaperForms processed invoices worth ₹124.6 Cr in FY26 and ₹39.9 Cr in Q1 FY27. Meanwhile, average revenue per customer improved to ₹9.8 Lakhs in the fiscal year ended March 2026 as against ₹9.2 Lakh in FY25. On the financial front, NoPaperForms reported an operating revenue of ₹115.6 Cr in FY26, up 25.2% from ₹92.3 Cr in the year ago fiscal. Meanwhile, the startup’s profits surged 534% to ₹11.9 Cr in the fiscal under review as against ₹1.9 Cr in FY25. The startup also posted an operating revenue of ₹44.8 Cr in Q1 FY27 against a net profit of ₹6 Cr in the quarter under review.

In late August 2026, a rumor spread online that claimed Canadian officials were refusing to grant passage through the Welland Canal — which connects lakes Erie and Ontario — to ships that had "Lake America" listed in their documentation, as opposed to "Lake Ontario."
The rumor circulated after U.S. President Donald Trump renamed Lake Ontario to "Lake America" in the United States.
Posts on X, Threads, Facebook (screenshott) and Reddit claimed Fox News had reported on the alleged Canadian blockade. Snopes readers contacted us to investigate the claim's legitimacy.
(X user @MykhailoRohoza)
This claim originated as satire. A search of Fox News' archives via its website found no evidence the news outlet had reported on such a claim.
Searches on DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo also found no relevant and credible news articles reporting on this claim as fact. If Canadian officials really were preventing ships using the term "Lake America" in their documentation from crossing the Welland Canal, it would certainly have made news, and search inquiries would have uncovered evidence of it.
The St. Lawrence Seaway Management Corp. oversees ship traffic on the Canadian side of the Welland Canal, which is part of the St. Lawrence Seaway. The Canadian Press reported that Serge Auclair, vice-president of commercial and external relations at the corporation, said vessels are traveling the canal as usual.
"Seaway operations are continuing normally and have done so throughout the weekend. Vessels are transiting the Welland Canal as usual," Nicole Giroux, a spokesperson for the St. Lawrence Seaway Management Corp., told Snopes.
The earliest version of the claim we found came from an Aug. 28 X post (archived) from a Russian X user listed as "Comedian" on the account's profile (archived). We reached out to the X user to confirm the account originated the claim and will update this story if we hear back.
Many of the earlier versions of the claim shared in English also labeled it as satire, or at least acknowledged its satirical origins.
Snopes has debunked similar pieces of media before. For example, in May, we alerted readers to a fake story about Canadian officials denying Trump a $573 billion railway bailout.
For more on Lake Ontario, we previously confirmed it was named by Indigenous people, not after the Canadian province of Ontario.
Since the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

Chinese man, Nepali woman found alive 10 days after flood
The man, named only as Luhaitao, was pulled out of a tunnel, while Chandrika Shrestha, 64, was rescued from her buried home
Rescuers pulled out a 64-year-old Nepali woman alive on Saturday from her home, buried under thick mud and debris when the region was struck by massive flooding 10 days ago, killing over 1,300 people and leaving at least 5,500 missing.

Philippine VP Duterte posts bail over 'grave threats' against Marcos
Sara Duterte was charged last month after she claimed to have hired a hitman to kill President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, his wife and a congressman cousin should she be cut down first.
MANILA: Philippine Vice-President Sara Duterte posted bail at a Manila courthouse on Saturday (Sep 5), a day after an arrest warrant was issued over her alleged death threat against the country's president.
Duterte was charged last month with "grave threats" stemming from a late-night news briefing in which she claimed to have hired a hitman to kill President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, his wife and a congressman cousin should she be cut down first.
She later said the comments had been misconstrued.
The alleged assassination threat also forms a crucial element of her ongoing Senate impeachment trial, where a guilty verdict would see her removed from office and permanently banned from politics.
"The vice-president voluntarily appeared before the court that issued the warrant, so there was no need for her to be arrested," her lawyer Lawrence Lim said after Duterte emerged from the regional courthouse holding a court order confirming she had posted a cash bond.
Prior to entering, Duterte had told reporters she feared for her life.
"I don't want to (post bail) if no one is watching," she said, claiming to be the victim of police harassment.
"Will they throw me into the (jail) and then one night I die in my sleep?" she said.
“GRAVE THREATS”
Under the Philippine legal code, a criminal conviction on the "grave threats" charge would carry a jail term of up to six months.
The vice-president's legal team issued a statement on Friday saying she had "no intention of evading the law and will continue to exercise all her legal remedies".
Justice department officials have rejected her lawyers' argument that she cannot be prosecuted for offences that are also tied to her impeachment.
Duterte was impeached in May by the House of Representatives, the lower chamber of parliament, on charges that also included graft and corruption.
A guilty verdict in the Senate - where her trial recently concluded its ninth week - would spell an end to a planned run for president in 2028.

Few films have woven themselves into India’s cultural imagination as deeply as Pakeezah. While the film is celebrated for its haunting melodies and its poignant portrayal of the mahaul and tehzeeb of nawabi Lucknow, one scene remains etched in the collective memory of cinegoers. Salim, played by Raaj Kumar, enters a train compartment and chances upon Sahibjaan, portrayed by Meena Kumari, asleep on an upper berth. Struck by the beauty of her bare feet, he leaves behind a note that came to epitomise mohabbat for die-hard aashiqs of the era: “Aapke paon dekhe, bahut haseen hain. Inhe zameen par mat utariyega, maile ho jayenge” (I saw your beautiful feet. Do not let them touch the ground, lest they be soiled).
Of course, the English translation can scarcely capture the poetic charm of the original Urdu. For generations raised on a more measured, pre-digital expression of romance, these words came to symbolise a love rooted in gentleness and respect.
The film itself is said to have been conceived by director Kamal Amrohi as an ode to Meena Kumari’s beauty and to the deep love they shared. Hence, he poured his heart and soul into the project. Though they were almost 16 years apart in age and Amrohi was already a father of three, their mutual love of literature and cinema brought them together. They married on Valentine’s Day in 1952. Pakeezah was often compared to Emperor Shah Jahan’s creation of the Taj Mahal in memory of Mumtaz Mahal.
Thanks to the Mumbai-based Film Heritage Foundation (FHF), the classic can once again be experienced on the big screen. When it was released in 1972, Pakeezah was a box-office success. Now, in a meticulously restored 4K version, it is set to travel to international film festivals, beginning with its world premiere at the Festival Lumière in Lyon, France. It will also be screened at theatres in India. FHF spent nearly two years working with the Amrohi family to restore the film, large portions of which had deteriorated over time.
A member of the International Federation of Film Archives (FIAF) since 2015, the Film Heritage Foundation (FHF) is a non-governmental organisation working in the field of film preservation. The Foundation has built a collection of around 700 films on celluloid and an extensive archive of film-related memorabilia such as cameras, projectors, posters, song booklets and books. Over the years, it has restored several classics of Indian cinema, including Shyam Benegal’s Manthan, Girish Kasaravalli’s Ghatashraddha, Satyajit Ray’s Aranyer Din Ratri, Bimal Roy’s Do Bigha Zameen andRamesh Sippy’s Sholay. Kamal Amrohi’s masterpiece will also be screened at the BFI London Film Festival, where it will be presented by FHF director Shivendra Singh Dungarpur alongside Kamal Amrohi’s children, Tajdar and Rukhsaar, and his grandson, Bilal Amrohi.
Recalling the challenging restoration process, Shivendra Singh says, “I first watched Pakeezah as a child with my grandmother in a theatre in Dumraon, Bihar. Ever since I ventured into film restoration, it had been my dream to work on Pakeezah. I eventually approached the Amrohi family with a proposal and was delighted to receive their enthusiastic support.
“I knew it wasn’t going to be an easy task. The original camera negative had almost melted, and the other film elements were not in good condition either. I often wondered how I would restore Kamal Amrohi’s original vision with the material available. Fortunately, we discovered original film stills, which proved invaluable. Equally important were Tajdar and Rukhsaar’s memories of the time spent on the sets.”
Tajdar, who was at the grand premiere of Pakeezah in 1972 with his father and choti ammi (Meena Kumari), remembers the film cans arriving at Mumbai’s famed Maratha Mandir in a palanquin. “Everything in our lives revolved around Pakeezah. My father had put in everything he had in the film and whenever we asked him for anything as children, his response would always be, ‘After Pakeezah’. This was his life’s mission. I have so many memories of the film as I would regularly visit the sets on Floor No. 3 at Filmistan. Pakeezah has influenced generations of filmmakers and even today I am sometimes asked how did he achieve some of the shots.”
The filming of Pakeezah, which remained in production for nearly 15 years, began in black and white in 1956. In 1958, the project shifted to Eastmancolor and was shot by the acclaimed German cinematographer Josef Wirsching. Frequent script revisions and the director’s obsession with perfection continually pushed up the budget. Matters worsened when a fire on the sets destroyed several negatives.
The film faced numerous hurdles before it finally reached the screen. Kamal Amrohi and Meena Kumari parted ways, and the actress was later diagnosed with liver cirrhosis. At the behest of friends, she returned to complete the film. Wirsching’s death meant that some of India’s leading cinematographers had to step in, one after another, to maintain the visual aesthetic he had established. The production suffered another setback with the death of composer Ghulam Mohammed, who had created the film’s celebrated songs, prompting Naushad to step in and compose the final background score. Pakeezah finally hit theaters on February 4, 1972, and Meena Kumari passed away on March 31, 1972, just weeks after the premiere.
An emotional Rukhsaar says, “As a13-year-old, I saw the many sacrifices my father made to make his vision a reality. I felt that my father’s legacy as a great master of cinema had been forgotten. I would like to thank Shivendra Singh for taking the initiative to restore Pakeezah with so much love and care. I cannot wait to see the restored film back on the big screen.”

Matthew Floca, the Kennedy Center's vice president of facilities, said in April 2026 sworn testimony that the center felled its weeping willows "because they were falling down." He also confirmed Trump was not involved in the decision.
In late August and early September 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the removal of weeping willow trees outside the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C.
"The iconic weeping willow trees outside the Kennedy Center have been cut down by Trump," Adam Parkhomenko, a former Hillary Clinton adviser, wrote on X.
The iconic weeping willow trees outside the Kennedy Center have been cut down by Trump. pic.twitter.com/5bZ0AnaPDx
— Adam Parkhomenko (@AdamParkhomenko) September 1, 2026
Similar claims also circulated on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived), Threads (archived), Bluesky (archived) and Reddit (archived). Snopes readers contacted us to verify them. One reader asked, "Did Trump have the willow trees at the JFK center cut down?"
That was not the case. 
Floca said in his testimony that the center felled the trees because of a "maintenance need" (Page 28) and that it was "contemplating" their replacements. Floca added that he had not spoken to Trump, who is the chair of the Kennedy Center Board of Trustees, about the weeping willows or what should replace them (Page 28).
Given the above, we rate the claim that Trump ordered the removal of the Kennedy Center's weeping willow trees false. Rather, the center's management said it felled the trees because of a maintenance need and confirmed Trump was not involved in the decision.
We contacted the Kennedy Center to ask when it cut down the weeping willows and whether it had any plans to replace the trees, but did not receive a response by the time of publication. A White House spokesperson referred our request for comment to the Kennedy Center.
Citing a spokesperson for the Kennedy Center, Newsweek reported that the center removed its weeping willow trees in October 2025. Snopes found one image published by Reuters that showed weeping willows at the Kennedy Center in September 2025 and a geo-tagged image from Google that showed at least one such tree cut down in October, supporting this reported timeline.
The neighborhood blog PoPville, which covers Washington, D.C., reported on the removal of the weeping willows on October 14, 2025. Snopes could not view metadata for the images in order to establish their authenticity, but had no reason to believe they were inauthentic.
What we know about the trees
Floca told a Washington, D.C. district court on April 29, 2026, that the weeping willows at the Kennedy Center had to be removed because they were in poor health. He said (Page 28):
Ninety percent of the trees were decaying and every time there was a heavy wind or rain a tree would fall down. If you walk around the center at that time, you would see limbs falling and trees falling down.
When asked whether he discussed what tree would replace the weeping willows with the Kennedy Center chairman (meaning Trump), Floca said (Page 28):
We haven't specifically talked about the weeping willows or the replacement. I think that a weeping cherry tree would be perfect. But we are going to come up with a complete landscape — a comprehensive landscape plan that doesn't only talk to the planters and the willow trees, and that will be part of the plan, the replacement.
As of this writing, it was unclear what tree would replace the weeping willows, which lawyer Abbe David Lowell claimed were meant to represent "the grief of the nation" for the death of former U.S. President John F. Kennedy (Page 27).
Trump posted digital renderings of his suggested "new, highly improved" Kennedy Center in March 2026 that replaced the weeping willows with either pink or orange-leafed trees. Though weeping willows change color in the fall, their leaves turn yellow or gold, not orange, red or pink like the trees in Trump's renderings, which appeared to suggest the president wanted to replace the weeping willows with a different kind of tree.
Floca's testimony was part of a lawsuit brought by several conservation groups that sought to stop Trump and the Kennedy Center's board from carrying out proposed renovations without third-party review. On May 29, a federal judge denied the conservation groups' request for a preliminary injunction that would stop the renovations while the court case was ongoing.
Nonetheless, the center remained open at the time of this writing, despite Trump initially saying it would close on July 4, 2026, for renovations.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether Trump cut down dozens of cherry trees in Washington, D.C., to make way for a golf course.

Former Premier League referee Mike Dean on Friday issued a clarification after his recent comments on a podcast drew criticism and questions were raised over the officiating standards in the England top flight.
“Throughout my 25 years as a professional referee, I have always applied the Laws of the Game to the best of my ability,” Dean wrote on Instagram on Friday.
“My approach as a referee was always to allow the game to flow and whenever possible I preferred to apply a high threshold for contact which the players liked. However, if I saw a foul challenge that needed me to take the appropriate action I would give it from the correct position.”
During the podcast appearance, Dean said he played “games” within a football match, challenging himself to let the game flow without blowing his whistle and trying to stay inside the centre circle for as long as he could.
Following Dean’s comments, several referees to pitched in and said the remarks brought into question the integrity of match officials in England.
“At no stage was it my intention to question, criticise or undermine the integrity of refereeing in this country. I have always respected the profession and the responsibility that comes with being a referee,” he added.

A federal judge recently blocked the Donald Trump administration from enforcing a new executive order which sets new rules to determine who qualifies for birthright citizenship. This isn't the first time that Trump sought to cut down the circumstances in which children born in the US would receive citizenship. What is US birthright citizenship, and what changes is Trump's government seeking? US birthright citizenship is the principle under which anyone born on US soil is generally considered a US citizen from birth, regardless of the immigration status of their parents. The right is rooted in the Citizenship Clause of the 14th Amendment, ratified in 1868, which established citizenship for people born in the United States and subject to its jurisdiction. The US Supreme Court has historically upheld this principle from time to time. A recent Supreme Court ruling in June 2026 also addressed the scope of the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause in litigation over the Trump administration's efforts to restrict birthright citizenship. Restricting birthright citizenship has been a major part of Donald Trump's broader immigration crackdown from earlier. His administration argues that the existing system can be exploited through what is being referred to as “birth tourism”, where foreign nationals travel to the US, including those on non-immigrant visas, with the sole purpose of giving birth in the country to obtain US citizenship for their child. In his August 6 executive order, Trump sought to limit birthright citizenship, including those whose parents work for foreign governments or are classified as “alien enemies”. It also restricts citizenship for kids born in the US whose parents are accused of using fraud or commercial arrangements to obtain citizenship. According to the White House, the changes in birthright citizenship are aimed at protecting the “meaning and value” of American citizenship. Trump's latest order arrived after an earlier attempt to restrict birthright citizenship. In June, the US Supreme Court ruled against the earlier order, stating that it conflicted with the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause, as reported by Reuters. Trump then issued a narrower order on August 6, which was also challenged in court. On September 2, US District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland blocked it through a preliminary injunction. The judge ruled that children covered by the lawsuit would remain US citizens at birth. The Trump administration reportedly argued that the case was premature as agencies had not yet issued rules to implement the order. However, the judge rejected that argument. The proposed changes to US birthright citizenship are likely to have an important impact. Under the draft reviewed by Reuters, parents or legal guardians applying for a US passport for their children could be required to submit proof of their own US citizenship or immigration status. Documents such as a US passport or birth certificate for citizens, or documents such as an I-94 form or permanent resident card of the parents, might be required to obtain citizenship for their child. Currently, parents can establish their relationship to the child by providing government-issued identification. For now, they are not required to submit evidence of their own citizenship or immigration status. The measure is expected to affect primarily families with children born in the US whose parents are non-citizens. This includes immigrants on temporary visas or families with complex immigration circumstances. Reuters reported that the State Department's proposed guidance would use parental citizenship and immigration information to determine whether a child falls within the categories covered by the executive order. For Indian-origin families, it can be a significant issue as well. A large number of Indians live and work in the US on employment-based visas, including H-1B visas, while many are permanent residents or are waiting for green cards. If the restrictions are implemented, affected parents could face additional scrutiny during passport-related processes as well. However, the executive order remains blocked by the preliminary injunction for now. Out in rural India, a crisis casts a dark cloud over the seemingly tranquil vistas of wheat fields and soy farms. Over the past 20 years, more than 400,000 farmers have killed themselves, beset by mounting debts and low market prices for crops. Shot in Maharashtra, the state with the highest rate of farmer suicides in India, Kinshuk Surjan’s documentary sensitively captures another tragedy that lingers after death: left behind by their dead husbands, generations of grieving widows struggle to find their way in a society still burdened by patriarchal values.
Sanjivani, a woman in her 30s, is one such case. Eight years after her husband killed himself, she has taken over some of the farming responsibilities, along with other odd jobs, to provide for her two children. The camera rarely finds her at rest; Sanjivani not only works in the fields but also performs domestic labour for her extended family – cooking, cleaning and doing laundry. Her resilience is stunning to witness, but even more impressive is the emotional support provided by a tight-knit network of other widows. Together, the women gather for counselling sessions where they can freely discuss their emotional, physical and financial issues.
One widow, for example, laments her former status as a child bride; another talks defiantly of her decision to remarry, still a taboo act in this conservative village. Though each has their baggage, the women all share the pain and anger of being rendered invisible by their widowhood. On certain celebration days, they are not even allowed to go out, for fear of inflicting bad luck on others. Sanjivani’s transformation over the course of the film, however, inspires hope. As she continues her education and works at a local pharmacy, Sanjivani’s steps towards independence show that, with the support of the collective, life can – and must – go on for the marginalised and forgotten.

It was only when Alex Lanier was doing his media interviews shortly after creating history at the Badminton World Championships in New Delhi that Carlos Rubio got his place in the spotlight, dousing the first French men’s singles champion in champagne. Until then, Rubio, the head of the Strength and Conditioning programme for the French badminton team, was happy in the background, making sure the athlete in front of him was physically ready for the moment.
Rubio, who recently retired from his position, speaks to Sportstar about what it takes to make a World champion, the biggest challenge for elite players, whether playing too many tournaments can be counterproductive, the physical demands of badminton and why he had to work to stop Lanier from becoming “too strong”.
Q. What does it take to build a World champion?
A. It takes a lot of dedication from their side. Then, we are merging, at least the way we have done it, the knowledge from different experts. We have the badminton coaches, physical coaches, like me, nutritionists, psychologists, data analysts, management and performance management.
We really try to work together to utilise all the expertise and make a really good plan for each player, because each player is different. We have to individualise it and make a very tailored programme to make sure each of them gets what they need to perform.
Q. When you joined the French badminton programme, what was your brief?
A. I joined in January 2025. The goal was simple: to try to create the best training process. We cannot guarantee the medals, but we can work for our players to be in the best situation possible to win the medal.
We cannot control the match because there is another part of the court, which is the opponent, who we can’t control. But we can control that we prepare our players the best, so when the chance arrives, they are in the best shape possible to win.
That was our goal — not to win any medal at some point. It was to do the best we could, to be in the best situation at the most important tournaments. Over time, we were sure that at some point that was going to give us the medals.
Q. Were there things you wanted to change when you started with the French team?
A. I think the project was very solid already. The project was already a change from what had been done traditionally in badminton.
My area is mainly about Strength and Conditioning, based on individualisation, science, data and coordination with the other experts. It was most important that we monitored and managed the load that every player received from every area — from Strength and Conditioning, from the psychologists as mental load, from the court and from the stress of life — to make sure that we didn’t overload or underload the player.
Q. At the elite level, everyone is working extremely hard. What separates someone who is physically exceptional from someone who is very good?
A. I think the answer is very simple. The application of the answer is not that simple. What I think is most important is load management.
From a Strength and Conditioning perspective, you want to put enough load that the player improves constantly, while making sure that you don’t overload or underload.
At the same time, World champions aren’t all built the same way. There are many things that go into building one and there are many strengths that you can utilise. If we compare Anders Antonsen with Lanier, we can see that probably Lanier’s physique is superior, but sometimes Antonsen performs better than Lanier.
That tells us there are different ways to achieve performance. Performance is a result of many components playing a part. Physical ability is one of them. There are also people at the top who are not good physically, but then the other aspects are very good.
You have to be in a range. If you fall below that range, you will probably lose because of the physicality. Or if you fall behind that minimum of shot quality, shot variety or tactical adaptability, then the person in front of you is going to be superior.
Not all of the components have to be at the maximum.
Q. What physical qualities do you need to be an elite badminton player?
A. The quality depends on the kind of player you are. If your playing style is more aggressive, you will need different things. If it’s more defensive, or it’s more about winning long rallies, or you want to focus more on winning short rallies, then what you need physically will be different.
But besides those individualisations, for sure you’re going to have huge maximum strength. You have to be able to use that in an explosive way. At the same time, you need endurance — enough endurance to go for the long rallies without losing technical, cognitive or decision-making quality.
You need to be durable enough to stay in the long rallies but explosive enough to do short rallies at a higher pace than your opponent for longer periods, and repeat that throughout the match.
Mobility has to be exceptional as well. Otherwise, you’re not going to move freely and you’re going to have to compensate or overuse some areas of your body because some others are not mobile, and that can make you prone to injuries.
Q. You’ve worked with athletes across different sports. What would people be surprised to learn about badminton?
A. I think they could be surprised about how many repeated high-intensity actions you have to do. Moving fast to the defence and then coming back; going fast to the net and coming back fast.
The faster you go, probably the less time you allow your opponent to have until the next shot. So, you can increase the pace of the rally. That’s way more tough than it looks.
That’s the main difference between the physicality of the top players and an amateur player. It’s the ability to do this repeatedly during the rally, repeat it during the points, repeat it during the sets [games] and repeat it over days.
ALSO READ | How France built two badminton world champions: Inside the system behind a historic day in New Delhi
Q. What’s the difference in how you prepare singles and doubles players?
A. Usually, a singles player needs to be slightly more prepared physically than doubles because the demands. This doesn’t mean that a doubles player should be less prepared. If they are very well prepared, they will also benefit from that physicality.
There are also differences in where the load is building. For example, the load on the shoulder in doubles is going to be higher because of the high-speed actions overhead and at mid-height. The demands for the shoulder and forearm are way higher than in singles.
In singles, they need to be more prepared in terms of horizontal accelerations and decelerations at a higher speed, repeated over time, because you are the only one on the court. There are also differences in the men’s and women’s singles. There are some studies that show that the frequency of strokes is higher in women’s badminton. It means there’s a lot less time between shuttles. That’s because in general women are not that tall or explosive so they have to do more without making the shuttle go as high.
Q. With badminton moving to a 15-point system, will the role of Strength and Conditioning change? There are theories that it could make it easier for less physically capable players to perform because the game is shorter.
A. I don’t think so. If you run a marathon, you don’t have to be more fit than the guy that runs 100 metres, right? But you have to be fit in a different way.
If you prepare for a marathon and you’re going to run a 100-metre dash, you will lose. If you prepare as a sprinter to win a marathon, you will lose as well. You have to make your Strength and Conditioning, your physical training, specific to what you’re going to compete in.
I’m still not sure how exactly the game will change in terms of activity patterns. It could be that they go more all-in during rallies, but I’m not sure. It also depends on the tactical approach that the players bring to this game.
It might not be as simple as going from stamina to explosiveness. Because the clock is only allowing you to rest for 25 seconds between points, you have to have the ability to sprint every 25 seconds, which is a metabolic and endurance ability.
Q. What is the biggest physical challenge for elite players?
A. Actually, I think the biggest issue for elite players is trying not to underload themselves during a tournament and not to overload during training weeks. But I think it’s more about underloading themselves during tournaments.
If you have to prepare for the World Championships or the Olympics, you can’t do it by constantly travelling for competitions. If you are constantly competing and travelling for two or three weeks on the Asian Tour or in Europe, plus jet lag, you cannot improve.
Actually, the competition doesn’t allow you to improve, if you don’t load during the competitions, at least a little bit.
But it’s not my view alone that matters. It’s the federation that has to be clear about what is the way in which we want to build performance. Then the practitioners like me, the coaches and the psychologists have to respect the philosophy of the federation and work towards it.
Every federation has a different perspective. Some feel the need to have a balance: we need to compete, but we also need to load and train and prepare for the big events. There are some other federations or teams that prefer to compete a lot because they think it’s a better strategy.
Q. How do you manage training load during competitions?
A. You have to train during the tournaments. You can always find a gym, you can always find a court to train. But most people, I believe, do too little during tournaments.
Q. But isn’t it hard to load when you have to prepare for a match?
A. I think it’s because of a lack of knowledge about how the human body reacts and works, and how to load without sacrificing the performance of the match.
Q. What are the challenges faced as the players get older?
A. If they have gone through a good training process, they will know themselves better. Players who do manage to play well into their 30s, like Chou Tien Chen, I think they are doing something right, which is changing the strategy.
You cannot play at 36 like you were playing at 21. You’re a different player. You should have more weapons. You should be more tactically aware. You should be more efficient in your movements. You should take better decisions.
Physically you are going to be worse than when you were 21. So, you have to play differently.
Of course, your management of the stress and the mental management of a tournament should also be better at 30-something than at 21. So, in the end, you also have some strengths compared to younger players.
Q. You’ve done a lot of work with Alex Lanier. What sets him apart physically?
A. Everything. He’s probably better than all the other people in everything. He has more strength, he’s more explosive, he has more endurance, he’s able to do very intense activities repeatedly at a higher intensity. He’s probably more mobile, he’s probably more aware of his body. I also think Alex has a genetic ability to be strong. He’s strong by default.
His biggest challenge is that he can become too strong! Sometimes we need to manage for him not to be too big. He’s very muscular. As you can see, his quads are big. His arms are big.
So, we need to find a way to prevent him from getting too big while still keeping him explosive. We can’t undertrain him and make him weak, but we can’t keep increasing his load because that will increase his muscular weight and at some point that isn’t beneficial.
When I arrived in France, he was already strong. We just made him strong in a better way. We modified in which areas he was strong and in which areas he was okay.
Q. France won two medals at the World Championships. What was the highlight of the tournament for you?
A. I think what I’m happiest about was how well we structured everything before the games.
Since I started working with the players, we got to know them and we started preparing routines for the tournament. The World Championships is a reference tournament. We really want to do well there. So, we need to practise the strategies we’re going to put in place beforehand.
From tournament to tournament, we were identifying what works and what doesn’t. In the end, at the World Championships, we arrived with all the strategies we had identified over one-and-a-half years that were working very well, and selected the ones we wanted.
We wanted to select them in a way where we were clear on exactly what to do on match day.
I think overall we got the right application of Sports Science on a daily basis.
Q. What is the role of data in Strength and Conditioning for badminton?
A. I can’t tell you what we have collected in France because that’s confidential. But I can tell you from my past what I believe as a physical coach.
Technology allows us to assess things that our senses as humans are not able to perceive with quality or without bias.
Simple things are: how strong a player is and how that strength is varying through the season, or how he wakes up every day, whether he has slept well, if he’s stressed or not, if he is very sore from yesterday’s training or not, if he’s in a good mood or not.
As we are seeing everywhere right now — in football, basketball and badminton — some teams measure the load that a player has during matches and practices.
Inertial measurement units, which are accelerometers, like small devices that analyse the acceleration and deceleration of the player, are also quite important. It’s quite nice information, if you know how to use it. It’s insightful.
I think the problem is not knowing which data you should collect. There’s more than enough. You can ask ChatGPT and it can tell you a million things about what to collect from the player. I think the real challenge is: which information do I collect, which do I not collect, and how do I make sense of this information feeding into each other to make a decision on an everyday or weekly basis?

‘Our leader is very clear’: Tamil Nadu minister reiterates TVK’s stance on 'Vijay as PM' pitch
Sengottaiyan's statement comes days after Congress leaders had threatened to resign from Vijay's cabinet if TVK did not accept Rahul as the PM candidate.
Tamil Nadu minister KA Sengottaiyan on Friday reiterated the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam's stand on party president and chief minister C Joseph Vijay being pitched for the prime ministerial post in 2029 by some supporters on Friday.
TVK leaders' and supporters' ‘Vijay as PM’ pitch had sparked rumours of a rift with the Congress on the issue. Sengottaiyan, responding to this, said the TVK's leader was “very clear.” The Tamil Nadu minister's statement comes days after Congress leaders from the state had threatened to resign from Vijay's cabinet if TVK did not accept Rahul Gandhi as the next candidate for prime minister.
Sengottaiyan said that Tamil Nadu had shown “faith” in Vijay by voting for him, while saying the chief minister would take “all necessary steps” to protect the people of the state, ANI news agency reported.
What did Sengottaiyan say?
When asked about Vijay being projected as a prime ministerial candidate, Sengottaiyan said, “As far as we are concerned, our leader is very clear. Tamil Nadu has voted with faith in him..”
The Tamil Nadu minister said that Vijay's TVK had “achieved a major victory” within two years of its formation and secured a new election symbol two months before winning the Assembly elections.
“The Chief Minister is taking all necessary steps to protect the people of Tamil Nadu and implement schemes that were desired by the public...” ANI cited Sengottaiyan as saying.
The remarks came a couple of days after TVK MLA Kanimozhi Santhosh said Vijay would be the prime ministerial candidate in 2029, adding that “a big and a shocking change in Indian politics will be seen in 2029”. “...you'll see in 2029. Who goes in and who goes out. It was our Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, who made Thalapathy sit in the CM chair. So he will only hold Vijay's hand and make him sit in the PM's chair in 2029,” Kanimozhi said.
Congress vs TVK over 2029 prime ministerial candidate
The debate began after some Vijay posters were seen in parts of Tamil Nadu's port-industrial city of Thoothukudi, with the phrase "Tomorrow’s PM” written on them.
The posters were put up by the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) functionary Sudhakar, who recently joined the Vijay-led party after leaving AIADMK. TVK leaders backed the projection of Vijay as PM for 2029, with TVK PWD minister Aadhav Arjuna saying that the country's top constitutional office should be held by a leader from Tamil Nadu.
However, the Congress leaders in the state showed displeasure, threatening to resign from Vijay's state cabinet. Congress is part of the TVK-led Tamil Nadu government with five MLAs, along with 107 of Vijay's party, two of Indian Union Muslim League (IUML), and two of VCK / Left Factions.
Tamil Nadu tourism minister S Rajesh Kumar stated that both Congress ministers will resign if TVK fails to back Gandhi in the 2029 general elections. Meanwhile, Tamil Nadu Congress president B Manickam Tagore said some TVK leaders were “still operating in a fan-club mode.”

I drink the blood of my fourth rat tonight. It’s only got so much life to give, so as soon as I drain it, I know I'll need to feed again. My hunger is not fulfilled. My health bar is only half full. I need more blood. Now.
I toss the rat away as my glowing eyes flicker to another, just across the street. I bare my sharp, bloody teeth, turn into a cloud of shadow and bats, and teleport to my unsuspecting prey. I bite down hard. It’s too late to realize my target has changed. As I swarmed, a human city guard happened to walk right in front of me. My teeth sink into his throat instead. I could let go, but I do not. I drink, drink, drink. Then he falls to the ground. Dead. I wipe my mouth as the last rat scurries away into the dark.
“Well, I guess I’m going to Hell anyway,” my character quips.
The Blood of Dawnwalker is a vampire simulator and role-playing video game that launches today. It’s a dark adventure where you play as the titular Dawnwalker—human by day, monstrous vampire at night.
You can’t talk about The Blood of Dawnwalker without talking about The Witcher 3. They’re both third-person monster-slasher video games starring handsome protagonists with cool scars on their faces, both made by some of the same people.
Konrad Tomaszkiewicz, a former director at the Polish game studio and Witcher developer CD Projekt Red, was one of three directors of the very popular The Witcher 3. His new studio, Rebel Wolves, even feels like a cheeky nod to Geralt, the main character of The Witcher series who is often called the White Wolf. The gameplay and graphics feel very similar. Combat involves swinging your sword and blasting magic abilities, while cutscenes and dialog have familiar dialog trees and quick-time events. You have a special sense that makes important items glow so you can find footprints and track down monsters.
The music also sounds almost identical to The Witcher 3 soundtrack—think somber swelling violin strings plucking away while you wander a gloomy open world. I was almost ready to allege copyright infringement before realizing that Dawnwalker features the work of fellow Witcher composer Mikolai Stroinski.
Ah, so, “We have The Witcher at home,” is that it? Well, not exactly. The sameness might feel derivative at first, but give it a minute. Once you get through the prologue, the world opens up in a way that invites exploration of its very pretty, blood-soaked world. There’s no way to beat The Witcher 3 in depth, breadth, or sheer volume, but The Blood of Dawnwalker doesn’t try to replicate or surpass that scale. Instead, it gives you a simple goal and a limited time to pull it off. That sounds restrictive at first, but it plays out in a way that's more freeing than you’d expect.
Dawnwalker takes place in a fictional plague-era medieval world. You play as Coen (I call him Young Geralt), a poor peasant who lives with his family in a town controlled by evil vampires. After some inciting events, the Draculean boss vampire kidnaps Coen’s family and turns him into the Dawnwalker—a vampire hybrid that manifests as a human in the daytime and a bloodthirsty vampire at night. You’ve got 30 in-game days to save Coen’s family. You’re already running out of time.
Gameplay is split into day and night cycles, each with eight time segments. Completing a quest or doing anything of consequence will pass one or a few time segments. Otherwise, time does not pass idly. If you’re running around and exploring, you have all the time to fart around in the world that you need. The game warns you when something you're about to do will pass the time, so you can choose to keep going or leave and find something else to do.
I worried this system would feel constricting, like being forced on a set path in an open-world game. Turns out, it was exactly what I needed to stay motivated and keep exploring.
My problem with The Witcher 3 and open-world games like it is that there is so much of it. You’re tasked with some time-sensitive mission—rescue your daughter before the world ends, etc.—but then you while away hours and hours on side quests. Games like this can punish you if you rush the main storyline, cutting off quests, choices, and even characters that those smaller efforts would have unlocked. When I play, I feel obligated to do all the small stuff first, then build to the main quests. When a narrative and world gets that dense, it can start to feel like a chore.
Dawnwalker gives you many activities across the world. Some are clearly story quests; many are treasure hunts or things that feel much smaller-scale. Knowing I can’t do everything lets me prioritize what needs doing. A ticking clock always counting down on the screen usually would make me anxious in games, since failing to do the right things at the right time means you lose. Weirdly, Dawnwalker’s countdown feels less punishing and more like motivation to do the very best you can with the limited resources you have. If you know you can’t see everything in a single playthrough, it’s easier to let go of the things you miss.
It’s by no means a perfect game. The Blood of Dawnwalker is a clunky name. It really should be Blood of the Dawnwalker or just Blood of Dawnwalker. (Dawnwalker is your character’s title after all, not his name.) There is also undeniable jank throughout, like when you sheathe your sword, it floats directly behind the center of Coen’s butt. When you run with your heightened vampiric sense, the sword bounces around and spanks Coen’s behind as he runs. It is very funny, and I hope the devs don’t change it.
It is particularly unfortunate for Dawnwalker that the game is launching in the shadow of news that The Witcher 3 is getting a free remastered update later this month and a whole new expansion pack in 2027, 11 years after its original release.
Despite all the blood, gore, and sorrow, Dawnwalker has charm and a lightness to it. Combat is bloody, wet, and satisfying. At night, Coen’s vampiric abilities are a hoot, letting you teleport around across the rooftops, drink the blood of any crawly creature you like, and sprint across the map as a wolf. Most of the vampires, aside from smokeshow Coen, are the truly monstrous kinds, all claws and teeth and gory bloodsucking. But the world slowly reveals some real beauty. The other characters develop and become much more interesting than they first appeared. The voice acting that carries some pretty wrenching story beats and character moments is stellar.
Above all, it does something remarkable: It takes an established game formula and really infuses it with its own personality and quirks. It takes a bite out of the Witcher formula and makes it its own. And has a bloody good time doing it.
