This rugged smartphone's camera is a removable action cam
It’s waterproof and can record up to 40 minutes of video.
Few companies are pushing back against the black, oblong smartphone design hegemony in 2026, but RugOne is one of them. It's part of Ulefon, which has been pumping out ruggedized phones for a few years, and its newest phone, the Xsnap 7 Pro, is very rugged but has a magnetic removable camera unit that can work like an action cam.
Yeah, it made me go "ooh" when I heard about it. (Unfortunately, my sample landed while we report on IFA 2026 here in Berlin. I'll update this story when I get to see the device in person later this week. The almost cube-shaped camera weighs 39 grams and can record video up to 2.7K resolution at 30fps — it's not coming for the latest GoPro quite yet.
RugOne says the module can run for up to 40 minutes on a full charge, with 64GB of built-in storage. It'll broadcast a preview feed to RugOne's companion app, up to 50 meters away. It also includes a handful of software features, including distortion correction, horizon lock and a Freeframe shooting mode that captures the full sensor area, so you can crop to vertical or horizontal footage as needed.
The camera is waterproof up to five meters (without any additional protective cases), and the company will also include a companion magnet pendant so you can wear it on your body for capture; it will also work with third-party accessories that support a universal mount.
The Xsnap 7 Pro also has a 50-megapixel "AI main camera" with optical image stabilization, plus a 64MP infrared night-vision camera with IR LEDs for "crisp black-and-white detail" during nighttime wildlife shooting — RugOne's suggestion, not mine.
And let's not forget: still a phone. The Xsnap 7 Pro has a 6.67-inch display with 1,700-nit peak brightness and up to 120Hz refresh rates. It packs a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 processor, and the device has strong durability credentials. It's rated IP68 and IP69K and can handle water submersion up to two meters deep for 30 minutes as well as 1.5-meter drops onto concrete.
While a prototype was teased at MWC 2026 a few months ago, the Xsnap 7 Pro is officially debuting at IFA, with early-bird sales opening on Kickstarter on September 7 at a discounted preorder price of 799 euros (roughly $930). The phone will then go on sale globally sometime next month on Amazon and RugOne's online store, priced at $999, in Sand Dune and Classic Black.

Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution significantly expanding presidential powers ahead of elections due in December.
According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago.
The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people.
The new constitution will reduce the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cut electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. New provisions will require presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for at least five years before the vote, which is believed to target diaspora-based politicians with significant followings.
The referendum’s outcome is expected to pave the way for December’s elections, which many hope will steady the political landscape in Guinea-Bissau, which has been through a series of politically turbulent periods since its declaration of independence from Portugal was globally recognised in 1974. Since then it has had at least 10 coup attempts, half of which have been successful.
The most recent came after last November’s disputed presidential elections. Both candidates declared themselves winners, citing electoral malpractice by the other’s camp. The military forcefully intervened, setting up a transitional ruling council headed by Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, a former military chief of general staff.
Na Man said: “What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance.”
Nelson Moreira, the second vice-president of the transitional council, said the outgoing constitution, which came into effect in 1993, had often been cited as “the cause of instability in Guinea”.
The leading opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which was barred from fielding a presidential candidate in the 2025 election, had asked its supporters to boycott the referendum, which it called a democratic farce.
“What will happen on 30 August is the continuation of the coup d’état carried out on 26 November,” its leader, Domingos Simões Pereira, had said.

What does Norris deal mean for Piastri? F1 Q&A
- Published
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli will try to tighten his grip on the drivers' championship on home ground at this weekend's Italian Grand Prix at Monza.
However, the 20-year-old can expect to face a challenge from a resurgent McLaren and in particular Lando Norris, who has won the past two grands prix.
And Monza is of course also home territory for Ferrari, although the long straights of the historic circuit may not suit the characteristics of their car.
BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before round 13 of the 2026 season.
What does Lando Norris' new contract extension mean for Oscar Piastri? There clearly is some tension behind the scenes and this season his development performance-wise has clearly dipped. - Juha
There is no question that Oscar Piastri has not started this season as well as he did last.
In 2025, the Australian for a large part of the year appeared on course for a first world title, until his season unravelled somewhat in the final third.
This season, team-mate Lando Norris has won two races - and should have won a third in Miami.
Piastri has only looked in contention for a victory in Hungary, when Norris took his first win of the year.
After taking the lead when Norris made an error on the first lap, there was some bad luck involved in Piastri losing the lead to Norris, when he was delayed lapping Carlos Sainz's Williams.
But Piastri acknowledged it would have been difficult to hold Norris back if he had retained the lead because his pace on the hard tyres was weak. It became academic when he retired with a broken gearbox.
Although the qualifying head-to-head statistics between them do not make pleasant reading for Piastri - Norris is 12-4 ahead - on actual pace, there is not a lot to choose between them over one lap. Norris is only faster by 0.071 seconds on average.
It's fair to say, though, that Norris has been comfortably the more convincing race performer - hence the 55-point and three-place gap between them in the championship
There seem to be a few things at issue here.
One might be that Piastri has always been strong in high-speed corners. But the numbers of these that are grip-limited has reduced this year because the engines are often using them to charge the battery, something about which all drivers have complained. So that reduces a point of potential advantage for Piastri.
Second, the cars have less downforce than last year, and Piastri is less comfortable than Norris in low-grip conditions.
Finally, there is no question that Norris upped his game consistently over the course of the second half of last season to win the world title, and has continued to raise his level through this year. Without question, he is one of the drivers of the season so far.
Team principal Andrea Stella said at the last race in the Netherlands: "Last year, we had seen already with Oscar that, from a technical driving point of view, when the car has this low level of grip, like we saw last year for instance in Mexico or in Austin, he needs to adapt the way he drives, the way he thinks, the driving, his expectations.
"This requires a bit of mental effort, which gets him to lose a couple of tenths of a second because you sort of have to process rather than drive through pure instinct because what happens is what you expect.
"So it's one of those cases in which you have to adapt your natural driving style to the demand of the car. So it stays in the space of driving and in the space of the technical side of things. I don't think it has anything to do with any psychological kind of opportunity. This is purely technical."
Stella points out that the top three teams are very close in terms of performance, which means, as he puts it, "as soon as things are not optimised, then you may have a very significant positional loss - it's very brutal from this point of view".
Both McLaren and Piastri reject any suggestion that there might be tension in their relationship.
It's a fact, though, that McLaren wanted to sign Max Verstappen this summer, and that if they had it's virtually certain it would have been Piastri who was replaced.
That possibility has receded for now, with Verstappen's new contract with Red Bull. But that contract has performance clauses, and if Red Bull are still struggling next year, it may well be that McLaren have another go for Verstappen.
For now, Piastri is under contract to the end of 2027 at least, and will be focusing only on getting back to where he knows he can be.

Why are Mercedes choosing to take a grid penalty for Kimi Antonelli at the next race in Italy? Why not take it at a future grand prix to give Kimi a better chance for a home win or is this not a concern for Mercedes? - Michael
Mercedes have been quite open about the fact that Kimi Antonelli will take a new engine for the Italian Grand Prix, and with it a significant grid penalty that is likely to mean him starting at the back.
The reality is that early season reliability meant this penalty - for exceeding the permitted number of engine parts - was inevitable, and Mercedes have calculated that Monza is the best place to take it for Antonelli.
They have tried to make the decision on facts, and not let the emotion of it being his home grand prix enter into the equation.
This decision will be based partly on the fact that Monza has long straights, and so is one of the tracks where a new engine and it's slight performance increase will translate most effectively into lap time.
But also important is Mercedes' analysis of how the engines in his 'pool' can be used most effectively over the remainder of the season
Team principal Toto Wolff said: "With Kimi, we are taking the full thing. In theory, our calculations say that it's the best track to take it. Obviously, algorithms don't take the nationality into consideration. I'm not ready to fight for a championship and get the best PR. That's what we're going to do."
Antonelli's championship lead is still very comfortable, at 59 points. So he can afford to be phlegmatic about this.
He says: "Of course, it's my home race and all that kind of stuff, but, you know, I think it's the best race to do so. So, I think it still will give me a chance to do a great result and bring home good points."
George Russell will have to take a penalty soon, too. This is most likely to be at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, for similar reasons to Antonelli's being at Monza.
Are Ferrari allowing emotion to get in their way? It's perhaps a stretch to say Ferrari can go on to win the title, but surely their best chance is backing the nearest challenger? Are they allowing the emotion of their attachment to Charles Leclerc, and his history with the team, to get in the way of making the clinical, ruthless decisions needed? - Alex
Presumably this question is a reference to the brief dispute between Charles Leclerc and the team at the Dutch Grand Prix, when Lewis Hamilton was coming up behind him on fresher tyres mid-race.
We dealt with what happened there in detail in last week's Q&A.
But in the context of the question, it's worth pointing out that they actually did ask Leclerc to move out of the way to optimise Hamilton's race in Zandvoort.
Ferrari operate a policy of equality between their drivers and only favour one over the other if it is obviously in the interests of the team.
That could work either way, and the most obvious time it would be employed is if a race victory was at stake.
Hamilton is their closest driver to the championship lead, at 59 points behind Antonelli. Leclerc is 28 points behind the seven-time champion - only four points further back than Lando Norris.
Hamilton and Leclerc have won one race each, and the qualifying battle between them is incredibly close.
Hamilton is ahead 9-7 on the head-to-head in races where a fair comparison can be made, but Leclerc is actually slightly quicker on average by 0.053secs.
Beyond that, the question seems to presume that the team would favour Leclerc emotionally. But why make that presumption?
Team principal Frederic Vasseur was instrumental in getting Hamilton to join Ferrari for 2025, but he has a long and close relationship going back many years with both drivers.
Why would he be emotionally connected to one more than the other, or consciously allow emotions to rule his management decisions?

Zandvoort is a great circuit and it's disappointing that they have pulled out of hosting the F1 grand prix for a second time. Is there any chance the circuit might return to the schedule some time in the future? - Lynne
In F1, one quickly learns to never say never, but the chances of the Dutch Grand Prix returning to the calendar seem remote for the foreseeable future.
The race was unique in that it owed its existence to the popularity of one driver - Max Verstappen.
The organisers did an impressive job to host a grand prix at a track that has many logistical challenges, in terms of both its location and its facilities, and to make it work financially for as long as they did.
It was highly popular with Dutch fans. But the event was privately run with no government financial support, and organisers decided that, as race fees went up, the risks that the event would not turn a profit were becoming too high.
This decision was influenced by the fact that there had been a slight decrease in interest in the last couple of years. Understandable, as the novelty wore off.
So organisers decided to end the event after a good run before any decline became more significant and they made a loss.
F1 has no shortage of events with which to replace it. Portugal and Turkey are both coming back to the calendar next year, for example.

The story so far: India’s food regulator has proposed a red, hexagonal warning label on the front of packaged foods high in added sugar, saturated fat or salt, in a move aimed at giving consumers a simple, at-a-glance signal about unhealthy products.
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), in an affidavit filed in the Supreme Court on August 28, has proposed that the warning initially apply to products high in two or more of the three “nutrients of concern” — added sugar, added saturated fat and salt — as well as specified highly sweetened beverages.
The proposal comes after years of debate over front-of-pack labelling and intervention by the Supreme Court. The Court is scheduled to consider the affidavit on September 10.
Also Read | FSSAI’s proposed warning labels could let unhealthy foods escape scrutiny, says expert
How the proposed system is expected to work?
FSSAI has proposed a two-phase rollout. In the first phase, products high in at least two of the three nutrients would carry the red hexagon, along with specified highly sweetened beverages.
In the second phase, the warning would extend to products high in any one of the three nutrients. However, FSSAI has not specified a firm timeline for moving to the second phase.
The thresholds are proposed to be based on the Indian Council of Medical Research–National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN) Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024. However, the FSSAI proposal refers to added sugar and added saturated fat, rather than total sugar and total fat.
Single-ingredient foods and products inherently rich in these nutrients, including ghee, edible oil, jaggery and honey, are also proposed to be exempt.
Also Read | Supreme Court slams FSSAI for not introducing front-of-pack warning labels on packaged food products
What do critics say about the proposed change?
Nutrition advocates say the biggest concern is the decision to initially require a product to be high in two nutrients before it attracts a warning. A product that is high in sugar but low in salt and fat, for instance, could escape a warning altogether.
“This defeats the purpose of a warning label,” Arun Gupta, convenor of Nutrition Advocacy in Public Interest (NAPI), told The Hindu. He has argued for a simpler principle: if a product is high in sugar, salt or saturated fat, it should carry a warning.
Also Read | Why the FSSAI is also putting liquor under the scanner
The distinction could matter particularly for products such as sugary beverages, which may be high in added sugar but contain little or no fat or salt and could therefore fall outside the warning requirement in Phase I.
Dr. Gupta has also raised concerns over the use of “added” rather than total sugar and fat, the size of the proposed warning and the absence of a firm deadline for Phase II. He has called for the warnings to be available in Hindi and English, arguing that language and visibility are essential if the labels are to reach consumers across the country.
He has urged the Court to examine the proposed nutrient thresholds, definition of high-fat/sugar/salt foods, warning size, language requirements and exemptions to ensure that the system remains visible and scientifically robust.
Also Read | From Bournvita to ‘100% Pure’: Why is FSSAI tightening the rules on food claims?
Why is this significant?
Front-of-pack warning labels have been under discussion in India since at least 2018. Draft regulations on high fat, sugar and salt (HFSS) foods were proposed in 2022, but did not become law.
The issue returned to the centre of the public-health debate in 2026 after the Supreme Court directed FSSAI to move towards interpretive warning labels for unhealthy packaged foods.
The regulator’s approach has also evolved rapidly in recent weeks. An earlier proposal placed before the Court in August relied on displaying nutritional information against recommended daily limits. Following the Court’s intervention, FSSAI returned with the red-hexagon warning framework in its August 28 affidavit.
Also Read | FSSAI proposes front-of-pack red pictorial warnings for foods high in fat, sugar, salt
For consumers, the proposed red hexagon is intended to make it harder for marketing claims such as “natural” or “multigrain” to obscure the nutritional profile of a product.
For the food industry, mandatory warnings could increase pressure to reformulate products by reducing sugar, salt and saturated fat. FSSAI has said the phased approach would give industry time to reformulate.
But the proposal is not yet a notified regulation. The immediate question before the Supreme Court is whether the framework provides a clear and meaningful warning or leaves products high in a single nutrient outside the net for an unspecified period.

The anger was impossible to miss.
As television reporters walked into Delhi’s Jantar Mantar and adjoining protest sites to cover the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, many were greeted with chants of ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’. Several journalists carrying microphones or wearing lanyards bearing the logos of prominent television channels — including NDTV, News X, ABP News, and Times Now — found themselves surrounded by protesters questioning their coverage of the movement. In some instances, reporters were heckled. In some instances, the confrontation turned physical: Times Now reporter Dev Kotak was roughed up by the crowd at Jantar Mantar, and video of the aftermath circulated widely. A Zee News reporter was filmed in Mumbai standing in the rain as youth protesters around him jeered.
The mood was most poignantly captured, perhaps, by a banner at the protest site. It contained the mugshots of six senior mainstream media journalist-cum-anchors: Arnab Goswami of Republic, Sudhir Chaudhary of DD, Chitra Tripathi of ABP, Anjan Om Kashyap of Aaj Tak, Amish Devgan then of News 18, and Rubika Liyaquat of Times Now Navbharat. Above their photos, the banner said, “India’s worst enemies — More dangerous that terrorists or anti-nationals”.
Taken together, the scenes that unfolded in Delhi raise the important question: Why did a large section of young protesters reserve some of their sharpest criticism not for politicians or police, but for television news channels?
Television Crew Faces Public Anger
The protests that erupted in Delhi in June-July brought together thousands of students and young people from across the country, turning a satirical political collective called the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) into the nucleus of a wider youth-led movement. What began as a mobilisation around the NEET-UG paper leak and concerns over the examination system expanded into a broader expression of anger against the government, with protesters demanding accountability from those in charge. The demonstrations grew in scale over weeks, drawing sustained public and media attention and eventually contributing to Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation.
As the protests grew, major television networks deployed reporters to cover the events. Instead of the routine interactions that often accompany live reporting, many ground reporters encountered open hostility from sections of the crowd.

Videos shared widely on social media show protesters chanting ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’ — a phrase originally coined by journalist Ravish Kumar, roughly translating to ‘lapdog media’ — as reporters prepared to go live. In one video, a protester says he stopped a News18 vehicle from being damaged despite his own anger towards the channel. “I am a Muslim myself. I protected their vehicle from being damaged. Though I know this evening, they will again do a Hindu-Muslim debate,” he said.
GODI MEDIA IS DEAD!

Traditional Mainstream Media has COMPLETELY LOST Gen Z’s Trust!

As reporters started being identified by the brands they represented, some began using unbranded microphones instead. NDTV’s Shiv Aroor and Vishnu Som, and India Today’s Preeti Choudhry were among those.
The outbursts were not confined to a handful of isolated incidents. Numerous videos from different locations captured similar confrontations, while comments beneath those videos echoed the protesters’ criticism of mainstream television news. Smaller outlets perceived as pro-government were heckled as well, suggesting the hostility was directed at a type of coverage rather than at legacy television alone.
At the same time, several incidents crossed the line from protest into intimidation. Videos also emerged showing journalists being pushed, chased or physically heckled by sections of the crowd.
This andhbhakti of CJP is now crossing all limits. You can tell godi media to walk away, raise slogans, but you can’t physically push, grope or beat them.

In Kolkata as well, reporters of mainstream media outlets were allegedly pushed and shoved after a march on July 24 in solidarity with the Jantar Mantar protest.
Why Were Protesters Angry?
The central allegation against sections of legacy media seemed to be that they had stopped acting as the voice of the people and had instead become the voice of the establishment.
For many of the demonstrators, the resentment did not begin with the July protests.
Television news channels have failed, over the years, to hold the Union government to account over a wide range of issues that affect ordinary citizens’ lives — from examination paper leaks and irregularities in recruitment exams to unemployment, price rise, public health etc. This is precisely the role the media is expected to play as democracy’s fourth pillar. Most television news channels that have ample airtime for communal debates and polarising studio confrontations show far less urgency when the failures of the government directly affect the lives and futures of citizens.
The dissatisfaction was not simply about what television channels were reporting during the protests, but what they had consistently chosen not to report. For a generation facing an increasingly precarious education and employment landscape, the perceived reluctance of mainstream television to question those in power became a source of deep distrust.
Explaining the reasons for the anger against the mainstream media, AISA leader and student face of the Delhi protests Neha Bora said, “The hate that the government peddles comes to our drawing rooms, our WhatsApp groups and our very personal lives, within the four walls of our homes, through the Godi media. The Godi media and the IT cell are single-handedly responsible for the venom that runs through the veins of this country presently. Through systematic targeting and organised campaigns, they have made enemies out of citizens, neighbours and friends.”
Elaborating on how they had failed in their duty, she added, “The government is not a God-like figure. They are there to do a job; they have been elected to serve us. They will have to be questioned. The Godi media has systematically dismantled this idea. We are told not to question the government, criticise its policies or talk about the problems we face. If I say that the answer sheet in the Class 12 examination is not mine, the Godi media and the IT cell are going to call me a Pakistani.”
In May, Doordarshan anchor Ashok Srivastav called Class XII student from Delhi Vedant Srivastava a Pakistani. After receiving unexpectedly low marks in Physics, Vedant had applied for photocopies of his answer sheets through CBSE’s reevaluation process. When the copies arrived, he discovered that the Physics answer sheet uploaded by the Board was not his. He made an X account to post about his grievances.
“The disrespect that the youth has for Godi media stems from this — the recognition that this Godi media and its anchors, who scream at the top of their voices on TV screens, have fractured the democratic, secular fabric of this country,” Neha added.
Asked for her response to ground reporters being heckled, Neha said, “We recognise that there are ground reporters in Godi media who do honest work, and that is why we urged our people not to disrespect them. Our differences need not be expressed through violence. We don’t believe in mobs. But there is no denying that the mainstream media has become a BJP propaganda cell, it seems.”
The protesters’ criticism was also shaped by how they believed the movement itself was being portrayed.
Arnab Goswami, for example, in an apparent bid to discredit the protest and question its legitimacy, mentioned China, US, Bangladesh, Pakistan, BitChat, the deep state, Greta Thunberg, Jeremy Corbyn, and even John Cusack as conspirators behind the CJP protest.
In a podcast hosted by Navika Kumar, lyricist and screenwriter Manoj Muntashir Shukla called protesters anti-nationals.
As clashes broke out between protesters and police on July 20, ANI did not post a single news update throughout the day which mentioned injury to protesters.
In Kolkata, Zee reporter Ayan Ghoshal said while interviewing BJP leader Dilip Ghosh, “For the last 3 days efforts are on in Delhi to break India. PM has shown restraint. We know how Pak or Indonesia curbed students’ protest. Dead bodies were strewn on sreets. But no tough action here. They’re getting encouraged.”
The mainstream media drew criticism on social media for what protesters described as coverage that closely mirrored the official version put forward by the Delhi Police and the government. The channels, on the other hand, maintained that they were reporting developments on the ground.

Rahul Shivshankar, editorial director of CNN News 18, amplified a video where RSS leader Atul Limaye called the CJP protest anti-national and “a weapon against the Constitution”.
It is worth noting that coverage of this kind carries risks beyond the newsroom. Framing a protest movement as anti-national, foreign-funded or a security threat can shape how the protesters are treated on the ground, by the state and by ordinary citizens alike. The Zee reporter’s on-air remarks, for example, were arguably not only biased, but amounted to incitement. Seen against this backdrop, at least some of the heckling and intimidation directed at reporters on the ground could be a reaction to this pattern of coverage.
A Widening Trust Deficit
The outpouring of anger at journalists points to a broader crisis of credibility confronting sections of India’s television news industry.
Alt News’s years of fact-checking work and media-watchdog journalism point to a pattern rather than isolated lapses: In the recent past, large sections of mainstream television media have functioned as an echo chamber for the government. The clearest symptom is the collapse of verification standards and rampant amplification of misinformation. During the India-Pakistan military escalation following the Pahalgam attack, several major channels aired unverified and outright false claims — old and unrelated videos and fabricated visuals presented as live combat coverage.
ALSO READ: Op Sindoor: As Indian media made false, outrageous claims, PIB looked the other way
Further in the past, we documented instances of mainstream media broadcasting misinformation targeting protesters and protest movements. During the 2024 farmers’ movement, Republic, News 18, India TV, Zee News, India Today, Navbharat Times — all ran a doctored video of farmer leader Jagjit Singh Dallewal without any context and amplified the misleading claim that he said Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s popularity graph had skyrocketed after the Ram Mandir inauguration and reached an all-time high.
More examples of such misreporting related the farmers’ protest can be found here and here.
It is worth noting that during the farmers’ movement of 2020–21, too, several mainstream television channels faced sustained criticism over their coverage, including banners at protest sites slamming Godi Media. Farmers accused sections of the media of portraying the agitation as foreign-funded or sympathetic to Khalistani groups rather than engaging with their demands. However, the scale and frequency of confrontations witnessed during the CJP-led protests appear significantly greater than what was seen during the farmers’ movement.
ALSO READ: The fictional strikes on the Karachi port and what it says about Indian media
A second, related failure is the normalization of communal debates on prime-time shows. On almost a daily basis, senior journalists anchor panel debates that are structured for conflict, with the hosts allowing and sometimes encouraging inflammatory rhetoric against minorities, because it drives engagement.
Check the thumbnails in the compilations from 2022 below. Each and every bulletin represented by these thumbnails was on communal issues. All on News 18:
Hosted by Aman Chopra:
Shows hosted by Amish Devgan:
The cumulative effect is to cloak hate-mongering as news content night after night. Several prominent channels have faced punitive action in the last few years for peddling communal propaganda on shows hosted by ‘star’ anchors. Related reports by Alt News can be found here, here, here, here and here.
After Operation Sindoor, when several mainstream channels aired unverified and absurd claims, including reports that India had attacked Karachi, the BJP’s official X handle shared a monologue by anchor Sushant Sinha defending the media’s coverage as part of a broader “information war” in national interest.
पाकिस्तान कभी नहीं सुधरेगा और हो सकता है कि युद्ध भी हो, लेकिन क्या ऐसे लड़ेगा भारत?
ऐसे भारत विरोधी तत्वों को पहचानिए, जिन्होंने #OperationSindoor के समय अपने देश, देश की मीडिया और देश की सेना का मजाक बनाया था…
हमारे जवान तो जंग के लिए तैयार हैं, लेकिन क्या आप मन से तैयार… pic.twitter.com/spQrwxqbTm
— BJP (@BJP4India) May 14, 2025
There could be no clearer indicator of the alignment of the mainstream media with the BJP government.
In a functional democracy, the public square is a space that should be open to everyone, equally, without fear, intimidation or violence. Whether that principle still holds in India is increasingly open to question. If sections of society — minorities, independent journalists and critics of the government — cannot live and function without fear of harassment, vilification or even incarceration, the mainstream media has played a significant role in creating and reinforcing that climate. And there appear to be few meaningful avenues for holding these media organisations accountable.
Structural Questions: The Nexus among Media, Corporate Power & the BJP Government
Structural factors help explain this pattern. Both the ownership and revenue models of India’s mainstream media organisations constrain their capacity for critical journalism. Several major outlets — including NDTV, IANS and News18 — are owned by large business conglomerates such as the Adani and Ambani groups, which have close ties to the Union Government.
The journalism produced by these organisations reflects those ties, more often than not. Television news, being capital-intensive, is also heavily dependent on government advertising and large corporate advertisers, who are often reluctant to fund critical journalism.
The incentive to toe the government line shows up not always as an explicit directive but more as a pattern of editorial choices: Aggressive coverage of opposition-ruled states, muted coverage of the same failures under the Union government or in BJP-ruled states; extensive coverage of minor opposition controversies, minimal coverage of major stories embarrassing to the ruling party. See here, here and here.
The closeness between media and corporate power was captured vividly when India Today anchor Rahul Kanwal was filmed tasting food meant for elephants at the Ambanis’ Vantara animal sanctuary, alongside Anant Ambani. For many viewers, the spectacle reinforced the perception of a media establishment more comfortable warming up to power than challenging it.
This was in March 2024. Exactly one year later, Vantara was in the news again. This time, after a South African wildlife coalition urged its government to investigate the transfer of wild animals to the Reliance-owned facility. A handful of Indian outlets reported the concerns, but within days, many of them took down their reports, leaving readers with ‘Error 404’ or ‘Page Not Found’ messages. The reasons for the removals remained unexplained. At least three media houses told Alt News that they had received threatening calls or emails.
In 2018, ABP News managing editor Milind Khandekar and anchor Punya Prasun Bajpai resigned after Bajpai’s show ‘Masterstroke’ fact-checked a claim made during a public interaction involving Prime Minister Modi. Chandramani Kaushik, a farmer from Chhattisgarh, had told Modi her income had doubled after she switched from paddy cultivation to processing custard apple. When ABP interviewed her, she said she had been coached by officials to make the claim. Senior anchor Abhisar Sharma was taken off air days later after e juxtaposed a Modi speech in Lucknow praising Uttar Pradesh’s improved law-and-order record with a shootout in the state on the same day.
Efforts to counter this nexus have had limited success. The Independent and Public-Spirited Media Foundation (IPSMF), set up with funding from Azim Premji and Nandan Nilekani to support independent journalism, has faced funding constraints in recent years and has been the subject of income tax investigations.
These dynamics are reflected in India’s global press freedom rankings, which have declined in the last two decades.
Reporters, like people in every other field of work, must be able to do their job without harassment or fear of violence. And physical retaliation can not become an acceptable response to disliked coverage. Once it is, it can easily be turned against any journalist doing legitimate reporting — not only those seen as compromised. But condemning those attacks should not foreclose an examination of the reasons behind the hostility.
The chants of ‘Godi Media Haye Haye’ were directed not merely at individual reporters standing in front of television cameras, but at institutions that many protesters believe have repeatedly failed to hold those in power accountable. Whether or not that perception is fair, the scenes from Delhi point to a widening gap between a section of India’s youth and parts of the country’s mainstream television news industry — a gap that did not emerge overnight, and is unlikely to close soon.

Union minister Chirag Paswan’s party seeks FIR against ‘influencer’ Swatantra Bhardwaj, calls for strict action
Union minister Chirag Paswan’s party filed a complaint at Parliament Police Station against Swatantra Bhardwaj, alleging that he had falsely used Paswan’s name.
Union minister Chirag Paswan’s party, Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas), on Friday sought registration of an FIR against self-styled influencer Swatantra Bhardwaj, accusing him of using Paswan’s name publicly to falsely suggest he had political backing.
Notably, a clip that went viral purportedly showed Bhardwaj admitting to a violent attack on the father of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activist Nishu Aazad.
In the same video, Bhardwaj allegedly bragged about Delhi Police refusing to take action over the incident, citing his political connections.
Chirag Paswan seeks FIR against Bhardwaj
The Union minister’s party filed a complaint at Parliament Police Station against Bhardwaj, alleging that he had falsely used Paswan’s name and publicly claimed an association with the LJP(RV) president, reported news agency ANI.
The party has urged the police to register an FIR against Bhardwaj and formally record that he has no association with the party or the matter in question.
It has also called for strict action against the accused.
Will ensure justice for Aazad's father: Paswan
The complaint comes after Paswan earlier said he was "taking full responsibility" for ensuring justice for CJP activist Nishu Aazad's father, who was attacked and seriously injured during protests at Jantar Mantar.
"In public life, many people come to meet us. But if somebody claims, on this very basis to be a personal acquaintance of ours, then that is a misuse of our name. The attacker has sought to give the impression that action has not been taken against him because of me and my party. I have lodged a formal complaint against this misuse of my name," Paswan was quoted as saying by news agency PTI.
He added, "It is indeed a serious matter that the student activist's father was beaten so severely that he could have died. The attacker has the temerity to brag about the incident on TV, and he roams scot-free. I take full responsibility to ensure justice to the aggrieved family by pursuing the matter with Delhi police."
Swatantra Bhardwaj detained
Bhardwaj was taken into custody in Uttar Pradesh’s Bulandshahr on Friday, just hours after Delhi Police allegedly assured CJP protesters that he would be arrested within 72 hours.
Police said Bhardwaj had tried to flee but was caught, HT has learnt.

After 12 years of fried chicken and flirting, hit YouTube series Chicken Shop Date to end
Creator Amelia Dimoldenberg interviewed dozens of celebrities, including some Canadians
After more than a decade of interviewing and flirting with movie stars, musicians and athletes while sharing some fried chicken, Amelia Dimoldenberg, the host of the popular YouTube talk show Chicken Shop Date, announced this week she's closing up shop.
"To me the show is my very own romcom and I have loved creating so many stories for you to watch. I am so grateful to everyone who has followed me on this journey and found some joy in these episodes," Dimoldenberg wrote in an Instagram post on Thursday.
"I never thought I'd stop Chicken Shop Date, I thought maybe it would be a part of me forever, and in some way it always will, but I feel like it's now time to move on from this adventure and onto a new one."
Dimoldenberg started the show 12 years ago, interviewing musicians in Britain's underground rap scene. Since then, she's gone on to chat with celebs, including Keke Palmer, Conan O'Brien, Paul McCartney and Jack Harlow and garnered close to 3.5 million subscribers to her YouTube channel.
Chicken Shop Date follows a simple format: Dimoldenberg goes on a date of sorts with a celebrity at a fried chicken shop in London and asks them a blend of questions that are flirty, funny and sometimes awkward.
It produces the type of banter you'd more likely expect on a first date than a typical sit-down, talk show style interview. In some cases, like her 2024 sit-down with Andrew Garfield, it's led to what seemed to be some actual flirting.
"This is called flirting, Amelia, this is called flirting," Garfield says at one point.
Dimoldenberg also has some Canadians among her dozens of interviews. That includes Ryan Reynolds, whom Dimoldenberg corrects when he gives the wrong name for the character his wife Blake Lively played on Gossip Girl.
"That is right, Brooke from Gossip Girl loves you," Reynolds tells Dimoldberg, hinting at Lively's fandom of her show. At that point, Dimoldenberg points out Lively's character was named Serena.
"I don't think there is a Brooke," Dimoldenberg says.
Shania Twain also sat down for a date with Dimoldenberg in 2023, where Twain revealed that she'd never actually met Brad Pitt (despite mentioning him in her hit song That Don't Impress Me Much).
The massive success of her YouTube channel has led to opportunities for Dimoldenberg outside the chicken shop, including working the red carpet at the Oscars this year, where she interviewed another Canadian, Hudson Williams.
It's unclear what Dimoldenberg's next move is after Chicken Shop Date, but it appears she has some irons in the fire. She's currently signed on to develop a young adult drama series for the BBC, according to Deadline.
But in her goodbye post on Instagram, Dimoldenberg also promised "a few final dates" before ending the show for good.

Clashes in southern Sudan leave at least 21 dead, medical group says
A doctors' group says at least 21 people, including women and children, have been killed in southern Sudan
CAIRO -- Clashes in southern Sudan have killed at least 21 people, including women and children, a doctors' group said Friday.
Sudan Doctors Network, which tracks violence throughout the war in Sudan, said that the rebel group Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, or SPLM-N, launched an attack on Thursday in the areas of Debi and Luweri in the town of Kauda in South Kordofan.
Rebel leader Abdel Aziz al-Hilu has aligned his fighters with the Sudanese paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, which has been battling the Sudanese military since 2023. The war killed at least 59,000 people, displaced some 13 million and pushed parts of the country into famine.
Al-Hilu’s group has been active in South Kordofan and joined a local government set up by the RSF. The group is a breakaway faction of the SPLM, the ruling party of neighboring South Sudan.
Thursday's attack was part of clashes that erupted between SPLM-N and the Otoro tribe, a minority group in the Nuba Mountains of South Kordofan.
The fighting came despite a ceasefire initiative backed by the RSF last month. The medical group said the attacks by al-Hilu's forces “constitute a clear violation of the agreement, a resumption of hostilities, and the targeting of civilians on an ethnic basis.”
Al-Hilu didn’t commit to the ceasefire agreement, and his forces launched attacks on 10 Otoro villages, displacing hundreds of civilians between Aug. 20 and 26, the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, a think tank, said in an analysis last week. It added that SPLM-N claimed in a video that it took control of Kauda.
Ali Mahmoud Ali, the group's Sudan analyst, said that the latest clashes risk bringing in more Nuba clans into the fight and could increase divisions across South Kordofan, where communities are facing an already dire humanitarian situation.
The group said it has recorded the killings of at least 158 people since violence erupted in March over land disputes.

Taylor v Pili - Irish icon's farewell fight predictions
- Published
Katie Taylor brings the curtain down on a remarkable career on Saturday when she faces unbeaten Flora Pili in front of 80,000 fans at Croke Park in Dublin.
Taylor is an Olympic gold medallist and two-weight undisputed champion who has won 25 of her 26 professional fights, with six victories by stoppage.
The 40-year-old has long dreamed of fighting at Croke Park and will finally get her wish in the final bout of her career.
French challenger Pili, 29, is undefeated in 12 professional contests, with two stoppage wins. She is former European champion, but has never faced anyone with Taylor's pedigree or experience.
Victory in the light-welterweight contest would provide a fairytale ending for one of Ireland's greatest sporting careers and see Taylor become an undisputed champion for a third time.
Can Taylor produce one final vintage performance on the biggest night of her career?
Or will the younger, unbeaten Pili spoil the occasion and pull off a mammoth upset?

"Saturday is the perfect tribute to probably the greatest female boxer that has ever lived in Katie Taylor. Flora Pili has the perfect style that will make Katie Taylor look great.

"100% Katie Taylor wins. It will be a night where she captures the hearts of not just Ireland but so many nations. She is the purest of souls and that is so much more of boxing. I pray that when she leaves that ring she knows what she has done for the people who will come through in boxing."

Prediction - Taylor

An experimental gene therapy for Angelman syndrome from Ultragenyx failed in a Phase 3 study, STAT reports. The medicine showed no benefit compared to a sham treatment in the rare disease, which causes severe intellectual disability and developmental delays. The drug, called GTX-102, had shown powerful results in early trials, raising the hopes of families affected by the devastating condition. The trial failure is also a significant blow to Ultragenyx’s business, and the company said it’s now planning “significant expense reductions.”
Just a week after the landmark U.S. approval of a game-changing drug for advanced pancreatic cancer, the same therapy is showing promise against the world’s biggest cancer killer, Nature tells us. In a small trial in non-small cell lung cancer, the drug, Revolutions Medicines’ Rasonque, shrank tumors in more than 30% of participants. Each patient had tumor-promoting mutations in a member of the RAS family of proteins, and had previously tried other therapies. A larger study in which participants with non-small cell lung cancer are randomly assigned to receive either the drug, also called daraxonrasib, or standard chemotherapy is underway.

Having An air quality monitor for your home is more important than you may think. As climate change speeds up and wildfires increasingly engulf large swaths of land, leaving behind smoke that makes air potentially hazardous to breathe, it's more important than ever to ensure you're breathing clean air. An at-home air quality monitor is a simple way to ensure that, whether it be car exhaust, wildfire smoke, pollutants from seasonal changes, or simply fumes from your gas stove, the air around you is safe to breathe.
These air quality monitors test the air quality both indoors and outdoors, and on top of measuring PM2.5 (particulate matter) in the air and AQI (air quality index), they can also give insights into the air you're breathing, including measuring temperature, humidity, CO2, VOCs, and more.
Our top pick, IQAir's Air Visual Pro ($330), measures for several factors and has an easy-to-read display, while our more basic budget pick, Temptop S1 PM2.5 Air Quality Monitor & Indoor Thermometer ($28), has been solid throughout prolonged testing.
For more ways to keep your air quality in check for a healthier environment, take a look at our guides to the Best Outdoor Air Quality Monitors, Best Air Purifiers, and Best Multiuse Air Purifiers. Plus, check out how we test them and how to pick the right air purifier for your home.

How I Tested
In the past, I've relied on my phone's weather app to measure the air quality around me, and the government’s free AirNow website, where you can plug in your zip code and see its easy-to-read air quality meter. Now, as I test air purifiers, I always make sure to corroborate the purifiers' built-in PM2.5 or AQI measurements with an independent outside source—a separate air quality monitor—to test both the accuracy of the machine and the purifier's efficacy in filtering pollutants and getting the air quality back to a healthy level.
These air quality monitors were tested in various locations around my house, when cooking on my unventilated gas stove, under my living room window that draws in a lot of building and exhaust fumes, and outside my cat's litter box. Plus, I did additional testing outdoors, where I measured the monitors’ readings against local weather apps. And when field testing air purifiers with a sealed tent and smoke pellets as mentioned above, I always use an air quality monitor to check pollutant levels and the purifiers' efficacy when timed to get back to healthy levels.
Why Do I Need an Air Quality Monitor?
Like I mentioned above, I think it's especially important to have an air quality monitor to test whether your air both inside and outside the home is healthy if you don't have an air purifier. But it's also important to have one to measure the efficacy of the air purifier(s) in your home to ensure they are doing their job as efficiently as claimed. Especially since after prolonged use (and time), the built-in sensors can clog and give inaccurate readings.
When placing or installing an air quality monitor, try to measure at the breathing zone height, around 3 to 6 feet off the floor. An air quality monitor is especially helpful against some of the more harmful effects of things like wildfire smog, which can't always be smelled or seen. But an air quality monitor can sense that there is too much bad air, and then you can adjust the air purifier fan(s) accordingly.
It can also help to instill healthy habits, as WIRED Reviews contributor Lisa Wood Shapiro notes, using air quality monitors taught her to turn on the kitchen exhaust fan and crank up an air purifier before she turns on her gas stove. In the past, she didn’t think much of a little smoke from cooking. Now she takes proactive steps to avoid inhaling harmful pollutants.
Once you start noticing bad air and take steps to correct it, you'll notice fewer allergy symptoms and, often, fewer upper respiratory sicknesses and improved sleep. Even innocuous household things like lit candles, cooking on a stovetop without an exhaust fan (guilty), or aerosol air fresheners can negatively impact indoor air in real time. Get yourself an air quality monitor and see for yourself.
What to Consider Before Buying
Even though many current air purifier models have built-in air quality sensors, having a designated air quality monitor is a great way to independently corroborate or monitor air quality and pollutants. Plus, these handheld monitors are also portable and able to more accurately test air quality outdoors.
Before you purchase your own indoor air quality monitor, here are some things to know: Sensors on the WIRED-tested AirVisual Pro and PurpleAir all performed well in an independent study. Low-cost consumer air quality monitors are much cheaper (in the $200 or less range) than what's used by the professionals, but are also less accurate and not as easily calibrated. When testing multiple air quality monitors, they will not usually give the exact same AQI, but they are usually very close.
Consumer air quality monitors use sensors to detect tiny invisible particles in the air and other contaminants, with some sensors using light scattering to detect fine particulate matter known as PM10, like the dust visible in light, and invisible health hazards like PM2.5, which can reach the deepest parts of the lungs and enter the bloodstream.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

A keenly observed class drama shown through the eyes of a child, Shalini Adnani’s “Our Share of Sand” overcomes its characters’ narrow construction through its brooding intensity. Set against a sand-mining crisis in modern India, it tells of a 12-year-old British Asian girl, Maya (Maya Mehta), who returns to the country to join her industrialist father Rohan (Mohammad Zeeshan Ayyub), and bears witness to a routine accident in his line of work. As notions of justice, power and inequity begin to shade her peripheral vision, Maya is torn between speaking out and adhering to the moral compartmentalization that goes hand in hand with her family’s generational success.
Adnani, a Chilean-born Londoner of Indian descent, draws on her memories of visiting India as a young outsider in crafting the film’s atmosphere, and her protagonist’s confined perspective. Such an approach runs the risk of gawking at an unfamiliar people, their hegemonies and their ways of life, even with the best intentions. But by rooting her tale in Maya’s family ties, the writer-director explores the complicity of well-to-do South Asian diasporas, and the foundations that afford them the luxury of emigrating in the first place. It begins with a brief, poetic prologue set decades ago — seemingly outside of time — as obscured day-laborers sift through sandy riverbanks and discover an enormous diamond. Their faces remain hidden, as a debate ensues about whether they should alert their boss to its discovery.
Popular on Variety
The next time we see this diamond, in a contemporary setting, Maya’s stern paternal aunt, Arti (Jyoti Dogra), shows it off while regaling her with their family’s mythology, wherein her grandfather discovered the gem and sold a fragment of it to uplift them after postcolonial partition. It’s worth noting that the aforementioned quandary, about alerting the laborers’ boss, is never answered: Did the grandfather really find the diamond himself, as a worker, or did he simply claim it from his employees?
There’s no way to prove the veracity of this “bootstraps” creation myth, a lingering doubt that informs the film’s saga of cyclical inequality. This initially takes unassuming form, as Maya grows friendly with Kiran (Krish Raj More), a boy of a similar age. There’s already a division between them — Maya doesn’t speak much Hindi or Marathi (the local language), while Kiran doesn’t speak English, though they just about understand each other — which is only reinforced when Maya’s father scolds Kiran to get back to work.
The adolescent turning out to be in Rohan’s employ ought to come as no surprise: Caste and class remain inflexible facets of Indian society, including on the outskirts of Mumbai, where the film is set. Kiran, dismissively treated, is one of Rohan’s divers, and a vital manual laborer in the cement production chain laying the foundation for India’s modern development. It isn’t long before Rohan’s regulation-skirting methods leads to an accident by nightfall, which leaves Kiran permanently injured. This in turn leads Maya (a key witness) and her British Indian mother Priti (Ellora Torchia) to quietly question what they ought to say to the police — if anything at all.
Although the film never gives its divisions a name — much of it unfolds through Maya’s sheltered perspective — its setting provides the perfect symbolism for a nation built on discrimination. Caste becomes a silent killer, as the expectations foisted upon Rohan’s workers collide with subdued pleas for their humanity. (Some of them are understandably furious, but others know there’s only so much they can say.) Granted, most characters barely exist outside the confines of the plot, and how they relate to social strata is their defining characteristic. We know little about Maya’s life before her arrival, or Kiran’s outside his work, or the family beyond their casual cruelty. But within this storytelling paradigm, Adnani imbues each scene with a dramatic wrath bubbling just beneath the surface.
This tension is often subtext enough, and it’s accentuated by cinematographer Adric Watson’s tight and dirty frames, which confine Maya and Arti through astute visual composition, as the reality of their cushy lives is gradually illuminated. There’s also occasional use of night photography, by way of the family compound’s security cameras where you wouldn’t expect them, gesturing at a thematic handshake between the upkeep of caste superiority and fascistic surveillance. It’s the closest “Our Share of Sand” gets to casting a wide net over India’s contemporary political milieu, and while this facet remains largely unexplored, the film’s confining focus on Maya’s point of view pays a number of dramatic dividends.
Not only does Mehta deliver a stunning debut performance, as a young girl perturbed by the world and her place within it, but the film’s sinister, shadowy tone makes even natural spaces feel imposing. The result is a twisted, naturalistic fairytale about structural realities; with the right boot-heel at one’s neck, even ostensibly life-giving forces like forests and rivers can be turned against innocent people.

Oscar-winner Marion Cotillard (“La Vie en Rose”) is at the Venice Film Festival in a new guise, as tutor of Biennale College Cinema, the workshop allowing emerging filmmakers to develop and produce micro-budget feature-length films, which is sponsored by Chanel.
Biennale College Cinemas was conceived 15 years ago by Venice chief Alberto Barbera in tandem with Torino Film Lab topper Savina Neirotti, who heads the unique Venice initiative.
During this time Biennale College has spawned 49 feature film projects made with micro-budgets with grants that after the first decade rose from €150,00 ($174,00) to €200,00 ($232) during the past five years. “These works provide a bird’s eye view of what it means to debut as a filmmaker today,” Neirotti noted.
Popular on Variety
“When Chanel told me about this program, I was very touched,” said Cotillard. “Above all, I think it’s very important to support films that are struggling to get off the ground financially these days,” she added.
“Not all films are destined to draw millions of viewers and turn a profit, and I think it’s very important to support artists — artists from all over the world – some of whom, even in their own countries, simply don’t have access to production opportunities,” she noted.
“And what’s really striking about the films I’ve seen — the four films I’ve seen – is their artistic passion; that need to tell stories,” Cotillard continued.
This year’s Biennale College projects, all first works, hail from China, Italy, Mexico, Spain and the U.S. They are: “Demeter in Exile,” by Italian director Maria Giovanna Cicciari who is teamed wth producer Raffaella Pontarelli. “Gu Shi” by Chinese director Yinan Song and produced by Yueyi Xing; “Moonfish,” by U.S. director Daniel Zvereff who is teamed with Spanish producer Mireia Villanova; and “Tijuana Todavía” by Mexian director Gabriel Gutierrez Morales working with producer Humberto Busto Marín.
Barbera also said he will soon be announcing the winner of the first edition of Biennale College Blend, the initiative’s new strand for artists looking to explore stories in the multi-media space comprising forms of expression such as music, visual arts, and performing arts.

What the Floods Say About Xi Jinping
China’s leader behaves more like an emperor than a man of the people.
When the Yangtze River flooded in 1998 and inundated villages in central China, Jiang Zemin, the Communist Party’s general secretary, was on the scene, bullhorn in hand, to encourage local relief efforts. Ten years later, his successor, Hu Jintao, stood among the rubble after an earthquake rocked Sichuan province, in the country’s southwest. Last week, after floodwaters caused by a collapsing glacier tore through the Himalayas between Nepal and China, leaving more than 1,100 people dead and thousands more missing, the party’s current general secretary, Xi Jinping, stayed largely and safely in Beijing.
In the United States, where politicians have to worry about the needs and feelings of voters, elected representatives are expected to be more visible and engaged in national crises. In 2021, Republican Senator Ted Cruz earned public condemnation when he was caught absconding to Mexico while Texas suffered a deep freeze and power outages. As a Communist dictator, Xi doesn’t have to fret over public-approval ratings. Yet his absence signals a bigger problem for China: Xi has become so powerful that he has lost touch with the country he governs.
Despite being professed Marxists, China’s leaders rarely interact with the working class. But Xi at least used to try to seem like a man of the people. In 2013, about a year into his tenure, Chinese media made a big deal out of his visit to a steamed-bun restaurant in Beijing; the state-owned China Daily praised him for showing his “common touch.”
Today, there’s nothing common about Xi Jinping. He has amassed greater personal power than any other Chinese leader since Mao Zedong, the Communist regime’s founder, who died half a century ago. To justify his outsize role in China’s government, Xi’s tireless propagandists portray him as something grander than a party boss: a philosopher king, whose doctrine of wisdom, called Xi Jinping Thought, is meant to be both studied and obeyed. He is the great global statesman, guiding foreign policy into a new era of peace and prosperity. His various “global initiatives” outline his vision for a reformed world order.
Mere mortals such as Jiang and Hu had to stomp around muddy disaster zones to prove their worth. But Xi “does not need to go to steam-bun shops to pretend he is with the people any longer, or, for that matter, to be visible when a major disaster has happened,” Steve Tsang, the director of the SOAS China Institute at the University of London, told me. “He no doubt thinks and therefore acts as if he is above all.”
In Xi’s calculus, the Himalayan communities destroyed by the floods are hardly worthy of his attention. The area in question is part of Tibet, a region that borders Nepal and was once independent. Xi has demonstrated a persistent hostility toward China’s minorities, who, in their stubborn resistance to Chinese civilization, threaten his vision of national unity. A new law that took effect in July aims to transform Tibetans, Uyghurs, Mongolians, and other minorities into properly loyal citizens by forcing them to adopt the majority Han Chinese culture. Until the Tibetans fall in line, “there is not really a compelling reason for him to visit them just because a disaster struck,” Tsang argued.
From Xi’s perspective, appearing at the scene of the floods would have involved more risk than reward. A purportedly all-knowing and all-seeing leader can’t make mistakes or even be associated with bad news, so Xi has good reason to avoid potentially tarnishing himself with an uncertain rescue operation. The politically safer option involves managing the crisis from afar while dispatching others to get their hands dirty. Beijing is also carefully controlling the information coming from the disaster zone. International journalists are already barred from Tibet, so any news about the disaster and the relief effort is from Chinese state sources. The state-run news agency Xinhua duly announced on Friday that Xi chaired a meeting of the party’s powerful politburo to “deliberate and make arrangements on rescue and relief efforts.”
The China-focused research firm Trivium noted that Xi’s response to the floods was in keeping with his usual approach to disasters, which is to visit long after the crisis has passed and the rebuilding has begun. Xi is “keeping himself above operational risk” and is focused on “owning the recovery rather than the chaos,” Trivium’s report said. Xi may at some point decide to show up on the ground, but probably well after the initial chaos has subsided.
The stories and images from the floods have moved hearts, but Xi has bigger things to think about than a mudslide on the far edge of his empire. One of his priorities has been to reshape Chinese culture by merging the party’s beloved Marxism with traditional Confucianism. Although that effort appears to have had little traction with the public, Xi himself seems to have taken these ideas to heart. He may speak like a socialist, but he governs more like an emperor, deserving of national veneration and shielded from scrutiny. But many emperors were remote figures, removed from the real world behind the walls of the Forbidden City, and reliant on courtiers for news from outside. As Xi’s absence from the flooding disaster demonstrates, he, too, has become detached from the daily struggles and sentiments of his citizens—and unresponsive to the nation’s mounting economic and social problems as a result.
How the Chinese people feel about Xi’s response is impossible to know. Assiduous censors deter candor and cleanse social-media platforms of any direct criticism. Perhaps life in an authoritarian political system breeds a practical indifference, given that people have no influence over who rules them anyway. But with a spare few hours on the ground among those who just lost everything, Xi could have at least shown that he cares. His loyal public has surely noticed that even that was too much.

On Feb. 24, 2025, the Food and Drug Administration did something it arguably should have done long ago: It removed the elaborate monitoring program that has governed one of psychiatry’s most important drugs, clozapine, for more than 30 years. For anyone who treats serious mental illness, this is welcome news.
But I want to say something more complicated about it, because I have spent a large part of my career prescribing this drug (or trying to) to the most vulnerable population there is: children with psychosis. The paperwork was never really the problem.
Very few things in all of medicine have struck me as close to miraculous. Vaccines. Antibiotics. And, in children with childhood-onset schizophrenia, clozapine. That will not surprise anyone who has worked with it in schizophrenia.
Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic we have for the sickest patients: the roughly 1 in 3 people with schizophrenia whose illness does not yield to other medicines. It is the only drug approved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, the only one shown to reduce suicide, and it is associated with lower death rates than the alternatives. When nothing else has worked, clozapine can, sometimes, give a person back to themselves. I have watched it happen in children, in the carefully controlled trials my colleagues and I ran, where young people who had been lost to relentless psychosis began, within days, to return to their families.
And yet it is one of the most underused drugs in all of medicine. In the United States, only about 4% of people with schizophrenia receive clozapine, though perhaps a third could benefit, and the figure should probably be higher still in childhood-onset schizophrenia, which tends to be even more treatment-resistant. There is, in plain terms, a proven, lifesaving, sometimes life-restoring treatment that American medicine mostly declines to give.
For years, simply to prescribe clozapine, a clinician had to enroll in an FDA-mandated registry. Patients submitted to regular blood draws, which are weekly at the start, with each result logged into a national database before a pharmacy could release the next supply. The goal was to catch the small number of patients in whom clozapine can sharply reduce the white cells that fight infection.
Whatever caution it began in, there is good evidence it also kept the drug from people who needed it. That is the very program the FDA has now retired, perhaps influenced by advocacy efforts, including those by parents.
But the deeper barrier was fear. Clozapine carries a fearsome reputation: the blood tests, the long list of side effects, the rare but genuine danger. This has scared clinicians; they just don’t want to take the risk. And the FDA can remove the registry, but cannot make the fear go away.
This is especially true when dealing with children, in whom neutropenia tends to be more common than in adults. I have watched capable, caring clinicians steer around clozapine for years, reaching for a fourth or fifth less-effective medication rather than the one most likely to work, because avoiding it simply felt safer. Recently I could not find a single child psychiatrist across four academic centers willing to start clozapine in a child with childhood-onset schizophrenia.
When I first started using clozapine, I was afraid as well. But it soon became clear that it was not a particularly difficult medicine to work with. Yes, you have to monitor the side effects carefully, but the benefits simply made the risk worth taking. And as I started seeing the benefits of clozapine, the fear quickly went away.
After all, in other areas of medicine, we treat children with many risky medications (such as chemotherapeutic drugs) because we know they are lifelines for those illnesses. We need to approach clozapine the same way when it comes to schizophrenia.
In my experience, parents were rarely the problem. They understood, they were desperate, had often done the work of getting over their fear, and were ahead of the curve. They typically had already heard and read about clozapine and were ready to be on board as soon as we were ready, partly because they had tried everything and nothing had worked. I used to say, after seeing what I saw at the National Institute of Mental Health, “If someone in my family was diagnosed with schizophrenia, I would want them on clozapine yesterday.”
The cost of our avoidance of clozapine is invisible but enormous, measured in people who stay sick, and in lives that end early, for want of a drug already sitting on the shelf.
I do not mean to minimize the side effects of clozapine. The risks are very real. My colleagues and I ran into them at the NIMH every now and then. We went on to study how often it happened in our children, and who was most at risk. The problem is concentrated in the first months of treatment, and it never quite reaches zero.
But we found ways through: We showed, for instance, that adding lithium could lift the neutrophil count enough to keep a child safely on clozapine, and we published it. Its other side effects, too, can be managed, and there is ample literature, including from our own group, on how to do that in children. In fact, as we published more, we began to notice something new: Some of the children referred to our study arrived already on clozapine, something we had never seen in the study’s earlier years.
Those of us who worked closely with clozapine had argued for years that its monitoring was stricter than the evidence justified; that a rigid, uniform schedule, largely unchanged for decades, treated every patient as though the danger were constant and equal, when in truth it was concentrated in the early months, foreseeable, and, in most cases, manageable. The FDA’s recent decision, in that sense, is less a reversal than an overdue acknowledgment of what the people closest to the drug had been saying all along.
Notably, the FDA still recommends the blood tests; it has simply stopped forcing them. This is a welcome change, and it means the responsibility that used to live inside a federal registry now lives where it probably always should have: in the judgment of the clinician and the informed choice of the patient.
That is the real opportunity in this decision, and the real test of it. Lifting the program is not permission to be careless; it is an invitation to be wise, and better informed.
Ideally it will empower clinicians to reach for clozapine sooner, for the people most likely to be saved by it, including the young. The worst outcome would be to lose the bureaucratic barrier and go on avoiding the drug anyway, only now without even a rule to blame.
And perhaps, and this is my real hope, it will move us to reach for clozapine earlier, rather than only as a last resort. To my colleagues who care for the youngest and sickest patients, I would put it as plainly as I can: Do not let fear make this decision for you. We have spent three decades treating clozapine as the door you open only after every other has failed. The science has never justified waiting that long. The government has now removed one of our excuses. Whether we use this moment to actually reach the patients who need it, or simply find a new reason to look away, is up to us. It always was.
Nitin Gogtay, M.D., is a psychiatrist, physician-scientist, and author of “The Vanishing Children” (HarperCollins, January 2027). He spent almost two decades studying and conducting blinded clinical trials of clozapine on childhood-onset schizophrenia at the National Institute of Mental Health.
