Trump admits he is putting his name on everything because nobody will after he’s ‘gone’
The president thinks his name ‘should’ be on the White House ballroom as he speedruns through legacy-defining construction projects
Donald Trump is hoping a massive ballroom and military installation on the White House grounds will one day bear his name as he speedruns through several multi-million dollar construction projects across the nation’s capital to secure his presidential legacy.
He recently admitted to New York Magazine’s Ben Terris that he is slapping his name on things because he knows nobody else will after he’s “gone.”
Trump conceded that Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, who remarked earlier this year that the president appears to be building monuments to himself because no one else wants to, may be right.
“That’s true,” Trump told Terris. “Nobody will do it once I’m gone. When I leave here, nobody will.”
The president’s remarkably candid comments to the magazine follow an unprecedented blitz across Washington, D.C., to either put his name or leave an unmistakably Trump-like imprint on buildings, monuments and other landmarks before the former real-estate mogul leaves the White House.
The president is embroiled in several lawsuits against his efforts to remake D.C., including renaming the Kennedy Center and its campus after him, overhauling the capital’s beloved golf course and renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
Trump also is planning to build his own version of the Arc de Triomphe to tower over the capital, and his face is printed on massive banners hanging from federal buildings, including the Department of Justice headquarters. The Department of State also created a commemorative “Patriot Passport” featuring an image of a scowling Trump leaning on his fists while standing in front of the Constitution, and the U.S. Mint is now circulating a commemorative $1 coin with his face on it.
He’s also naming his policy achievements after himself — there are “Trump Accounts,” “TrumpRx,” and a “Trump Gold Card” that offers a fast-track to legal residency in the U.S. for the price of $1 million. The U.S. military is also developing a line of “Trump-class” battleships as well as the USS Donald J. Trump aircraft carrier.
But his biggest and most-expensive project yet is the transformation of what was once the East Wing of the White House into a gold-filled, bullet-proof ballroom sandwiched between a “military complex” that includes a sprawling underground bunker and with a “drone port” roof.
Recently revealed designs for the project show plans for an ornate, gold-stuffed interior with golden marble floors and a chandelier, as well as gold finishes on the exterior that were not previously included in plans approved by federal agencies earlier this year.
The Supreme Court has allowed the president to continue construction while federal judges — and even Chief Justice John Roberts — question the legality of the entire project after the administration destroyed the East Wing to make way for a 90,000-square-foot facility that officials say is vital to national security and the president’s safety.
Trump told New York Magazine that he hopes his name is on it.
“It should,” he said. “I don’t know if it will, but it should.”
A senior administration official told the magazine that “his rush to get it done in this term is so important because it’s something the Democrats would have a hard time taking away or getting rid of.”
“When the ballroom is built, everyone will always know in perpetuity that it was built by Donald Trump,” the person said. “Are Democrats going to come in and rip it down? I have a hard time believing that.”
Trump said he doesn’t believe it can even be physically torn down — a point of argument brought by preservationists who have tried, and failed, to stop him in court from further construction. Materials for the project are intended to be nuclear-blast resistant.
“I don’t think they could, physically,” Trump told the magazine of potential efforts in the future to tear it down.
“It’s made with the most powerful steel welded together and concrete that is so hard and so strong it’s used in nuclear-power plants,” he added. “You could take a jackhammer and go to those columns and stand there for two days at full blast and you wouldn’t even see a mark. It’s nuclear concrete. I think it would be very hard. It’s meant for if there’s a nuclear attack. I’m not sure you could take it down.”
Trump also appears to be more focused not just on his legacy — as he faces the likelihood of impeachment proceedings and investigations in his remaining years in office — but his mortality, as the 80-year-old president prepares for a second half of his administration as the oldest one ever.
The president appears to have grown more introspective and openly discussed the end of his life following a series of alleged assassination attempts. He has even mused publicly about whether he will go to heaven.
“I want to try and get to heaven, if possible,” Trump told Fox & Friends last year as he discussed ending Russia’s war in Ukraine. “I’m hearing I’m not doing well. I’m really at the bottom of the totem pole. But if I can get to heaven, this will be one of the reasons.”

Kolkata school teacher suspended for asking student to wipe off tilak: Adhikari
S Chowdhury, the school’s secretary, told HT that the action was taken after the institution received a notice from the district inspector (DI) of schools on Thursday
A Kolkata school teacher has been suspended and a police case has been registered against her because she forced a student to remove his sandalwood tilak from his forehead, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari announced on Friday.
“A teacher from the Holy Mission English Medium School has been suspended for repeatedly forcing a boy to wash off his sandalwood tilak. An FIR (first information report) has also been lodged against the teacher,” Adhikari said.
The school, established 25 years ago, is located in New Alipore, south Kolkata. It is affiliated to the West Bengal Board of Secondary Education and has around 1200 students and 60 teachers.
S Chowdhury, the school’s secretary, told HT that the action was taken after the institution received a notice from the district inspector (DI) of schools on Thursday following a complaint lodged by a Class 5 student.
“The teacher was asked to explain the matter before the school’s disciplinary committee,” he said.
According to the teacher, the boy was asked to wash his face on Wednesday because the tilak had smudged in the heat and spread across his forehead. “The boy possibly misconstrued this,” Chowdhury said.
“The teacher has been suspended until the matter is decided by the school management committee. Around 80 % of our students are non-Bengalis, and the majority are Hindus. Many of them come to school with tilaks. We never stopped anyone from following any religious custom,” Chowdhury said.
The official, however, underlined that neither the government nor the police had informed the school that an FIR had been lodged. “We came to know about this when we saw the video of the chief minister’s press conference,” Chowdhury said.
At the press conference, Adhikari also announced that a state employee at Bikash Bhawan in Salt Lake, Paromita Sen, had been suspended for an objectionable social media post about Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
“Nobody can post such things about the Prime Minister. These matters will be dealt with strictly,” he said.

When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.
She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.
India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.
Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.
While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.
Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.
She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.
“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.
Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.
She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”
India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.
When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.
Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.
She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.
At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.
But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.
On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.
Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.
Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.
But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.
Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.
She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.
In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.
“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.
The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.
She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.
“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”
Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.
“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”
She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.
Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.
And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.
Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.

Indian state gives taxi and tuk-tuk drivers a year to learn local language
- Published
An Indian state has given taxi and tuk-tuk drivers one more year to learn the local language after a new rule making it mandatory sparked protests.
Transport officials in the western state of Maharashtra had begun testing drivers' ability to conduct basic conversations in Marathi, the state's official language, on 20 August. Those who failed were given a month to learn the language, after which they risked having their licences suspended or cancelled.
The government said the requirement was meant to improve communication between drivers and passengers and ensure safer journeys.
But the rule alarmed drivers' unions, who argued that workers should not risk losing their livelihoods while they were still learning the language. Many of the drivers are migrants who came to Maharashtra from other parts of India in search of work, including the populous Hindi-speaking states of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.
Amid protests, Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis announced last week that the drivers would be given another year to learn Marathi, as many had been out of the formal education system for years and needed more time.
State Transport Minister Pratap Sarnaik has said that drivers will be expected to learn Marathi during the year and that there will be more extensions.
Maharashtra has almost 979,000 valid tuk-tuk and taxi permits, nearly half of them in the Mumbai metropolitan region.
The extension has brought some relief to drivers who had feared losing their ability to work.
"We were worried that if our licences were suspended, our daily income would be affected," says Lakhan Pandey, a taxi driver in Mumbai. "Now we feel somewhat relieved."
But the row has reopened a much older debate in Maharashtra, where questions of language, migration and jobs have shaped politics for decades.
"The issue is not simply about communication between drivers and passengers, but about Marathi identity, migration and employment," says Prakash Akolkar, a journalist, author and political analyst.
Those tensions stretch back to the creation of Maharashtra itself. The state was formed in 1960 after a long campaign for a Marathi-speaking state.
As Mumbai grew into India's financial centre, it drew generations of migrants from across the country in search of work. Language became increasingly entwined with arguments over jobs and opportunities for Marathi speakers.
In 1966, the Shiv Sena, a regional political party rooted in Marathi nationalism, was founded on a "sons of the soil" platform, arguing that Marathi speakers were losing jobs to migrants. It went on to become one of Maharashtra's most powerful political forces, with Marathi identity at the heart of its appeal.
Today, Maharashtra is governed by a coalition led by Fadnavis's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and one faction of the Shiv Sena, which split in 2022. The rival faction and another regional party, the Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS), have also championed the Marathi cause.
Akolkar says it is reasonable to expect people who move to a state to learn some of the local language. But he draws a distinction between that and the politics around it.
"Ordinary people do not always treat language with the same intensity as political parties," he says, adding that parties have often raised the issue when it suits the political circumstances.
Deepak Pawar, a political scientist and president of the Marathi Abhyas Kendra (Marathi Training Centre), which promotes the language, takes a stronger view. He argues that people who have lived in Maharashtra for years should already have acquired at least a basic knowledge of Marathi.
Refusing to learn the local language after living and working in the state for years is "linguistic arrogance", he says.
It's a tension that has played out in other states including Karnataka, where language activists fear their local language - Kannada - is being marginalised as many migrants believe they can get by using Hindi or English.
In Maharashtra, the government says drivers are not expected to read or write Marathi, or to speak it fluently. Under changes to the state's motor vehicle rules, they are required to have a "working knowledge" of the language.
To help them learn, the government has organised classes focused on Marathi words and phrases drivers might need at work - asking passengers where they want to go, discussing fares or giving directions.
Around 166,000 drivers have completed the training and passed an oral test, according to the state's transport department.
Munawar Sheikh, a 58-year-old tuk-tuk driver, was among those who signed up.
Over four days at a training centre in Thane, near Mumbai, he and other drivers learnt 16 commonly used questions and phrases, including "Where do you want to go?", "don't worry" and "the fare will be according to the meter".
At the end, they took an oral test, with those who passed receiving a certificate they could show transport officials during inspections.
Sheikh says the course taught him enough Marathi to manage basic conversations with passengers.
But for some drivers, finding the time to learn is part of the problem.
Ajay Singh, a taxi driver in Mumbai, says he wants to learn Marathi but has struggled to fit classes around his working day.
"From the time we wake up until late at night, we have to drive. Otherwise, there is no food on the table," he says. "Taking a few hours out of the day for a class is financially difficult for me."
Singh says he earns between 1,500 and 2,000 rupees ($17-$23; £13-£17) a day and worries that losing even a few days' income could leave him struggling to pay rent and his children's school fees.
Instead, he is trying to learn while he works - listening to Marathi radio stations while driving and practising with Marathi-speaking passengers.
Lakhan Pandey, also a driver, says the extra year has made a significant difference.
He says he never objected to learning Marathi - he just wanted enough time to do it.
"We live here, we work here. Of course we should learn Marathi," he says. "Just give us the time to learn it without putting our livelihoods at risk."

In Summary
- As concerns around smart glasses and privacy grow, Meta has ensured that users cannot use the cameras on its smart glasses if they cover or tamper with the LED that lights up during recording.
- While Meta’s move is a step in the right direction, it still does not go far enough to address the privacy issues posed by smart glasses.
- Smart glasses brands need to do more to prevent misuse. This includes informing and educating not just users, but also the public, who could unknowingly end up in footage shot on these devices.
Smart glasses have existed for a while but have attained a whole new dimension of popularity since Meta invested in them. For those of you who might not be aware (welcome to high-tech planet, folks), smart glasses look like regular glasses but come with a number of tech add-ons, such as displays, speakers, and most notably, cameras. These smart glasses can take photos, record videos, handle phone calls, play music, let you speak to an AI assistant, figure out your way around town, get recommendations, and more.
Table of Contents
Smart glasses? Pervert glasses, more like!
Sound uber cool, cutting-edge and futuristic, don’t they? Unfortunately, this tech rose comes with a stack of thorns that would make a cactus turn even more green with envy. While the tech world and content creators may be going gaga over all these smart glasses can do, more and more people are beginning to refer to them as “pervert glasses.” There is a sound reason for this – these glasses are increasingly being used to record people (often women) without their consent and knowledge, resulting in a massive breach of a person’s privacy. There have been a number of incidents in which people have been recorded without their knowledge and the footage shared in public or private groups, causing severe trauma to those who appeared unknowingly in the footage.
What’s worse, the onus of figuring out that they are being recorded fell on the person being recorded. Being vigilant, actively looking for signs of someone wearing smart glasses, and catching up on tech cues were all part of the package – we also did a story on ways one could find out if they are being recorded as smart glasses moved from being content creators to destroyers of privacy. As incidents of “secret recordings” through these glasses increase, pressure has finally started building on the brands making these devices to make them safer not just for their users, but also for those in their vicinity.
Meta finally moves, but is it enough?
Recently, Meta finally fixed a flaw that was making it easier for users to covertly record others. In a post made on Threads (https://www.threads.com/@ahimel/post/DcjTatTGyn-), Alex Himel, Vice President of Wearables and Vice President of Augmented Reality at Meta, said that the camera on the glasses would stop working if the LED on the glasses was covered.
He was referring to a small LED indicator on the glasses that lights up when the glasses are recording. While the cameras on the glasses would not allow users to record if the LED was covered, many users found ways around this. One method was as simple as covering the LED light after starting to record the video. Following Himel’s announcement, an update will ensure that if the LED is covered at any stage (before or after starting a video recording), the glasses will automatically stop recording the video or taking photos. What’s more, if users tamper with the LED light and destroy or disable it, the glasses will now disable the camera feature permanently.
While this is definitely a step in the right direction, it does not really solve the biggest issue around these glasses. We have seen Meta’s glasses in public, and it is very difficult to spot when they are recording, especially in daylight or if the person is some distance away. The LED light is bright, but can easily be missed if one is not looking for it. What’s more, one can place a hand in front of it to stop others from seeing it, without actually covering it. We really think more needs to be done to safeguard the privacy of users in the vicinity of these devices. Brands need to come up with stronger measures that can help people spot those who may be wearing smart glasses and steer clear of their line of vision, if they so wish.
Making smart glasses safer: five more things brands can do
Given how limited the LED indicator can be, here are five measures that tech brands can take to make smart glasses safer for those in front of them:
Just make them look different…VERY different
One of the reasons why it is extremely difficult to find out if a person is wearing smart glasses is because they look exactly like usual glasses. Clear, tinted, or even running smart glasses all come with designs/frames that make them look like “normal” glasses. This makes them difficult to spot and enables users to record footage without being noticed.
We think that, given the privacy nightmares they can potentially pose, smart glasses need to look fundamentally different from everyday glasses. Visible badging, colors, even frame size or design should make them easy to spot. Who knows, this might even catch on as a style statement, but at least it will alert those in the vicinity that the person is walking around with a camera literally on their eyes!
Better, brighter (and maybe even more) LED lights
An LED light blinking while recording or taking photos is currently the only way to find out if someone is recording video or taking photographs from their smart glasses. As we have said before, a single light can be missed or even discreetly covered. The solution? Brands could perhaps use multiple LEDs of different colors, and which are of larger size, to pretty much advertise that a smart glasses’ camera is in use. Something like Nothing’s Glyph UI would be very handy!
Pump up the volume
Smart glasses should also give clear audio signals when their cameras are functioning. It should not be possible to take photographs without a loud camera shutter sound, and adding low but constant beep sounds when video is being recorded would also alert people to the presence of a camera in their vicinity.
Mandatory identifying apps
There are already apps like Zuckoff in the market that notify users if they are around someone wearing smart glasses. But these are unofficial and a little hit and miss. We think it would be wonderful if smart glass manufacturers took the initiative to come up with an app that can alert people in a small radius (say, 10 meters if based on Bluetooth), letting them know that they are in the presence of someone wearing smart glasses. Yes, it does violate the privacy of the person wearing smart glasses, as it is likely to make people in their vicinity notice them, but then that’s the price one pays for wearing such a device.
Better marketing and awareness
Brands have been pouring sackfuls of money into normalizing and promoting smart glasses. It would be great if they could allocate some of these funds to also highlight the dangers they can pose, and how they can be misused. Some might think this is counterproductive, but we feel this is the socially responsible thing to do – to make people aware that the device has its dark side too. And it is best that the brands do it themselves before they are forced to do it by Governments around the world.
The Government needs to step in as well. While new tech does make lives easier, there are always people who can find ways to misuse it. It happened with the Internet, it happened with smartphones, it is happening with AI, and it is happening with smart glasses too. To make sure that technology is not misused, there need to be strict privacy laws that are implemented effectively and come with stringent punishments. Perhaps statutory warnings on devices, advising consumers not to misuse them, might be an option worth considering. People need to realize that with great tech comes great responsibility.
Smart glasses need a Meta-morphosis, pun intended. They do not need to blend in, but to stand out and make people realize that they are present in a room. People need to know that they could be on camera. And the onus for this lies not just on those doing the recording, but on the brands who facilitate this.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Maria Diaz Valdez, a 29-year-old based in Spain. It's been edited for length and clarity.
I feel like a relationship with a founder is a relationship on steroids because it's so intense in the trust and patience it requires. I've had to be committed to his journey, but I'm not in charge of it, and that's very scary.
My partner, Emil, and I met as roommates in a shared household in Norway, and we've been together for four years. I was lucky enough to get to know him so well as a friend before we started dating because we had all sorts of honest conversations about our goals without trying to impress each other. That level of honesty and communication has been the foundation of everything we've built in our relationship.
It's been strange to take a backseat role to build my career to help him build his, and there are times we feel more like business partners than life partners, but I'm in this for the long haul. I trust this journey, and I know he'll support me the same way as I build my own entrepreneurial journey.
We created a contract toward the start of our relationship
Emil didn't start his current entrepreneurial journey until right before we started dating, so I've kind of been through everything with him. I was even his first client. I was building a jewelry brand at the time and hired him to help me develop my website.
At the start of our relationship, we had a lot of conversations about his vision for the company, my role in it, and whether he saw this future with me. Our discussions made me feel confident that he'd actually pursue his goals, but I still had to put a lot of trust in him. I lent him money those first couple of months, which was scary, but I believed in him.
We wrote a contract that tracked the money I was sending him and established a deal that there would come a day when he'd need to support me in return.
I've had to take a backseat to his dreams, but I know he'll return the favor
I've always been a career person — someone with direction who works very hard. Now I'm with someone who's outperforming me in that area. I'm not blindly trusting everything will go well; we have conversations about this constantly.
It's strange, but it's a conscious choice I've made because I view this person as somebody I want to experience my whole life with. I write a lot in my diary, trying to figure out what I truly feel and want. The biggest challenge to wrap my head around is that his passion and project are taking priority, and I must remember that things will change as I figure out what I'm most passionate about.
Emil and I have very compatible skills and knowledge; I focus on design, marketing, and branding, while he is in tech and business development. With his help, I've even started creating my marketing platform, CrazeAI.
Work sometimes comes before the relationship, so we focus on presence with each other
Emil is the type of person who really values quality time. If we watch something on Netflix, for example, we're not going to be on our phones. We're in this together. I think we're very conscious of the distractions we have around us.
Because of that, I'm very lenient in times when he has to step away for something at work. There are times we'll be on a walk together, and one of his partners calls, and he suddenly forgets he's on a walk with me. He'll just walk away.
I don't worry about it too much because I've been in that position before. When I was building the jewelry brand, I would wake up in the middle of the night having to answer emails. I have a lot of understanding that he's in a position where these moments can make it or break it for his business.
Our baseline is one of presence, so when something comes up, it's OK.
Most of our conversations go back to business
It's very hard not to talk about the development of the business because that's the stage we're in. We're both very passionate about it, and we work together on it, so it doesn't feel like a dragging conversation.
There are times we go out to have a drink and try not to talk about business, but then we start dreaming and saying things like "Imagine when we get to this level or through these things." It feels supportive to talk through these things.
We also try to play chess every once in a while and take salsa classes. That's a time when we're not talking or thinking about work at all.
We set aside moments to remind each other we're life partners, not business partners
We're often in a mode where we have to buckle down and figure issues out about the business, and those conversations aren't happening in a candlelit dinner setting. We're sitting down with an Excel sheet, sourcing out financials. It's not very romantic.
Recently, we've been trying to get out of our usual environment, whether for a day trip, a hike, or a trip back home to Norway to see family, to remind us that we have identities outside of being a doer and fixer. That's when we usually find each other again and remember, "Oh wait, I'm also a girlfriend."
I'm also very persistent about spending two minutes before we go to bed without distractions to just be together and settle. It's very important to have routines like that.
You need a strong sense of self to date a founder
If you're entering a relationship with a founder, you need your own strong support system and lifestyle. Your whole life cannot be the relationship, because it's not theirs.
Founders can be so focused on chasing their dream that they can forget your needs or your dates. You need to have your own life so those moments don't feel too heavy, and find a balance between forgiveness and setting boundaries.
Founders are dreamers, and they often dream about what their life will look like when their business succeeds. Are you a part of that dream? Are they saying "when we get to that point.." or is it "when I get to that point.."? Little things like that are so important.
We dream a lot together, so I know his success is my success.

Since the dawn of Silicon Valley, there’s been a widespread perception that San Francisco is, put gently, not exactly a dating mecca.
The city famously has a skewed male-to-female ratio (per census data, there are about 105 men for every 100 women), and there’s a perception among many women that men who work in tech tend to have poor social and emotional skills and a lack of style—opting for Patagonia vests and Meta glasses rather than putting substantive effort into their appearance.
On August 31, however, Celeste Amadon, the founder of the AI-powered dating app Known, valiantly attempted to reverse that stereotype. In an X thread accompanied by a moody, upward-angled selfie, she announced that she and her team were compiling a list of “SF’s most dateable people,” titled “San Francisco’s Hot List.” She attached a link for people to nominate their single friends according to criteria like “ambition,” “accomplishment,” “reputation,” and “aura.”
The post was skewered online by many in and outside of the tech scene, with some referring to it as “cringe” or mocking the lack of eligible singles in San Francisco: “The solution to dating in SF is to leave SF,” posted one female founder. But it was an extremely effective bit of marketing for Known, garnering more than 15,000 submissions 24 hours after the tweet was posted, according to Amadon. It was also an effective piece of counter-propaganda to the stereotype of San Franciscans, officially heralding that San Francisco Is Hot.
“Not to be cheesy, but I think the SF dating scene deserves some defending,” Amadon tells WIRED. “It gets so much flak for being a place where it’s hard to meet people, but there are many people who are super eligible in not just their physical attractiveness but in their holistic dateability.”
Known’s Hot List is part of a broader conversation focused on the general attractiveness of the San Francisco populace—and why some locals seem to be placing more importance on being perceived as hot.
Last summer, two women who work in tech—Madison Kanna (who is on the Hot List) and Cat Orman—threw an “enforced ratio” party at a Tesla showroom in the city, ensuring that there were as many women as men. The invite stipulated that the vibe would be “unapologetically feminine and fun” and that “Patagonia vests will be turned away at the door.” On August 28, Mantis Biotech startup founder Georgia Witchel posted an X thread titled “Tech Is Having a Hot Girl Renaissance.” In the thread, Witchel describes how social media has been deluged with “young, attractive women taking tastefully slutty duck-faced mirror selfies” to promote their startups, citing Known and the insurance company Corgi as examples.
Witchel says her argument is not so much that she objects to young women using their attractiveness as a marketing strategy—it's more to explain how and why it has emerged as a marketing strategy to begin with, telling WIRED the trend is a result of “a renaissance of sales culture in SF.”
Throughout much of Silicon Valley, software marketing was “nerds selling to other nerds,” she says—but with the emergence of vibe coding, the barrier to entry for the industry has gotten lower, and the standards for marketing a product higher. “The fact that you are able to build a complicated product is not enough to give you the leeway of not being charismatic,” says Witchel. “People are recognizing that.”
When reached for comment, Brooke LeBlanc, head of community at Corgi, who Witchel cites in her thread, referred WIRED to an X post. “My mom just heard about the hot girl in tech renaissance and she’s absolutely thrilled by the news,” she wrote. “No one in my family from Georgia can believe that it’s breaking news for a woman to care about how she looks.”
Amadon says the Hot List has “minimal” connection to Witchel’s thread, but she understands why Known’s marketing “draws interest” (though she notes that X specifically is “not a primary marketing channel” for the app). She concedes that the list was intended to capitalize on the discussion and create “positive discourse” around dating in San Francisco.
And it’s working: On September 1, Known posted the first round of Hot Listers, including LeBlanc and startup founders like Jasper Carmichael-Jack, the CEO of the AI-driven company Artisan. There was nary a Patagonia vest in the bunch.

Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?
- Published
Houston's historic Old Braeswood neighbourhood is affluent and tree-lined.
These are not the kind of streets where you would expect to see co-ordinated vandalism. Yet here, four surveillance cameras were attacked and cut down in the middle of the night.
The metal poles were severed, leaving the distinctive black oval cameras and accompanying solar panels lying on the ground. On some of the cameras was a red sign reading: "Notice. 24/7 video recording."
These cameras are run by a company called Flock Safety and this sabotage, which happened in late July, is a signal of growing concern over the nationwide spread of sophisticated AI-powered surveillance systems. Similar vandalism incidents have occurred in Minnesota, California and Georgia.
Proponents say they have made communities safer and have helped dramatically increase the rate at which crimes are solved. But recent examples of misuse have caused concern. Critics say the cameras, which take pictures of the rear of every car that drives past, are overly broad investigative tools that treat civilians like suspects.
They see the little black poles popping up in their neighbourhoods as visible reminders of state power, at a time when public confidence in institutions is historically low and many are concerned about the accelerating pace of technological change and the influence of AI on people's lives.
A new age of surveillance
Founded in 2017, Flock Safety has become one of the country's biggest makers of Automatic Licence Plate Readers (ALPRs). These AI-powered cameras take a picture of the rear of every car that drives past. Footage is retained for a specified amount of time.
But little is known about the extent to which Flock is being used - the company does not publish exact data, but says it works with more than 7,000 communities nationwide and estimates that there are approximately 100,000 cameras deployed.
Records obtained by the BBC provide a rare glimpse into the extensive network of cameras and surveillance tech being used in America's fourth largest city, Houston, including the use of controversial facial recognition software powered by artificial intelligence.
Flock is not just selling cameras - it is selling access to a database that can include thousands of cameras from around the country. Older ALPRs did not have this vast network, which is a major selling point for law enforcement.
For example, Houston's Metro Transit Authority owns 35 cameras. But documents show Metro has access to around 20,000 devices in the Flock network - including some as far as Albany County, New York.
And as Flock expands, so too can the scope of investigations. Documents released to the BBC show how the network has grown year-on-year. In the Cypress-Fairbanks independent school district, a typical licence plate lookup in April 2024 searched around 270 networks of cameras.
By April 2025, the typical search scope had almost doubled to around 500 networks. In April 2026, 20% of searches were conducted across more than 6,000 networks.
Critics in Houston say this national network concerns them more than individual cameras. Christopher Rivera, from the Texas Civil Rights Project, worries that authorities could use "these databases to search our everyday routines, which ultimately scrapes out our routes to work, where our children go to school, and where we worship - and that's very problematic".
There have been recent incidents of privacy breaches that have caught national attention. Last week, a police officer in Kentucky was charged after using the Flock system to track his ex-girlfriend - who filed a protection order - over 2,000 times.
He was caught using Flock's newly mandatory, AI-powered audit tool that flags suspicious use.
Others are concerned about Flock being a way for police to avoid warrants, which are usually required to search a person's property or tap their phone. In 2025, a detective in Johnson County, Texas, searched over 80,000 images to locate a woman suspected of having an abortion. He did not have a warrant.
CCTV cameras, licence-plate readers and surveillance are not new. But the scale of Flock's network and the integration of AI in modern surveillance tech is a recent development and it's turned Flock into a household name. Americans who otherwise ignored the cameras in their cities have started to notice and tune into the capabilities of the technology around them.
With AI, unlike older licence-plate readers, law enforcement can search surveillance footage with a string of words like "Caucasian man, blue shirt" - not just a licence-plate image.
One thing Flock does not use is facial recognition. But that does not mean police departments are avoiding that tech. Critics say it violates human rights, is susceptible to misidentifying innocent people, and can be biased against minorities.
The BBC has received documents revealing that Harris County Sheriff's Office, which covers Houston, uses other facial recognition technology, Clearview AI.
The tool includes a database of more than 70 billion images, many of which were scraped from public internet sources including social media. The documents, including purchase orders and a license agreement, show that the county's Clearview AI contract currently runs through to March 2027.
Several European countries have issued the company with data protection fines, including a £7.5m penalty from the UK's Information Commissioner.
Harris County Sheriff's Office use of this facial recognition technology has not been reported before. It did not respond to requests for comment.
Police say surveillance technology like this, including Flock cameras, is important for fighting crime.
"It's a very good tool," says Chief Ray Schultz of the Memorial Villages Police Department - a small jurisdiction within Houston. "It makes the community safer."
Before purchasing a Flock ALPR, his department would recover an average of three stolen cars a year. Now, this figure is 45, Schultz says.
Some crimes solved in recent years would have been "impossible" without Flock, he adds. Last month, Schultz used the tool to find an elderly woman with dementia who had driven 60 miles from Galveston to Houston and had gotten lost. "We were able to find her and reunite her with her family."
Schultz says that it is important for agencies to have strong policies governing ALPR use and officers that misuse the system should be held accountable.
"But don't throw out a tool that is valuable, that can help recover a missing child."
'I feel like I'm being stalked'
Jasmine Khadem Gonzalez, an immigrant rights organiser, is worried that law enforcement might "use [the Flock] database to tell ICE where somebody is".
The federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency does not have a contract with Flock directly. However, there have been reports of police officers citing "immigration" or "ice" as a reason for searching for a licence plate.
Jessie, an immigrant from Central America, noticed a Flock camera outside her house last month. She asked the BBC to not use her real name out of fear it could impact a pending case to extend her green card.
"It makes me feel as if I'm being stalked," she says.
In response, she's changed her commute to work. "I try to take different routes every day so there's not a pattern."
But whether individual law enforcement agencies share info with the federal government is unclear. Federal immigration enforcement cannot access Flock data directly, Flock's CEO says. But some police departments have standing agreements with federal immigration enforcement to work together.
In Harris County, a proposed Flock contract amendment initially included the explicit authorisation to share camera data with federal law enforcement, but this provision was later removed after push-back from campaigners.
Hundreds of contracts cancelled
Some jurisdictions have opted not to renew contracts with Flock as a result of these concerns, including large metropolitan areas like Los Angeles, Seattle and Austin.
In total, more than 200 communities have cancelled or not renewed their contracts since 2021 - including 90 in August alone - according to advocacy group Secure Justice, external. Their reasons for cancelling may include cost and concerns about data privacy.
Nationally, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have suggested that there ought to be guardrails and several candidates have made it a campaign issue for the upcoming midterms. Republican Congressman Keith Self has proposed legislation that would require federal agencies to get warrants before accessing Flock data.
The company itself has also amended some of its policies, such as requiring mandatory audits and reducing the default period that data stays on a server from 30 days to seven, unless flagged as part of an investigation. But individual agencies can choose to retain data for much longer.
Flock's founder and CEO Garrett Langley told the BBC that it was up to individual cities to decide how long to store data and what information to share with whom.
"I don't think a technology company should be making decisions like that," he says.
"As long as it's a lawful investigation, we are not going to tell cities what laws they should or should not enforce."
Flock is a safety, not surveillance, company, Langley says. Yet three patents filed between 2020 and 2025 have the word "surveillance" in the title.
He boasts that the tech helped solve "about a million crimes" and helped find more than 10,000 missing people.
"The debate of how we build a society where safety and privacy coexist" is worth having, he says, but the ongoing vandalism is "disappointing".
But there is nothing Flock or law enforcement could say to make Jessie feel at ease with this technology, she says. "I just don't trust that they're doing it to keep us safe."

US midterms begin with chaos over mail-voting crackdown
North Carolina became the first state authorised to begin sending out ballots, formally launching an election season that culminates on Nov 3 and will determine control of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term.
WASHINGTON: America's midterm elections opened Friday (Sep 4) in a fog of confusion over mail voting, with ballots already going out as President Donald Trump presses courts to let him impose sweeping new restrictions on how they are handled.
North Carolina became the first state authorised to begin sending out ballots, formally launching an election season that culminates on Nov 3 and will determine control of Congress for the final two years of Trump's term.
Yet voters and election officials still do not know what rules may govern millions of mail ballots, as Trump asks the Supreme Court to revive curbs blocked by a federal judge and as states scramble to prepare for changes that could come after voting has begun.
The dispute has been compounded by whistleblower allegations that a new Postal Service verification system was rushed, inadequately tested and could delay or even disqualify entire batches of ballots because of a single barcode problem.
A federal judge on Friday extended her previous temporary block on Trump's plan, a day after warning that hurried changes could cause widespread disruption.
"We're not playing an intellectual puzzle game," Judge Indira Talwani reportedly told a lawyer defending the restrictions, in remarks widely picked up by US media. "We're talking about people's right to vote."
The Trump administration is expected to appeal to the Supreme Court against Talwani's new order, which extends her previous block.
RULES IN LIMBO
Trump's March executive order would require states to provide the US Postal Service with lists of eligible mail voters through a new federal portal.
Ballot envelopes would also need individual barcodes and other design features, with USPS empowered to refuse mailings that fail to meet its requirements.
The administration says the rules are meant to protect election integrity, although it has produced no evidence of significant fraud through mail voting.
Trump has repeatedly denounced the practice as corrupt while using it himself - including to vote in Florida's Republican primary just last month.
The uncertainty comes on top of a voting system that already differs dramatically from state to state.
Some automatically send ballots to registered voters, others require voters to request them, while identification requirements, return deadlines and rules for counting late-arriving ballots vary across the country.
Election officials now face the additional prospect of federal requirements changing while voting is already underway.
"The states set the time, place and manner of elections in this country, not the president," Marc Elias, the founder of voting rights platform Democracy Docket, said on his YouTube show.
"In fact, the Congress can override the states in many instances, but in no instance can the president. The president is given no power over federal elections."
North Carolina officials said Friday's mailings would proceed normally and that the state has no plans to use the federal portal at the center of the dispute.
But time is rapidly running out for any nationwide overhaul.
"RUSHED, CHAOTIC"
Friday marks 60 days before Election Day - the deadline Trump's order itself envisioned for states to submit voter information - while another 18 states are expected to begin distributing ballots roughly 45 days before Nov 3.
That leaves little room for officials to redesign envelopes, update computer systems, train workers and upload voter data if the courts suddenly allow the restrictions to take effect.
Concerns intensified this week after an anonymous USPS whistleblower alleged that the ballot portal had been developed through a "rushed, chaotic, and fundamentally flawed" process.
The official warned that under a proposed "zero-percent failure" policy, one barcode that fails to scan or match could result in an entire batch containing thousands of ballots being rejected until it is checked again.
USPS told AFP no mandatory verification procedures were being performed and that election officials would initially use its portal only voluntarily.
The fight - alongside disputes over partisan redistricting in around a dozen states - comes with high political stakes.
Republicans hold narrow congressional majorities, but Democrats are favored to capture the House as Trump's approval ratings remain weak and voters voice frustration over living costs and the continuing war with Iran.
A new Cornell University forecast gives Democrats an eight-in-10 chance of taking the chamber, projecting a roughly 226-209 majority.

Ecuador intelligence chief and five Americans killed in Kenya helicopter crash
- Published
Ecuador's intelligence chief and his wife have been killed in a helicopter that crashed at Mount Ololokwe in central Kenya.
Michele Sensi-Contugi, 44, and his wife, fashion designer Stephany Hollihan, 42, were among the group of seven people - six tourists and the pilot - killed in Samburu county at approximately 09:13 (06:13 GMT) on Wednesday.
Five of victims were Americans, a US State Department spokesperson said. The Reuters news agency reports that Hollihan also held US citizenship.
The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority (KCAA) said the helicopter was on a scenic flight from a wildlife conservancy in Loisaba to Ewaso Nyiro, a river that flows along several national reserves.
Samburu county is a popular tourist destination with many private wildlife conservancies and is renowned for its stunning landscape.
Images from the scene show smoke at the wooded crash site on Mount Ololokwe, as members of the Kenya Red Cross approach the still-burning wreckage.
Ecuador's President Daniel Noboa named Sensi-Contugo director of the country's Centre of Strategic Intelligence (CIES) in January 2024.
The office of the president and Ecuador's National Assembly expressed their condolences over his death and that of Hollihan.
The Italian-Ecuadorean businessman had had close links to Noboa even before he was chosen to lead the intelligence service and was considered a close ally of the president.
Shortly before being named head of the CIES, he had served for four months as a minister in his cabinet.
Noboa has declared three days of national mourning starting on Thursday.
Newspapers in Ecuador have also run obituaries of Hollihan. The Guayaquil-based designer founded Sensi Studio, a brand praised for incorporating traditional Ecuadorean elements and materials in its designs.
Lady Lori Helicopters, which operated the Eurocopter EC130 B4 aircraft, said it was "deeply saddened" by the accident.
"Our deepest sympathies are with the guests, crew, their families and loved ones, and all those affected by this tragic accident," a statement read.
According to a memo seen by the BBC's US partner CBS News, external one of the Americans killed in the crash was NBCUniversal journalist José Alberto Suárez.
In the memo, NBCUniversal called Suárez "a deeply respected leader and beloved friend and colleague.
"José was an exceptional colleague and mentor to many," the memo read.
Miami restaurateur Roger Duarte was among the Americans killed in the crash, according to local and US media.
Commenting on his death on X, US Rep Carlos Antonio Gimenez wrote: "Our prayers are with their loved ones during this incredibly difficult time. May their memories be a blessing."
The other victims have not yet been identified.
Helicopter crashes are not uncommon in Kenya.
In February, a helicopter crash in the Rift Valley county of Nandi killed six people, including a member of parliament.
In 2024, the military chief, Gen Francis Omondi Ogolla, died after an army helicopter that was carrying 11 people crashed in the west of the country, with only two survivors.
In June 2021 at least 10 soldiers were killed when their helicopter crashed while landing near the capital, Nairobi.

A Michigan Democrat wants to put Canada on the ballot during the midterms. Are voters listening?
State's open Senate seat is shaping up to be a tight race in the shadow of a trade war
It's just past noon at Richfield Bowl on the outskirts of Flint, Mich., and already the sounds of rolling bowling balls and crashing pins fill the large hall.
Here, strikes and spares are serious. So are splits. And not just when two pins are left standing.
"President [Donald] Trump's trying to keep American people working instead of sending it overseas," said Scott Holmes, moments before his turn to bowl.
"My son just lost his job a few months ago because they sent it over to Africa."
His teammate Dick Hunt sees the U.S. president's tariffs another way.
"The people, we end up paying for it," he said.
CBC News recently travelled to Michigan to get a temperature check on how Americans are feeling about the tariff war with Canada — the state's largest export market.
MAGA supporter Tina Bentley says she trusts the president's handling of the economy.
"I think he's a smart man. And I think that he cares 100 per cent about America," she said.
"The way I look at it is God didn't use perfect people to do his work. He used people like Trump to do his work."
A few lanes down, longtime bowler Peggy Banks can't disagree more.
"Our tariffs have not done anything for the people except make everything more expensive," she said.
Bowling league-mate Lisa McFadden nodded along.
"I think now everybody is starting to see it regardless of if you're a Democrat or a Republican because now it's affecting everybody's pocket," she said.
Trump's tariffs on the ballot
Michigan, heart of the auto industry, is one of the states hardest hit by the trade dispute. Just this month the U.S. National Taxpayers Union Foundation published a study suggesting Michigan households face the highest per-household tariff costs in the country.
- Whitmer told Trump in private that Michigan auto jobs depend on a tariff change of course
- Sault Ste. Marie in Ontario and Michigan share a border — and now a very big tariff threat
That puts the already hotly contested race for U.S. Senate this November in the shadow of an escalating trade war.
Winning Michigan's open seat is crucial for the Democratic Party if they want to regain control of the Senate during the second half of Trump's term. The Republicans are hoping to flip the seat red. So far, polls suggest the two candidates are neck and neck.
Abdul El-Sayed, considered a progressive-left choice for this party, is hoping to capitalize on Michiganders' frustrations with the trade war. He's been pushing Canada into the conversation while campaigning, repeatedly calling Trump an "asshole" for starting a trade war with the country's northern neighbour.
"People don't want to have to keep paying more for stuff that they need to buy. And this is the logical outcome of an illogical trade war. So here we are," El-Sayed told CBC News during a campaign stop in Waterford, Mich., on Thursday.
The Democrat — who was quick to raise his childhood memories of watching Hockey Night in Canada and his love of lacrosse, Canada's actual national sport — isn't ruling out all tariffs.
He cited duties on windmill parts or solar rigs as an example of tariffs he would keep if it would help build up his state's renewable energy industry.
"But it's because you're being very particular about exactly what kind of industries you're trying to protect. This is just across the board, ridiculousness, for no particular reason," El-Sayed said.
"So I can't quite explain it. Except for that everything Donald Trump does is ham-fisted, chaotic and self-serving."
His Republican rival has largely stayed away from talking about Trump's tariffs on the campaign.
Mike Rogers's camp didn't respond to CBC's request for an interview, but was recently asked by Fox News if he supports Trump's handing of the trade deal with Canada and backed the president's objectives.
"The Canadians have not been good partners on this," Rogers said in an interview on Fox & Friends on Monday. "I think they think that the Republicans are going to lose in the midterms, and then that the Democrats are going to open up the borders again and absolutely undercut the people who build cars and car parts right here in Michigan."
Voters mixed on if tariffs play into their vote
Residents in Genesee County were mixed on whether the tariffs will impact their votes.
Carl Olson, teammates with Holmes and Hunt, offered a quick "no."
"I think eventually everything will level out and everything will go back to normal," he said.
"If anything, it made it stronger that I will never vote Republican," said Joan Castor, when stopped in the Flint downtown core.
Down the street, Matt Zastrow said work and housing are his main concerns. If he votes, it will be for the Republican candidate.
"I think Trump's doing a good enough job right now. I'm not sure where we would be if we had somebody else in there," he said.
So far, industry in the region is largely staying out of politics. Businesses CBC contacted didn't want to speak on the record, citing the atmosphere.
Glenn Stevens Jr., executive director of MichAuto at the Detroit Regional Chamber, said businesses he speaks to want to see the cloud of uncertainty this trade war has brought cleared.
"Politics is not what this is about," Stevens Jr. said. "This is about making cars, in our perspective, moving lumber, moving energy, moving agriculture to the market and employing people.
"So the politics and the rhetoric are one thing, and that's at a crescendo right now, but the economics really are what speaks."

Not a mistrial, yet. Clancy's lawyer asks for emergency appeal in her murder trial
The judge in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy has granted the request of her defense attorney to appeal to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court to seek an emergency stay in the case. This came moments after the judge said he intended to declare a mistrial Friday morning.
Clancy, 36, was charged with strangling 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan, in the family's home in Duxbury, Mass. Her defense argued she should not be held criminally liable because she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time, an approach often called the insanity defense. The prosecution argued Clancy was well enough to plan and act intentionally.
The jury has been deliberating for six days and told the judge they could not reach a verdict. Defense attorney Kevin Reddington asked Judge William Sullivan to dismiss a holdout juror on Thursday. Reddington referenced two notes the jury foreperson sent the court about the juror, who, according to Reddington, admitted doubt but refused to join the other 11 jurors in finding Clancy not guilty.
However, Judge William Sullivan denied that request. He did however instruct the jury on the meaning of "reasonable doubt."
When making his request for a stay on Friday, Reddington said of the holdout juror, "I believe that this is a situation where there is a clear and present danger that this individual, for some reason, what it is we don't know, but is taking a position that's intractable, regardless of proof beyond a reasonable doubt."
Reddington also asked the judge to survey the jury to see if they could reach an agreement on a lesser charge, such as second-degree murder or manslaughter, before declaring a mistrial, so that Clancy couldn't be tried again for first-degree murder. The judge denied that request as well.
The judge agreed to give Reddington an hour to make his appeal to the state's top court.

Anthropic’s prospective public-market investors must reckon with an external group of trustees that control the majority of the AI company’s board, as its planned blockbuster initial public offering forces close scrutiny of its experimental governance structure.
The company’s Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) is a small group of advisers created to safeguard the lab’s mission of developing AI for the long-term benefit of humanity, even as commercial pressures intensify.
The trust holds no equity in Anthropic, but has significant influence, with the San Francisco-based company planning to preserve its role after a stock market debut that could value the Claude maker at as much as $2 trillion.
The LTBT, which is the controlling governance mechanism of the Anthropic public benefit corporation, has the right to appoint or dismiss the majority of the company’s board. It has selected four of Anthropic’s seven directors, including Netflix’s co-founder Reed Hastings and Vas Narasimhan, chief executive of Novartis.
Currently, the LTBT has three members out of a potential maximum of five, chaired by Neil Buddy Shah, chief executive of the Clinton Health Access Initiative, alongside former Federal Reserve chair Ben Bernanke and Richard Fontaine, CEO of the Center for a New American Security. Mariano-Florentino “Tino” Cuéllar, a former California Supreme Court justice, left the trust after a few months to work as Anthropic’s chief global affairs officer.
Anthropic is attempting to establish a template for future AI governance through the trust, said multiple people close to its plans.
They said the ambition for the LTBT is to provide an industry blueprint, similar to the GAAP accounting principles, which initially emerged as voluntary standards proposed by private companies. Bernanke’s appointment in July signals this intention to build a more institutional body, one person added.
The trustees are required to receive advance notice of major company actions, including the launch of new AI models. They meet weekly among themselves, while also meeting Anthropic’s leadership as frequently as every other week, according to people close to the matter.

Why are European countries moving their gold out of North America?
- Published
When the central bank of the Netherlands confirmed this week that it had moved tonnes of the country's gold out of North America, it said the relocation would make it "better prepared for severe crises".
Some 86 tonnes from the combined total of about 313 tonnes held in the US and Canada were relocated to London "in view of increasing geopolitical unrest", it said, so the shiny stuff could be "readily available for use in a crisis situation".
Questions were bound to follow. Why were the Dutch doing this? Were they anticipating some major economic shock on the horizon?
It seems not, but the move was clearly in response to the unstable and uncertain state the world finds itself in, with trade and military wars prompting countries to take precautions and hold their gold closer to home.
Earlier this year, France announced it had removed its gold reserves from the US to home shores. Meanwhile, Germany's Bundesbank transferred more than 216 tonnes of the metal from storage locations abroad - 111 tonnes from New York and 105 tonnes from Paris - over a few years ending in 2016., external
It is a strategy which has played out before in times of global instability. "Some European central banks moved part of their gold holdings to New York during the Cold War," said research analysts Lina Thomas and Daan Struyven of Goldman Sachs.
Joseph Cavatoni, senior market strategist at the World Gold Council, told the BBC while wars and trade tensions were "playing into some of these decisions", it didn't "top the list" of motivating factors.
Inflation, interest rates and just having gold in a place where it can be traded quickly also played a role.
"I don't get a sense that there's an impending doom," Cavatoni said, "but what I do think is people are being better educated around how to manage their reserve assets, growing their reserve assets, and actually thinking more effectively around how to make the most of those assets."
De Nederlandsche Bank said the gold removed from the US and Canada between March and August this year was now being held in the vaults of the Bank of England.
"We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness," said the governor of the Dutch central bank, Olaf Sleijpen.
London was seen as the best choice due its position in the world as a major trading centre. If you want to be able to buy or sell gold fast in a crisis, London is the place to be, which makes the Bank of England a popular storage spot.
The Bank is one of the largest custodians of gold in the world. Underneath the 300-year-old institution in central London sits about 400,000 bars worth more than £200bn.
According to industry surveys by the World Gold Council, the Bank of England remains the most popular vaulting location, but central banks are increasingly diversifying where they store the precious metal.
Where to store your country's gold is "increasingly top of mind for reserve managers", according to Thomas and Struyven of Goldman Sachs.
In the modern world, there are many ways to shift your treasure around. The Dutch sold about 59 tonnes in New York and then bought more stocks in London, meaning that amount didn't need to be hauled across the Atlantic.
But more than 27 tonnes were "physically transferred" from the US and Canada to the Dutch town of Zeist. A similar quantity was also sent from Zeist to London.
Companies that perform such services are tight-lipped on how operations are carried out, but it's fair to say the security measures and planning are extensive to avoid the risk of a real-life Italian Job.
Cavatoni, of the World Gold Council, said one standard approach to move gold stocks was to sell the commodity in one place and buy it in another. "Let's say I want my gold in New York and I have it in London. I could sell it in London, buy it in New York, same day, same time, effectively book transfer without actually having to put it on any other logistical change."
There are only a few select companies which handle gold shipments across borders, one of which is Brink's Global Services, who told the BBC it had seen "increased demand" from the likes of central banks in recent times.
"Heightened geopolitical and economic uncertainty, along with gold's growing role as a strategic reserve asset, appear to be contributing to this trend," said Nader Antar, Brink's executive vice president.
The reason gold storage is such a topic in the minds of central banks is because they have been increasingly buying the stuff. But storing it at home comes at a cost, said Thomas and Struyven of Goldman Sachs.
"Domestic storage requires investment in physical security, audit infrastructure, and insurance; costs that can be disproportionate for smaller central banks," they said.
Over the past four years, central banks have accumulated an annual average of 1,000 tonnes of gold, up significantly from the 500 tonnes average over the preceding decade, according to the World Gold Council.
The trend stretches back to the global financial crisis. And that is only expected to go up in the next year.
Gold has been having a moment in recent years. Its price has surged to hit a series of record highs, passing $5,000 an ounce in January.
There are several reasons behind its value jumping, but a major factor has been the precious metal's position in the human psyche as a so-called safe haven asset, to invest during periods of financial and geopolitical turmoil caused through trade and military wars.
Inflation and interest rates also influence gold's popularity. Due to the commodity's scarcity and the value placed on it across thousands of years, it is somewhat resistant against rising prices, and so is seen as a good investment.
"Over the past half-century, gold prices have risen much faster than the Consumer Price Index (CPI) - the most closely watched measure of inflation," according to investment bank Charles Schwab.
While the price of gold has fallen from the record high seen early this year, it still remains at a high level historically.
According to researchers at Goldman, the price is forecast to rise to $4,900 (£3,624) per troy ounce by the end of 2026, $300 more than it was in August.
The demand for gold from central banks is one key reason why prices are surging, according to Thomas and Struyven.

No Brits left in US Open singles - but are there reasons to be positive?
- Published
For the fourth time in five majors, there will be no British interest in the second week when the US Open moves into the latter stages.
Underwhelming performances at this year's Australian Open, French Open and Wimbledon led to a series of inquests into what was going wrong.
But there is not quite the same sense of doom and gloom, despite everyone being wiped out after the second round in New York.
"Do I think there could be an inquest? I always think there's things that British tennis could do better. So yes, definitely," said British women's number three Francesca Jones.
"Do I think it's something that's concerning? No, not at all.
"The level is getting better and everyone is dangerous on their day."
With the Grand Slam season now over for the singles players, BBC Sport analyses the positives and negatives in British tennis.
Another Slam semi-final and more top 100 players - the positives
Arthur Fery's extraordinary run to the Wimbledon semi-finals is the clear highlight.
The 24-year-old was ranked 114th in the world and needed a wildcard to play at the All England Club, but took full advantage to produce a performance which nobody could have predicted.
Fery was the only player to reach the second week at a Slam this year and has been heralded by British tennis bosses as proof their talent development pathway is working.
Nine Britons competing in the US Open main-draw singles - the most since 1981- is also highlighted as a sign of recent improvement.
That figure does not include 2021 US Open champion Emma Raducanu and Jack Draper, who both missed out with long-term injuries.
"We obviously want more and more competitors in the second week of Slams - just like the British public," said LTA chief executive Scott Lloyd.
"But the fact we've had four different British players make Grand Slam semi-finals since 2021 - you have to go back 30 years before Andy Murray to have four - shows there is no question that the direction of travel has improved.
"We've just got to keep driving for more - and that's what we're trying to do day in and day out."
Five British men are set to feature in the world top 100 after the US Open, with Fery, Cameron Norrie, Jan Choinski, Toby Samuel and Jacob Fearnley representing the highest tally since February 2024.
On the women's side, there will be two players - Katie Boulter and Raducanu - in the top 100, although Jones and Harriet Dart moved back to the cusp after reaching the Flushing Meadows second round.
"We've sent 12 players to the world's top 100 over the past eight years and four of those have played Grand Slam semi-finals," said LTA performance director Michael Bourne.
"I'm not sure what other period in the modern era where we've had that level of productivity. Hopefully the number in the top 100 will rise over the next year."
Injuries, trailing other nations and coaching issues - the negatives
Despite those figures, some will argue that Britain - with its rich tradition and spending power as a Grand Slam nation - is still punching well below its weight.
A glut of injuries for many British players over the past year has not helped the cause.
Former world number four Draper has barely played over the past year because of an arm injury, while Sonay Kartal - who cracked the top 50 last year - has also dropped outside of the top 100 following a long-term back issue.
Britain has fewer players inside the top 100 than the United States, Australia and France, who also benefit from the revenue generated by hosting Grand Slam tournaments.
It also trails nations such as Spain, Italy, the Czech Republic and Argentina, who are all heralded for their talent production.
But Britain cannot simply "pick up a plan" of what others are doing as every country has its own "tennis ecosystem", says Bourne.
Lloyd adds: "We're competing in one of the most internationally elite sports out there and the landscape is vastly different to 40 or 50 years ago in terms of the number of countries which have representation at the top.
"We're ambitious, we want to drive for more, but we honestly believe the indicators are positive. We're moving in the right direction and stronger than where we have been historically."
Encouraging more British children to pick up a racquet from an early age is crucial to developing the next generation of stars.
Draper, Raducanu and Fery - who entered the LTA system at a young age - provide the blueprint.
There are 4.3m juniors playing tennis annually with 1.9m playing every month, which Lloyd says are both all-time records.
But there is a concern that a lack of high-level coaching is stunting the development of many more promising talents.
Bourne admits the UK needs a "higher base" of coaches, adding that one of the LTA's key strategies is "spending time and effort" on developing them.
Chris Marshall, a senior performance coach with over 25 years' experience, fears many youngsters are being priced out of tennis because parents cannot afford quality coaching.
"To fund a 12-year-old at county level right now requires anywhere from £500 to £1,000 a month for coaching, travel, and tournament fees," Marshall, who founded the Young Champs programme to provide free and discounted coaching for children, told BBC Sport.
"It is a massive, stressful financial barrier that makes the sport a non-starter for the vast majority of British families.
"We can't sit around lamenting the lack of British interest in the second week when we are restricting the pipeline that feeds it."
