The meme provides some factual information about both stories and, as of this writing, an accurate GoFundMe tally of donations earmarked to defray Clancy's parents' travel and housing costs as they attended the trial. Also, it's true that a Swedish news outlet reported that a church deacon in that country organized a fundraiser equaling, at current currency conversion rates, about $42,000. However …
… the meme omits additional fundraisers and sponsors who pledged to help rebuild Schols' home, according to information found in the same Swedish news outlet mentioned above and her 2022 book.
In late August and early September 2026, people shared a meme comparing the alleged stories of two mothers.
The right side features Lindsay Clancy, the mother at the center of a highly-publicized Massachusetts murder trial — which ended in a mistrial Sept. 4 — in which prosecutors charged her with killing her three young children, along with a purported GoFundMe fundraising figure exceeding $1 million.
X user @CodyManners2 posted (archived) the meme, which reads under photos of Schols: "Mother pulls all 6 of her children out of raging house fire, going back in three times despite burns covering 93% of her body. Money raised: $42,000." Clancy's caption reads: "Mother kills all 3 of her children by strangling them to death with exercise bands. Claims she is victim. GoFundMe: $1,044,318+."
(@CodyManners2 via X)
Other users widely shared the meme, or a similar one, on Facebook (archived), Reddit (archived), TikTok (archived) and X (archived).
In sum, Schols' book and news media outlets' reporting confirm the meme features a few specific facts but also omits key information. For these reasons, we have rated the meme's content as a mixture of true and false information.
Snopes emailed Kevin Reddington, Clancy's attorney, and Schols to request comment. A reverse image search found no posts displaying the meme older than X user @CodyManners2's post. We reached out to that user to ask whether they created the meme and will update this article if we receive further information.
Breaking down the Schols-Clancy meme
Schols, who lives in Sweden, saved all six of her children in a Sept. 3, 2019, house fire, taking three trips to remove all of them from the inferno. Her 2022 coauthored book, "Ärren bär jag med stolthet: branden i Edsbyn och livet efteråt," which translates to "I Carry the Scars with Pride: The Fire in Edsbyn and Life Afterwards," tells her harrowing story, including the fact that 93% of her body sustained burns, as the meme claims.
In September 2019, Swedish news media outlet SVT, quoting church deacon Christer Schwartz, reported Schols' fundraising total at 400,000 Swedish krona, or at current exchange rates about $42,000. According to that report, Schwartz's fundraiser was one of several on Schols' behalf but no other figures were reported.
On top of Schwartz's and other fundraisers, a February 2020 charity hockey match reportedly collected an additional 200,000 Swedish krona ($21,000). Schols says in her book that people and companies also initially pledged to sponsor the rebuilding of her house, though she adds some of those sponsors pulled out after she separated from her partner.
As for Clancy, The Associated Press, Reuters and other outlets reported she admitted strangling her children with exercise bands on Jan. 24, 2023, and pleaded not guilty to her initial charges, which included three counts each of first-degree murder, strangulation and assault and battery with a dangerous weapon. Prosecutors later dropped the strangulation charges, saying they were redundant to the murder charges.
The organizer of the Clancy case GoFundMe (archived), titled "The Musgrove Family Fund," described the purported recipients of the fundraiser as Clancy's parents, Mike and Paula Musgrove, citing their hotel, travel and relocation costs to stay close to their daughter over more than three years. The in-question meme does not mention Clancy's parents, instead making the allegation that Clancy herself will one day collect the funds. At last check, the fundraiser had grown to more than $1.1 million with a goal of $2 million, bringing in more than 33,500 individual donations.
The meme adds that Clancy has claimed she's the victim. During her criminal trial in summer 2026, Reddington, her attorney, said "there is evidence of lack of criminal responsibility" and suggested "a required finding of not guilty should be entered on the case." He repeatedly argued Clancy suffered from postpartum psychosis, a disorder an estimated one or two in 1,000 women experience after giving birth that can include delusions, depression, hallucinations, insomnia, paranoia and other changes in behavior. Prosecutors, on the other hand, argued she knew what she was doing.
Schols' harrowing rescue story
On Sept. 3, 2019, Schols awoke before 6 a.m. in her home to early-morning light shining through her window, with the faint memory of minutes earlier hearing some of her children playing in another room.
In Schols' book, which we translated to English, she said her then-partner, Anders, was working a night shift, leaving her to sleep alone. She wrote of the morning, "Great, I think, now I have a few minutes to lie down and catch up before I have to start my morning routine."
Moments later, the book recounts, she felt a very different sense of "fear, panic and desperation" when one of her children screamed from downstairs, "Help, mom, there's a fire. There's a fire in the TV room!"
She wrote, "To make sure all the children have woken up, I scream at the top of my lungs: 'Everyone has to get out of the house!'"
In the minutes that followed, Schols first managed to guide her
Schols became unable to move from the flames covering her body. She wrote, "If I have managed to give birth to six children, I will swear to get six children out of this burning house," and that she gathered strength, picked up Mollie and looked to escape. She described William as positioning a ladder they happened to have left out from a long-neglected painting job as their method of escape from the balcony.
Once outside, Schols described hearing her dog, Sally, inside making noises and thinking of
Several Swedish outlets published news of the fire on the same day.
Following extensive hospital stays for her burns and a period of rehabilitation, Schols returned home.
In her book, Schols wrote of Schwartz, the deacon, organizing the fundraiser following the fire. A Facebook post from days after the incident mentions Schwartz by name.
Schols said locals helped find clothes for her children, writing, "I am struck by the incredible care that exists in our country." Other examples of that care included "Playing for Emma," a charity hockey match organized in Schols' honor in February 2020. Schols wrote about the match, as well as her family's home insurance situation at the time of the fire:
On Sunday, February 2nd, a tribute match will be held for me, where the money raised will go to help me and my family get back on their feet. For all the years we have had home insurance, but just a month or so before the accident, we had, due to our financial situation, fallen behind on that particular bill. This fact is something I am ashamed of today. As I have been mulling this question over here in the hospital. This very month, when the house burns down, we were forced to skip that bill. What are the odds of that?
Later in December 2020, the Swedish Heroes Gala awarded Schols the title "Lifesaver of the Year."
Near the end of her book, Schols wrote that some companies and people sponsoring the rebuilding of their former home pulled out after she and Anders separated.
To close her book, Schols thanked numerous locals and medical personnel, as well as her family, former partner and friends, saving a message for her children for last:
My biggest thanks go to William, Nellie, Melwin, Albin, Oliwer and Mollie. I may have saved your lives, but you are the absolute biggest heroes in this whole story. You are my everything and I love you with all my heart.
For further reading, we previously reported about other rumors involving Sweden, including investigating whether the country imports trash to fulfill its energy needs, as well as fact-checking whether the city of Södertälje truly trained wild crows to pick up cigarette butts.

Is 'disruptor' Antonelli winning hearts in Italy, where Ferrari is F1?
- Published
Kimi Antonelli has been hailed as a generational talent in Formula 1; the driver who can end the 73-year wait for an Italian world champion.
In March, Antonelli became the youngest-ever championship leader when he sealed victory in Japan at 19 years, seven months and four days.
And he has stayed there ever since.
This weekend, Antonelli arrives at the Italian Grand Prix with a 59-point advantage at the top of the standings after winning six races so far this year.
There is just one small issue: the young star drives for Mercedes, not Italy's beloved Ferrari.
"Ferrari is my heart," says Thomas, who is Monza born and bred, to BBC Sport at the circuit on Friday.
"It's a religion," says Emanuele, who is at the grand prix with his daughter, Matilde. "In Italy, we do support other teams and other sports, but there is only one Ferrari."
Ferrari is Formula 1 in Italy; natives joke that the position of Scuderia team principal is just as important as the identity of the Pope.
So, with fans flocking to worship at the Temple of Speed, just how do Italians feel about Antonelli battling Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc for race wins and the drivers' championship?
When a Ferrari driver triumphs in F1, the team's spiritual home of Maranello rejoices.
"It's like the second coming effectively; everyone's in the streets singing, dancing, church bells are ringing. It's a party in the streets," says Adrian Hussain, who is a member of the Scuderia Ferrari Club Silverstone and half-Italian.
Those famous bells last rung out in honour of a Ferrari world champion in 2007, when Finn Kimi Raikkonen won his only title by a single point.
Italy has not produced a world champion driver since Alberto Ascari claimed back-to-back titles for Ferrari in 1952 and 1953. For most Italians, seeing a title winner draped in il Tricolore - for any team on the grid - has been a dream rather than a reality.
But Antonelli's ascendancy this year has opened the door for Italy to embrace a new hero - even if he does drive for the direct competition.
"Antonelli is disrupting the traditional rules of fandom in Italy," Giulia Toninelli, a journalist for La Gazzetta dello Sport, Italy's most widely read sports newspaper, tells BBC Sport.
Toninelli says Antonelli's "strong personality" has won over the Italian public, especially the younger fanbase. "And the fact that he is racing for Mercedes matters very little to them."
In the fanzone at Monza, a household is divided. While Alessandro is decked out in Ferrari red, his girlfriend, Emma, is wearing the silver of Mercedes.
"Of course, I am a little bit of a Ferrarista because I'm Italian. But honestly, I love Kimi, I support him," says Emma.
If Antonelli does win this year's world title, with the season finale possibly being held at Imola, about 25 miles from where he grew up in Bologna, both Emma and Alessandro agree it would mean "Italy is back on top".
Five-time MotoGP race winner Marco Melandri and 2012 GP2 series champion and F1 TV's Davide Valsecchi present the Chiacchiere da Box, external (Paddock Chatter) podcast, where the two ex-racers discuss and analyse everything that's happened during F1 and MotoGP weekends.
"I think Kimi is living the dream, even of the Italian fans," says Italian Melandri. "But in Italy, a lot of people are very close to Ferrari, they are pushing for Ferrari. So sometimes they are fighting themselves to understand, to choose who is their favourite driver. But I think Kimi is doing something amazing."
Compatriot Valsecchi feels the same: "We are loving it. It's a big surprise for everyone, knowing that an Italian driver, so young, is leading the championship, is driving so well, and is mentally so strong. So, at the moment, everything is perfect for us."
'Sometimes in Italy, we lack a bit of patience'
1 of 5
Antonelli has been a Mercedes protege since he was 11 years old.
After just one season in Formula 2, Silver Arrows team principal Toto Wolff fast-tracked him into the seat vacated by seven-time world champion Hamilton in 2025, after the Briton left to join Ferrari in a blockbuster move.
Antonelli's introduction to F1 last year was a steep learning curve, and after a bruising European leg of the season that featured four retirements and only three points, he finished his debut campaign seventh in the championship.
Mercedes have made sure to put an arm around Antonelli whenever there has been a mishap. When the then 18-year-old crashed during his very first practice session in Monza two years ago, Wolff was straight on the team radio with five soothing words: "All good, Kimi. All good."
"I think Kimi is in the right place at the moment," says Toninelli. "Mercedes is a family he has known for a long time, one that has nurtured him as a driver and given him a level of protection that would be impossible for him to have at Ferrari right now."
Being separated from the sometimes "extreme" Italian fanbase can only work in Antonelli's favour, believes Valsecchi.
"Sometimes in Italy, we lack a bit of patience," he says. "We just push for you when you are strong and then underline with red pen every time as soon as you make little mistakes.
"For this reason, as a rookie, it is better to be away and to be on another side, and then come to Ferrari only when you are a big man with already a championship and a complete driver."
Do fans 'dream' of Antonelli at Ferrari?
If Antonelli does clinch his maiden title this year, he will surpass four-time winner Sebastian Vettel as the youngest driver in Formula 1 history to become world champion.
German Vettel was 23 years and 134 days old when he claimed his first title in 2010. Antonelli would be three years younger.
If that happens, Daniele, who is enjoying Monza with his two sons, Tommaso and Demis, says they will feel "so-so" about Antonelli's victory.
"We support Hamilton and Leclerc - we support Ferrari," says Daniele emphatically, although youngest son Demis, while still loyal to the Scuderia, is an Antonelli fan, whispering the Mercedes driver is "really good".
"I'm happy for Kimi, of course. But I'm not supporting him like Ferrari, because Ferrari is up there," Thomas adds, gesturing high into the air.
Antonelli has already rewritten the history books this season, becoming the youngest driver to take pole position, converting it into his first victory in China in March, before becoming the youngest driver to win the prestigious Monaco Grand Prix.
An engine-related retirement in Barcelona and a 15th-placed finish at Silverstone have been the only real blips of Antonelli's campaign, up until Monza's grid penalty as a result of taking a new power unit, which means he will start at the back in Sunday's race.
While his title lead has ebbed and flowed in recent races, a victory in Belgium, plus podiums in Hungary and Zandvoort, has given Antonelli a decent buffer to Mercedes team-mate George Russell and Hamilton, who are both level on 183 points.
"It would be very nice to have an Italian driver in Italian colours winning races and championships," says Hussain. "Everybody within the club, certainly in our group chats, everyone's supportive of Kimi winning races. There's no animosity towards him."
Melandri, too, thinks Antonelli driving the red car could happen somewhere along the line. "It should be a dream to see Antonelli get a victory in Ferrari in the future. That's for sure," he adds.
A result to bring both fanbases together?
At the drivers' news conference at the Belgian Grand Prix in July, after Antonelli had been hanging out with tennis' five-time Grand Slam champion and compatriot Jannik Sinner, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson asked Antonelli who, out of the two of them, is more famous in Italy.
His light-hearted reply was rapid. "It's Charles," he said, pointing to Ferrari's Leclerc sat next to him. "He's probably the most famous man in Italy right now."
Monegasque Leclerc has become the surrogate son of the Scuderia since his arrival in 2019, carrying the hopes of the tifosi on his shoulders for the past eight seasons.
Fluent in Italian and deeply embedded in Ferrari's culture, the 28-year-old, who has won twice at Monza, signed a new long-term deal with the team in June, and has said his desire to be the driver that delivers success back to Maranello is what fuels his title ambitions.
But with just nine wins for the team in 162 grands prix, doubts as to whether Leclerc is truly the chosen one for Ferrari might be starting to creep in.
"I start to see, after many years, for the first time, some fans start to say, maybe he's not as strong as we think before, because Hamilton is doing better than him, and Antonelli is doing much better with another car," says Melandri.
With Antonelli hamstrung by his grid drop this weekend, Ferrari have a head start on their rival. If he does manage to recover and finish in the top three, would a Scuderia one-two accompanied by some Antonelli magic be the ideal race result?
"Of course, sharing the podium with a Ferrari would make it even more special, but regardless of that, he will have the full support of his fans," says Toninelli.
"Part of the Italian audience may indeed favour Ferrari over Kimi, while another section may feel the opposite, but that won't stop the Italian celebration at Monza, which will bring both fanbases together."

Scientists map key protein interactions linked with profound autism
Scientists map the interactions of key proteins linked with profound autism
Scientists have now gotten closer to understanding how gene mutations may lead some people to develop profound autism.
The clues, they say, lie in the murky space between genes and disease — where key proteins come together and interact.
A team of researchers from UC San Francisco mapped more than a thousand interactions between many proteins that come from certain autism risk genes. This molecular atlas, published in the journal Science, could point researchers toward new and promising treatments.
"It's an unprecedented resource for the field," says Dr. Daniel Geschwind, a professor of human genetics, neurology, and psychiatry at UCLA who was not involved with the study. "A lot of people interested in understanding autism and drug development are going to be using this."
For families affected by profound autism, it offers hope for eventual drug therapies. "This is the kind of scientific advance we have been waiting for and praying for," says Alison Singer, president of the nonprofit Autism Science Foundation, who has a daughter with severe cognitive impairment. "There's still a lot of work ahead, [but] this paper makes the path from genetic discovery to treatment much clearer."
The work builds on progress made in recent years to identify single genes that harbor mutations found in a subset of individuals with profound autism.
Getting past the "wall"
People with profound autism often live with severe intellectual disability and require around-the-clock care. They're nonverbal or minimally verbal, and often have serious medical conditions like epilepsy.
Pinning down the biology behind profound autism has always been a complicated endeavor — while both genes and environmental factors play a role, those factors can vary widely from person to person.
In the past decade or so, some genetics researchers have had remarkable success in identifying high-impact genetic differences in a subset of people with profound autism.
"They've discovered several hundred genes and corresponding mutations that are prevalent in [these] individuals," says Nevan Krogan, director of the Quantitative Biosciences Institute at UC San Francisco.
"But they kind of hit a wall," he added — because scientists haven't been able to turn those gene discoveries into many promising drugs and treatments.
"There was this huge missing piece," says Dr. Matthew State, a clinical psychiatrist and geneticist at UCSF: The genes serve as blueprints for making proteins that drive brain development, but researchers lacked visibility into how those proteins do the work.
State has been a pioneer in identifying high-risk genes, and the mutations in those genes, that are associated with profound autism. Krogan has been at the forefront of using new technology to look into protein interactions.
More than a decade ago, the two researchers were introduced by their mutual boss, the chancellor at UCSF, who encouraged them to collaborate. "[State] had the genes and the mutations. I had the technologies to look at the corresponding proteins," Krogan says.
They focused on filling a knowledge gap. "What we've been missing is the mechanistic understanding of how these mutations [on the genes] are seemingly resulting in autism," Krogan says. "In order to understand that, you need to go to the proteins."
Proteins are the complex molecules that come together to build the body, based on instructions encoded in the genes. "What makes an eye cell an eye cell, and a muscle a muscle, are the proteins and how they work together," State says. "They are the machinery of life."
In this case, the researchers wanted to find the molecular machinery of profound autism — to understand which proteins came from those high-risk autism genes, and how those proteins worked together.
The research was slow at first, but more recent advances in technology — including artificial intelligence — have sped things up.
To start, the researchers went on a "fishing expedition" for protein interactions. They chose 100 proteins from these high-risk autism genes, injected them into lab-grown cells, and then pulled them out, along with the additional proteins that attached to them.
Then, they used an AI system called AlphaFold, developed by Google DeepMind, to help determine which proteins in the clumps were directly touching. "Where AI is playing an important role is being predictive about who's talking to who," says Krogan. "Sometimes they take years to figure out. Now, we can get these insights in an hour." While imperfect, the system has worked well enough to save significant time and money, Krogan says.
Then, they wanted to see what happened to the proteins when the genes got tweaked. They introduced mutations that appear in patients with profound autism, and assessed what changed. "We broke the proteins in the way that they're broken in autism," says State. "That allows us ultimately to answer the question of, when they're going wrong in autism, how are they going wrong?"
They conducted this research in frogs and in organoids, which are lab-grown tissues that model the human brain. In one example, the mutations weakened the connection between two proteins related to which genes turn on and off in a cell. Then, one went rogue, turning on other genes that led to neurodevelopmental defects in organoids.
Molecular convergence
There are hundreds of rare, high-risk autism genes, acting in more than a thousand different ways.
But in mapping more than 1,800 protein interactions, the researchers found that many of them moved along shared biological pathways — particularly those related to early brain development, such as how synapses get constructed, and which neurons develop and when.
The convergence found in this study aligns with other recent publications, adding to an emerging understanding in the field, says Dr. Geschwind of UCLA.
"If we look at multiple mutations and they converge on the same process, that's strong evidence that you're dealing with the things that you want to treat," State says.
Identifying this more limited set of protein complexes that likely contribute to the development of profound autism could change the approach to treatments, says Singer with the Autism Science Foundation. "We've been working gene-by-gene to correct mutations," she says.
And if future drugs could target these shared protein pathways, she adds, "we may not need that separate therapeutic strategy for every autism gene."
Setting sights on new drug-development targets
It takes years to go from a biological discovery like this to an approved drug that treats humans. The findings would need to be translated into drug candidates, then tested for safety and effectiveness.
"It takes time and a lot of persistence and focus," State says. "This [paper] is unlikely to lead to therapies tomorrow — but it lays an important foundation for them."
Most human drugs are made to target proteins, Geschwind at UCLA says, so the newly published map of protein interactions offers an accessible entry point for pharmaceutical development.
And researchers hope to combine recent technological advances in ways that accelerate that progress even more. "When you put together the ability to borrow from successes in other fields [such as cancer treatments], and the development of AI, we're at an inflection point that will hopefully shorten the time cycle," State says.
Last week, Krogan's Quantitative Biosciences Institute received a $46 million grant from the Aligning Research to Impact Autism initiative, funded by philanthropist and Google co-founder Sergey Brin. The researchers are already working on next steps.

I've never spoken to Everton owner Friedkin - Moyes
- Published
David Moyes says he has never met or spoken to Everton owner Dan Friedkin since returning as manager in January 2025.
Friedkin is head of The Friedkin Group, which runs the club from its base in Houston, but has not attended a home game since completing a takeover of the club in December 2024.
How the club is run and who is responsible for making key decisions came under close scrutiny during the summer transfer window.
Speaking to reporters before Everton's match against Manchester United on Sunday, Moyes reiterated his commitment to the club despite a chaotic end to the window.
When asked if he had ever met or spoken to Friedkin in the 20 months since he was reappointed as manager, Moyes' answer was a simple "No".
Friedkin leaves the day-to-day running of the club to his son-in-law Rishi Majithia, who works in tandem with chief executive Angus Kinnear.
"My real contact is Angus," said Moyes. "Angus is the one who I would go to see. Rishi is the next one and then the head of the Friedkin family in America.
"I don't really get any direct conversations with them, but I do through Rishi, he is the one I would speak to."
Fans reacted angrily during last Saturday's match at Bournemouth following news the club had accepted a £40m bid from Nottingham Forest for one of their prized assets, England Under-19s midfielder Harrison Armstrong.
Everton eventually pulled out of the deal, but supporters remain frustrated by decisions made by the board in the remainder of the transfer window.
Beto was sold to Fiorentina on deadline day on Tuesday, before the club had secured a replacement striker, with USA forward Folarin Balogun then backing out of a move to Everton from Monaco at the 11th hour on Tuesday.
Everton finished the transfer window with a squad of just 18 senior players, including only one striker, one right-back and one left-back.
Moyes aligned himself with Everton fans last weekend when asked about plans to sell Armstrong, saying the club was "managed by an Evertonian" and "supporters aren't always wrong".
And he acknowledged on Friday that there was work to do done on the club's structure behind the scenes: "We've got new owners in who are still feeling their way in the club. I think if we get to know each other more it will get better."
But the former Manchester United and West Ham boss said he would not walk away from the challenge of unifying a club that he led to a succession of top-five finishes in the Premier League between 2002 and 2013 in his first stint as manager.
"Everton's different," said Moyes, when asked if he had considered quitting. "I wouldn't have come back for anybody but Everton.
"I think the club here has had enough days where the people find a way of recovering. People saw the face of Evertonians last week and it can be really powerful. I would expect them to be really powerful now.
"But powerful for the team, powerful for the players. What we're going to need from them is extra because we're short, so we need them. If they're not with us, then it's terrible. And they are with us, I believe they are with us."

Kerala minister takes dig at university heads attending RSS events: ‘Not befitting of a democratic society’
The minister's remarks come amid differences between the state government and Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar.
Kerala Higher Education Minister Roji M John on Saturday criticised the association of heads of higher education institutions with organisations promoting what he described as “divisive agendas”, in an apparent reference to vice-chancellors who participated in an RSS programme attended by its chief Mohan Bhagwat in June.
“It is not at all befitting of a democratic society that those heading institutions of higher education, which should be centres of independent thought and constitutional values, forget the dignity of the positions they hold and confine themselves to platforms of organisations that promote divisive agendas,” he said in a Facebook post on Teachers' Day.
The minister's remarks come amid differences between the state government and Governor Rajendra Vishwanath Arlekar, who is chancellor of universities in Kerala, over various issues concerning state universities, including the appointment of vice-chancellors and nomination of Senate members.

RSS event draws criticism
The issue also acquired an ideological dimension after some vice-chancellors participated in an RSS programme attended by its chief, Mohan Bhagwat, in June.
Roji had then criticised their participation, saying that the position of a vice-chancellor represented academic and administrative neutrality.
“Such tendencies, which surrender the privilege of academic autonomy before narrow political interests, question the very essence of education and teaching,” the state Higher Education minister said.
RSS centenary celebrations
The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) plans to conclude its ongoing centenary celebrations with a programme in the national capital in November, to be addressed by its chief Mohan Bhagwat, HT reported earlier.
The RSS, founded in 1925 in Nagpur, is the ideological fountainhead of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party. Its centenary celebrations began last year on Vijayadashami (October 2).
“The celebrations began in Nagpur and will conclude with a programme in Delhi, to be addressed by sarsanghachalak Mohan Bhagwat. As part of the celebrations, programmes were held across India and abroad,” a functionary said. The Delhi programme is likely to be held on November 29.
The organisation, credited with mobilising support for the BJP through a vast network of cadres linked to its more than 40 affiliates, has been expanding its footprint across the country and strengthening its overseas outreach. Bhagwat attended programmes in nearly all of the 46 prants, or provinces, besides delivering public addresses in Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai and Bengaluru, the functionary said.
“In many states, he interacted with prominent people and heads of other faiths, and addressed smaller gatherings. Several senior functionaries, including Dattatreya Hosabale, also travelled extensively,” the functionary said.

The doors to Europe’s largest consumer tech show officially opened to the public today following a week of news coming out of IFA 2026 in Berlin, Germany. If you’re struggling to keep up with what has been announced, here are some of the best new gadgets and upgrades from the show — including a smartphone that attempts to finally rid the world of screen bezels and a powerful robovac that carries a smaller sidekick for cleaning spaces it can’t squeeze into.
The best tech and gadgets announced at IFA so far
Double-decker robovacs, a smartphone that eliminates the screen bezel, and another laptop with an expanding screen.

To catch up on everything announced at IFA 2026 you can follow The Verge’s complete coverage right here.
By tucking the edges of its 6.78-inch, 144Hz OLED panel underneath the phone’s thin metal frame, Tecno managed to create a smartphone that nearly entirely eliminates a visible bezel, maximizing screen real estate. The aptly-named Bezelless made its debut at IFA with a MediaTek Dimensity 7400e chipset paired with 8GB of RAM, 256GB of storage, a 6,000mAh battery, and a trio of front and back cameras including a 50-megapixel main shooter. The company hasn’t announced any plans to put the concept into production, but its unique design could eventually inspire other devices.
Why build one robovac that can do it all when you can split the work between a pair of them? That’s the idea behind iRobot’s Roomba Duo concept. The main vacuum is the most powerful robovac the brand has ever made. It can suck up messes like spilled pasta, steam-mop hard floors, and vacuum and wash carpeting while navigating a home using a combination of LiDAR and cameras. But it’s big, so to reach and clean tighter spaces the Roomba Duo carries a Roomba Plus 757 on top in a small garage it can raise and lower to deploy its robovac sidekick.
One of the most portable projectors on the market is getting some welcome upgrades. The $579.99 Aurzen Zip Pro carries forward the same tri-fold design of the original including features like autofocus and automatic keystone adjustments but is getting a bump in brightness from 100 to 200 ANSI lumens and an increase in resolution to 1080P. It’s a bit bigger than its predecessor thanks in part to a battery that now offers up to 2.5 hours of runtime and added connectivity including the ability to tether to the Nintendo Switch using only a USB-C cable.
First announced at MWC 2026 earlier this year, the RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro is an extra durable $999 Android 16 smartphone with dust and water protection, a beefy 9,300mAh battery, a 6.67-inch 120Hz AMOLED screen, and four cameras. The three on the back include a 64MP night vision camera assisted by infrared LEDs and one that can be removed and used as a standalone action camera capable of capturing video at up to 2.7K/30fps. The pop-out camera module has a battery good for up to 40 minutes and 64GB of built-in storage. When either are depleted you can reattach to the camera module to the phone where its battery will recharge and the footage will be copied over automatically.
Lenovo continues to experiment with ways for laptops to take advantage of flexible OLED displays, but its latest concept feels a bit tame compared to the Legion Pro Rollable gaming laptop it debuted at CES 2026. The 14-inch Project Swan concept is much smaller by comparison with a display that unfurls horizontally to grow to 17-inches with a 16:9 aspect ratio. It keeps the laptop compact while boosting productivity with extra screen real estate but accommodating the OLED panel and motors leaves the laptop’s lid feeling unusually heavy with a design that limits how far back it can be tilted.
At its thickest point the Muse measures around 3.8mm and will be available in 512GB or 1TB capacities with read and write speeds topping out at 1,050MB/s and 1,000MB/s, respectively. There’s not much compromise on performance, but there is with connectivity. To slim down the drive Lexar skipped a standard USB-C port in favor of a magnetic pogo-pin connector and a proprietary USB-C cable. Not only do you have to keep tabs on a special cable, if you want to stick the Muse to the back of your smartphone while recording video you’ll need to use an included magnetic sleeve that negates the drive’s slim design.
There are two new versions of Anker’s sleepbuds that can help quiet a snoring roommate, but the $349.99 Soundcore Sleep Earbuds 4 Pro introduce a new charging case with a round OLED display on the case. Without having to reach for your phone you can select a preset soundscape, browse your recent sleep stats, and set alarms. The sleepbuds also feature in-ear PPG sensors, so while you doze, they can keep tabs on the quality of your sleep, heart rate, HRV, and other health metrics that may provide insights if you wake up exhausted each morning.
Borrowing an idea that Lenovo proposed in a laptop concept last year, Oukitel’s RG14-P features a solar panel on the lid that can recharge the laptop’s battery at up to 10W under “optimal sunlight conditions.” It would take approximately six hours to bring a dead battery up to a 50 percent charge, but you won’t have to be scrambling to find a power outlet. It’s expected to launch in November with a 14th gen Intel Core i7 processor, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage.
With most rope lighting solutions you can easily see the individual LEDs illuminating it from within, but Philips Hue’s new Liane 360-degree Rope Lights emit an even diffuse light in all directions using the company’s OmniGlow technology with the ability to adjust their color. The ropes can be used to line and illuminate architectural features, simply hung from a ceiling, or shaped using clear clips and mounts. But they’re not cheap. A 3-meter version is $399.99 while a 5-meter option is $549.99.
At $5,999 when it launches later this year, Awol Vision’s latest ultra-short throw projector will strain budgets, but at a distance of just 7.5 inches from a wall it can project a 4K/120Hz image with 6,000 ISO Lumens of brightness up to 120 inches in size, so it’s actually more affordable than a comparably sized flat panel TV. The LuxVision can be customized with various finishes and colors to match a room’s decor or furniture, but its most appealing feature is the projector’s ability to physically shift its lens so you can adjust and reposition the image on a wall or screen without having to rely on digital image corrections.
TCL’s Nxtpaper technology is one of the better ways to merge the functionality of a modern smartphone with the benefits of a dedicated e-reader. A push of a button activates a Max Ink Mode with a paperlike monochromatic display and a streamlined version of the Android UI that reduces distractions and boosts battery life. What sets the new P80 Ultra apart is that it’s the first Nxtpaper phone to feature a 6.83-inch, 120Hz OLED screen with a 1.5K resolution and 3,200 nits of peak brightness with an anti-glare coating you won’t find on other devices.
Packard Bell dates back to 1933, but most remember the brand from when it was resurrected in 1986 and used for a line of popular and affordable home PCs in the 90s. Acer is bringing it back again for its new 14.5-inch DotBook laptop as well as a bunch of other colorful accessories including keyboards, speakers, a 4G feature phone, audio glasses, and a record player.
The smart home long ago expanded to include devices that can help care for cats and dogs, but Dreame’s LumaTempo is one of the first to help fish thrive. The smart tank can be controlled using a mobile phone on your app letting you use and schedule its build-in feeder, see a history of when your fish last ate, and keep tabs on the water temperature. It’s expected to launch next year, but pricing isn’t known yet.
Flipping the gaming laptop script, Acer’s latest concept is a Windows-based gaming handheld, similar to its Predator Atlas 8, that can transform into a tiny portable PC thanks to a swiveling design that repositions its screen atop a mini keyboard. The DualPlay Mini’s display is just 8-inches in size, which could make productivity a challenge if work involves sprawling spreadsheets, but the concept could be used for answering emails during a daily commute and then connected to a larger display at work for more demanding tasks.
The Dell 14S isn’t as thin or light as its recently launched XPS 13, but the company is looking to make this model even more accessible for students or others on a tighter budget. The laptop starts with 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, and those specs can be bumped to 16GB/1TB. It features a 1080P webcam with face unlock support, two USB-C ports, a headphone jack, and like Apple’s MacBook Neo, will be available in four bright color options: linen, dusty rose, washed denim, and velvet green.
The $1,199 Roomba Max 875 Combo is iRobot’s latest flagship floor cleaner and introduces a new feature the company calls “SealForce.” When it detects it’s cleaning carpeting, the robovac lowers a skirt around the cleaning head to create a better seal that increases suction for a deeper clean. The Max 875 also offers up to 35,000 Pa of suction power, mopping capabilities, lidar and camera-based autonomous navigation, and the ability to climb over obstacles and thresholds up to 3.5cm tall.
Released under Jsaux’s new Voidjoy brand, the $49.99 SkyLark S1 Pro is a compact portable controller that appears to do a lot of things right. It’s got drift-resistant TMR thumbsticks that are recessed so they won’t get snagged on other devices in your bag, a pair of analog triggers ideal for racing games, and three different ways to connect to devices and consoles: Bluetooth, USB-C, and 2.4GHz. If you opt for a 2.4GHz connection, you can also pair two S1 Pros to a single transmitter and swap back-and-forth between what character you’re controlling in a multiplayer game, making it useful for parents playing with a kid who may struggle with some challenges.
Is Framework’s approach to easily repairable and upgradeable laptops finally rubbing off on other companies? Acer’s 16-inch Vero 16 offers tool-free access to several internal components including its user-replaceable SSD and battery. The company says the laptop’s processor can also be upgraded down the line, but that will require it to be sent in to an Acer service center. Pricing is still unknown, but the Vero 16 is expected to launch early next year outside North America.
If you’re lucky enough to have an original Nintendo Switch Pro controller that hasn’t succumbed to joystick drift and want to expand its capabilities, Jsaux’s new Elite Extender is an easy aftermarket upgrade. For $39.99 it attaches to the back of the controller and adds four mappable buttons that can be programmed to reproduce multiple button presses. It’s got its own rechargeable battery, but does hinder Amiibo functionality while it’s piggybacking.

Choosing the right race can give your character useful passive bonuses throughout Grand Blue. Some races are built around combat, while others offer better mobility, exploration benefits, or bonuses for specific playstyles. In this Grand Blue race tier list, we rank every available race from S to D so you can decide which one is worth keeping after a reroll.
Grand Blue Race Tier List
Races provide passive bonuses that affect how your character performs during combat, exploration, and general progression. A good race can complement your fighting style or make certain activities easier. You can combine them with the best Grand Blue fruits and easily go through even the hardest challenges.
However, if you use weaker races, it may leave you with fewer useful advantages. This is especially important when deciding whether to spend your limited Race Rerolls available through the Grand Blue codes.
| Tier | Races | 
|---|---|
| S | Celestial, Seafolk | 
| A | Beastfolk, Skyfolk, Half Fish | 
| B | Long Arm, Dwarf | 
| C | Human | 
| D | None | 
S Tier races in our Grand Blue race tier list provide the strongest overall advantages and are the best races to keep. A Tier races are excellent choices with strong benefits; B Tier races are useful but more specialized; C Tier races are serviceable options that are usually outperformed. We did not include any race in the D Tier, as you must reroll a race to create a proper build.
Grand Blue Tier List for Best Races Explained
As you can see in our Grand Blue race tier list above, Celestial and Seafolk are extremely stronger than others. Wondering why? Here is our detailed explanation for the tier list rankings:
- Celestial (S Tier): Extremely rare and one of the most desirable races in Grand Blue. It offers strong overall potential and is an excellent long-term choice, although its 0.1% drop chance makes it extremely difficult to obtain.
- Seafolk (S Tier): Provides strong swimming-related advantages that make exploration and travel between islands easier. Its benefits become less important once you are familiar with navigating the world.
- Beastfolk (A Tier): A versatile race with strong general usefulness and Cat and Bunny variants. It is particularly good for players who value mobility, although it lacks the specialization of the top S Tier races.
- Skyfolk (A Tier): Focuses heavily on mobility and movement. It is a strong choice for players who like repositioning during combat, though its value depends more on your playstyle than the more universally useful races.
- Half Fish (A Tier): Offers useful exploration benefits and is a good option for players who spend plenty of time traveling around the world. It does not provide the same overall value as Seafolk.
- Long Arm (B Tier): Has an interesting combat-focused identity that suits players who prefer close-range fighting. Its benefits are more specialized and do not provide as much value for exploration or general progression.
- Dwarf (B Tier): Provides a distinctive option for certain bruiser-style builds. It can work well for specific playstyles, but its overall benefits are less obvious than those offered by higher tier races.
- Human (C Tier): The default race and the easiest one to obtain. It is completely viable for progressing through the game, but lacks the specialized advantages that make the rarer races more appealing.
Celestial is the race to aim for if you want the strongest overall option, while Seafolk is especially useful for players who spend a lot of time exploring. If you roll Human, there is little reason to panic, but most other races offer a more specialized advantage worth keeping.
So, which ones from our Grand Blue race tier list are you picking up first? Let us know in the comments below.
How do you change your race in Grand Blue?
You can reroll your race through the character customization screen. The game shows the available race options and their chances when you use a Race Reroll.
Should I reroll Human in Grand Blue?
You can keep Human if you are comfortable with it, since it is fully viable for progression. However, most other races provide additional specialized benefits, so a better race is worth keeping when you roll one.
What is the best race in Grand Blue?
Celestial is the best race in Grand Blue. It is extremely rare and offers strong overall value for long-term progression.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is still secretly counting two measles deaths that were deleted from the agency’s public measles data—a deletion that occurred at the direct request of anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., according to two reports released today.
Early today, Reuters reported that Kennedy instructed new CDC director Erica Schwartz to delete the two deaths from the agency’s website. CDC staff had reportedly already reviewed information about the deaths and accepted the characterization that they were measles-related. Still, Schwartz deleted the deaths without objection, insiders told Reuters. According to previous reporting, the two deaths were added and then removed from the CDC’s website within hours on August 30.
The deaths were of a newborn and a child, and they were reported last week by health officials in Pennsylvania. The state’s ongoing measles outbreak has sickened 540 so far, including 119 just in the last week.
This afternoon, Inside Medicine reported that an internal CDC database still includes the two deaths, according to a screenshot that was reportedly verified by CDC staff. The database, called “One CDC Data Platform,” is accessible to state and local health officials as well as CDC employees.
Ars Technica reached out to the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) about the discrepancy, but it did not immediately respond.

Eye donation is said to be one of the most meaningful forms of donation, as a single donor can potentially restore sight to two individuals through corneal transplantation. India has made considerable progress in eye banking; the country currently has 396 functional eye banks, and corneal collections increased from 62,370 in 2022–23 to 69,848 in 2024–25. However, the need for donor tissue substantially exceeds its availability. There are approximately 2 million corneally blind people in our country, but only 40,000 corneal transplants performed per year.
Role of stakeholders
The government has a crucial role in strengthening the eye donation ecosystem through the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI). Government support includes funding for eye bank infrastructure and equipment, training of ophthalmologists and eye bank technicians, promotion of eye donation, and provision of corneal storage media. Government hospitals can further improve donation rates by establishing Hospital Cornea Retrieval Programmes (HCRP) and integrating eye donation into routine end-of-life counselling.
Non-governmental organisations and service organisations have an equally important role in creating awareness, dispelling myths, encouraging pledges and, most importantly, counselling families at the time of death. Organisations such as eye bank networks, Lions Clubs and other community-based groups can take the message of eye donation to schools, colleges, workplaces and rural communities.
Private eye hospitals and institutions can complement these efforts by establishing or strengthening eye banks, developing efficient corneal retrieval networks, maintaining high standards of tissue evaluation and preservation, and providing advanced corneal transplantation. Recent initiatives such as the expansion of the National Eye Bank at AIIMS, Delhi through partnerships with additional hospitals demonstrate the value of collaborative retrieval networks.
Building strong PPPs
Ultimately, the future of eye donation in India lies in a strong public–private–NGO partnership. Awareness must translate into timely family consent, consent into retrieval, and retrieved tissue into high-quality transplantation. Strengthening this entire chain will be essential to bring down the burden of corneal blindness and make the gift of sight a reality for many more Indians.
The goal is clear: to transform the gift of eye donation into the gift of sight. Every donated cornea carries a legacy of compassion—allowing one person’s life to bring light into another’s.
(Dr. Mohan Rajan is chairman and medical director and Dr. Sujatha Mohan is executive medical director, of Rajan Eye Care Hospital. drmohanrajan@gmail.com)

Serbian club punished by Uefa over fan chants in honour of war criminal Ratko Mladic
Ratko Mladic died last week at the age of 84 while serving a life sentence for genocide
Uefa has issued a fine to Serbian club Red Star Belgrade following chants by supporters in tribute to convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, who died on the day of their European fixture last week.
Visiting fans chanted Mladic's name, saluted him and unfurled a banner praising him during a 5-1 defeat by Czech side Viktoria Plzeň on 27 August.
Mladic, a Bosnian Serb commander, directed the 1995 massacre of over 8,000 Muslims in Srebrenica as well as other war crimes. He died last week at the age of 84 in The Hague, where he was serving a life sentence for genocide.
Uefa announced late on Friday that Red Star must pay 90,000 euros (£77,000) for breaches including inappropriate chanting and "racist and/or discriminatory behaviour."
Furthermore, the Serbian champions are prohibited from selling tickets to supporters for their next away fixture in European competition, when they play Swiss club Lugano in the Conference League.
A secondary away ticket ban has been deferred subject to a two-year probationary period.
The 1991 European champions have a history of Uefa disciplinary actions regarding fan behaviour, including racist slurs targeting Roma people.
Mladic was sentenced to life in prison back in 2017 for what was called one of the “most heinous” crimes in human history by the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia (ICTY), which convicted him.
The massacres took place in July 1995 when Mladic’s troops rounded up thousands of unarmed Muslim men and boys in the town of Srebrenica, lined them up while tying their hands behind their backs and shot them over a period of several days. Women and girls were systematically raped.
Remains of the deceased were then bulldozed into mass graves, which were later dug up and hauled away in order to hide the extent of the killings.
Earlier this year, his attorneys requested his release on humanitarian grounds as his defence teams said he was in a state of “advanced, irreversible medical decline”.
Reports said that Mladic died in a UN prison hospital in the Hague, in the Netherlands. A family member confirmed the news to the Associated Press.

Trump says Witkoff, Kushner heading abroad in latest U.S. effort to end Ukraine war
Zelenskyy says U.S. envoys will arrive in Ukraine Sunday after going to Moscow first
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law, are heading abroad to attempt to forge a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, the U.S. president told reporters on Friday.
During comments in the Oval Office, Trump suggested the U.S. had a fresh concrete proposal aimed at ending the war, which is now in its fifth year. He did not, however, elaborate on what that proposal would be, nor did he say if Witkoff and Kushner would be travelling to Ukraine, Russia or both countries.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday said the two men would fly to Ukraine on Sunday after visiting Moscow.
"We have an idea for peace," Trump said.
"I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two great negotiators. They've done a great job, and we sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done. And there may be a good chance that we'll do it."
Itinerary has been in flux: sources
The duo had been planning to travel to Moscow over the weekend followed by a visit to Kyiv, two sources previously told Reuters. However, the itinerary has been in flux in recent days, and the Kyiv section of the journey was still not completely certain, one of the sources said on Friday.
The Trump administration's attempts to settle the war in Ukraine have largely come to nothing, and negotiations stalled out in recent months.
In late August, Central Intelligence Agency Director John Ratcliffe travelled to Moscow in part to press counterparts there to consider a settlement, Reuters and several other media outlets reported.
Most Western intelligence officials doubt Russian President Vladimir Putin is interested in a short-term deal, while Ukrainian intelligence believes he is in fact likely to escalate, rather than de-escalate the war in the near term.
A Russian drone hit the headquarters of Ukraine's SBU security service in Kyiv on Friday in one of the most high-profile targets struck during the war.
Witkoff, who is effectively the lead U.S. negotiator with respect to the war in Ukraine, has travelled to Moscow numerous times but has not yet visited Ukraine.

Five years ago, people who hang out in the stranger corners of the web started arguing that the internet was mostly fake. It had been this way since about 2016, they said, when Google introduced its artificial neural network for machine translation. Supposedly, from that point forward, online interactions began to be replaced, until nearly every message and picture had been posted by a bot. Everywhere you looked, websites were “empty and devoid of people,” as one scholar of the theory put it.
This wasn’t true, but the core idea was tethered to a real phenomenon. Even way back then, in 2021, social platforms were awash in fake views, fake likes, fake traffic, and fake engagement. Some people figured that automation might one day take over the entire web and then our world. They were mostly being silly, or paranoid. Today they seem like … prophets?
“Dead Internet” theory is seeing a revival, this time in mainstream conversation. It’s no longer strange to think that AI might be everywhere, edging out all forms of human interaction: bots talking to bots, all the way down. Every week we seem to take another step in that direction. In June, the Pew Research Center reported that nearly a quarter of American adults now use chatbots every day. Two months later, OpenAI announced an official ChatGPT integration for iMessage. Chatbot-generated text is already widely used for website filler, business emails, and cover letters. Will it soon be commonplace in private messages between friends and family?
The ChatGPT-iMessage integration works on your desktop, not your phone. It doesn’t send messages on your behalf until you’ve reviewed and approved its suggestions. A similar plug-in has long been available for Anthropic’s Claude, and many messaging apps already offer AI-suggested replies. To some extent, OpenAI’s new product simply formalizes something that people had been doing on their own, either by pasting text from one window to another, or by improvising personal ChatGPT-linking software. (The Atlantic has a corporate partnership with OpenAI.)
“Low-effort communication has always existed,” Michael Pfister, a software developer living in Colorado, told me. He said that he had already vibe coded his own version of the iMessage tool months ago. ChatGPT pings him daily to let him know if he’s missed any important questions in his group chat. He tried having it write a text to his friends, just as an experiment, but they immediately noticed that the message was AI. “They tried to prompt-inject me,” he said: They asked the agent what Michael thought of them, in the hopes of tricking it into sharing his private thoughts. He told me that he mostly uses the tool for work and that he isn’t interested in having AI communicate with his friends on his behalf in the future. “I think relationships are experiential,” he said.
Max Weinbach, an analyst at a market-research firm in Connecticut, told me he uses ChatGPT to text with his bosses about work. “It just makes life easy,” he said. It’s hardly different from using Google’s suggested email responses, which have been available for nearly a decade. Weinbach had no ethical qualms about switching to LLM-assisted communication, although he recognizes that it can be taken as a sign of disrespect. “It’s not accepted or polite,” he said. “It’s just kind of a rude thing to do.”
These two are on the bleeding edge, yet exhibiting more restraint than some others. All over Reddit, my favorite repository for human drama, people are worrying about human drama that has a nonhuman interloper. New posts appear each day requesting help in figuring out whether something might have been created with AI: Is this apartment listing real? What about this dating-app profile? What about this video of a cute animal doing something amazing? (A bobcat flagging down a biker to help her rescue her kitten from the bottom of a random hole?)
Many of the requests have a moralistic tone, and the poster comes to the crowd solemnly, with hesitation, because they know the truth may be painful. The most fraught discussions concern AI-generated personal messages. Guys on dating apps are using the technology. Sometimes long-term partners, friends, siblings, or parents do it too. “Is this text apology written by ChatGPT?” someone will ask. Or “Did my mother use ChatGPT to write me a text of support on the morning of my divorce?” The implication is betrayal.
I spoke with Melissa Crowder, a 47-year-old from Alberta, Canada, who shared her own experience with AI texting in a July post on Reddit. She’d spent all day having a “nice conversation” with a match from the dating app Feeld, then finally noticed that their repartee was off when he copy-pasted her own message back to her by mistake. At that point she realized all of his previous messages had been structurally similar—usually two paragraphs of text followed by a question on a single line. And he’d been using the word dangerously way too much. When she asked if he was using ChatGPT, he replied, “Busted” with a bunch of emoji, which also struck her as something ChatGPT might do. “I’m like, this is still ChatGPT.” Then he unmatched her.
Crowder would not have been that mad if the guy had just fessed up and said something normal in his own voice. She sometimes uses AI tools to help her express herself too. She said she has a tendency to ramble on and overexplain her feelings, so she’ll use a site called Goblin Tools to self-edit. She might make a message to her ex-husband “Less emotional” (one of the choices in a drop-down menu) and get straight to the point. She also has a friend who sends AI-written texts from time to time. “Where I would draw my line is where you take the person out of the conversation,” she said. “If I’m vibing with a chatbot and then I meet the person in real life, what is that conversation going to look like?”
For a recent paper, a group of researchers from the University of Washington and Arizona State University studied two popular Reddit forums—r/RealOrAI and r/isthisAI—to figure out how people go about determining which material is AI-generated and which is not. The most common mode of analysis evaluates the fundamental plausibility of an image or a video. (“Babies do not nearly have that much coordination to both be standing up, talking so well and holding up that large cat.”) A smaller number of comments in the study addressed some alleged telltale signs of AI-style texting, including the prevalence of “overly ornate but meaningless phrases.” Other people have noted LLMs’ overreliance on certain words (delve is an oft-noted one), sentence structures (negative parallelisms), and punctuation (em dashes).
The paper ends in an ominous tone. “Our findings suggest that people are developing mental models of what AI-generated content looks like, built on personal experiences and beliefs developed over time,” the authors wrote, before arguing that these mental models were unlikely to be accurate for long. The LLMs will evolve and stop doing the things that now make their output so easy to spot. In fact, the tricks enumerated in the paper are already getting old, one of the paper’s authors, Tina Yeung, told me. “I definitely think this is a snapshot in time,” she said.
The mere fact of people’s concern about AI, and their anxiety over its incursion into day-to-day life, may be a snapshot too. Perhaps the stigma that now exists around using ChatGPT to text a friend or message on a dating app will fade in the years ahead. Maybe one day it will disappear altogether, and even our phones will end up empty and devoid of people. Or else I guess it’s possible—just possible—that the Dead Internet theory is as silly as it ever was.

Why former East Germany became the stronghold of far-right AfD
Eastern Germany commissioner says economic disruption and anti-immigrant sentiment are driving voters towards the AfD
More than three decades after Germany’s 1990 reunification, lasting east-west divisions may be thrown into stark relief at Sunday’s election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
The anti-immigration and Moscow-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to win big and even hopes to take power at the state level, which would be a first for a far-right party in German post-war history.
As much of the east has become an AfD stronghold, the government’s commissioner for eastern Germany, lawmaker Elisabeth Kaiser, herself from Thuringia state in the east, spoke about the historic and cultural factors shaping the region’s distinct politics.
When the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, spelling the end of the communist German Democratic Republic (GDR), many state-owned enterprises were closed, sparking large-scale unemployment and population flight, especially by young women.
“That was a difficult experience for many East Germans, one that has persisted across generations, becoming part of a collective East German memory,” Kaiser said.
“It involved this sense of devaluation, this experience of loss and the realisation that everything can change overnight.”

Sheeppox is a highly contagious, often fatal viral disease that was largely eradicated from much of European livestock in the 20th century. But there is still the occasional regional outbreak, such as the one that afflicted many flocks of sheep in Greece last year. In order to reconstruct how the virus has evolved over the last 3,500 years, scientists extracted and sequenced sheeppox DNA preserved in the animal skins used for the parchment of numerous medieval manuscripts. They reported their findings in a new paper published in the journal Science Advances.
“The recording of ancient DNA of pathogens has completely changed our understanding of infectious disease in the past, and here we show that parchment can also preserve animal pathogen DNA. It is possible that archives and libraries around the world also contain the genetic traces of disease outbreaks in animals in the past,” said co-author Louis L’Hôte, a graduate student at University College Dublin. “These genomes help us understand how these pathogens evolved and how they impacted past societies—such as sheeppox virus, which we show has been affecting Eurasian sheep herds for at least three and a half millennia.”
Per the authors, the earliest known written evidence of sheeppox infection dates to the first century CE, when Roman accounts described outbreaks of skin lesions (“pustules”) in the animals. There are more frequent mentions of deadly outbreaks of “pockes” or “variola” in sheep by the Middle Ages, recorded in various agricultural texts and accounting documents in France, Spain, and England. There seemed to be a decline in outbreaks in 17th-century France, although frequent outbreaks re-emerged in the 18th and 19th centuries, often with high mortality rates in the flocks. Great Britain did not experience a sheeppox resurgence until 1847.
However, very little was known about the genetic history of the sheeppox virus. That’s why L’Hôte et al. turned to analyzing DNA in medieval manuscripts—the parchments were often made from sheep leather. A number of analytical techniques have emerged in recent decades to help create these kinds of historical molecular records.

Canadian 'banking' company linked to sanctioned money-laundering network
Visual investigation reveals 'red flags' experts say should prompt review of secretive firm
Maple Digital Financial Solutions describes itself as a "revolutionary banking" company, with an address in a skyscraper in the heart of Vancouver's financial district.
On paper, the company is registered with Canada’s financial intelligence agency, and offers "fast and easy" global currency transfers and "convenient banking" with the click of a button.
In practice, however, it’s a shell company. Its website offers no option to open an account and provides no employee names, while phone calls go straight to voicemail and emails go unanswered.
A CBC News visual investigation, in collaboration with the Centre for Information Resilience (CIR), reveals this shell company is closely linked to the TGR network, accused by international law enforcement of laundering billions of dollars for ransomware gangs, drug cartels and wealthy Russians.
"Red lights are flashing, there are a number of red flags here," said Denis Meunier, former deputy director at the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC), who reviewed the findings.
A report by CIR, a U.K.-based research organization, used digital clues to connect Maple Digital Financial Solutions with a series of companies called The OneGate and the TGR network.
CBC shared its findings with multiple legal and financial experts, and each had a similar takeaway: Maple Digital Financial Solutions, also known as Maple Finance, is at "high risk" for suspicious activity.
Unlike traditional banks, money services businesses (MSB) such as Maple Finance already pose a threat of laundering illicit funds due to a lack of transparency and the fact that they don’t require an operating licence in many provinces.
This, coupled with ties to a sanctioned network and individuals known for money laundering, should put authorities in Canada on alert, said Meunier.
TGR network: transnational money-laundering
The CIR report and the experts CBC News spoke to acknowledge there's no definitive proof of money laundering. But there are substantial digital clues that connect Maple to TGR — primarily Andrejs Carenoks, a Latvian sanctioned by the U.S. in 2024 for his role in a sophisticated money-laundering operation allegedly led by Yury Maksakov, a Ukrainian national born in Russia.
Carenoks, according to corporate records, was a director at Maple Finance in 2021.
The current director is Janis Zvigulis. He is also director of The OneGate and a registered director of TGR Wealth Solutions in the U.K., which was sanctioned in 2024.
Zvigulis has not been sanctioned.
Authorities in the U.S. and U.K. described TGR as a full-service shadow financial hub, offering unregistered crypto exchanges, prepaid credit cards and sanctions evasion services, helping cybercriminals and drug traffickers.
For example, if a Russian cybercrime group held $1 million US in cryptocurrency paid by the victim of a ransomware attack and a drug gang in the U.K. had a similar amount in cash that needed to be laundered, TGR would arrange for the U.K. drug gang to be paid in crypto in exchange for their cash. The cash would then be laundered through a network of international business accounts.
Investigators at the U.K.’s National Crime Agency (NCA) have seen similar exchanges where cash handovers were followed almost immediately by the movement of a similar denomination of crypto.
Both Carenoks and Maksakov are accused of playing major roles in the TGR network, according to authorities in the U.K. and U.S.
"TGR is massive. It's really, really huge," said Elise Thomas, senior open-source investigator at CIR and author of the OneGate report. "To have Carenoks’s name on the actual company documents [for Maple Digital Financial Solutions], I think it's some really strong connections to TGR."
CBC tried reaching out to Maple Finance and The OneGate through email and phone but did not receive a response.
The registered Vancouver address on the Maple Finance website led to Canadian business law firm Osler, Hoskin & Harcourt LLP.
In a call, Osler lawyer and partner Matthew Burgoyne said, "the Law Society code of conduct doesn't let us disclose who our clients are and who they're not. So, unfortunately, I wouldn't even be able to tell you if we acted for them or not."
CBC followed up via email requesting that the lawyer ask Maple Finance for comment on this story. The firm wrote in an email, "we cannot help with your story."
"I think it sort of underscores that this is not a normal business. Because normally, when you call the business, they answer," said Thomas. "And when you try to contact them through the channels that they've given to be contacted by customers, they would respond."
'Silent director'
CBC News reached out to Careneks, Zvigulis and Maksakov but did not receive a response.
Attempts were also made to reach former directors of Maple Digital Financial Solutions.
One of those former directors, Elen Kazarian, is based in Ontario. In an email, she told CBC News she was appointed as a "silent director" because the “owner and CEO of this company are foreigners I was told by my cousin — who knew these owners to help them to register this Corporation."
She said she didn’t do anything during her tenure as a director and wasn't paid.
Maple Digital Financial Solutions is part of a group of companies connected to The OneGate.
The financial network offers products such as virtual and physical payment cards, and services such as cryptocurrency trading through shell companies spread across at least seven jurisdictions, from the U.S. to Switzerland to Hong Kong.
"OneGate seems to be presenting [itself as a] payments service company that provides a number of different financial products and services," Thomas said. "Under the hood, there are all these deep historical connections to TGR, which obviously is accused of being a transnational money-laundering ring."
The TGR network was disrupted in 2024 after a three-year international probe led by the NCA codenamed Operation Destabilise. It was a global effort to dismantle a multibillion-dollar shadow banking and cryptocurrency network that laundered proceeds for violent drug cartels, ransomware gangs and Russian intelligence operations.
It resulted in 128 arrests worldwide and the seizure of more than $44 million Cdn in cash and digital assets.
The OneGate network was operating in parallel to TGR and started with a virtual office in Vancouver when Maple Finance was still called Fexcool Payments.
The CIR report further detailed the digital forensic connections. When it changed its name to Maple Digital Financial Solutions, it registered a website: maplefinance.ca.
Andrejs Carenoks was the one who registered that domain.
At the same time, Carenoks was the director of a TGR entity later sanctioned by the U.S.
The overlap between Maple Finance and TGR went beyond Carenoks. Archived records of that website show that Maple Finance listed a Toronto-area phone number also used by TGR Partners.
Maple Finance provided clients with a branded payment card issued by OneCard — a service in part operated by TGR at the time.
In 2023, Maple Finance became the acting primary legal entity behind The OneGate. Its customer portal was fully merged into the main OneGate domain a short time after.
TGR Partners also actively recruited staff for Maple Finance online, including posting job listings for an IT project manager to work out of TGR's physical office in Podgorica, Montenegro, under a TGR human resources manager.
PDF files created for Maple’s privacy agreements contained metadata listing the author as "Max Travel," a likely digital trace left by TGR leader Yury Maksakov, who uses the username "Max Traveller" on Facebook.
The digital clues and overlaps between Maple Finance and TGR are consistent with "illicit financial activities," said Peter Dent, a former forensic services lead for global professional services firm Deloitte who is also part of the Vancouver Anti-Corruption Institute.
"I'm certainly concerned," said Dent. "They share a common directorship, they share a phone number with another entity that has been alleged to be involved in illicit financial activity. They don't even have a phone number in Canada."
FINTRAC registration
Following the global crackdown on the TGR Network in December 2024, Maple Finance was scrubbed from the active provider list on The OneGate website, as its FINTRAC registration expired.
The FINTRAC registration has since been renewed and Maple Finance now advertises itself as an "innovative financial ecosystem for modern business owners to manage their finances on their own terms."
FINTRAC wrote in an email to CBC News that it is "prohibited from disclosing information on the compliance history of individual entities... except in the case of a public notice of an administrative monetary penalty imposed."
"If I was the government authority in charge of money-laundering enforcement, like FINTRAC here in Canada, I think I'd be looking at this report," said William Pellerin, international trade lawyer at McMillan LLP, who also reviewed the report and CBC’s findings.
