Trump gets testy and calls Iran war ‘small potatoes’ when pressed on length of fight
The president argued the conflict was minor compared to something like the Vietnam war and said the U.S. had ‘essentially taken over’ the country
President Donald Trump has backed up comments from his vice president and insisted the Iran conflict is a relatively minor operation, rather than a full-on war.
"I call it a military conflict because it's small potatoes for us,” the president told reporters in the Oval Office on Friday. “It’s not a big thing.”
When pressed by Rachel Scott of ABC News about the record-setting deployments of certain service members as part of the fight, the president lashed out, repeatedly asking, “How long were we in Vietnam?”
President Trump claimed the U.S. had successfully stopped Iran from getting a nuclear weapon and alleged U.S. satellite intelligence would spot any future threats from the country the moment they arose. The U.S. had “essentially taken over” Iran, the Republican said.
The question of whether the fight is a war has profound implications.
The widow of John A. Klinner, an airman killed as part of the campaign against Iran, alleges she has been denied some military benefits because the Trump administration has not formally declared war.
“As much as our heart breaks, I can’t possibly fathom a young widow, what she’s feeling, and dealing with it,” Vance said Thursday when asked about the situation.
“We very much take very seriously our commitment to get you what you need to get,” he added.
Bipartisan critics allege the president has ignored the Constitution and War Powers Act by continuing the fight against Iran without congressional authorization. Both houses have approved resolutions demanding the president seek clearance.
The president dismissed the Senate’s June vote on the war as “poorly timed and meaningless.”
During his comments on Friday, the president also downplayed the centrality of the Hormuz Strait, another important aspect of the war.
The president claimed that new pipelines, shipping routes and overland oil transport would replace the key waterway, which is a major global oil hub.
“The Hormuz Strait is not what it used to be,” Trump said.
Iran has used its proximity to the strait to hamstring global oil trade and continues to exert leverage over the U.S., though the president claimed the waterway was dwindling in importance.
“They’re going to end up with a Hormuz Strait that’s not very necessary anymore,” he said.

The Dutch central bank has moved around $12 billion worth of its gold holdings from United States and Canada to London, amid concerns over rising geopolitical tensions worldwide. London is home to the world’s most active and liquid gold market, with precious metal worth hundreds of billions of dollars traded there each week. This has made the Bank of England a long-standing storage partner for central banks, allowing them to buy, sell or lend large amounts of gold quickly when needed. Gold kept at the Bank of England also complies with global standards for bar weight and purity. This means the bullion can be readily exchanged and traded across international markets. From March through August, the bank relocated about 86 metric tonnes of gold, representing more than a quarter of its bullion stored in the US and Canada. Following the transfer, London now accounts for almost one-third of the Netherlands’ gold reserves, making it the largest holding location. The Dutch central bank carried out the transfer by selling around 59 tonnes of gold in New York and purchasing an equivalent amount in London. It also physically transported more than 27 tonnes of bullion from the US and Canada to Zeist, with a similar volume subsequently moved from Zeist to London. Finance Minister Eelco Heinen said the preparations for the transfer were kept confidential until the operation was completed, as the move was considered a matter of vital public interest. Dutch Central Bank Governor Olaf Sleijpen said on Wednesday that relocating the country’s gold reserves to London had made them easier to trade, while the move was also intended to enhance the Netherlands’ resilience and preparedness. He noted that the country does not expect to need to use the reserves. “With this relocation, we have improved the tradability of our gold reserves. We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness,” Dutch Central Bank Governor Olaf Sleijpen stated on Wednesday, according to Bloomberg. The Dutch central bank said bullion held at the Bank of England “is considered the most easily tradable gold in the world,” adding that “This makes it the quickest for DNB to deploy in a crisis situation.” It stated that holding a greater portion of its gold reserves in London helps reinforce gold’s role as a trusted financial anchor. It keeps 30.8% of its total 612.4-tonne gold reserves at its cash centre in Zeist, located southeast of Amsterdam. Central banks have traditionally stored their gold in multiple locations, weighing the safety of keeping reserves at home against the need to access and mobilise them swiftly through major global financial hubs. Over 60 central banks keep their gold reserves at the Bank of England, its Governor Andrew Bailey said in a recent interview with Sky News months ago. The institution stores roughly 430,000 gold bars in nine vaults, allowing central banks to trade gold among themselves without physically moving the bars out of the Bank of England’s custody. Where countries keep their gold has become an increasingly important consideration, particularly for nations that are expanding their reserves. India has increased its total gold holdings in recent years while simultaneously cutting the amount of gold it keeps at the Bank of England. Jan Kubicek, a board member of the Czech central bank, said London serves as Europe’s gold market and that storing reserves in Bank of England vaults helps the country reduce transaction costs. “London is the market for gold in Europe. We save money on transaction costs by using Bank of England vaults," The New York Times quoted Kubicek as saying. Central banks generally avoid revealing where their gold holdings are kept, with many treating the information as highly confidential. China’s central bank has emerged as one of the biggest gold buyers in recent years, adding to its reserves for 17 straight months. However, little information is available about where those holdings are stored. Brazil’s central bank also boosted its gold reserves late last year for the first time in four years, but similarly did not disclose their storage location. London and New York have been the world’s leading gold storage hubs for decades. However, Hong Kong is seeking to establish itself as an alternative, potentially giving central banks an option outside traditional Western storage centres. 'If you started running, they shot you' - inside Nigeria's growing kidnapping crisis
- Published
"If you ran into a room, they set the room on fire," says Fatima, describing a recent attack on her village in Zamfara, north-western Nigeria. "If you came out and started running, they shot you."
The gunmen, who struck at 02:00, split into groups to surround residents: one at the village entrance, one in the centre and one at the back.
"They opened fire without a care in the world, shooting indiscriminately," the 55-year-old quietly tells the BBC World Service.
It was one of many attacks that have caused havoc in the mainly Muslim community where residents live in fear of being kidnapped for ransom.
Fatima explains how the raids unfold: "You could have 100 motorcycles, and each one could be carrying three people."
About 70 people, including children, were killed from the village of Bia Buki in June, according to Fatima.
She describes how the attackers also targeted villagers as they fled and children were injured falling into ditches. Among the dead were her husband and six of his seven siblings.
Fatima is one of an estimated 800,000 Nigerians who the UN says have been displaced in the country's north-west. One of the main reasons people have left their homes is violence.
Some attacks have been carried out by militant Islamist groups, but the majority in this region are by gangs, locally referred to as bandits, who often move around on motorcycles and attack quickly then ride away, escaping before security forces arrive.
Thousands of people have joined government-backed vigilante groups to fight, and the BBC spoke to one who said his armed group had killed many bandits.
But the gangs keep attacking in what appears to be a deteriorating pattern of violence and abductions that is spreading southwards.
Fatima says when the bandits attacked her home, she ran into the nearby forest with other villagers to hide: "The forest became our sanctuary. We ran with our kids, if you couldn't find your child you'd take your neighbour's child."
She says people slept in the forest before moving on to the state capital, Gusau, "where we found a little bit of peace".
Fatima now lives in an informal camp in Gusau with her seven children, who are aged between nine and 30.
Dozens of women sit in groups on the dusty ground of the makeshift compound, many wearing brightly coloured hijabs. More than 1,000 people are here, she believes.
Conditions are tough with "no proper place to even lay your head". Food is scarce and assistance arrives irregularly.
Fatima describes two occasions where "good Samaritans" brought rice or potatoes. Children are sent out to gather firewood to sell so families can buy food, but 22 have been kidnapped by bandits, she says.
Gesturing towards a nearby building, Fatima says that there "you will find 100 or more women… maybe just two or three have had breakfast.
"When we had peace, we had our own wealth, but now the tables have turned and we have become beggars."
Her eyes fill with tears and she cries for a few minutes, wiping her face with her hands.
Despite being 16 miles (25km) from her village, the threat Fatima fled has not disappeared.
When she first arrived at the camp, the sound of gunshots kept her awake at night. Things have since quietened, she says, crediting patrols by the army and government-backed vigilantes, but the atmosphere is still tense.
The bandits are mostly people from the Fulani ethnic group, who traditionally make their living by raising animals. Some of them have swapped cattle trading for kidnapping and extortion, which is seen as a faster, easier way to make money.
They attack towns and villages or ambush travellers, abducting people for ransom, stealing whatever they want - and sometimes killing those who resist. They also force communities to pay protection money, only allowing farmers into their fields if they hand over large sums of cash.
Attacks are now more frequent than ever. In the bandit heartlands of north-west Nigeria, the number of incidents recorded by the international conflict monitoring group Acled rose 78% in the first half of this year compared to the same period in 2025.
One security consultancy estimates that kidnappers across Nigeria collected nearly $5.8m (£4.3m) in ransoms over the past year as the number of abductions surged. SBM Intelligence estimates that 7,825 people were kidnapped between July 2025 and June 2026, a 66% increase on the previous year.
The increase in bandit activity appears to be a key driver in this trend.
Malik Samuel at Good Governance Africa, a research and advocacy non-profit group, says that "there is no region in northern Nigeria currently that does not experience one form of mass abduction or the other".
Nigeria's battle with bandits is just one part of a more complex security situation facing the country.
As well as the bandit gangs in the north-west, there is an Islamist insurgency in the north-east, separatist unrest in the south-east and clashes in central regions, where the main grievance is over access to land and water for grazing and farming and where ethnic and religious elements have also fuelled some of the unrest.
Most analysts agree that armed groups have waged campaigns of violence that affect all communities, regardless of background or belief.
- The kidnap gangs, jihadists and separatists wreaking havoc in Nigeria 
  - Published28 November 2025
Schools are a common target. When the Islamist Boko Haram militant group infamously kidnapped more than 200 schoolgirls from the north-eastern village of Chibok in 2014, it made global headlines.
At the time the group forced its captives into sexual slavery, domestic servitude or used them as suicide bombers.
But a range of groups across Nigeria now use kidnapping to raise funds, focusing on soft targets such as schools, churches, mosques and remote villages.
This was mainly confined to the Boko Haram strongholds of the north-east or the bandit zones of the north-west - areas that are largely Muslim.
Then, in May this year, gunmen on motorcycles attacked three schools in Oyo state, south-west Nigeria, one of the few regions that was previously considered relatively safe. Thirty-nine children, the youngest just two years old, were abducted along with seven teachers. One teacher was killed during the raid, another's murder was filmed and shared online.
After 56 days, the remaining 44 hostages were released. The government said it refused to pay a ransom and that the children were released after an operation by security forces. Three men were sentenced to life in prison for the attacks and confessed to being members of an affiliate of Boko Haram.
The abduction spread fear throughout the south-western town of Oriire, with parents in the community pulling their children out of school.
"There is fear because many residents have run away and are yet to return," says the traditional ruler of the area, Oba Tajudeen Abioye, whose niece was among the kidnapped children.
"And for those of us who are left here, we are relying on the security officials, the soldiers" who were sent to protect the community, he says.
Nigeria already has one of the highest numbers of out-of-school children in the world: the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (Unesco) estimates the number is about 19 million.
The multiple, overlapping security issues mean Nigeria's military and police are overstretched and as a result struggle to tackle the violence.
A 2025 UN report said that police stations were often underfunded and not fully operational, citing independent sources that accused officers of lacking skills in hostage negotiation and forensic investigation.
President Bola Tinubu's administration has allocated the largest defence and security budget in the country's history, raising it by 10% in December 2025 compared to one year before. He has recently approved the recruitment of 28,000 new soldiers.
In the meantime communities are still suffering and in Zamfara thousands of residents have joined government-backed vigilante groups to fill the gaps in security.
But there are concerns about their involvement. In 2020 Zamfara banned a large vigilante group over concerns that extrajudicial killings were driving more violence, according to AFP.
The authorities say the new vigilantes are better trained, but Samuel, from Good Governance Africa, calls them a "time bomb waiting to happen".
"If citizens arm themselves how do you control them at the end of the crisis, how are you able to disarm them?" he asks.
One of the vigilantes meets us outside his group's headquarters, a single-storey concrete building, and agrees to speak on the condition of anonymity during our visit in July.
He perches on his motorcycle, an AK-47 slung over his shoulder, a scarf across his face as a makeshift balaclava, gold and silver skull rings on his fingers.
"We are some of the people the governor hired to protect the community," he says, explaining that they are sometimes told where the bandits are and "with the help of God we fight them and defeat them".
"Let the bandits understand that when they attack a place and kill, they can also be killed," he adds.
He estimates he has fought bandits at least 20 times and says the calls for his group's help keep coming.
"It's hard to go a week without these reports," he says. "There are regions that became safer… but there are other regions where the same cannot be said."
He calls on the state governor, whom he supports, to hire and arm more people to take on the bandits. "These people won't be afraid of you unless you have proper weapons to fight them," he says.
Fatima also calls for more action: "These kidnappers are in every nook and cranny.
"I am not saying the government has failed but even if it is trying, it needs to do more. There are problems and we think with more effort and more security agents, villages will be peaceful."
She wants to return home, but is doubtful that will happen as she has heard her village has now been turned into a camp for the gunmen that attacked it.
The local bandit leader has become the de facto authority, and that families look to him to solve domestic disputes, she says.
Another nearby village "is completely empty, not even a chicken lives there… empty villages like that are countless", Fatima says.
"Even if you go back to our area, it's just difficulty you will face. There's nothing there, no food… you farm and when you go to harvest, they stop you or kidnap you."

Are Jan 6 rioters getting taxpayer payouts? New lawsuit claims DOJ refuses to say
Hundreds of defendants are ‘seeking millions of dollars’ from the government after Trump’s DOJ killed plans for a slush fund, lawsuit says
Donald Trump’s administration insists that a compensation fund for pardoned January 6 rioters is dead for good, but the Department of Justice has refused to say whether government lawyers are working on backdoor plans for taxpayer-funded payouts.
The Justice Department has denied several Freedom of Information Act requests filed by a nonprofit watchdog group, according to a newly filed federal lawsuit. The group is now asking a judge to intervene to force the government to answer.
Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington wants to know whether the Justice Department is working on settlement deals with pardoned rioters after hundreds of members of the mob filed lawsuits against the government “seeking millions of dollars for what they claim are injuries incurred during the investigation and prosecution of their federal crimes,” according to the lawsuit.
They’re all suing under the Federal Tort Claims Act, which taps into the government’s permanent Judgment Fund used to pay court judgments and other settlements involving the federal government.
“While the status of the slush fund is unclear, the DOJ and other Trump administration officials have assured President Trump’s allies, in the face of pushback on the slush fund, that the DOJ’s plans to pay January 6 Defendants through the alternate means of the [Federal Tort Claims Act] remain on track,” the lawsuit says.
The administration abandoned plans, at least for now, for a nearly $1.8 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund” to reward the president’s political allies.
As an apparent condition to win the votes of skeptical Senate Republicans, Attorney General Todd Blanche conceded that those plans have been “rescinded and shall have no force or effect.”
But Republican lawmakers and top Justice Department officials have suggested that the government has alternate plans to funnel millions of dollars to the president’s aggrieved allies, including the hundreds of people charged and convicted in connection with the Capitol assault.
Attorney Peter Ticktin, who represents hundreds of January 6 defendants, has said he has already filed claims for approximately 200 clients.
According to Mark McCloskey, an attorney representing many January 6 defendants, most are seeking “$1 million to $10 million” for their alleged injuries.
Earlier this year, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham wrote that “victims” of Joe Biden’s administration should still be able to collect checks if they “can prove their claim against the federal government” through the Federal Tort Claims Act.
“We have a legal system already in place for people to make claims against the government,” he wrote on X at the time. “That does not need to be reinvented.”
In response to Graham, Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward wrote: “We’re on it.”
Woodward later deleted the post.
Woodward told reporters at a news conference that the Justice Department has the ability “to settle any claim that is brought against the United States of America.”
The Judgment Fund is intended to “eliminate the procedural burdens involved in getting an appropriation from Congress to pay a particular judgment,” according to the Department of Treasury.
The Trump administration has already tapped into the fund to settle other multi-million dollar Federal Tort Claims Act claims from his supporters and allies since returning to office, including to pay the family of Ashli Babbitt nearly $5 million.
The Independent has requested comment from the Justice Department.
Hours after his inauguration last year, Trump granted clemency to more than 1,500 people who were charged or convicted in connection with the Capitol attack on January 6, 2021. Hundreds of defendants pleaded guilty to crimes in connection with the attack, and more than 200 others were found guilty at trial.
The president has said he “loves” the idea of the "Anti-Weaponization Fund.”
“It’s dead, but you know, I wish it weren’t,” he told reporters at Camp David in July. “I’d like to see them compensated.”
In June, he told NBC’s Meet the Press that he wouldn’t be “inclined” to approve taxpayer-funded payouts to January 6 rioters who attacked police officers, but he hasn’t ruled it out.
He claimed that hundreds of defendants pleaded guilty because they were “frightened” and that “dirty cops” were at fault for the attack.

Instagram uses icons for likes, comments, reposts, saves, messages, Reels, Stories, calls, profile tools, notifications, active status, and more. This guide explains what every major Instagram symbol means and what happens when you tap it.
Instagram is the most popular app with billions of users around the world. The platform has lately been getting plenty of new features and fixes.
Instagram is also one of the few platforms that are known for experimentation. Meta often changes their layout very often, which can sometimes confuse users. If you are new to Instagram, or even an existing user, the new features and some icons you never use can be confusing.
Some of the features on Instagram don’t have an undo option, so it is better to know what they do before pressing them. In this guide, you will learn everything about Instagram icons, their meanings, and what they are used for. To make it easy for you, we have included each and every icon on every page of Instagram and explained what it does.
Table of Contents
What Do Instagram Symbols and Icons Mean?
Instagram Post Symbols Meaning
Instagram posts are what we see and interact with most on a daily basis while using the app.
They come with several engaging elements. Most of them are easy to understand, but if you are confused, here is what they mean:
- Like: Wherever you see this heart symbol on Instagram, it represents a like for posts, comments, and all
- Comment: This represents a comment on the post. Tapping on it reveals all the comments, and you can also add a comment.
- Repost: Instagram has recently introduced the ability to repost. The reposted post also appears on your feed.
- Save: The save feature lets you save posts; in other words, it works like a bookmark.
Instagram Home Screen and Bottom Navigation Bar Icons Meaning
Now let’s look at what the icons mean on the home screen and on the bottom navigation bar.
You won’t find many icons on the home screen, except for the ability to create a new post and to view all your notifications.
If there is one area that Instagram constantly experiments with, it is the bottom navigation. Meta keeps changing the positions of the icons and also changes their designs frequently.
Here is what they mean:
- Notifications: The heart symbol here represents notifications. Here, you can see all the notifications you receive inside the Instagram app.
- Create: The plus symbol here represents “create,” which you can use to create a post or a story and more.
- Home: Tapping on the home icon takes you to the home screen. It is part of the main bottom navigation. Tapping on it also takes you to the latest posts.
- Reels: Instagram has added a dedicated Reels tab, where you can tap on it to go to the Reels section.
- Messages: Tapping on this icon takes you to the Instagram Messages screen, previously known as DMs.
- Search: Tapping on the search icon takes you to the Explore page.
- Profile: This is a profile icon, which takes you to your profile page.
Instagram Reels Tab Icons Meaning
Instagram offers a dedicated Reels tab where you can see all the latest Instagram Reels. It also comes with several interactive elements, some of which are already used for posts.
Here is what each and every icon means in the Instagram Reels tab:
- Create: You can also add new posts directly from the Reels page. You can tap on the Plus icon.
- Like: It lets you like the Reel you are watching. You can like it, and tapping on it removes your like.
- Comments: Lets you add a comment and see comments for the Reel you are currently watching.
- Repost: It lets you repost the Reel you are currently watching.
- Share: It lets you share the Reel with your friends. You can also copy the Reel link using this option.
- Save: You can save or bookmark the Reel using this icon.
- More options: Gives more options for Reels, including Playback controls, Meta AI, and much more.
- Audio: It represents the audio used for the Reel. Tapping on it reveals more details.
Instagram DM Page Icons Meaning
Instagram DMs are among the most feature-packed, yet Instagram somehow manages to keep them minimal. However, they do come with several icons. Here is what each icon means in the Instagram message space:
- New message: It lets you create a new message. After tapping, you can select the user and send a message.
- Notifications off: It appears if you turned off notifications for Instagram.
We missed highlighting the Instagram Instant feature that the company introduced very recently. It lets you share a random photo with other users without complex editing.
It is turned on by default, and tapping on it shares whatever your phone camera sees, so be careful before pressing it. There is also an option to turn it off completely
Instagram Profile Page Icons Meaning
Instagram profile page also comes with plenty of icons. Here is what they mean:
- Create: Lets you create a new post, Reel, or Story from your profile page too
- Menu: Lets you access main and global Instagram app settings
- Threads: Lets you open the Threads app by Instagram.
- Discover people: The icon lets you discover new friends. It appears when you have a lower following count.
- Posts: Represents the Posts tab
- Reels: It represents the Reels tab
- Tagged posts: It represents the tagged posts where you can see all the posts you were tagged in by your friends.
- Pinned post: It means the user has pinned the post. Instagram lets the user pin up to three posts.
Instagram DM Message Icons Meaning
The chat interface also comes with plenty of icons, which can be confusing for a beginner. Here is what each icon means inside Instagram chats:
- Instagram Blend Feature: This is an Instagram Blend feature where you can invite the user to the Blend, where you can see each other’s suggested Reels, new Reel suggestions based on the chat, and much more.
- Voice call: Lets you make a voice call to the user
- Video call: Lets you make a video call to the user
- Voice message: Lets you send a voice message in the chat
- Photo library: Lets you select the local photos on your phone and send them to the chat
- Stickers: Lets you access the stickers
- More options: Gives you more options, including the ability to send location, draw, and access Meta AI and much more
- Camera: Lets you access the camera, where you can quickly take a photo and share it with the user.
Instagram Share Screen Icons Meaning
The share screen on Instagram is very simple. It is very similar to the other share screens, but it comes with one unique icon that lets you create groups. Here is what that icon means:
- Create group: This is the share screen that appears when you tap on the share button under the post or the Reel. The user icon means you can create a new group.
Instagram Call Screen Icons Meaning
Instagram calling screen also comes with several icons during the call, and here is what each of them means:
- Camera off: During the video call, it lets you control the camera. If you see a cross line, it means your camera is turned off
- Mute microphone: Lets you mute or unmute your camera
- Speaker off: Lets you turn on or off sound from the other user
- End call: End the video or voice call using this button.
Instagram Story Editor Icons Meaning
If you are adding a story for the first time, it can be confusing because Instagram Stories are feature-packed and let you customize everything you upload. Here is what each icon means on the Instagram Stories screen:
- Add text: While adding an Instagram Story, tapping on this icon lets you add text
- Stickers: It lets you add stickers to an Instagram Story
- Music: Lets you add and select music.
- Effects: Lets you add effects
- More tools: More creator tools. Tapping on it lets you access more tools
- Next: Once added, you can move to the next screen while adding a Story
Instagram Profile Bio Options Icons Meaning
Instagram profile bio also comes with plenty of icons. Here is what each icon means and what it does:
- Notifications: Lets you turn on or off notifications for this account.
- More options: Gives you more options about the Instagram profile you are viewing
- Profile link: Instagram lets users add links in their bio. The link icon represents the link the creator added to their Instagram bio. It is also available for regular users.
More Instagram Profile Icons Meaning
Here are more icons that you see when you visit any Instagram profile, including icons in the top right corner of the post and the verified blue checkmark right next to the profile. Here is what they mean:
- Verified badge: Instagram has verified the account, which means it represents the official account. Also, Instagram allows users to pay for the verified badge.
- Video or Reel: If you see this on top of the post, it means the post contains a video or Reel.
- Carousel post: If you see this with a number, it means it is a carousel post.
Instagram Reels Controls Icons Meaning
In the Reels tab, when you pause the Reel, Instagram displays more icons. Here is what they mean, including the recent Friends tab icons:
- Create: The plus icon lets you create a new post or Reel
- Trending audio: If you see an arrow next to the audio file name, it means that audio is trending
- Sound: Lets you turn off sound or turn on sound for the video. It appears when you tap on the video
- Play: It appears when you pause the video. Lets you play the video again
- More options: Again, tapping on this option gives you more Reel options
- Reposted by a friend: If you see a purple arrow icon, it means the Reel is reposted by your friend. If you see the like, it means the Reel is liked by your friends.
More Instagram Messages Icons Meaning
Here is what the different icons mean in the Instagram DM space. If you have multiple accounts and unread messages, Instagram will notify you with different color badges. Here is what they mean:
- Pinned chat: It appears when you pin the chat for any user in your Instagram DMs.
- Muted chat: It means you muted the chat. You won’t receive any notifications for their messages.
- Unread message: It shows the unread messages inside the chat. If it appears, it means you have unread messages.
- Account switcher: Lets you switch between accounts, and if you see the red icon, it means you have unread notifications from the other account
More Instagram Post Icons Meaning
Instagram recently launched collaborations, which allow users to collaborate with each other and publish posts. It joins with older tags, the ability to add music, and much more. Here is what each icon means:
- Collaborative post: Instagram lets you add collaborative posts. If you see multiple profile pictures, it means it is a collaborative post from those accounts.
- More options: It lets you access more options for the posts
- Explicit audio: If you see an E icon right next to the sound or audio, it means the song contains explicit content
- Tagged people: It lets you view all tagged users for the post. Tapping on the user takes you to their profile
- Sound: It lets you mute or unmute the sound for the post.
Paid Instagram Post Icon Meaning
You don’t need a special introduction for the ads on Instagram. If you see a post and you are confused about whether it’s a regular post or not, you can find a little “Ad” label under the profile.
- Ad: If you see Ad, it means it is a sponsored post or ad inside the Instagram feed.
Instagram Story Viewer Icons Meaning
Fortunately, Instagram has kept stories minimal. They also come with several interactive elements. One is the ability to like them and also share the story with others.
- More options: Gives you more options for the Instagram Story you are viewing, which includes options like the ability to report it and more
- Like Story: Like means you can like your friend’s Story
- Share Story: You can also share the Story with others. Tapping on it lets you share the Story with your contacts.
Instagram Close Friends Story Icons Meaning
If you see a green icon in the stories, it means that the user has added you to their close friends list. It comes with an extra “Close Friends” tag, and while the rest of the elements look the same, it doesn’t come with a share option.
Here is what each icon means in the Instagram Close Friends Story screen:
- Close Friends: If you see this green star, it means they have added you to their Close Friends list and shared a Story with you
- More options: Lets you access more Story options
- Like Story: Lets you like your Close Friend’s Story.
Instagram Reels Comments Symbols Meaning
Finally, ending this guide with the post or Reels comments, it also comes with several elements which can be confusing for the beginner. Here is what each icon means in the Instagram post or Reels comments section.
- Sound: You can turn the Reel sound on or off using the icon
- Like comment: You can like any comment made by users. The number below shows how many people liked it.
- Photo: Instagram recently announced the ability to add a photo as a comment.
- GIF: You can also add a GIF in the comments.
- Gift: Send a gift in the comments. You can tap on it and buy points with real money and help the creator to make money.
Instagram Active Status Symbol Meaning
- Green dot: If you see a green dot, it means the user is active on Instagram. If you hide your active status, it won’t appear for you even if others are online.
Story Rings Meaning
- Grey colored ring: If you see a grey-colored ring, it means you have already viewed their story.
- Colorful gradient ring: It means they added a new story or a story you have not watched yet
- Green ring: If you see a green ring, it means a story for a close friend that the user added. In simple words, the user added you to their close friends list and shared a story with close friends.
Still Confused About an Instagram Icon?
Those are the icons and symbols and their meanings on Instagram. Instagram constantly tests new icons and new features, and also changes existing features. As I said before, the platform has undergone several fresh layouts over the years.
To stay updated with the latest, we also update this post regularly when Instagram changes the layout and announces a new feature. We update this post regularly to keep the same layout and make it less confusing compared to what you currently see on your Instagram app.
Fortunately, Instagram also uses the same icons for its desktop version and for the Instagram app on other platforms as well. If you still find any icon confusing on Instagram, you can comment below, and I am happy to guide you.

China’s carbon dioxide emissions fell by 1% after the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran, thanks to a sharp reduction in oil consumption and a steady rise in the use of electric vehicles and public transport, analysis shows.
The report reveals the role of clean energy in cushioning the price shocks caused by the strait of Hormuz crisis to the world’s biggest oil importer. It also reinforces hopes that China, which is the world’s biggest greenhouse gas emitter, may be nearing a turning point in decarbonising its economy.
China was able to increase overall transportation use, despite cutting oil imports by 32%, according to second-quarter energy data reported by the country’s National Bureau of Statistics and analysed for Carbon Brief by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
The reduction – equivalent to about a million barrels a day – from the world’s biggest petro-customer helped to stabilise global oil prices, which nevertheless surged by about 60% in the weeks and months after the first US airstrikes in late February.
How that was achieved has been the subject of considerable speculation. The analysis indicates that about two-thirds of the fall in imports came from running down, rather than building up, strategic oil stockpiles. The remaining third was largely covered by a reduction in demand.
The country’s use of oil fell by 9% overall and by 16% for transport. While large numbers of petrol and diesel vehicles stayed off the roads, there was a surge in journeys by electric cars, buses, trains and trucks.
This electrifying trend had begun long before the strait of Hormuz crisis. China is by far the world’s biggest manufacturer, user and exporter of batteries, e-vehicles, wind turbines and solar panels. The disruption of oil supplies from the Gulf has strengthened the economic and strategic imperative of reducing petro-dependence.
In the first half of 2026, China’s shift towards electric vehicles displaced the equivalent of the UK’s entire oil consumption over a six-month period.
Analysts predict much of this demand will not return even if global oil prices fall. “In a qualitative sense, there’s no question that the transport sector decarbonisation has been accelerated,” said Lauri Myllyvirta, the lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. “It’s a validation of the energy security strategy that China has in place … It’s very clear that electrification is the winning strategy to insure against these kinds of shocks.”
Myllyvirta noted this was the first time China’s overall emissions had fallen due to a reduction in oil use rather than in coal consumption.
In fact, coal generation rose during the quarter due to shifting economic incentives and delays in adapting the country’s grid, which caused considerable wastage of wind and solar power. Despite this, observers believe the longer-term trend in China is away from fossil fuels.
Dr Muyi Yang, a senior analyst at Ember, which will next week publish a separate overview of China’s energy trends, said a fossil fuel peak was coming into view at the provincial and sectoral level. “The Iran crisis reinforces the case. The way China has been able to absorb its impact strengthens the confidence to go deeper and further.
“The risk of oil-import dependence increasingly comes from the geopolitical domain. This is a risk no country can effectively manage. So the more effective strategy is to reduce that exposure altogether. And China’s experience is demonstrating that this works.”

For 26 days, India watched as Sonam Wangchuk wasted away. His hunger strike, held in solidarity with India’s “Cockroach” youth protest movement, would prove to be one of the most politically consequential fasts held in the country’s modern history.
Many in the country view the gruelling fast, which began on 28 June, as the crucial spark that helped propel the Cockroach movement into one of the most formidable challenges to the government of prime minister, Narendra Modi, in more than a decade.
Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, said Wangchuk had “awakened the conscience of an entire nation” through his sacrifice.
The Cockroach movement was launched in May, following the cancellation of a key nationwide exam to enter medical college after a paper was leaked. The cancellation was devastating for the 2 million students who had already sat the exam, a dozen of whom reportedly took their lives.
The movement took its name from comments made by India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, who had compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches and parasites in a court hearing.
Dipke’s demand for education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, to show accountability for the leak by resigning struck a nerve, and anger that had been seething below the surface surged out on to the streets.
The protest ballooned into a nationwide movement. For weeks, deadlock prevailed between the government and Dipke, backed by thousands who flocked to his sit-in protest in Delhi. Eventually, after an unprecedented police crackdown which further influenced public opinion in its favour, the protesters triumphed and Pradhan resigned on 25 July.
The victory was not a foregone conclusion and Dipke has acknowledged the importance of Wangchuck’s fast in determining the outcome. Unlike the students, Wangchuck was a well known and respected figure, recognised for his decades-long efforts to secure educational reforms and environmental protection. Last year, he was arrested in Ladakh on charges of inciting anti-government protests.
The timing was also key: crowds at the Delhi protest site had been thinning before he started his fast on a stage there on 28 June, injecting new energy and momentum into the movement.
Wangchuk had declared he would not end his strike until the government had listened to the demands of India’s protesting youth. He lay outdoors at the Cockroach protest site in the heart of Delhi, day and night, enduring rain, torturous heat and mosquitoes. Already a lean and slight figure, he lost 11kg over the 26 days.
“I felt confined, trapped … like a prison,” he told the Guardian. “The heat and humidity were awful.”
In the aftermath, Wangchuk, a softly-spoken engineer, environmentalist and educationist, remains humble about his role. “I was a known entity and that helped,” he said. His reverence is reserved for the hundreds of thousands of young people in the Cockroach movement, which he says has changed Indian politics for good.
Wangchuk is adamant that the Cockroach movement’s success is far bigger than a single resignation. In an era where dissent is routinely criminalised, young people, he said, had seized back the power of political protest.
“They have stripped away the curtain of fear that existed,” he said. “They are now engaged. They have tasted success in getting results and I expect them to continue.”
The 60-year-old admits the hunger strike took a gruelling toll. By the time he broke his fast on 24 July, he had pushed his body to the limit and was perilously close to organ failure. But as thousands of young people and politicians flocked to his side, his spirit remained unbroken throughout.
The greatest test, he says, came when he was forcibly removed by police from the protest site and taken to hospital against his will. Videos of his frail body being dragged away by burly police went viral and Wangchuk was hailed by young people online as a national hero. When mass protests erupted the following day, Wangchuk’s name was chanted and held aloft on placards.
Wangchuk was not always an obvious figure of anti-government resistance. Born in Ladakh, he rose to international prominence as an engineer and environmentalist, best known for inventing the ice stupor, a unique technique for water storage in human-made glaciers. He became a prominent champion of the rights of Ladakhis and set up his own school and cultural and environmental institution.
He had been a vocal supporter of several prominent policies of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) but it soon turned to resistance as he accused the BJP of failing the people of Ladakh. Last year, as protests in Ladakh escalated, he was imprisoned by the government for almost six months under draconian anti-terrorist laws.
While his focus has been on rebuilding his body in recent weeks, regaining about 60% of his previous weight, Wangchuk has also continued his call for political reform, albeit without any overt criticism of the Modi government.
In a video message posted before India’s independence day in August, Wangchuk called for a “second independence movement” and urged Indians to choose men and women of “character and substance” to lead the country.
He has urged people to share the names of individuals of integrity who can be trusted and once he has a list, he plans to meet them in Mumbai and Delhi to discuss how elections can be cleansed of those with a criminal background.
“Indians have to trust those at the top,” he said. “At the moment, there is no trust in anything, not in elections, not in exams, not in civil servants. Clean and honest leaders are the first step to a better future.”
He expressed his support for the decision by the Cockroach movement to resist calls to become a political party and instead focus on being a pressure group, championing issues of education. “When we used to talk during the long days of the fast, I used to advise them that being a pressure group is the best way to keep clean and neutral,” he said.
For now, he is back living quietly in Ladakh, finally able to enjoy the one food that lingered on his mind during his hunger strike. “I did dream of apricots,” he said, “but that was just because I was wondering if mine back home had ripened.”

How the Early Dreams of the Internet Changed
Technology was once seen as countercultural. What happened?
This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here.
During the 1984 Super Bowl, an advertisement launched a technological revolution. If you were alive, you probably know the one. Directed by Ridley Scott, the minute-long spot showed men in gray uniforms, heads shaved, eyes blank, marching in unison toward a lifeless auditorium. A Big Brother figure speaks from a giant screen, droning on about “the first glorious anniversary of the Information Purification Directives.” All the while, a woman in red shorts and a white tank top is running to the auditorium. She looks like she’s just come from an aerobics class, but she has a sledgehammer, and authorities are in pursuit. Entering the room, she hurls the sledgehammer into Big Brother’s face. There’s a flash of light, and a wind blows over the stunned, awakened audience. A different voice—a comforting one—announces, “On January 24th, Apple Computer will introduce Macintosh. And you’ll see why 1984 won’t be like 1984.”
Although the ad did not show an actual Macintosh computer, it worked. Apple went on to sell 250,000 of its user-friendly, mouse-driven little machines in that year alone. The ad also asserted what was to be a defining idea of the emerging digital age: that personal computers, far from massive instruments of centralized control, were vessels of individual freedom. The coming of the internet, with its invitation to universally accessible knowledge and the free exchange of ideas, seemed to affirm the promise: Our machines wouldn’t enslave us; they would liberate us.
The dystopia depicted in the ad came by way of George Orwell’s imagination, but the fears underlying it had deep American roots. As mass consumer culture expanded in the early 20th century, American artists, intellectuals, and critics worried over the problem of “conformity” and the loss of individualism that came with it. Most didn’t see the dark totalitarianism of 1984; instead, they saw a world of ready-made desires, a soulless existence brought to you by corporations, advertisers, media, and politicians. As The Atlantic’s review of Sinclair Lewis’s Babbitt put it in 1922, “the ‘standardized American’” was becoming “as much a national product as the Ford car”—a person like Babbitt himself, whose entire life and very personality were shaped by forces beyond him. Such criticism formed a fault line that ran from the cultural commentary of the ’20s to the outbursts of Beats, folkies, and academics in the ’50s.
The earthquake, of course, would come in the counterculture of the 1960s. No longer would people need to be stuffed into “Little Boxes,” as the folk singer Malvina Reynolds worried early in the decade. The counterculture promised liberation from such confinement. Visiting San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury district for The Atlantic in 1967, the novelist Mark Harris wondered whether he was seeing Babbitt’s descendants finally rebelling against conformity in ways that Babbitt himself could not. The counterculture’s sensibilities migrated into the mainstream, where popular culture and advertising absorbed its language of liberation and transgression, so that admen could pitch 7 Up using hippie iconography or Virginia Slims cigarettes by way of the women’s-liberation movement.
Digital culture would prove especially receptive to these countercultural ideals. Northern California, after all, was the center of both the counterculture and the tech industry, and the cross-pollination between the two was considerable, as the historian Fred Turner has shown. By the 1990s, as the internet was becoming a mass medium, some of its first boosters (many of whom had roots in the counterculture) were presenting it as the realization of countercultural ideals. John Perry Barlow, a poet and sometimes Grateful Dead lyricist, wrote his 1996 “Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace” in response to an early effort to regulate the internet. It reads like a Port Huron Statement for digital culture, describing a realm of individual freedom and free-flowing ideas that would break from existing forms of cultural and institutional authority. According to Barlow, a new “civilization of the Mind” was coming.
In the dot-com and digital revolutions that followed, many of the people who sold the hardware, coded the software, and built the platforms were seen as iconoclasts themselves. Digital entrepreneurship became a form of transgression, not just in the casual dress and informal culture of the Silicon Valley office but also in what it promised to users. Tech visionaries pledged to create a world that would make possible precisely the kind of self-expression, open exchange, and communal connection that the counterculture had promised. It was no coincidence that by the late 1990s, Apple’s advertising—again with almost no reference to the machines themselves—simply pictured groundbreaking figures such as Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr., Bob Dylan, and John Lennon, alongside the slogan “Think Different.”
In many ways, those promises were fulfilled. The internet did splinter 20th-century mass culture, and the effects have been every bit as revolutionary as promised. We don’t all watch the same networks anymore; we don’t see the same movies; we don’t get our news from the same places or read the same books (mostly, we just don’t read); we “do our own research.”
Even as the conditions of mass culture and conformity that shaped the counterculture and the early dreams of the internet have faded, we continue to live in their shadow. In the fractured age of social media and the unknowable algorithm, our devices give us the feeling of freedom, even as they serve the interests of corporate forces that track our movements, catalog our interests, and profile our wants. The oppressive monoculture has been replaced by countless minicultures, each with their own devoted acolytes; we still inhabit little boxes, partially of our own making.
The transgressive ethos, meanwhile, continues to thrive. Subversion is perhaps the dominant language of digital culture, spoken across the political spectrum by podcasters “just asking questions,” wellness gurus swilling at-home health hacks, manosphere kingpins lashing out against wokeness, and lefty influencers denouncing the billionaire class. Everyone, it seems, is hurling a sledgehammer at something.

On a Monday evening in May, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent sat down for dinner at a ritzy Japanese restaurant tucked inside a 400-year-old garden in central Tokyo.
Across the table was Satsuki Katayama, Japan’s sharp-tongued finance minister. Bessent was set to meet Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, the next day. But first, he had grievances to air.
Over two hours, Bessent, who closely followed the country’s economy as a hedge fund manager, unloaded his frustration with the economic direction set by the Japanese leader. Takaichi had expanded government spending while leaning on the Bank of Japan to keep interest rates low. The strategy was driving capital out of Tokyo, sending Japan’s currency to four-decade lows.

After U.S. President Donald Trump announced in August 2026 that he would rename Lake Ontario to "Lake America," social media users spread a screenshot appearing to show a Truth Social post from the president that announced the construction of the "Melania Canal" that would 
The screenshot circulated across Facebook (screenshot) and Threads. Here's what Trump allegedly said:
The FAKE NEWS is saying we need the Canadian canals that connect to LAKE AMERICA. Total lie! We don't need their small, low-energy Welland Canal! America built the Panama Canal, we built the Suez Canal — incredible, beautiful, high-IQ canals! I have officially instructed the Army Corps of Engineers to build a much BIGGER, DEEPER, WIDER, and far more powerful canal bypass connecting straight into Lake America! It is going to be magnificent! And we are naming it after my stunning, beautiful wife: THE MELANIA CANAL. Every American will be able to EASILY enter the Melania Canal from BOTH the front end and the back side for a very minimal fee! Thank you for your attention to this matter.
Some users seemed to interpret the rumor as true, and Snopes readers contacted us to investigate its legitimacy.
A closer look at the screenshot indicated that this post was labeled as satire, both under the usual spot for "Likes" on a Truth Social post and as a watermark across the image.
According to the watermark, this post originated with a Facebook account called Mrs. Putin, which identifies itself as "Satire/Parody" in its description. Mrs. Putin first shared the post (screenshot) on Aug. 29.
As Mrs. Putin pointed out in a Facebook message conversation with Snopes in 2025, the account's posts often include several indicators that they are satire, including misspelled names. In this case, aside from the "satire" label, other indicators that the post is fake include that Mrs. Putin changed "Likes" to "disLikes" and misspelled Trump's social media tag, "@realDonaldTrump," as "@realDotardTurmp" and his last name as Turmp.
(Mrs. Putin)
A search of Trump's social media accounts using the databases Trump's Truth and Factbase also determined that, as of this writing, the president has not declared the construction of a "Melania Canal." He did, however, float renaming the Strait of Hormuz to "Trump Strait" in a Sept. 2 Truth Social post.
For more on Lake Ontario and its renaming, Snopes previously debunked a claim that Canadian officials were refusing passage to ships with "Lake America" in their documentation and confirmed that Lake Ontario was not named after the Canadian province.
Snopes also has previously written about numerous satirical Mrs. Putin posts.
Because the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

Basketball has always given me a different kind of adrenaline, be it in real life, 2K games, or even in Roblox. I have played plenty of sports games over the years, from EA FC to WWE 2K, but there is something about watching a game slip away and then fighting your way back that keeps me returning to NBA 2K. So, the moment I got to review NBA 2K27, I had to be HIM.
NBA 2K27 makes several meaningful improvements to its basketball fundamentals. Yet, it also feels remarkably familiar in many areas, and some of the same design decisions that have bothered me for years are still here. That leaves NBA 2K27 in an awkward position. So, before you dunk your wallet purchasing the game, check out my honest NBA 2K27 review here.
NBA 2K27 Finally Makes Defense Feel Important
The biggest change I noticed on the court is how much more aggressive the defense feels. Getting into the paint without thinking twice is no longer a guaranteed route to an easy bucket, as help defenders are much more aware of what is happening around them.
Drive straight into two defenders, and there is a good chance you are walking away with nothing. Sometimes, you don’t even walk away with your dignity intact after watching a defender launch into a spectacular block animation.
This makes shot selection more important than in all the previous games. The paint feels like an actual defensive zone now, and I appreciate that because previous NBA 2K games could sometimes make interior defense feel secondary to simply scoring more points.
However, my experience with reaching for the ball was much less enjoyable. I was called for fouls far too often when trying to strip the ball, even on lower difficulty settings, and it quickly became frustrating.
The new shot contest system is more interesting. Being able to make aggressive or conservative contests gives defending more control, although the system can sometimes feel inconsistent when a shot that looks heavily contested registers as only a light contest.
Player collisions are another area that still needs work. There were plenty of moments where bodies interacted in ways that looked awkward, especially during crowded plays. But what did feel right was the attacking part. That takes me to…
Dribbling and Dunks Feel Better, Even If Movement Does Not
Dribbling is one of the more enjoyable parts of NBA 2K27. Chaining moves together feels more natural, and there is less of that feeling where your player simply phases through a defender because you pressed the right combination of buttons.
I especially enjoyed how much more unpredictable the ball feels around defenders. Creating separation now requires better positioning rather than simply memorizing a sequence of moves, which makes successful ankle breakers feel more satisfying.
The movement itself is not perfect, disappointingly. Sharp changes of direction can still feel sluggish, with players occasionally rounding an angle instead of making the precise cut you intended.
Dunks, on the other hand, are another bright spot of 2K27. Sprint dunks feel smoother in most situations, while timed dunks give contested finishes more weight because you actually have to earn them.
The meter also reacts to traffic, which I liked once I got used to it. If you are a fan of shooting from distance and right angles, scoring three-pointers will make you feel like a king. Open dunks are generally straightforward, while contested attempts require more attention and timing.
Shooting and passing remain polished overall, like the old times. The combination gives NBA 2K27 a strong foundation because when the game gets out of your way and lets you play basketball, it can be genuinely excellent.
The Ratings Still Matter More Than the Skills
One issue I kept noticing was the relationship between player ratings and actual skill. 2K has talked about putting more emphasis on player skill, but I often had better results simply using highly rated players without putting much effort into them.
That creates moments where the rating feels like an auto-win stat in any game mode. It is difficult to feel like you outplayed someone when the difference between players can sometimes do so much of the work for you.
This does not ruin the entire experience, but it takes away some of the satisfaction from mastering the mechanics. I want my knowledge of basketball and execution to matter as much as the number sitting beside a player’s name.
MyCAREER Remains Fun, While Eras Brings a New Crossover
I am not going to spend too much time on MyCAREER because the basic appeal remains familiar. Creating a player, developing them, and watching them grow is something I have enjoyed across EA FC, WWE 2K, and previous NBA 2K games.
Fire & Concrete gives that progression a new story with 11 chapters, and I found the presentation and acting stronger than last year. Some of the objectives can become tedious, especially when the game asks you to follow specific plays or hit certain statistical targets instead of simply letting you play.
The bigger attraction for me is MyCAREER Eras. Creating a player and dropping them into different periods of NBA history is a fun concept, especially when you can play alongside stars such as Allen Iverson or go up against legends from earlier generations.
At the same time, much of the experience is already familiar to anyone who has spent years with NBA 2K. The presentation is new, but there are not many genuine surprises once you understand how the mode works.
The WNBA career changes that for me. Being able to create a female player and experience a career in the WNBA feels more interesting because I have far less familiarity with that side of basketball compared to the NBA. Unfortunately, one part of the game is yet to grow on me, and that is The City.
The City Still Feels Like a Lobby with Extra Steps
I have never been particularly convinced by NBA 2K’s open-world approach. When the concept first arrived, I imagined something much closer to a living basketball city, but what we eventually got felt more like a giant online lobby with buildings scattered around it.
NBA 2K27 continues that approach. There are new environments, new arenas, Casual Corner, and other activities, but I rarely felt like I was exploring a world that needed to exist.
Casual Corner is useful for players who want a lower-pressure way to jump into 3v3 or 5v5 games. The new environments also help keep things from becoming completely stale during late-night Rec sessions, but the novelty wears off quickly.
The co-ed City is a welcome addition. Female MyPLAYERs can participate across the City multiplayer modes, which makes the online ecosystem more inclusive and gives players another way to experience the same basketball systems.
Still, I think NBA 2K needs to reconsider this entire approach. WWE 2K26 has experimented with similar ideas, and I would rather see these resources used to make the core sports experience deeper than to maintain an open world that mostly functions as a menu you can walk around.
MyNBA and MyTEAM Add Depth Without Changing the Formula
MyNBA has received several useful additions, including expanded trade possibilities, international prospects, contract buyouts, and more detailed team management. These systems give dedicated franchise players more control, although the mode still feels like an evolution of what we have already had rather than a major reinvention.
Simulation accuracy was a bigger concern for me. Some players ended up producing numbers that felt completely disconnected from what I expected, while free agency could send young players to the market or move marquee names between teams without much logic behind it.
MyTEAM’s unified Auction House is probably what you will notice as a key change here. Bringing the auction economy together across platforms is a welcome quality-of-life improvement, although the mode still carries the familiar progression and monetization structure that longtime NBA 2K fans know.
NBA 2K27 Performance Review: Great Visuals, Questionable Performance
Visually, NBA 2K27 looks excellent. Player models, arenas, lighting, and animations continue to make it one of the better-looking sports games around, and watching a game unfold can genuinely look like a television broadcast.
Performance is a different story. I tested the game across multiple setups, and one thing remained consistent: NBA 2K27 appeared heavily dependent on frame generation to deliver the kind of frame rates I expected.
My Setup:
CPU: AMD Ryzen 5 3600 @ 4.1GHz
CPU Cooler: CORSAIR H150 RGB
Motherboard: MSI B450 Tomahawk Max II
GPU: Sapphire Pulse AMD Radeon RX 9060 XT 16GB GDDR6
RAM: Corsair (2x16GB) 3200MHz DDR5
SSD: XPG 1TB GAMMIX S70 Blade Gen4
Monitor: 1080p @ 165Hz
On my Radeon RX 9060 XT setup, I was averaging around 30 to 40 FPS without frame generation. With frame generation enabled, that jumped to roughly 100 to 120 FPS, which is a massive difference.
Another key issue was the CPU utilization compared to the GPU. Until you turn the frame generation setting on, the CPU can even go above 100% usage. Yes, pretty scary if you are not using a cooler.
That tells me the game is leaning heavily on frame generation rather than simply delivering a strong native performance baseline. NVIDIA GPU users should also pay close attention to their settings, especially if they are expecting high native frame rates without relying on frame generation.
I also experienced two crashes while playing NBA 2K27, including one during shader building. The game asks you to use all available CPU threads during the shader process. That can apparently become a problem on CPUs with fewer than 12 threads, so I recommend leaving some headroom rather than maxing everything out. But performance is not even the main culprit in the game.
DLSS 5 Impressions
Nvidia’s DLSS 5 in NBA 2K27 held up better than I expected, given its reputation. Running on an RTX 5080 Founder’s Edition at 1080p, Ultra settings, ray tracing on, and DLSS 5 set to Quality, I noticed less shimmering or jagged edges and player and ball ghosting versus the native rendering engine.
Reflections, lighting, and material definitions on players and their uniforms all improved, with sharper sweat highlights and facial stubble. Skin occasionally looked too glossy under arena lights, but it never felt like an AI filter slapped onto the game. The real downside was the crowd with low-poly faces that stood out more next to upgraded players. Since the engine itself can’t add geometry that it never rendered, it was a significant trade-off.
Performance made the strongest case for using DLSS 5 in NBA 2K27, where framerates jump to 600 FPS from the native rendering’s 81 FPS average. CPU utilization also dropped to 20-25%, and GPU power draw reduced to a more forgiving 235W. In practice, that meant cleaner motion, no visible ghosting, more responsive controls on layups, and a better gameplay experience overall. Check out our full in-depth analysis of DLSS 5 in NBA 2K27 right here.
(With Nvidia DLSS 5 testing and input from Rishabh Sabarwal)
Ads Are Your True Opponent in NBA 2K27
My biggest annoyance has nothing to do with basketball mechanics; not even the performance. NBA 2K27 cuts to advertisements far too often, and while I understand the desire to make the presentation resemble a real sports broadcast, it becomes distracting when it repeatedly interrupts the flow.
The constant post-score animations have a similar problem. After almost every point, the game wants to show another presentation sequence, and eventually I just want the ball back so I can play basketball.
Sports broadcasts can have advertisements, celebrations, and presentation packages without making the actual game feel fragmented. NBA 2K27 needs to learn that sometimes the best transition is simply letting me play the next possession. I mean, you are still trying to grab more cash through monetization.
NBA 2K27 Review Verdict: Game Is Fun When It Lets You Play
Despite everything I have mentioned, I still had moments where NBA 2K27 reminded me why I love basketball games. My favorite came when I turned a 50-20 deficit into a 59-60 game, and that comeback gave me exactly the adrenaline I want from a sports title.
Those clutch moments are why I kept coming back to NBA 2K27 even when the ads, strange fouls, collisions, and performance issues started getting on my nerves. The actual basketball underneath all of this remains entertaining, and several of the gameplay improvements make it more satisfying than the previous entries in certain areas.
But as an NBA 2K27 review, I cannot ignore how familiar the overall package feels. The game improves enough to be enjoyable, but not enough to make the last five years feel like a distant memory.
As a basketball fan, I still enjoyed NBA 2K27. I just wish I could spend more time enjoying the game and less time dealing with everything around it. NBA 2K27 has too many issues keeping it from becoming the definitive basketball experience it could be.

Voters are fed up with data centers. Both parties are trying to cash in for midterms
In campaign ads airing everywhere from Georgia to Iowa, Republicans and Democrats are confronting the same enemy: data centers powering the artificial intelligence boom.
An NPR analysis of political advertising data from the firm AdImpact found that since January, campaigns and outside groups have spent more than $45 million on ads mentioning data centers in this year's gubernatorial, House and Senate races.
The two major parties driving that spending are largely making the same argument: the sprawling facilities get too many tax breaks, drive up electricity bills and need reining in.
From January to August, spending was nearly identical: over $22 million supported Republican candidates and more than $21 million for Democratic candidates, with independents driving the rest. Still, Democrats ran almost twice as many ads as Republicans — 127 compared to 67 — and spread their messaging across more states and races. The ads are clustered in states with competitive races, like Wisconsin and Michigan.
Mentions of data centers have grown from just a handful in ads from January, to 62 in June, more than 110 in July and about 164 in August, as the election draws nearer and the issue continues to heat up.
A June Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 77% of Americans are concerned about data centers raising electricity costs and two-thirds of Democrats and half of Republicans said they'd oppose a data center in their community.
This bipartisan anxiety helps explain why candidates in both parties are talking about the issue. Michael Franz, co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks political advertising, said data centers give each side the talking points it wants.
Apart from a chance to talk about affordability, "Democrats can latch on to environmental concerns," Franz said, adding that for Republicans, criticizing data centers is a way "to go in opposition to big corporations, in opposition to a system that doesn't care about you."
Data centers are a unique issue where "MAGA Republicans and liberal Democrats" land in the same place, he said.
The convergence around affordability
Ads from both parties are tying data centers to rising energy costs.
A Believe in Wisconsin PAC ad for Wisconsin's Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Crowley, which the group spent $634,795 to air in August, promises that Crowley "will lower costs, make housing affordable, stop AI data centers from making your energy bills skyrocket."
Byron Donalds, Florida's Republican gubernatorial nominee, casts himself as a check on data centers, by vowing to "protect Florida families and communities from data centers that jack up utility rates and make everything else more expensive," and "fight for a ratepayer protection plan." The Friends of Byron Donalds PAC paid over $2.5 million to air the ad.
Similar ads have run in support of Democrat Rob Sand in Iowa and Republican Ty Masterson in Kansas.
A Republican Party operative spoke to NPR about this on condition of anonymity, and said the party is not commenting publicly on data centers because the views within the party vary. They said "The most popular answer that we've seen is: We could potentially have data centers as long as they pay for their own energy," adding that data centers are necessary to win the race against China "and increase jobs in local communities."
Similarly, Olivia Davis, a spokeswoman for the Democratic Governors Association said data centers are creating deep concerns around affordability and utility costs.
"That's why it's being included in paid media," she said.
Georgia and Ohio: where data centers take center stage
According to data from AdImpact, more than half of the GOP's spending on ads mentioning data centers has been in Georgia and the state has captured about 30% of total spending on data center ads.
Georgia's contest for governor is the race that has spent the most on ads mentioning data centers — $12.8 million across nine ads.
Six ads discouraged voters from backing Republican Lt. Gov. Burt Jones who lost the June runoff to healthcare billionaire Rick Jackson. The ads, some of which were run by Georgians for Integrity, a group that has dropped millions attacking Jones since 2025, used data centers as a bogeyman for Jones' alleged corruption.
In Ohio's U.S. Senate race, supporters of Democratic nominee Sherrod Brown have spent millions to describe his opponent, Republican Sen. Jon Husted, as the "the face of data centers," and accuse him of "giving corporations over $2.5 billion in out of control tax breaks and causing electric bills to spike by thousands of dollars."
Republicans are aware of the shifting tide. In an internal memo obtained by NPR and first reported by Axios, the National Republican Senatorial Committee singled out the Ohio race, called data centers a "sleeper issue for the entire election cycle," and warned the tech industry that a Husted loss would make politicians nationwide wary of them.
Husted isn't airing ads on the topic. He championed data centers as Ohio's lieutenant governor but has since introduced congressional legislation to protect ratepayers from the higher electric rates that data centers can cause.
In an interview with Spectrum News, Husted addressed a seeming shift in his position.
"It's not really a shift. I was always trying to hold these companies accountable by making them pay local property taxes," he said, also highlighting his push to require the companies to hire locally. "So this is very consistent for me, holding them accountable."
A local issue with national attention
The Ohio contest is a rare Senate race with heavy spending on ads mentioning data centers.
According to AdImpact data, gubernatorial races spent the most on such ads, about $32 million, with House races in second place, spending $8 million and Senate races coming in third at roughly $5.3 million.
"The federal government doesn't really play a role in permitting the construction of new data centers," said Darrell M. West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution's Center for Technology Innovation and co-editor in chief of TechTank. "Governors are under a lot of pressure to slow the construction of new data centers just based on public opposition to them."
The issue, however, has spilled beyond gubernatorial races. In some of the country's marquee Senate contests, candidates such as Texas's Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico have said that Washington should step in.
The Republican turn against data centers is more striking because experts say that the party has positioned itself as pro-business. West said Republican incumbents and nominees "want to slow down the movement towards data centers because they can see so many of their own voters are opposed."
That leaves the party at odds with President Trump who has urged states to keep building data centers while admitting that they could "use a little public relations help."
"Trump seems oblivious to public opinion on a number of fronts," said West. "Typically, when the public shifts, politicians shift with them. Trump is not doing that on data centers."

Third seed Anmol Kharb lost to China’s World No. 81 Xu Wen Jing 21-16, 21-19 in the women’s singles semifinals of the Indonesia Masters 2026 in Pontianak, West Kalimantan, on Saturday, September 5.

Anmol quickly regained the lead at 13-12 and stretched it to 15-13, only for Xu Wen Jing to fight back again and level at 16-16. Trump downplays war with Iran, in which 18 US service members have been killed so far, as 'small potatoes'
Donald Trump minimized the war with Iran while speaking with reporters in the Oval Office on Friday. When asked how he would describe the conflict, if not a war, the president called it “small potatoes”.
“A lot of people don’t call it a war. I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us. It’s not a big thing,” Trump said. “We did Venezuela and we did this. In Venezuela we lost nobody. In this we lost 18 people and in Vietnam we lost 100,000 people and in other conflicts you lost tens of thousands of people.”
When a reporter followed up, saying 18 service members have died and there are record-long deployments, Trump retorted: “Why is it record long? How long were we in Vietnam? How long were we in Vietnam? How long were we in Vietnam? We’re at five months now.”
The war with Iran started in late February, nearly seven months ago. During the conflict, thousands of Iranians have been killed and more than 750 US service members have been wounded. The war has also brought soaring gas prices and disrupted food supply chains worldwide, as the blockade over the Strait of Hormuz has stifled trade and oil supply.

Trump told reporters Friday that “there’s no fighting right now”, despite a sharp escalation in the war this week with US strikes on Iran. He also said “we’re taking out a lot of oil” and “we control the Hormuz Strait”, both of these statements are not accurate. The president added that the US could hit Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, where nuclear facilities are reportedly housed, “very soon”.
The week ended with court rulings that were seen as wins for democratic elections in the country. A federal judge ruled that mail voting can continue for the midterms and Missouri’s supreme court denied a Republican-drawn congressional map meant to carve up a Democrat-held district.
Donald Trump also, once again, downplayed the war in Iran, calling it “small potatoes” and threatened to axe trade with dozens of countries unless the Federal Reserve agreed to cut interest rates.
Here’s what else happened today:
Aiming to catch leakers, Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon subjected 50 members of the military’s Joint Staff to polygraph tests. According to the New York Times, the tests came after a deluge of leaks to the press about diminishing stock pile munitions.
A federal judge extends block on Trump’s executive order, aimed at stifling mail voting. For a second time, a judge ruled that the presidents order to make a nationwide list of verified voters would result in “nearly guaranteeing significant disenfranchisement for eligible voters”.
Despite 18 service members being killed so far in the Iran war, Trump called the conflict “small potatoes”. While speaking with reporters, the president minimized the war saying it wasn’t even a “war”, but rather a “military conflict”. He compared it to Vietnam and said it’s “not a big thing”.
