You also get dedicated new toggles for accessibility features such as “Select to speak,” which reads aloud what is displayed on your screen.
Redesigned media player
The media player Quick Settings tile has also been refreshed. Noticeably, the album and podcast get new circular toggles for play/pause, rewind, and skip. The visualizer waveform on playback now dynamically extracts hues and colors from your currently playing album art. This gives your lockscreen a visual overhaul and a rich look.
Network restriction controls
Let us face it. We have been in this situation so many times where we download an offline game, a calculator app, or even a flashlight tool, and are suddenly bombarded with full-screen ads. These ads not only waste a lot of time, but sometimes they are so intrusive that you cannot close them, or they force you to purchase the pro version. One UI 9 fixes this and introduces a feature that power users have been begging for.
Network Restriction Controls is the new setting that is buried within the main Settings app; you now have a master kill-switch to block specific applications from connecting to the internet entirely. This is a massive win for privacy and data management. If an app does not strictly need an external internet connection to function, you can cut its Wi-Fi and mobile data access with a single turn of a toggle. This will stop ad-filled apps from quietly phoning home with your personal data in the background.
A unified phone app
Calling is no longer limited to standard cellular calls. You now make calls on WhatsApp, Google Meet, or message family members on Viber. But the problem with all this is that all of your call logs are scattered across various apps. WhatsApp calls will be available in its app, Google Meet’s call history is available in its app, and so on. You have to switch between apps just to view the call history.
One UI 9 fixes this issue and introduces a unified phone app. It fixes the headache by merging all of your calling applications into one centralized feed inside the Samsung Phone app. Now, when you open your dialer, your WhatsApp calls, Google Meet calls, and standard carrier calls all live in one neatly organized timeline.
Status bar enhancements
If you are someone who loves keeping a close eye on the device’s performance, then One UI 9 brings a highly requested feature: a native network speed indicator in the status bar. While this has been a staple on many Chinese smartphone brands, Samsung models will finally get a built-in way to see real-time download and upload speeds. It is an incredibly useful diagnostic tool to quickly see if your Wi-Fi is acting up or if you are getting the correct speed with it or not.
Note that you still need to make use of the Good Lock “Quickstar” module to enable it. But it is well worth the two minutes if you want to keep an eye on your internet speed. Plus, Samsung has also adjusted the size of the status bar pill area, basically the area that shows background activities like active calls or screen recordings. The pill is noticeably larger now, which allows it to display more content.
Everyday usability and multitasking tweaks
When it comes to multitasking, Samsung has always been the king. The One UI 9 update brings a few quality-of-life improvements that only help get things done much easier.
- Browser Windows in Recents menu: After using Google Chrome for years, I ditched it for Samsung Internet Browser as my default. One UI 9 brings a massive usability bump, as you can now configure individual browser tabs to show up as separate cards in your phone’s Recent Apps menu. This way, you don’t have to open the Samsung Internet Browser app just to close these tabs. You can do that from the Recent Apps menu.
- Mandatory PIN for shutdown: Smartphone theft is a real concern. Just the other day during a stroll around Hyde Park, my phone was almost snatched by a thief. While my phone was not stolen, thieves, when they get their hands on a phone they usually turn it off to stop tracking immediately. One UI 9 adds a crucial security layer, and you now you need to enter your PIN, password, or biometric data before the phone lets you restart or power off your phone.
- Clearer Routines: For those who use Samsung Routines to automate their device, they will be happy to know that Samsung has finally added plain-English explanation text for all the presets. You no longer have to guess what a specific routine means.
- Floating Bars return: Throughout various first-party apps, Samsung has brought back floating action bars. This gives you a cleaner gesture area at the bottom of your screen, good for those who customize their home screen.
- Bypass Charging: Mobile gamers are getting a new Bypass Charging feature. With this, the phone will route the power directly to the processor rather than charging the battery. This will reduce heat and protect your battery in the long-term.
- Dual Vertical Video: Samsung’s Camera app is packed with features, but One UI 9 adds some more elements to it, especially tailored for social media creators. You can now record vertical video using both the front and back camera simultaneously. The phone will record the footage in a 1:1 square aspect ratio.
Final thoughts
One UI 9, based on Android 17, may not be the biggest visual overhaul update that you might be expecting, but that was already done with the One UI 8 update. Now, with the latest update, Samsung is aiming to give users more control. It is a mature, polished, and thoughtful update that makes every Galaxy device a little bit more intuitive. More details will come about the update after the stable update is pushed.

Clean tech startup Leanwatts, which manufactures EV chargers, has raised $2 Mn (around ₹18 Cr) in its seed funding round led by Trivest Partners. The round also saw participation from angel investors Abraham George and Alok Rungta. The startup plans to utilise the fresh capital to accelerate research and development (R&D), strengthen its supply chain and ramp up manufacturing capabilities. “As we scale, our focus is on strengthening our supply chain, increasing localisation and continuing to invest in manufacturing capability. The new capital will allow us to accelerate this journey and build the capabilities required to reliably scale India-engineered power electronics,” said Leanwatts cofounder Abhilash Reddy. Founded in 2023 by Reddy, Pradeep Chowdary and Sujith Kumar, Leanwatts designs and manufactures power electronics products for EV OEMs. Its product portfolio includes portable and onboard chargers, ranging from 500W to 6.6kW, which cater to electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers and tractors. It claims to have developed in-house capabilities across hardware design, embedded firmware and software, product engineering and testing. The startup also operates a manufacturing facility in Hyderabad. Going forward, Leanwatts plans to expand into new areas including public charging solutions, rectifiers, power modules, hybrid inverters and other power conversion applications. On the back of this, the startup is targeting an annualised revenue run-rate (ARR) of nearly ₹60 Cr by March 2027. “... At Leanwatts, we are investing in our laboratories, engineers and ability to industrialise efficient architectures, cost-effective designs, advanced materials and emerging technologies, with the objective of building technological capability that compounds over the long term,” added cofounder Chowdary. The fundraise comes amid the rapid build-out of India’s charging ecosystem. As of December 2025, the country was home to 29,151 EV charging stations, including 8,805 fast-charging stations. To fuel this, the Centre has rolled out a slew of sops under the PM E-DRIVE scheme to improve the EV charging network. As a result, investors are slowly making a beeline for the space. Earlier this week, Zenergize, which also manufactures chargers for EVs, raised $4 Mn in its Pre-Series A funding round led by Giraffe Studios. In February, EV charger manufacturer Statiq also secured $18 Mn, via a mix of equity and debt funding, in a round led by Tenacity Ventures. Last year, IPEC also bagged $3 Mn in a funding round from Gruhas.

Body of world's youngest traditional king returns home to Uganda amid succession row
- Published
The body of a popular traditional ruler who was the world's youngest reigning monarch has been flown home to Uganda where President Yoweri Musveni was amongst the mourners gathered at Entebbe airport to pay their respects.
King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV died in the US last week aged 34 after receiving treatment for an aggressive form of cancer.
The Tooro king will be buried next Saturday - the day he had hoped to celebrate the anniversary of his coronation. He had ascended the throne aged just three and was crowned when he turned 18.
The return of his body marks the start of the Tooro kingdom's official nine-day mourning period amid a growing dispute over who should succeed him.
Uganda is governed by an elected president and parliament, but it has several traditional kingdoms that continue to have significant cultural influence despite not having political power.
Oyo, who Guinness World Records listed as the world's youngest reigning monarch, external, ruled over more than two million people. He was the 13th monarch of a kingdom that was founded in the early 19th Century.
After a brief ceremony at the airport, his body was flown by military helicopter to Kyegegwa in western Uganda, where the Tooro Kingdom is located, before being taken by road to the royal palace in Fort Portal.
It will lie in state at Karuziika Palace for the mourning period and members of the public will be allowed to pay their respects and prayers will be held there each evening.
On Thursday, Uganda's parliament held a special tribute to King Oyo, with MPs remembering him as a modernising monarch who championed education, health and opportunities for young people.
Prime Minister Robinah Nabbanja described him as a "symbol of unity" and praised his work raising awareness about HIV and Aids among young people.
Opposition MPs also paid tribute, with acting opposition leader Patrick Nsamba Oshabe saying: "Heritage and development were never rivals in his hands."
President Museveni has ordered an official burial for the monarch and national flags will fly at half-mast for three days around the funeral.
On Wednesday, the Tooro kingdom's Prime Minister, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, said the king had asked officials not to disclose the seriousness of his illness because he believed he would recover and return to his people.
He said the monarch had hoped to return home for this year's Empango - the annual celebration of his coronation - on 12 September.
"He was confident in his recovery," Akiiki said.
His death has triggered uncertainty over the future of the monarchy as Oyo was not officially married.
But Akiiki has said the king had a young son, whose identity would be revealed later in accordance with Tooro customs.
President Museveni also said the king's mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, had told him that her son had left an heir.
But Charles Kamurasi, who is head of the Babiito royal clan from which Tooro's kings are chosen, said he knew nothing about the reported child, prompting an unusual public disagreement among senior figures in the kingdom.
Others within the royal clan have questioned why they were apparently unaware of the child.
"The prime minister is not supposed to talk about the king's heir. It is a cultural process," one royal clan member was quoted as saying by Uganda's state-owned New Vision newspaper.
"How can we, blood relatives, not know of the child, and the prime minister says he knows? That is totally out of order," the clan member added.
Akiiki has since appealed for the dispute to be dealt with privately, saying he wanted to meet other elders to resolve their differences.
"Words spoken in moments of grief can deepen divisions that may take years to repair," he warned.
The Ugandan government has also intervened, urging people not to spread speculation about the succession on social media.
Culture Minister Henry Tumukunde said Ugandans should rely on official information from the government and the Tooro Kingdom, adding that any dispute would be dealt with under law governing traditional and cultural leaders.
"The whole world is watching how Uganda mourns its king," he said, urging people to show "restraint and respect".
The Tooro Kingdom follows a hereditary system in selecting its monarch.
King Oyo ascended the throne in 1995 and became an international curiosity because of his young age.
Before his burial, a church funeral service will be held at a local church.
His body will then be carried in a traditional procession to the Karambi Royal Tombs, with burial is expected to be completed by 14:00 local time.
According to Tooro tradition, kings are not buried in the evening.

On the evening of 1 April 2024, a team of aid workers from World Central Kitchen (WCK) stood on Gaza’s Mediterranean shore overseeing the unloading of a barge full of desperately needed food on a makeshift jetty made of sand and rubble.
The Gaza war had been raging for six months and Israel’s closure of land crossings had left the whole territory facing the threat of famine. WCK and local Palestinian contractors had constructed the jetty out of everything they could lay their hands on, including debris from the bombed house of one of the contractors, so that the pallets of humanitarian assistance could be delivered by boat from Cyprus.
A consignment of 200 tonnes of rice, flour and other proteins had arrived two weeks earlier, the first sea shipment to dock in Gaza since 2007. This was the second shipment and it was even bigger, with enough food to prepare more than 1m meals, as well as a Ramadan gift of dates from the United Arab Emirates.
The choreography of the delivery had been coordinated over several days with the Israeli army, and an officer was on the jetty to observe the proceedings. In the midst of a devastating bombing campaign after the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023, this humanitarian effort was supposed to be carried out under internationally agreed military protection.
The shipment had been unloaded by 8.30pm but despite the lengthy planning, there was a delay in receiving final Israeli security clearance for the eight hired trucks and two WCK escort vehicles to leave the jetty. By the time the green light came from local Israeli commanders and the convoy began to move south, night had fallen.
There was no initial overhead surveillance but two drones joined somewhere along the route to the first stop, a WCK welcome centre 6 miles to the south. Those drones were assigned to the Israel Defense Forces’ (IDF) Nahal brigade, which had not been fully briefed on the aid convoy’s itinerary.
A special adviser assigned by the Australian government to assess the case (in the interests of justice for the Australian victim Lalzawmi Frankcom), found that “specific details about the pre-coordinated WCK aid mission had not been passed down from higher levels of Southern Command to the brigade and UAV [unmanned aerial vehicle] operator”.
Local guards
At the WCK welcome centre, a few local men hired as guards were waiting, at least one of them armed. At a time of widespread hunger, many food convoys had been mobbed by desperate crowds as well as organised gangs, some of whom may have had been linked to Hamas, though Hamas never had the grip on food deliveries alleged by the Israeli authorities.
Using local security for aid deliveries was not unknown in Gaza, but it was directly against WCK policy to use armed escorts. The WCK says it is unclear why the local team on that night agreed to accept armed guards. The official Israeli version of events suggests it was “due to the convoy’s delayed departure, during night-time hours,” and noted it “was not coordinated with IDF authorities”.
The official Israeli version does not say how many armed men were waiting for the convoy (unofficial versions vary between two and four), but drone footage reportedly showed one of them climb on top of the cabin of one of the trucks and fire a shot in the air shortly afterwards, for reasons that remain unknown.
The Nahal brigade officers and the drone operators assigned to them concluded it was a Hamas hijack, based in part on the false assumption that such hijackings were commonplace.
“The troops also identified vehicles surrounding the trucks in a manner that, in their assessment and based on accumulated operational experience, corresponded to a scenario in which the Hamas terrorist organisation had taken control of the convoy,” the official account says.
The Israeli military prosecutor’s version of events, published last month to justify his decision not to pursue criminal proceedings, does not mention the breakdown in communication between the army’s coordination and liaison administration, which handles humanitarian needs in the territory, and the Nahal brigade controlling that sector of the Gaza Strip.
Furthermore, the prosecutor’s version says efforts by IDF personnel to contact WCK were unsuccessful. But according to WCK sources and the Australian report on events, contact was established that night with WCK headquarters in the US, which in turn got in touch with an employee in Gaza.
According to the Australian report, the WCK worker on the ground told headquarters staff the guards only had “fake guns”. It remains unclear what the basis for that claim was, but the WCK assured the IDF that it had not lost contact with the convoy and it had not been hijacked.
Arrival at destination
It is unclear whether this exchange with WCK was relayed to the Nahal brigade before the strikes. But even if it was not, the fact that the convoy of eight food trucks continued on its journey and arrived at its intended destination, the WCK warehouse in Deir al-Balah, should have been ample proof that the aid had not been seized by Hamas.
The military prosecutor’s summary acknowledges that the “convoy arrived at the designated warehouse and unloaded the aid” but does not address the seemingly straightforward conclusion that it had therefore not been diverted. The IDF has yet to release audio recordings of military communications that night.
After the trucks entered the warehouse, the WCK workers and the local guards stayed outside by their own vehicles for about 10 minutes. That short period, observed by operators of Israeli drones, appears to have helped seal the aid workers’ fate. As far as the Nahal brigade’s chief of staff, reserve Col Nochi Mendel, was concerned, they were “mingling” with Hamas.
Under the very loose procedures of “incrimination” that delegate much to the discretion of field commanders like Mendel, the WCK workers became unwitting targets as they celebrated the completion of a successful delivery of aid, because they were in the proximity to armed men.
“There was incrimination. The incrimination was according to the rules,” Mendel said. “There were armed men there with certainty. With certainty, they [the aid workers] had mingled with armed Hamas men.”
Other IDF officers have confirmed to the Guardian that such a process of guilt by association is used widely to determine targets, though different field commanders use different standards in making decisions. The Israel military prosecutor, in making his assessment on criminal responsibility, did not address the practice of incrimination in targeting.
Parting of ways
After the brief pause outside the WCK warehouse in Deir al-Balah, the guards and the WCK workers went in separate directions. “The WCK vehicles departed together west towards the coast. Concurrently, the vehicle containing the locally contracted security personnel, including the previously identified gunmen, drove north,” the Australian report says. It also makes clear that the IDF was aware of this parting of the two groups.
“One UAV tracked the locally contracted security vehicle heading north for approximately three minutes until it arrived at another warehouse where up to four gunmen were identified exiting the vehicle and entering the building,” the report says. “A decision was made to discontinue targeting them due to the time available before they entered the northern warehouse.”
The military prosecutor’s version makes no mention of this drone or the fact that the suspected gunmen were seen driving off in a different direction and entering a separate building. It claims instead that “several individuals mistakenly … identified as armed persons” were observed getting into WCK vehicles.
That is at odds with the Australian report and the accounts of Israeli officers familiar with the investigation. They said a bag was spotted by a drone operator being put in a WCK car, and that the operator mistook it for a gun, though sources briefed on the drone video said that later analysis showed no sign of a suspicious bag.
Whether or not it was a gun was irrelevant as far as Mendel was concerned. He saw his task as carrying out the government policy of crushing Hamas governance in Gaza, which included stopping its seizure of aid deliveries.
“If a Hamas operative takes over a truck and after that he sells it and that’s how he recruits more people, then what does it matter if he’s armed or not?” Mendel said.
In its economical, dry prose, the Australian report describes what happened next as the WCK workers left the warehouse at about 11pm. “The WCK vehicles proceeded west to the coast. Due to the time delays encountered, rather than return to the WCK welcome centre as planned, a decision was made to return directly to the accommodation in Rafah,” the report says.
“After turning south on to the coast road, the three WCK vehicles were struck in relatively quick succession, each strike being approximately two minutes apart. There were two survivors from the strike on the first (up-armoured) vehicle who quickly moved to the second vehicle, then two survivors from the second (up-armoured) vehicle who moved to the third vehicle. There were no survivors from the third (soft-skinned) vehicle. Over the four-minute period 23:09 – 23:13, the seven WCK workers were killed – likely one in the first vehicle, two in the second and four in the last.”
The seven victims of the IDF drone strikes were from the UK, Australia, Poland, Palestine and the US. The Britons John Chapman, James Kirby and James Henderson were working as security consultants. Saifeddin Issam Ayad Abutaha, a Palestinian driver and translator, was the youngest killed, at 25. Frankcom, Damian Soból, a Pole, and Jacob Flickinger, a US-Canadian dual citizen, were humanitarian workers for WCK.
The military prosecutor claimed that in turning south towards Rafah, the WCK workers were “deviating from the route that the organisation had coordinated in advance with the IDF”, giving weight to the Nahal brigade’s mistaken impression that “Hamas operatives had taken control of the convoy”.
Mendel also mentioned this “deviation” as a mitigating factor. However, the Australian report found that the fact that the WCK workers had changed their route only became known after they were killed, and “as such it did not play a factor” in the decision to open fire.
The official Israeli version of events says Mendel and his brigade fire support commander ignored an order on the night of the airstrike from a superior officer to cease any attacks on humanitarian convoys, but Mendel has said the order is a fabrication.
“It never happened, never existed.” Mendel said. “No operational directive reached the brigade to cease the strikes … We checked it a thousand times.”
In explaining his own decision-making, Mendel stressed he was carrying out Israeli government policy by stopping Hamas taking control of food deliveries. He had been lauded by his superiors for ordering strikes on several earlier alleged Hamas attempts to hijack aid. In his mind, the events on the night of 1 April 2024 fitted the same pattern.
“I didn’t plan to kill the aid workers,” Mendel said, but added: “They were not innocent because they were connected to Hamas.”
Justifying this conclusion, he said: “They were mixed together with Hamas operatives …near them, talking, playing, hanging out and so on.”
In a written statement, WCK said: “It is extraordinary to learn now that some in the IDF considered our humanitarian work to be enemy activity based on the flimsiest evidence, or no evidence at all.
“This undefined, unjustified and unlawful view is a mortal threat to all humanitarians. The IDF’s shifting excuses and explanations for these unlawful airstrikes are precisely why we continue to demand an independent investigation with the full release of the IDF’s evidence.”

India is ageing, and the most recent official figures show how quickly this is happening. The National Family Health Survey - 6 factsheets, released in August 2026, indicate that the proportion of Indians aged 60 years or older has reached 12.9%, up from 11.8% in NFHS-5, some four years earlier. This represents a small national increase, and while significant, is not the most interesting aspect of what the data reveal.
The more important conclusion is that India is not ageing as one country. Keralam, which was already the oldest state, now has 20.7% of its population aged 60 and over; Goa is at 17.2%, Himachal Pradesh at 16.4%, and Tamil Nadu at 16.3%. On the other hand, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh had their proportions of elderly people increase by only 0.4 and 0.3 percentage points, respectively and remain young by any measure. There is also the case of Ladakh, where the percentage of people over 60 rose from 8.9% to 14.6% in four years, a 5.7 percentage-point increase, which is greater than the increase Kerala achieved over the same period.
It is impossible to apply a single national template to such different populations. In States that are already ageing, there will be increases in the demand for care of chronic diseases, geriatric services and long-term care. Although younger States have more time ahead of them, that time is exactly when preparation should take place. Putting off action until the elderly population is large enough to be seen when looked at as a group, means responding to demographic change rather than predicting it.
What the fact sheets cannot tell us
The NFHS-6 State and national fact sheets include 101 key indicators. The only one of these relating to older Indians is the proportion of the population aged 60 and over; all the other information that could tell us about their health is either included in age groups that are too broad to be of any use or is given in a form that does not allow linkage to individuals.
When it comes to hypertension and high blood sugar, the two main indicators of India’s burden of non-communicable diseases, both conditions are recorded for adults aged 15 and over. Thus, a 25-year-old and an 85-year-old are placed in the same statistical category. Based on the available fact sheets, there is no way to know how common hypertension is among the elderly in India, how this prevalence differs from State to State, or whether the States ageing most rapidly are also experiencing the steepest increase in chronic disease among older adults.
When it comes to nutrition, the gap is even more apparent. Body mass index is reported only for adults between the ages of 15 and 49, and not because older adults were measured and then left out of the tables. They were never weighed. Height and weight are recorded only for women up to 49 and men up to 54. The population whose nutritional and functional status matters most as a society ages does not appear in the data at all.
With regard to health insurance and financing indicators, they are provided at the household level. These indicators tell us whether a household has coverage, but they tell us very little about whether the older person in that household is financially protected when their healthcare needs become intensive and long-term.
There is a deeper design issue underneath this. NFHS interviews women up to 49 and men up to 54. Above that age, Indians appear in the survey only as a line in the household roster and, if selected, a blood pressure cuff and a glucose reading. So even where we have a measurement for a 70-year-old, we have very little to explain it with: nothing on their tobacco or alcohol use, whether they are on treatment, whether they sought care, whether they still work. The elderly are enumerated. They are not interviewed.
This does not mean that NFHS-6 is a flawed survey; it is, in fact, one of the most valuable sources of information on population health available anywhere in the world, and it was intended to track overall population health rather than to answer all the questions raised by an ageing society. But as India’s age structure changes, so must the information system used to formulate health policy.
The evidence is older than the policy
This is no longer just a theoretical issue: since the Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB PM-JAY) has been extended to all citizens aged 70 and over, the government has now assumed responsibility for financing the health of a very large number of elderly people.
To serve that population adequately we need to know more than simply how many people are eligible. How many live with chronic diseases? How many need help with everyday activities? How much are they paying out of pocket? Only on the basis of this information can we tell whether the money and the services are being directed towards the right needs in the right States.
India possesses the necessary equipment to deal with these questions. The Longitudinal Ageing Study in India, conducted by the International Institute for Population Sciences, was designed precisely for this purpose. In its first phase, it included more than 73,000 adults aged 45 and over, gathering information on their health conditions, their use of and expenditure on healthcare, economic circumstances, social networks, functional health, and biomarkers. It is a major piece of infrastructure.
The problem is that the first wave covers the period 2017 to 2018. For a policy programme being expanded this year, a baseline that is eight years old cannot be considered up-to-date evidence. Once data has been collected, it loses relevance over time, and this decline in value is most rapid in cases where the underlying population is changing quickly.
Staying current
When a gap in data is identified, the reflex is to call for a new survey. That is the wrong instinct here. India already runs two surveys. The NFHS gives a regular, broad picture of population health across the country. The LASI does a deep dive into ageing and its social and economic consequences. They were built to do different jobs, and turning the NFHS into a second LASI would be expensive and would damage what it already does well.
What is needed is more modest. Keep the ageing data current, rather than letting a decade pass between one wave and the next. Report the numbers by age where the NFHS already collects them, particularly for hypertension and blood sugar. And design the two surveys so they can be read against each other, instead of sitting in separate silos.
An ageing India will have to do more than simply count its older population; it will also need to find out what their requirements are, where these needs are appearing first, and whether the health system is able to meet them. With regard to the first of these questions the data are now fairly good, but with respect to the others we are still making guesses.
(Tanya Singla is a research student, tanyasingla.india@gmail.com, and Megha Jacob is an assistant professor in the department of economics at Jesus and Mary College, University of Delhi, mjacob@jmc.du.ac.in; Karan Babbar is an assistant professor of economics at XLRI Jamshedpur. phd17karanb@iima.ac.in)

Electric two-wheeler maker Ola Electric has opened its first dealer-operated stores across India, less than a month after announcing a shift from its company-owned retail model. The first dealer-led outlets have gone live across Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Bihar, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh. The company said the stores will cater to local demand for its electric scooters and motorcycles while expanding its presence across regional markets. Ola Electric is now looking to build a network of more than 500 dealerships over the next two quarters. Meanwhile, its existing company-owned stores will transition into product experience centres. The development marks the beginning of a major overhaul of the Bhavish Aggarwal-led company’s distribution strategy. Ola Electric opened its sales and service network to dealers on August 6, five years after launching its first escooter through a fully company-owned retail network. Under the new model, dealers will handle local sales and service, while the company’s outlets will largely focus on showcasing its products and building the brand. The partner-led model is expected to allow Ola Electric to expand across cities and towns without incurring the costs associated with setting up and operating company-owned stores. The company had earlier said that it received more than 1,200 expressions of interest from prospective dealer partners. It added that the dealer network would help the EV maker take its products deeper into regional markets. The dealership push is also expected to support Ola Electric’s attempt to address its long-standing after-sales service issues. The company has faced sustained customer complaints related to delayed repairs, inadequate spare parts, and service centre capacity. Under the dealer-led model, partners will handle both sales and service and maintain Ola Electric’s spare-parts inventory locally. While announcing its Q4 FY26 financials, the company said service was the largest constraint on demand and brand trust through the fiscal year, but claimed that average service turnaround time fell 88% from around nine days in October 2025 to nearly one day in March 2026. Service backlog declined from 14 days to six days, while same-day closures reached about 87%. The rollout comes as Ola Electric looks to regain lost ground in India’s increasingly competitive electric two-wheeler market. The OEM has seen a turnaround in recent months, and commanded a 7.6% market share in E2W registrations in August. To penetrate further into the mass market segment, Ola Electric launched the new S1Z range, priced from ₹79,999. Offered with 3.1 kWh and 5.1 kWh battery options, the scooters have claimed ranges of up to 179 km and 301 km, respectively. Beyond new models, the EV major is also using the S1Z to showcase its battery technology, with the scooter becoming its first model to use its indigenously developed Bharat Cell LFP technology.

With an eye on expanding its health intelligence platform, smart ring maker Ultrahuman has raised $70 Mn (nearly ₹662 Cr) in a fresh funding round, which saw participation from Qualcomm Ventures, Alpha Wave, Blume, Nexus and Alteria and others. The startup plans to use the fresh proceeds to scale research and development (R&D) in sensing, AI, miniaturised electronics and health algorithms. A chunk of the capital will also be utilised to expand its blood testing product ‘Blood Vision’ and continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) platform Ultrahuman ‘M1’ globally. The startup also said that the funding will help it expand beyond wearables and build an integrated platform combining physiological, biochemical and environmental data. “Building this requires us to go unusually deep across sensing, materials, electrical engineering, algorithms, physiology and clinical science… This capital lets us push much harder on it, and bring what we build to millions of people around the world,” said Ultrahuman cofounder and CEO Mohit Kumar. Founded in 2019 by Kumar and Vatsal Singhal, Ultrahuman has built a health tracking ecosystem around its smart rings. Its platform currently combines data from the Ultrahuman Ring, Blood Vision, CGM, environmental sensors and software and AI tools. Including the current round, the startup has raised more than $173 Mn in funding to date and counts the likes of Nexus Venture Partners, Steadview Capital, Blume Ventures and Premji Invest as backers. Going forward, it plans to create a broader computing platform that can continuously understand signals from the human body, including sleep, cardiovascular health, metabolism, hormonal rhythms, blood biomarkers and recovery. Alongside, it is also building a software layer around its hardware. This includes PowerPlugs, which allow users to derive insights and add specialised health capabilities across areas such as cardiovascular health, reproductive health, circadian alignment, respiratory health and pregnancy. Earlier this year, the startup also launched Pulsomics, an opt-in research platform that allows Ring users to participate in large-scale studies that use longitudinal real-world data. Ultrahuman’s Many Troubles The funding comes as Ultrahuman continues to douse fires on multiple fronts. In March this year, the startup suffered a cybersecurity breach after hackers gained access to certain personal information of its users. This, as per Ultrahuman, led to the leak of wellness data of about 0.1% of its users. On the other hand, Ultrahuman is locked in a legal tussle with Finnish competitor Oura in the US. Last year, the US International Trade Commission (ITC) ruled that Ultrahuman’s smart rings infringed on a patent held by Oura, which resulted in a months-long import ban. It re-entered the US market in March 2026 with Ring Pro, a redesigned smart ring it claimed addressed the patent claims that triggered the ban. On the financial front, the smart ring manufacturer posted a net profit of ₹71.5 Cr in FY25, against a loss of ₹37.7 Cr in the previous fiscal. However, Ultrahuman’s operating revenue grew nearly 5X to ₹564.7 Cr in the year under review, up from ₹104.6 Cr in FY24. The funding comes as India’s wearable ecosystem is rapidly moving beyond conventional fitness trackers, with startups pivoting towards AI-powered preventive healthcare, recovery and stress management. This comes amid surging consumer demand for integrated wellness platforms spanning diagnostics, coaching, nutrition and skincare. As a result, investor appetite for the segment has also grown notably in recent months. In May this year, wearable startup Sychedelic raised $3.5 Mn in its seed round, while rival Gabit also bagged around ₹36.2 Cr. Prior to this in March, another healthtech startup Mave Health also secured $2.1 Mn its seed round led by Blume Ventures, while Deepinder Goyal’s wearables startup Temple raised $54 Mn in a funding round in February this year. At the heart of all this is the Indian healthtech market, which is reportedly projected to become a $106 Bn opportunity by 2033.

Although dieticians are a bit apprehensive about the high-calorie content of traditional Sadya (feast) of Keralam, a grand vegetarian feast served on a banana leaf comprising around 26 to 28 dishes, Kerala Tourism is exploring the possibility of turning the delicious Sadya of the State into an international brand.
Kerala Tourism has requested Apple CEO John Ternus, who assumed office on September 1, to include an emoji representing Keralam’s Sadya on iPhone. The request was made through the official social media handle of Kerala Tourism in response to a post by Mr. Ternus after assuming the office.
Speaking to The Hindu, a senior bureaucrat said, “We are not sure whether Apple would entertain such a request from Kerala Tourism. However, given the growing appeal of Sadya, especially during festival seasons such as Onam across the globe, we thought it would be a wise move to make such a request to the Apple CEO.”
Buzz on social media
Although the petition by Kerala Tourism has not evoked any response from the CEO so far, it has generated a buzz on social media platforms, with the move receiving widespread support from netizens as Sadya is a hallmark of festivals as well as various religious ceremonies and wedding celebrations in the State.
According to James Kodianthara, a tourism expert and former chairperson of the Kerala chapter of the Indian Association of Tour Operators (IATO), Sadya is definitely a grand product from Keralam that could be marketed as an international brand across the globe.
“There are a lot of examples across the world, like steak in American cuisine and pork knuckle in Czech cuisine, which have brought fame and international recognition to destinations. Perhaps, after Kathakali and snakeboat regatta, Sadya can fetch international spotlight to Keralam,” said Mr. Kodianthara.
Main dishes
A lot of airlines serving southern India serve Sadya aboard their flights, especially during festival occasions such as Onam. The feast includes dishes such as Kaalan made with coconut; cucumber Pachadi, a garnished salad; and Puli Inji, a sweet and tangy ginger-based chutney; along with Payasams and other dishes.
Meanwhile, Dr. Anupa Jose, a dietician, attached to a private clinic, said that although Sadya is an integral part of Keralites' lives, the amount of rice served on the banana leaf should be reduced, given the high-calorie content of the traditional feast. Instead, curries prepared with legumes and lentils should be given equal prominence in the feast to limit total calorie intake to less than 1,000 while ensuring adequate protein.

The US Bradley Fighting Vehicles were visible on the horizon as they raced toward the city. Smoke, deployed to conceal movement, formed wisps around the outskirts. Assault forces, preparing to storm the enemy stronghold, gathered on the northern edge, navigating barbed wire, cars, and concrete blocks — enemy obstacles meant to slow the assault down.
The urban assault, part of a simulated conflict against a formidable peer adversary, followed days of combat.
The US Army exercise tested soldiers on moving through a city caught in conflict, pushing them to clear streets and buildings while fighting. The fight also had another layer. Though not at scale the way combatants in Ukraine are, soldiers were integrating new technologies, including drones and software, to determine whether these systems made a difference in how they saw, sensed, and engaged the enemy.
Traditional warfighting skills remain central to combat operations though.
At the Army's Project Convergence Capstone exercise at Fort Irwin in California this summer, close to 10,000 soldiers gathered to experiment with new weapons and technology while fighting a mock war. Enemy forces consisted of troops from Irwin's 11th Armored Cavalry Regiment, known as "Blackhorse."
Across the hot, dusty Mojave Desert, soldiers grappled with the heat's effects on themselves and their equipment.
A little over an hour before assault forces breached the training city, Blackhorse drones were flying above, scouting the area.
Inside a building, a unit commander asked a drone operator flying a Black Widow quadcopter to use it to assess vehicles pushing into the city. The drone could fly up to four kilometers away, extending the unit's view beyond what soldiers could see from the ground.
"I'm able to find with my UAS [uncrewed aerial system], I'm able to fix with fires, and then I finish with my AT [anti-tank] weapons systems," Capt. Mohamed Elmaola with the 4th Infantry Division told Business Insider.
While remotely piloted uncrewed aircraft proved advantageous for early surveillance operations, they were used only sparingly once the fighting moved into the city, occasionally flying above to scout positions, terrain, and movement. Soldiers said that the use cases for the drones had changed as the exercise went on, with the focus shifting toward the on-the-ground fight.
One ground robot, an uncrewed ground vehicle called the NOMAD, had been put to use outside the city limits earlier that morning, but it didn't see use in the assault.
"What we really want to be able to do is not just saturate the environment with a bunch of technology" because "that becomes so distracting" that soldiers can't train efficiently and effectively, Brig. Gen. Daniel Hibner, head of the Army Joint Modernization Command, told Business Insider.
The simulated city, which the Army calls Razish, was sprawling, with winding streets, buildings of different heights, underground tunnels, and hidden positions. During the training exercise, two key objectives for the assault forces were the jail and a large palace at the center of the city.
As the two opposing forces clashed inside the training city, troops dismounted from their fighting vehicles and began checking buildings for enemies. Dismounted infantry and Bradley crews work together in combat, with each protecting the other as they advance.
Bradleys equipped with heavier weaponry engage threats farther away while soldiers on foot armed for close-in combat clear buildings and eliminate threats to the vehicles nearby.
"You don't want your Bradleys to outpace your dismounted infantry," one soldier told Business Insider, explaining that dismounted enemy troops armed with anti-vehicle weaponry will "just shoot your Bradley."
Enemy forces hid in alleys and on the top floors of buildings, occasionally taking a shot at a gunner exposed atop a Bradley vehicle or a dismounted soldier running across the street. At one point, enemy forces successfully hit a Bradley. The turret shot up, signaling that the vehicle had been destroyed. In many respects, this kind of fighting wouldn't have been unfamiliar to veterans of the Global War on Terror.
The sounds of the fighting came in waves, loudest when assault forces raided the jail and palace. Even in quieter moments, bursts of gunfire could be heard in the distance.
Soldiers positioned on rooftops or in windows would peek up, aim, and fire their weapons before ducking back down. If "killed," soldiers would stop fighting and sit or stand where they were.
Hours into the fight for the city, some of the assault forces gathered inside and alongside a low building just across the street from the gates surrounding the palace. They were assessing whether they had enough ammunition to keep fighting.
One asked where they were located and whether any friendly forces were around them. Another opened his End User Device, a smartphone mounted to his chest, and checked out a map, reading off the building number aloud.
The soldier was using the Army's prototype Next Generation Command and Control, or NGC2, a software- and artificial intelligence-enabled battlefield network.
At Project Convergence Capstone, troops were examining how NGC2 performed in a large-scale combat scenario, marking the latest iteration of a series of tests. Prior tests had taken place at Fort Carson in Colorado, where the Army's 4th Infantry Division developed NGC2 with industry partners.
One soldier said he was using NGC2 to see where friendly forces were located within the city and where enemy forces might be hiding. Another soldier said that connection issues, either problems with the NGC2 system or the result of electronic warfare and jamming, had left it mostly unusable.
That mix of success and failure was exactly what Army leaders said they wanted to see at the exercise, characterizing it as a chance to gather feedback on what worked and what didn't.
"We're gonna have some failures out here in the desert, and that's good," Gen. Christopher LaNeve, the Army vice chief of staff, said on a call days after the exercise concluded. "If there is something out here that's not living up to what has been advertised, we're going to walk away from that."
The urban assault showed both the advantages and the challenges of training while experimenting with new technology.
Soldiers had to answer big questions about whether experimental systems were actually useful while still being judged on basics such as whether they properly cleared or marked buildings.
The training environment gave the Army a demanding place to test new technology, but the experimentation also gave soldiers one more thing to manage while trying to win a fight.

Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) is likely to remove former Test cricketer and chief selector 
Aaqib Javed
 from the national selection committee as part of a wider "clean-up" exercise being carried out within the board, news agency PTI reported.
The development comes days after senior players Mohammad Rizwan, Imam-ul-Haq and 
Salman Ali Agha
 were sent home from England. The decision has raised questions over Pakistan's selection policy and team management.
“Aqib is also likely to be told to focus on his role as Director Development at the Lahore High Performance Centre,” a source was quoted as saying by PTI.
According to the PTI quoted source, the decision to send back Rizwan, Imam and Salman was part of the PCB's wider plan. He claimed that Rizwan and Imam were dropped not only because of their form but also because of their behaviour in the dressing room.
“The rest of the players sent back were done so on the recommendation of interim red-ball head coach Mike Hesson, who wanted to try out some players he had worked with in the white-ball camp,” the source was further quoted as saying by PTI.
It added that the PCB chairman Mohsin Naqvi was keen on a "clean-up" and that the selection committee could be the next area to see changes.
“Aaqib, who is considered the blue-eyed boy of the chairman, is also likely to be told to just focus on his role as Director Development at the Lahore High Performance Centre,” he said.
Another member of the selection committee, former Pakistan captain Misbah-ul-Haq, has already offered to step down.
The PCB has also issued notices to members of the selection committee and advisory committee, asking them to explain the selection of Imam and Rizwan for the England tour and the criteria used to formulate the selection policy.
Aaqib has been one of the influential figures within the PCB and has had a significant role in selection and other team-related matters.
Pakistan suffered an innings and 103-run loss in the series opener at Headingley before going down by 194 runs at Lord's on Sunday as England took an unbeatable 2-0 lead in the three-match series.
The Pakistan Cricket Board responded to those defeats in dramatic fashion, taking the extraordinary step of sending seven players home, calling up another seven and replacing sacked Test coach Sarfaraz Ahmed with Hesson, already Pakistan's white-ball boss.
Senior players Imam-ul-Haq and Salman Ali Agha, who was Pakistan's captain at Headingley when Babar Azam was injured, were among those told to leave.

Tesla's Cybercab is under federal investigation almost immediately after hitting the streets
Regulators will review the process and data Tesla used to self-certify the vehicle.
Tesla's Cybercabs are now in service, but almost immediately after they hit the streets of Austin, Texas, they were under federal investigation. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) has begun a probe that covers around 1,000 of the vehicles.
The agency said in a notice that Tesla began commercial service of the Cybercab with a small number of vehicles on Thursday after self-certifying that they're compliant with all relevant Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS). The company indicated that it plans to expand Cybercab operations with more vehicles and in additional locations.
"The vehicles lack permanently attached, conventional manual controls, such as a brake pedal, gas pedal, steering wheel and mirrors," the agency said. "NHTSA is opening this [audit query] to examine the process and technical data on which Tesla relied when certifying the Cybercab and related issues. Among other things, NHTSA will consider the extent to which Tesla's certification depended on determinations that certain FMVSS are inapplicable to the Cybercab."
According to Reuters, Tesla has registered 420 autonomous vehicles in Texas, 45 of which are Cybercabs. It's not clear how many of the latter are actually ferrying customers to their destinations and how many are used for testing. Tesla is also offering robotaxi rides in Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando and Tampa using Model Y vehicles.

Home Minister Priyank Kharge said there is no question of diluting any evidence in the ongoing investigation into alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations conducted by the Karnataka Public Service Commission (KPSC), irrespective of the political or official position of those accused.
“Nobody, be it any party or commission, has any right to play with the future of our youth. Rest assured, I will not allow any evidence to be diluted as long as I am the Home Minister, no matter whether the accused is an IAS or IPS officer, or a BJP or Congress leader,” he said.
Speaking to mediapersons at the Aiwan-e-Shahi Guest House in Kalaburagi on September 5, Mr. Kharge said the government is committed to safeguarding the interests of candidates appearing for various recruitment examinations in Karnataka.
“I had introduced a private member’s Bill in the Belagavi Legislature session when we were in the opposition seeking to prevent malpractices in recruitment examinations. After we came to power, we have passed the Bill. The draft rules have been published,” he said.
Referring to the arrest of an IAS officer in connection with alleged irregularities in a KPSC recruitment examination, Mr. Kharge said the action had been taken under the new legislation.
“Around 35 lakh candidates are appearing for various recruitment examinations. Most of them belong to middle-class, lower-income, and poor families and had studied in government educational institutions. It is our duty to protect their interests,” he said.
Drought declaration
Asked about the declaration of drought in only five taluks of Kalaburagi district, Mr. Kharge said drought had to be declared in accordance with the norms prescribed under the National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF) guidelines.
“It is the Union Government that has framed the norms according which the drought-hit taluks are declared. The BJP leaders, instead of asking the Union Government headed by their party, are protesting in Kalaburagi. These leaders make a hue and cry in Karnataka, but do not have the courage to open their mouth before Prime Minister Narendra Modi,” he said.
Prison reforms
To another question, Mr. Kharge said a high-level committee headed by Additional Director-General of Police (Law and Order) R. Hitendra had submitted its report on the administration, security, and reforms in prisons in Karnataka. “The recommendations would be discussed with Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar and steps would be taken to implement them,” he said.
MLC Tippannappa Kamaknoor was present at the press conference.

New Jersey yesterday asked the Supreme Court to rule on whether states can regulate sports betting on prediction markets such as Kalshi.
“Companies like Kalshi claim to offer legal sports betting in all 50 states, but they refuse to follow the gambling laws of any state,” New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport said in a press release announcing the lawsuit.
In April, the US Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit ruled that New Jersey cannot regulate sports bets on prediction markets. The court determined that sports-related event contracts meet the legal definition of “swaps,” giving the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) exclusive jurisdiction.
New Jersey’s petition to the Supreme Court said, “The issue is one of tremendous practical and legal consequence: Kalshi seeks to federalize the multi-billion-dollar sports betting industry at the expense of every state sports gaming law. And the decision [by the 3rd Circuit] is badly mistaken.”
New Jersey’s petition to the Supreme Court came about a week after the 9th Circuit appeals court ruled that Nevada can stop Kalshi from allowing sports bets. Unlike the 3rd Circuit, the 9th Circuit judges determined that sports betting labeled as swaps is just gambling with a different name.
The split between circuits “has tremendous importance, as it will determine whether a multi-billion-dollar gaming industry can suddenly operate free from state sports-gaming laws,” New Jersey’s petition said.
Circuit split raised odds of Supreme Court taking case
The circuit split dramatically raised the odds that the Supreme Court will step in and determine who’s right, although Kalshi reportedly said it won’t allow bets on the case. Davenport’s office said New Jersey’s petition asks the Supreme Court “to hear a question that divided courts nationwide: whether prediction markets can offer sports wagers without following state sports-gambling laws.”
“Litigation regarding these questions has erupted across at least 20 states, with dozens of active suits pending and the gambling laws of several states currently enjoined by the federal courts,” Davenport’s office said. “This is the first certiorari petition filed with the US Supreme Court regarding the legality of this business model—of offering sports wagers self-certified by Kalshi with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) without following state laws.”

After more than a week since the devastating flash floods in Nepal, the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) shared an update on missing Indian nationals on Friday. While 275 Indians remain missing, 166 others were rescued after the floods along the Nepal-Tibet border last month. The Indian government said that 1,907 Indians have safely crossed over to Nepal from China, leaving no traveller stranded. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India has supplied around 95 tonnes of relief material to Nepal since the flash floods on August 26. "As per our information, 275 Indian nationals remain missing. We continue to be in close touch with the Nepali government," Jaiswal said during the latest media briefing. "We deeply appreciate the efforts of the Nepalese authorities in this regard. So far, 166 Indian nationals have been rescued and 1,907 Indian nationals have safely crossed into Nepal from China," he said. "As per official sources in China, there are no Indian travellers who are stranded in the Tibetan Autonomous Region in China," Jaiswal added. The MEA spokesperson said India will continue to provide assistance to Nepal in this hour of need. "We do plan to send more forensic kits, Bailey bridges and other materials that are requested by the government of Nepal," he said. Jaiswal said India has already supplied around 95 tonnes of relief material on seven aircraft to Nepal. "In addition to the relief material, we have also sent 54 personnel to support relief and rescue efforts in Nepal. This comprises 30 tunnel rescue experts, 19 forensic experts, and a five-member medical team. Our rescue and forensic teams are deployed on the ground, and they are working closely with the Nepalese authorities," he added. At least 1,295 people were killed in the floods in Nepal districts, reported Nepalese authorities. Several bodies were recovered by the rescue workers. More than 12,000 people have been rescued from the affected areas. However, almost 5,000 remain missing as rescue operations are still underway. The floods have damaged 35 motorable bridges, 45 suspension bridges and 40 km of black-topped roads, affecting parts of central Nepal, according to local authorities. According to a report by the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA), more than 32,000 people and properties have been affected by the flash floods. A detailed assessment of the damage is yet to be released publicly. The floods were triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border. In a car collision in Kerala's Thrissur, eight individuals believed to be students from Tamil Nadu were killed, local police informed PTI on Saturday. The tragic road accident happened on Friday around 11.40 pm when the vehicle the youths were travelling in collided with the rear end of a parked lorry on the highway at Panambikkunnu in Kaipamangalam. The lorry number was registered in Maharashtra.
Keralam police in a statement said, “Eight people were killed after a car rammed into the rear of a parked goods lorry on the National Highway at Kaipamangalam in Thrissur district. The accident occurred around midnight at Panambikunnu Centre. The car was completely mangled in the impact, and the occupants had to be extricated by cutting open the vehicle. Preliminary information suggests that those travelling in the car were students of an engineering college in Dindigul, Tamil Nadu,” ANI reported.
Although locals, fire and rescue personnel and police rushed to the spot to rescue the passengers but six of them died on the spot. The impact of the crash left the car severely mangled due to which rescue teams had to cut open the wreckage to recover their bodies.
Two of the injured who survived the impact were taken to a nearby hospital but later succumbed to injuries and were declared dead on arrival, police informed PTI.
Their bodies were pulled out of the car, which was registered in Tamil Nadu, and were taken to the mortuary of Thrissur Medical College for postmortem. The car was reportedly heading towards Kodungallur from the Guruvayur. The police suspects that the deceased were students from Tamil Nadu.
As per media reports, the victims were engineering students from Dindigul’s PSNA College.
The FIR suggested that the Maharashtra-registered lorry was parked illegally on the right side of on an under-construction stretch of NH-66. This section was barricaded and traffic had been diverted. According to the police, the car was travelling at high speed. The fatal accident occurred because its driver apparently failed to notice the diversion barricade and rammed into the rear of the lorry.
Kaipamangalam police registered a case against the lorry driver and six of the deceased have been identified. Four of the occupants were from Dindigul — Surya, Yuvasanjith, Vishva and Johua — while two others were from Madurai — Santhosh and Prasanna. The identity of the other two has not been established yet. Identity cards recovered from the bodies were used to identify the deceased. Charges under Section 105 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita have been levied against the lorry driver for culpable homicide.

OpenAI announced Thursday the launch of its next generation AI model, GPT-6 Astra, which the company claims is state of the art at navigating computers and web browsers, writing software, and solving difficult math problems.
It plans to make GPT-6 Astra available to paid customers in the coming days, starting with enterprise clients in its Daybreak early access program, followed by ChatGPT Plus, Pro, and Business plan subscribers. OpenAI did not say whether GPT-6 Astra will be available to free users of ChatGPT.
In a press briefing with reporters, OpenAI executives made it clear that they feel very confident about the company’s latest AI model. President and cofounder Greg Brockman says he personally believes the world is now in the era of artificial general intelligence, or AI systems that are generally smarter than humans.
“It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era,” Brockman told reporters. “I think that if we fast-forward a couple of years, when we look back and say, ‘When was it really that AGI was created?’ I think it's going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model."
OpenAI is releasing GPT-6 Astra at a critical moment for the company. The ChatGPT maker is trying to rapidly advance its technology and boost sales ahead of a planned initial offering while simultaneously avoiding compromising on safety and security. OpenAI is also facing stiff competition from Anthropic, its most important rival, which is also working on an upcoming IPO.
In a blog post, OpenAI calls GPT-6 Astra the “world’s best computer use model,” claiming it can navigate computers and web browsers on behalf of humans far better than its predecessors. AI companies have historically struggled to make models that can reliably browse websites, fill out forms, and manipulate software tools quickly and accurately enough to replace humans. In tests, OpenAI says GPT-6 Astra was able to book DMV appointments, search for job listings, and apartment hunt faster than the average person could.
The company also claims GPT-6 Astra is also the most safe and aligned AI model OpenAI has ever released. Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI’s chief scientist, told reporters that the company is monitoring GPT-6 Astra’s chain-of-thought—the model’s internal scratchpad it uses to work through problems—to ensure it is deployed safely. However, Pachocki said that making sure advanced AI models don’t cause unintended harm is increasingly a challenge, and may present a bottleneck to further AI progress.
“We kind of take this visibility for granted, and we are seeing that as model capabilities are increasing, monitorability is getting more challenging,” said Pachocki. “We think confidence in monitoring may constrain further development, because we would not accept degradation in our ability to monitor model alignment beyond a certain level. We would withhold scaling until we can regain enough confidence.”

Climate breakdown is happening on one Earth, but two different worlds. In one, its impacts increasingly encroach on everyday life; longer periods of discomfort and shorter periods of sharp pain. Endless, hotter summers, and within them sudden wildfires, evacuations, homes burned to cinders in a matter of hours. In another, catastrophe. This summer has been a snapshot of that split-screen. The hottest day on record in parts of Europe, and a wave of water, mud and ice in Nepal that so far has claimed more than 750 lives. Thousands of people are still missing.
The difference is also one of resources. The climate crisis has an economic cost, but some places can absorb it better than others. Responses to this summer of wildfires in Europe included a rapid scrambling by the French government to provide everything from tax breaks for businesses affected by the fires to relocation costs and aid to rebuild homes. The UK government had deployed almost £100m before the summer to strengthen wildfire resilience.
Entire industries exist to absorb the impact, undergirded by sophisticated technology, disposable income and evolved sectors. Wildfire insurance in the US is being powered by AI, which spits out numbers to estimate risk based on location and construction material. Outside North America and Europe, there is little of that buffer. The result is asymmetry. While developed countries will still be stressed as events triggered by climate breakdown become more regular and chronic, and they are still not immune to globalised outcomes – rising food costs, droughts, water shortages – what they experience and how disruptive that will be are far removed from other parts of the world.
The difference in scale and resources is colossal. What is needed to rebuild Nepal’s flood damage may constitute up to a 10th of its entire economy – something like $5bn, and that’s not even factoring in all the technical foreign assistance, equipment, expertise and labour required. Also colossal is the difference in exposure to the obliterative effects of events.
Take the death of coral reefs, and how that disproportionately affects coastal populations. Across the Caribbean, coral bleaching caused by rising ocean acidification and temperatures not only dramatically reduces marine life, which is a source of food and income for entire populations – 90% of Jamaica’s economic income is generated alongside its coasts – but also increases the scale and intensity of storms. Coral reefs are a sort of natural storm barrier, absorbing the force of sea waves and buffering coastal areas from flooding. The intersection between these geographical and economic features means countries in the Caribbean are being pummelled on the weather front (climate breakdown also increases the power of hurricanes through warming ocean water), as well as having their incomes drastically reduced and therefore their ability to bounce back.
Then there is the heat. Temperatures are not just jumping far above the average in Europe but also in warmer areas where the base temperatures are already high. Last week, a Harper’s Index summary of estimated heat-related mortality in India showed some staggering numbers: 3,400 excess deaths “caused by a single day of extreme heat”; 30,000 deaths “caused by five consecutive days of extreme heat”. In April of this year, all 50 of the world’s hottest cities were in a single country, India, something which according to the air-quality monitoring platform AQI “has no modern precedent across global weather data”.
This is another double whammy for poor communities without access to shelter or cooling systems of unlimited fresh water. These are the so-called climate breakdown hotspots, identified as “areas where strong physical and ecological effects of climate change come together with large numbers of vulnerable and poor people and communities”. Few places on Earth demonstrate this category more vividly than Sudan. A country already in the grip of war and food insecurity is now succumbing to the delayed rains caused by the El Niño climate pattern, cracking the dry earth and draining the Nile. The risk of famine stalks populations that are already acutely hungry.
And what is felt asymmetrically has been caused in that way too. These poorer, more vulnerable countries are paying the price for the emissions caused by wealthy countries, and not even being extended the full, remedial support from the coffers of those nations that accumulated the wealth generated by industries that contributed to climate breakdown and global heating. We are not just battling complacency, or indifference to the importance of climate justice, but a political climate that has in recent years, led by Donald Trump’s second term, seen its own collapse.
Look closer and the problem isn’t only historical failure but a casual disregard, an adventurism that launches wars and stresses economies with buffers already damaged by the climate crisis. The Iran war in combination with El Niño is a weather and politics collaboration that has hiked fertiliser costs on the one hand and choked rain on the other. More broadly, what was a generously named albeit tenuously implemented “rules-based order”, which at least had some bedrock of global cooperation and aid, has been cancelled altogether. Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris agreement set the tone, while the dismantling of USAID cut the funds that diverted billions of dollars from the rich to the developing world to help with the fallout of extreme weather and reduce greenhouse gas emissions.
Here is another cascade. As the US withdraws from its commitments, sending the signal that there are no rules or duties, and indeed no problem with climate breakdown at all, pressure will rise on other countries to contribute more. They will need to figure out a way to hold together a coordinated response in the shadow of a destabilising hegemon, as well as try to foster that sense of social obligation in a time of political sociopathy.
The foolish shortsightedness of it all is that even though there is a large gap between experiences, and so a sense that glaciers and floods and famines are happening all the way over there, their knock-on effects and food supply challenges, and political and refugee crises, will affect us all. Things will get dramatically worse for the hotspots, but there is still no outrunning it all in the long term. It seems that at precisely the moment when this realisation should yoke us together in all the ways life is rapidly changing, we are all being untethered. But ultimately, whatever different spheres we inhabit, we are all still trapped on the same planet.

It has been hard not to despair while watching the ruinous floods swallow parts of Nepal, and harder, still knowing that the agony compounds each passing day for dozens of Indian families whose members remain unaccounted for.
Social media is awash with desperate pleas, photos and details of the young and old, men and women, from Mumbai to Kolkata, posted by families searching for traces of life. The disaster unfolded when a melting glacier slammed into the valley below, unleashing a deadly cascade of rock and ice down the Bhote Kashi River, which flows from Tibet into Nepal.
Among the 275 Indians missing at the time of writing are workers of a hydropower project and people undertaking the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Another 128 people of Indian origin, including a large group of Sadhguru’s Isha Foundation spiritual group, are also missing; 149 Indian people have been rescued as of Monday.
For Gauri Joshi, whose five relatives remained unaccounted for over the weekend, the last few days have been a blur of calling their numbers in vain, watching news of rescue operations and trying to reach Indian officials – over and over again. What she has pieced together so far is that her relatives, part of a pilgrim tour group from Maharashtra, cleared immigration at the Gyirong border between Nepal and Tibet and boarded buses shortly before the flood waters destroyed the crossing.
“Chances appear very bleak now. But maybe a miracle will happen,” Joshi said.
The tragedy has reignited the question of how vulnerable the Himalayas are to climate change, and what its implications are for India. To understand the risks of glacier collapse and thawing permafrost leading to sudden floods and debris flows, I spoke to Dr Ashim Sattar, a professor at Indian Institute of Technology Bhubaneswar and an expert on glacial lake outburst floods. The conversation has been edited and condensed.
What are the climate- or glacier-related risks emerging across the Himalayas?
“There are different forms of cryosphere and how they pose a hazard. In a layperson’s terms, the cryosphere is where water exists in solid form, for example a glacier. When it melts, it forms glacial lakes. If they have an outburst, they can cause damage downstream.
Another cryospheric component is glacier ice. This is what we’ve seen in Nepal, where a glacier detachment happened. The frontal part of the glacier detached from the main glacier and eventually led to a debris flow.
The third component is permafrost. They exist widely in the Himalayas, but there has not been much monitoring because it’s very difficult. Everything – these lakes, glaciers and permafrost – are all hazards. Unless they’re triggered, they would not cause damage.
With climate change, these grounds will go above zero degrees and will start to degrade. These would need very little … to mobilise debris. We might expect a higher frequency of debris flows in the future. We won’t know how they are getting conditioned, unless we have some monitoring stations and scientific investigation.
And given the Himalayas are very vast, monitoring every part of it becomes tricky. It can be the mountain ranges within India, or maybe outside India, eventually, which drains into the Indian subcontinent. That needs to be well studied.”
How big are the downstream risks for India?
“Right now, this is a gap in scientific studies; nothing [is] quantified yet. There is direct evidence of climate impacts, even in the Indian part of the Himalayas. The number of glacial lakes is increasing, the size of glacial lakes is increasing, the volume of glacial lakes is increasing, and glaciers are retreating. The risk exists because it might happen any time.”
Which parts of India are the most vulnerable?
“Everyone in the Himalayas, every Himalayan state has hazards. We can’t deny it. If you look at the eastern side, they have a lot of glacial lakes. They have already reached their maximum extent. Most full-grown lakes are about to reach their limits, like maximum extent. In the western Himalayas or even the central Himalayas, there’s a lot of scope for the lakes because they have not reached their full extent. As the glaciers would retreat, they would keep on growing.
We are still unsure when the status is going to change for any of these states. That’s a very, very difficult question, and I don’t think anyone [can] answer it at this moment without any scientific investigation.”
How would you describe India’s early warning systems and disaster preparedness?
“The National Disaster Management Authority is taking proactive steps now with the glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) Risk Mitigation Programme to install early-warning systems.
Maybe an early warning system should be community-based. It should be for the people and by the people. It’s not always the scientist or the policymakers who can actually make this work at its full potential. We need to have local knowledge, involve the communities to make them more effective.”
How long will it take to have these systems in place?
“I have no idea because each of these organisations are working at their own pace. They have their own style of working. I’m sure it is going to happen soon. I can just comment on the areas where I know, and I’ve been in touch.”
Is prevention possible, or can it only minimise the damage?
“Prevention is possible, but it is very expensive: computationally, financially and manpower-wise. Minimising is also possible. It would require a lot of intervention in the high mountains, which is very difficult in those terrains.
We know that the mountains are changing and the hazard levels are increasing, so the only way forward is to minimise the exposure to the risk below. That means how much of the hazard is going to interact with the downstream. If something is in the path, we remove them.”
